en: The country of Ṭakka (磔迦國) is over ten thousand *li* in circuit; it borders the Vipāśā River to the east and faces the Sindhu River to the west. The capital city of the country is over twenty *li* in circuit. The land is suitable for non-glutinous rice and produces much winter wheat; it yields gold, silver, brass, copper, and iron. The climate is hot, and the land is subject to many windstorms. The customs of the people are violent and wicked, and their speech is vulgar and obscene. Their clothing is bright white, consisting of so-called *kauśeya* (silk) garments, *chaoxia* (morning glow) robes, and the like. They have little faith in the Buddhadharma and mostly serve the heavenly deities. There are ten *saṃghārāma*s and several hundred *deva* temples. In the past, this country had many charitable houses to provide for the poor and needy, where medicine or food was distributed; with such provisions for their sustenance, travelers were never in want.

Fourteen or fifteen li to the southwest of the great city, one arrives at the old city of Śākala (奢羯羅故城). Although the walls are ruined, the foundations remain solid. It is more than twenty li in circumference. Within it, a smaller city has been built, six or seven li in circumference, where the inhabitants are wealthy and prosperous; this is the former capital of this country. Several hundred years ago, there was a king named Mihirakula (摩醯邏矩羅), who established his capital in this city and ruled over all of India. He possessed talent and wisdom, and his nature was brave and fierce; there was no neighboring country that did not submit to him. During his leisure from state affairs, he wished to study the Buddha-dharma and ordered the monks to recommend a person of outstanding virtue. At that time, the assembly of monks dared not respond to the command, for they were few in desire and practiced non-action, not seeking fame or status; those who were learned and brilliant feared his majesty. At that time, a former servant of the royal household, who had long worn the dyed robes (of a monk), possessed elegant rhetoric and was eloquent and quick in speech, so the assembly collectively recommended him to respond to the command. The King said, "I respect the Buddha-dharma and have sought out famous monks from afar, yet you all recommend this menial to engage in discussion with me. I always thought that the wise and brilliant among the monks were comparable to one another, but knowing this now, what is there to respect?" Thereupon, he issued a decree throughout the five regions of India that from then on, the Buddha-dharma was to be utterly destroyed, and the assembly of monks was to be expelled until not a single one remained. King Bālāditya (婆羅阿迭多) of the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) revered the Buddha-dharma and loved and nurtured his people; because of the excessive punishments and tyrannical rule of King Mihirakula, he guarded his own borders and did not offer the customary tribute. At that time, King Mihirakula prepared his troops to launch a punitive expedition. When King Bālāditya (幼日王) learned of this news, he told his ministers, "I hear the invaders are coming, but I cannot bear to let my soldiers engage in battle. I hope my officials and the common people will forgive me for this, but I shall grant this humble body of mine the chance to slip away into the marshes and wilderness." Having finished speaking, he left the palace and took refuge in the mountains and wilds. More than ten thousand people in the country, moved by gratitude and admiration, followed him and hid away on islands in the sea. King Mihirakula (大族王) entrusted his troops to his younger brother and set out across the sea to attack. King Bālāditya guarded the strategic passes and sent light cavalry to lure the enemy into battle; at the first sound of the gongs and drums, ambushers rose from all sides, capturing Mihirakula alive and leading him forward with his hands tied behind his back. King Mihirakula, ashamed of his failure, covered his face with his garment. King Bālāditya sat upon his lion throne, surrounded by his officials, and ordered his attendants to say to Mihirakula, "Uncover your face; I wish to speak to you." Mihirakula replied, "The positions of subject and master have been reversed, and we look upon each other as enemies. Since we are not on friendly terms, what is the use of speaking face to face?" Though they urged him again and again, he would not comply. Thereupon, the King issued a proclamation enumerating his crimes, saying, "The Three Jewels are a field of merit upon which the four forms of birth depend. You, however, acted like a jackal or wolf, destroying these noble works. Fortune has not protected you, and you have been captured by me. Your crimes are unforgivable, and you must face the penalty of the law." At that time, the mother of King Bālāditya, who was widely learned and possessed a keen memory, was skilled in the art of physiognomy. Hearing that Mihirakula was to be executed, she hurriedly told King Bālāditya, "I have heard that Mihirakula possesses an extraordinary appearance and great wisdom; I wish to see him once." King Bālāditya ordered that Mihirakula be led into his mother's palace. The mother of Bālāditya (幼日王) said, "Alas, Mahirakula (大族), I pray you do not feel ashamed! The world is impermanent, and honor and disgrace alternate. I am like a mother to you, and you are like a son to me; you should remove the cloth covering your face and speak to me face to face."  Mahirakula said, "Formerly the ruler of a hostile state, I am now a captive prisoner. Having ruined the royal enterprise and extinguished the ancestral sacrifices, I am ashamed before the spirits of my ancestors above and the common people below; I am truly disgraced to show my face. Looking up and down between heaven and earth, I cannot bear the loss of myself, and that is why I wear this covering."  The King’s mother said, "Rise and fall follow the times; survival and extinction have their destiny. If you equalize things with the mind, then gain and loss are both forgotten; if you equalize the mind with things, then praise and blame arise in turn. You should believe in karmic retribution and move along with the times; remove your covering and speak with me, and perhaps you may preserve your life."  Mahirakula thanked her, saying, "Being a man of no talent, I inherited the royal enterprise, yet my governance strayed from the Way, leading to the ruin of my kingdom. Although I am now in bonds, I still cling to the hope of living for a little longer. I dare to accept your great kindness and will remove my covering to thank you for your profound grace."  Thereupon, he removed the cloth and revealed his face. The King’s mother said, "Take care of yourself, for you shall live out your natural lifespan."  Shortly after, she told King Bālāditya, "The ancient scriptures contain the teaching to forgive transgressions and cherish life. Although King Mahirakula has accumulated evil for a long time, his remaining merit is not yet exhausted. If you kill this man, for twelve years there will be famine and people will look at one another with the pallor of starvation. However, he possesses the energy of a restoration; he will not be a king of a great country, but he shall occupy the north and possess a small territory." King Bālāditya, obeying his compassionate mother’s command and pitying the sovereign who had lost his kingdom, gave him a young daughter in marriage and treated him with extraordinary courtesy; he assembled the king’s remaining troops and provided additional guards before they had even left the island. The younger brother of King Mahirakula (大族王) returned to his country and established himself as ruler; having lost his throne, Mahirakula fled to hide in the mountains and wilderness, eventually seeking refuge in the north in the kingdom of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國). The King of Kaśmīra treated him with great courtesy and, pitying him for the loss of his kingdom, granted him a territory as a fief. After much time had passed, he led his people, treacherously killed the King of Kaśmīra, and established himself as ruler. Taking advantage of the prestige of his victory, he attacked the kingdom of Gandhāra (健馱邏國) to the west; by deploying hidden troops and an ambush, he killed its king and completely exterminated the royal clan and the high ministers. He destroyed stūpas and abolished saṃghārāmas, totaling one thousand six hundred sites. Beyond those killed in battle, there were nine hundred million people whom he intended to execute, leaving no survivors. At that time, his assistants all remonstrated, saying, "The Great King has intimidated powerful enemies and, without engaging in battle, has executed the chief culprit. What fault have the common people committed? We wish to offer our own humble bodies to die in their stead." The King replied, "You believe in the Buddha-dharma, value merit in the afterlife, aspire to attain the fruit of Buddhahood, and speak extensively on the Jātakas—do you wish to transmit my evil to future generations? You should return to your positions and speak no more of this." Thereupon, he took three hundred million of the upper-class families and had them killed at the edge of the Sindhu (信度) River; three hundred million of the middle-class families were drowned and killed in the Sindhu River; and three hundred million of the lower-class families were distributed among the soldiers. Having seized the wealth of the ruined state, he gathered his troops and returned. Before a year had passed, he suddenly died. At that time, clouds and fog grew dark and gloomy, the great earth shook, and violent winds raged. A person who had attained the fruit (of the path) felt pity and sighed, saying, "By unjustly killing the innocent and destroying the Buddha-dharma, he has fallen into the Avīci hell, where he will transmigrate without end."  In the old city of Śākala (奢羯羅故城), there is a saṃghārāma (伽藍) with more than one hundred monks, all of whom study the Hīnayāna teachings. The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (世親) formerly composed the *Paramārthasatyasāstra* (勝義諦論) while in this place. Beside it is a stūpa (窣堵波) over two hundred feet high, where the four past Buddhas preached the Dharma. There is also a site marking the traces of the four past Buddhas walking in meditation. Five or six li to the northwest of the saṃghārāma, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王), which is the place where the four past Buddhas preached the Dharma. More than ten li to the northeast of the new capital city, one reaches a stone stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka, which is the place where the Tathāgata halted midway while traveling north to transform beings. The *Account of India* (印度記) says: "There are many relics within the stūpa, and on days of fasting, it sometimes emits light."

Traveling eastward from here for more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Cīnabhukti (至那僕底國). The country of Cīnabhukti is more than two thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city is fourteen or fifteen *li* in circuit. The crops are lush and abundant, but fruit trees are sparse. The households are settled in their occupations, and the national resources are plentiful. The climate is warm and hot; the customs are timid and weak; the people study both the true and the conventional, and their faith includes both the heterodox and the orthodox. There are ten *saṃghārāmas* and eight *deva* temples.  In the past, when King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王) reigned, his reputation shook neighboring countries and his prestige extended to distant lands; the border tribes west of the river feared his power and sent hostages. Once King Kaniṣka had received the hostages, he treated them with great generosity and favor, changing their residences according to the three seasons and providing guards from the four branches of the military. This country was his winter residence, and it was therefore called Cīnabhukti. Because it was the place where the hostages resided, it became the name of the country.  Before this time, throughout the various regions of India, there were no pears or peaches. They were planted by the hostages, and thus peaches are called *cīnānī* (至那爾) and pears are called *cīnarājaputra* (至那羅闍弗呾邏). For this reason, the people of this country deeply respect the eastern lands, and pointing to one another, they say, "These are the people from the original land of our former king."

Traveling more than five hundred *li* to the southeast of the great city, one arrives at the Tamasavana Monastery (答秣蘇伐那僧伽藍; Skt. *tamasa-vana*). There are more than three hundred monks who study the Sarvāstivāda school; their deportment is solemn and their virtuous conduct is lofty. They are particularly well-versed in the studies of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). It is said that the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa all gathered gods and humans in this place to preach the profound and wonderful Dharma. Three hundred years after the Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the master Kātyāyana composed the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (《發智論》) here. Within the Tamasavana Monastery, there is a *stūpa* over two hundred feet high, which was built by King Aśoka. Beside it are the sites where the four past Buddhas sat and walked in meditation. Small *stūpas* and various large stone chambers (大石室) stand facing one another like the scales of a fish, in numbers too many to detail. These are all places where sages who have attained fruition since the beginning of the *kalpa* have entered into extinction; it is difficult to enumerate them all, yet their teeth and bones still remain. The monasteries surrounding the mountain cover a circuit of twenty *li*, and there are hundreds of thousands of *stūpas* containing the Buddha’s relics, standing so closely that their corners join and their shadows touch.

From here, traveling northeast for one hundred forty or fifty li, one arrives at the country of Jālaṃdhara (闍爛達羅國). The country of Jālaṃdhara is over one thousand li from east to west and over eight hundred li from north to south. The capital city of the country is twelve or thirteen li in circumference. It is suitable for grain crops and has an abundance of non-glutinous rice; the forests and trees are lush and sparse, and flowers and fruits are abundant. The climate is warm and hot; the customs of the people are fierce and unyielding, their appearance is coarse and ugly, and their households are wealthy and prosperous. There are more than fifty saṃghārāmas (monasteries) and over two thousand monks, who study both the Great and Lesser Vehicles. There are three deva-temples, and more than five hundred followers of non-Buddhist paths, all of whom are ash-smearing ascetics. The former king of this country revered non-Buddhist paths, but later he met an arhat, heard the Dharma, and attained faith and enlightenment. Therefore, the king of Mid-India, appreciating his pure faith, entrusted him with the general supervision of all affairs concerning the Three Jewels throughout the five Indias. He made no distinction between his own people and others, forgot preferences and aversions, supervised the monks, and thoroughly investigated their virtues and vices. Consequently, those whose moral conduct was renowned were treated with utmost sincerity and respect, while those whose precepts were violated were severely punished. At all sacred sites, he erected memorial structures, whether stūpas or saṃghārāmas, which are found everywhere throughout the territory of India.

From here, traveling northeast, crossing steep ridges, passing through deep valleys, traversing perilous routes, and wading through dangerous paths for more than seven hundred li, one reaches the country of Kulūta (屈露多國). The country of Kulūta is more than three thousand li in circuit, with mountains surrounding its four borders. The capital city is fourteen or fifteen li in circuit. The soil is fertile, crops are sown in their proper seasons, flowers and fruits are abundant, and trees and plants flourish. As it borders the Snow Mountains, it is rich in precious medicinal herbs and produces gold, silver, red copper, as well as fire-pearls and rain-stones. The climate is very cold, and frost and snow fall lightly. The people are coarse and ugly in appearance, and they are prone to goiters and swollen feet; their nature is fierce and impetuous, and they value courage and strength. There are more than twenty saṃghārāmas (伽藍) with over a thousand monks, most of whom study the Mahāyāna, while few practice the various schools. There are fifteen deva temples, where followers of different sects live together. Built against cliffs and situated on ridges, there are stone chambers at intervals, some of which were inhabited by arhats and others by rishis. In the country there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata came to this country, preached the Dharma to save people, and left behind these traces as a record.
From here, the northern route extends for one thousand eight or nine hundred li; the path is perilous, crossing mountains and traversing valleys, until one reaches the country of Lāhula (洛護羅國).
More than two thousand li to the north of this place, the route is difficult and obstructed, with cold winds and flying snow, until one reaches the country of Marasā (秣邏娑國).

Traveling south from the country of Kulūta (屈露多國) for over seven hundred li, crossing great mountains and fording a great river, one arrives at the country of Śatadru (設多圖盧國). The country of Śatadru is over two thousand li in circuit and borders a great river to the west. The capital city of the country is seventeen or eighteen li in circuit. The grain crops are abundant, and fruits and flowers are plentiful; it produces much gold and silver, and yields pearls and precious stones. The people’s clothing is fresh and plain, though their garments are elegant and fine. The climate is hot, the customs are honest and harmonious, the people are naturally compliant and obedient, and there is order between those of high and low status. They are devoted to the Buddha-Dharma and are sincere and respectful in their faith. Inside and outside the royal city, there are ten saṃghārāmas, but the courtyards and buildings are desolate, and the number of monks is very small. Three or four li to the southeast of the city, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, which was built by King Aśoka. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas.

From here, traveling southwest for more than eight hundred li, one arrives at the country of Pāriyātra (波理夜呾羅國). The country of Pāriyātra is more than three thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is fourteen or fifteen li in circuit. The land is suitable for grain crops and is abundant in winter wheat; there is a unique variety of rice that is harvested in sixty days. There are many cattle and sheep, but few flowers or fruits. The climate is hot, and the customs of the people are fierce and impetuous. They do not value learning or the arts, and they believe in and follow non-Buddhist paths. The king is of the Vaiśya (吠奢) caste; his nature is brave and fierce, and he possesses much martial strategy. There are eight sanghārāmas, which are in a state of great ruin, and the number of monks is small; they study the Hīnayāna. There are more than ten deva temples, and over one thousand followers of non-Buddhist paths.

From here, traveling east more than five hundred li, one arrives at the country of Mathurā (秣菟羅國). The country of Mathurā is more than five thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than twenty li in circuit. The land is fertile and rich, and the people are devoted to agriculture. Āmra (mango) trees are planted by every household, forming forests; although they share the same name, there are two varieties: the small ones are green when raw and yellow when ripe, while the large ones remain green from beginning to end. The country produces fine striped cotton cloth and gold. The climate is hot, and the customs are gentle and compliant; the people love to cultivate merit for the afterlife, and they esteem virtue and value learning. There are more than twenty saṃghārāmas (monasteries) and over two thousand monks, who study both the Great and Lesser Vehicles with equal diligence. There are five Deva temples, where followers of different sects live together. There are three stūpas, all of which were built by King Aśoka (無憂王). There are many traces of the four past Buddhas. There are stūpas containing the relics of the holy disciples of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, namely those of Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, Upāli, Ānanda, and Rāhula, as well as stūpas for the various bodhisattvas such as Mañjuśrī. Every year during the three long fast months and the six fast days of each month, the monks compete with one another, leading those of like mind to carry offerings and prepare many rare curiosities, which they present before the images of the figures they venerate. Those who study the Abhidharma make offerings to Śāriputra; those who practice meditation make offerings to Maudgalyāyana; those who recite and uphold the sūtras make offerings to Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra; those who study the Vinaya make offerings to Upāli; the various bhikṣuṇīs make offerings to Ānanda; those who have not yet received the full ordination make offerings to Rāhula; and those who study the Mahāyāna make offerings to the various bodhisattvas. On these days, at the various stūpas, they compete in performing offerings; pearl-adorned banners are arrayed in rows, and precious canopies are gathered together. The smoke of incense is like clouds, and scattered flowers fall like rain, obscuring the sun and moon and shaking the valleys. The king and his ministers make the practice of virtue their primary duty.

Going five or six li to the east of the city, one arrives at a mountain monastery (saṃghārāma), where the cliffs have been hollowed out to form chambers and the valleys utilized as gateways; it was built by the Venerable Upagupta (鄔波毱多). Within it is a stupa containing the nail-parings of the Tathāgata. In the cliffs to the north of the monastery, there is a stone chamber over twenty feet high and over thirty feet wide, filled with fine bamboo tallies four inches long. When the Venerable Upagupta (known as Jinhu, 'Near-Protector') preached the Dharma and provided guidance, whenever a husband and wife both attained the fruit of an Arhat, he would place one tally inside; those from different households or separate lineages, even if they attained the fruit, were not recorded. Twenty-four or twenty-five li to the southeast of the stone chamber, one reaches a large dried-up pond, beside which stands a stupa. In the past, when the Tathāgata was traveling through this place, there was a monkey that brought honey to offer to the Buddha. The Buddha instructed it to mix the honey with water and distribute it to the great assembly. The monkey, in a state of joyful excitement, fell into a pit and died; by the power of this merit, it was reborn among humans. Not far to the north of the pond, in a large forest, are the remains of the places where the four Buddhas of the past walked in meditation. Beside these are the places where Śāriputra (舍利子), Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅子), and twelve hundred and fifty other great Arhats practiced meditation; stupas have been built at these sites to mark the remains. During the time the Tathāgata was in the world, he frequently traveled through this country, and at all the places where he preached the Dharma, there are markers and trees.

From here, traveling northeast for more than five hundred li, one arrives at the country of Sthāneśvara (薩他泥濕伐羅國). The country of Sthāneśvara is more than seven thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than twenty li in circuit. The land is fertile and rich, and the crops are abundant. The climate is warm and hot. The customs are degenerate; the households are wealthy and compete in extravagance. The people are deeply skilled in magical arts and highly esteem extraordinary abilities. They mostly pursue profit and pay little attention to farming; rare goods from various regions are mostly gathered in this country. There are three sanghārāmas with more than seven hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). There are more than one hundred deva temples, and there are many heterodox sects.

As for the boundaries of its territory, they may be described. The realm of the Five Indias (五印度) measures more than 90,000 li in circumference. On three sides it borders the great sea, and in the north it rests against the Snow Mountains (Himālaya). It is broad in the north and narrow in the south, shaped like a half-moon, with the land divided into more than seventy countries. The climate is exceptionally hot, and the ground is often damp with springs. To the north, mountains and ridges rise in succession, and the hills are of saline-alkaline soil; to the east, the plains are fertile and moist, and the cultivated fields are rich and productive; in the south, the vegetation is lush and flourishing; and in the west, the land is stony and barren. This is the general situation, which can be briefly stated.

Within a radius of two hundred li around the great city, the people of that land call it the Land of Blessedness (Kurukṣetra). According to the records of former times, the Five Indias were once ruled by two kings; their territories bordered each other and were subject to mutual invasions, with wars never ceasing. The two rulers conspired together, wishing to decide the matter through a decisive battle to determine the victor and bring peace to the populace. The common people were all resentful and would not follow the kings' commands. The kings thought that it is difficult to plan the beginning of an undertaking with the masses, but that the divine can move living beings and authority can establish merit. At that time, there was a Brahman known for his great talent; the king secretly presented him with a gift of silk and ordered him into the rear palace to compose a sacred text, which was then hidden in a mountain cave. As time passed, the trees grew to the size of a man’s embrace. The king sat in court and told his ministers: "Because of my lack of virtue, I unworthily occupy this high position; yet the Emperor of Heaven has looked down upon me and granted me a spiritual book in a dream, which is now located on a certain mountain, hidden on a certain ridge." Thereupon, he issued an order to search for it, and the book was found beneath the mountain forest. The officials offered congratulations, and the masses were joyful; it was proclaimed far and near, so that all might hear and know of it. Its general purport was: "Life and death are without bounds, and the cycle of transmigration is endless; sentient beings are submerged and drowning, with no way to save themselves. I, through a marvelous stratagem, shall cause them to depart from all suffering. Now, this royal city and its surroundings of two hundred li were a land of blessings and merit in the ages of former emperors. As the years and months have been extremely long, the inscriptions and records have been obliterated; living beings do not realize this and have consequently sunk into the sea of suffering. If they are drowning and not saved, what is to be said of it?" "All you sentient beings, if you die facing the enemy in battle, you will be reborn among humans; if you slaughter many of the innocent, you will receive the blessings and joys of heaven; and if obedient grandsons and filial sons who serve their elderly parents travel through this land, they shall obtain infinite blessings. With so little effort yielding such great merit, how could you let this advantage slip away? Once you lose this human body, the three paths (the three lower realms of existence) are dark and obscure. Therefore, let all living beings each apply themselves to their practice!" Thereupon, the people all engaged in battle, viewing death as a return home. The king then issued an order to recruit the brave and fierce; the two kingdoms joined in battle, and the piled-up corpses were like dense grass. Down to the present day, skeletal remains are scattered across the fields; as the events took place in ancient times, the human bones are of a massive size. Local custom passes down the name of this place as the Land of Blessings (Kurukṣetra). Four or five li to the northwest of the city, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, which was built by King Aśoka (無憂王). The bricks are all a yellowish-red color and are very bright and clean. Inside is one *dou* of the Tathāgata’s relics, which emit light from time to time and manifest many divine wonders.

The country of Lampāka (濫波國) is over a thousand *li* in circuit. To the north, it has the Snow Mountains at its back, and on the other three sides, it borders the Black Range (黑嶺). The capital city of the country is over ten *li* in circuit. For several hundred years, the royal lineage has been extinct, and powerful men have contended for strength, leaving the country without a great sovereign; only recently has it become a dependency of the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國). The land is suitable for non-glutinous rice and produces much sugarcane; although trees are numerous, they yield little fruit. The climate is gradually becoming warmer, with light frost but no snow. The customs of the country are prosperous and joyful, and the people are fond of singing and chanting; however, their dispositions are timid and weak, their hearts are deceitful, and they engage in mutual deception and mockery, lacking any sense of deference. Their physical stature is small, and their movements are restless. They mostly wear white cotton cloth and their attire is bright and decorative. There are more than ten monasteries with few monks, most of whom study the teachings of the Mahayana. There are several dozen *deva* temples, and the followers of heterodox paths are very numerous.

Traveling more than one hundred li to the south of the city, one arrives at the Gukhunda (俱昏荼) monastery. Multi-storied pavilions have connected roof ridges, and terraced platforms stand interspersed between them. The community of monks is pure and disciplined, and their deportment is calm and elegant.
The capital city of the country (Lanpo 濫波國) is more than ten li in circuit.

From here, traveling southeast for over a hundred li, crossing a great mountain range and fording a large river, one arrives at the country of Nagarahāra (那揭羅曷國). The country of Nagarahāra is over six hundred li from east to west and two hundred and fifty or sixty li from north to south. Mountains surround its four borders, which are precipitous and dangerous. The capital city of the country is over twenty li in circuit. There is no great monarch; the ruler is subject to the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國). The land is rich in grain and crops, and abounds in flowers and fruits. The climate is warm and hot. The customs of the people are simple and honest; they are fierce, valiant, and brave, and they value wealth lightly and love learning. They revere and respect the Buddhadharma and have little faith in heterodox paths. Although there are many monasteries, the number of monks is small, and the various stūpas are desolate and ruined. There are five Deva temples and over a hundred followers of heterodox paths.

From here, traveling northeast for more than four hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Srughna (窣祿勤那國). The country of Srughna is over six thousand *li* in circuit; it borders the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) to the east, rests against great mountains (pravaragiri) to the north, and the Yamunā River flows through the middle of its territory. The capital city of the country is over twenty *li* in circuit; it borders the Yamunā River to the east, and although it is very desolate, its foundations remain firm. The produce of the land and the suitability of the climate are the same as in the country of Sthāneśvara (薩他泥濕伐羅國). The people are honest and simple by nature, and they revere and believe in non-Buddhist paths. They value the arts and sciences, and esteem merit and wisdom. There are five *saṃghārāmas* with over one thousand monks, most of whom study the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), while few study other schools. They deliberate on subtle doctrines and engage in pure, profound discussions; talented scholars from distant regions seek them out to debate and resolve their doubts. There are one hundred *deva* temples, and the non-Buddhist sects are very numerous. To the southeast of the great city, on the west bank of the Yamunā River and outside the eastern gate of a large *saṃghārāma*, there is a *stūpa* built by King Aśoka. In the past, the Tathāgata once preached the Dharma here to save people. Beside it is another *stūpa* containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata. Surrounding it on the left and right are several dozen *stūpas* containing the hair and nails of the arhats Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana and others. After the Tathāgata entered extinction, this country was misled by various non-Buddhists; they accepted erroneous teachings and abandoned correct views. The five *saṃghārāmas* that exist today were built because they were places where masters from other countries debated and triumphed over various non-Buddhists and Brahmins.
The capital city of the country of Nagarahāra (那揭羅曷國) is more than twenty li in circuit.

Two li to the east of the city is a stūpa over three hundred feet high, which was built by King Aśoka (無憂王). It is constructed of piled stone rising prominently, with exquisite carvings and a unique design; it is the place where the Bodhisattva Śākya (釋迦菩薩) encountered the Buddha Dīpankara (然燈佛), spread out his deerskin garment, and laid down his hair to cover the mud, thereby receiving his prediction. Although aeons have passed and the world has been destroyed, this trace has not vanished. On certain fast days, the heavens rain down various flowers, and the populace, vying in their devotion, perform offerings. To its west is a saṃghārāma with few monks. Further to the south is a small stūpa; this is the site where the mud was once covered, which King Aśoka built in this secluded spot to avoid the main road. Inside the city are the old foundations of a great stūpa. I have heard from the records of the ancients that there was once a Buddha tooth here, which was tall, broad, and magnificent. Now that the tooth is gone, only the old foundations remain. Beside it is a stūpa over thirty feet high. Local tradition says, without knowing its origin, that it descended from the sky and established its base here. Since it was not made by human hands, it possesses many spiritual marvels. More than ten li to the southwest of the city is a stūpa marking the spot where the Tathāgata, traveling through the air from Central India to convert beings, descended; the people of the country, moved by admiration, built this spiritual foundation. Not far to its east is a stūpa where the Bodhisattva Śākya once encountered the Buddha Dīpankara and purchased flowers.

Traveling over eight hundred *li* east from the Yamunā River, one reaches the source of the Ganges River (Gaṅgā), which is three or four *li* wide; where it flows southeast into the sea, it is over ten *li* wide. The color of the water is a deep blue, and the waves flow vast and wide. Although there are many spiritual anomalies, they do not harm living beings. Its taste is sweet and delicious, and fine sand flows along with the current. According to the records of the local customs, it is called the "water of merit." Even if one has accumulated sins and transgressions, bathing in it removes them. Those who hold life lightly and drown themselves are reborn in heaven and receive blessings; those who cast their remains into it after death do not fall into the evil paths; and by splashing the waves and agitating the current, the souls of the departed obtain salvation.  At that time, the Bodhisattva Deva (提婆菩薩) from the country of Siṃhala (執師子國) had deeply penetrated the true reality and attained the nature of all phenomena. Pitying these foolish people, he came here to guide and instruct them. At that time, men and women had all gathered, young and old alike, and were splashing the waves and agitating the current on the riverbank. The Bodhisattva Deva, mingling with them to draw the water, lowered his head and pushed the water in the opposite direction, his behavior differing from that of the crowd. A non-Buddhist asked, "Why are you acting so strangely, sir?" The Bodhisattva Deva replied, "My parents and relatives are in the country of Siṃhala. I fear they are suffering from hunger and thirst, and I hope to provide them with relief from afar." The non-Buddhists said, "You are mistaken, sir! You have not thought this through and are performing this act in vain. Your home and country are far away, separated by vast mountains and rivers; to splash this water here to relieve their hunger there is like walking backward to try and reach a destination in front—it is unheard of." The Bodhisattva Deva replied, "If those burdened by sins in the dark paths of the afterlife can still receive the benefit of this water, why should it not reach those separated by mountains and rivers?" At that time, the various non-Buddhists (外道), realizing that they were defeated by his logic, abandoned their false views, accepted the true Dharma, reformed themselves, and wished to follow his teachings.

Traveling over twenty *li* southwest of the city to a small rocky ridge, there is a monastery with lofty halls and multi-storied pavilions, constructed from piled stones. The courtyards and buildings are desolate, and there are absolutely no monks. In the center is a *stūpa* over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). Southwest of the monastery is a deep, precipitous ravine with a waterfall flowing down and cliffs standing like walls. On the stone wall of the eastern cliff is a large cave, which is the dwelling place of the dragon Gopāla (瞿波羅龍). The entrance path is narrow, the cave is dark and gloomy, the cliff rocks drip with moisture, and the path is wet with the remaining flow. In the past, there was a shadow of the Buddha, shining as if it were his true form, with all the marks and characteristics complete, appearing just as if he were present. Since recent times, people have not been able to see it fully; even if they do see it, it is only indistinctly. Those who pray with utmost sincerity and have a spiritual response may see it clearly for a moment, but it cannot last long. Formerly, when the Tathāgata was in the world, this dragon was a cowherd who supplied milk and curds to the king, but he failed to present them properly. Having been reprimanded, he harbored resentment in his heart; he then used gold coins to buy flowers to offer to a *stūpa* of prediction, wishing to become a wicked dragon to destroy the country and harm the king. He then rushed to the stone wall and threw himself to his death. Consequently, he resided in this cave and became a great dragon king, intending to emerge from the cave to fulfill his evil vow. Just as this thought arose, the Tathāgata perceived it. Compassionate toward the people of this country who were about to be harmed by the dragon, he exercised his supernatural powers and arrived from Central India. When the dragon saw the Tathāgata, his poisonous intent ceased; he accepted the precept against killing and vowed to protect the True Dharma. The dragon then requested the Tathāgata, "May you always reside in this cave, and may your holy disciples constantly receive my offerings." The Tathāgata replied, "I am about to enter nirvana, but I shall leave my shadow for you and send five arhats to constantly receive your offerings. Even when the True Dharma has faded away, this practice shall not cease. If your poisonous heart should flare up in anger, you should look upon the shadow I have left behind; because of its compassionate nature, your poisonous heart will cease. In this Bhadrakalpa, the World-Honored Ones who are yet to come will also have compassion for you and will all leave their images behind."  Outside the entrance of the Shadow Cave (佛影窟), there are two square stones. On one of the stones is the footprint of the Tathāgata, where the wheel mark is faintly visible and light occasionally shines forth. To the left and right of the Shadow Cave are many stone chambers, all of which are places where the various holy disciples of the Tathāgata entered into meditative concentration. In the northwest corner of the Shadow Cave is a stūpa, which marks the place where the Tathāgata used to walk. Beside it is a stūpa containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata. Not far from this is a stūpa, which is the place where the Tathāgata manifested and expounded the True Doctrine, and where he spoke of the aggregates and realms. To the west of the Shadow Cave is a large flat rock where the Tathāgata once washed his kaṣāya robe, and the faint traces of its pattern are still visible.
Thus, from the silver ox's mouth on the eastern side of the pond flows the Ganges River (殑伽河; Skt. gaṅgā), which circles the pond once and enters the southeastern sea.
From the golden elephant's mouth on the south side of the lake flows the Sindhu River, which circles the lake once and enters the southwestern sea.

From the lapis lazuli horse's mouth on the western side of the pond flows the Vakṣu River (formerly called the Bocha River, which is a corruption), which circles the pond once and enters the northwestern sea.

Crossing the river to the east bank, one arrives at the country of Matipura (秣底補羅國). The country of Matipura is over six thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is over twenty li in circuit. It is suitable for grain and wheat, and there are many flowers and fruits. The climate is mild and pleasant, and the customs are honest and simple. The people value learning and the arts, and are deeply skilled in magical incantations. Those who believe in heterodox paths and those who believe in the orthodox path are about equal in number. The king is of the Śūdra caste; he does not believe in the Buddha-dharma and reverently serves the heavenly deities. There are over ten monasteries with more than eight hundred monks, most of whom study the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hīnayāna teachings. There are over fifty temples to the heavenly deities, where followers of various heterodox paths live together. Four or five li to the south of the great city, one reaches a small monastery with over fifty monks. In the past, the śāstra-master Guṇaprabha (瞿拏鉢剌婆) composed the *Tattvavibhaṅga* (辯真) and other treatises here, totaling over one hundred works. The śāstra-master was heroic and outstanding in his youth, and broad-minded and quick-witted in his maturity; he was widely learned and possessed a retentive memory. Originally, he studied the Mahāyāna, but not having fully fathomed its profound mysteries, he read the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (毘婆沙論), abandoned his former studies, and turned to the Hīnayāna. He composed several dozen treatises, refuting the principles of the Mahāyāna and establishing the tenets of the Hīnayāna. He also produced several dozen secular works, criticizing and rejecting the treatises composed by his predecessors. He pondered the Buddhist scriptures deeply, but there were over ten points he could not resolve; though he studied them with great refinement for a long time, his doubts remained. At that time, there was an arhat named Devasena (提婆犀那) who traveled back and forth to the Tuṣita Heaven. Guṇaprabha wished to see Maitreya (慈氏) to resolve his doubts and request further instruction. The arhat, using his supernatural powers, took him up to the heavenly palace. Upon seeing Maitreya (慈氏), he merely bowed and did not prostrate. The heavenly host (天軍) said to him, "Maitreya Bodhisattva is the next to succeed to the Buddha’s throne; why are you so arrogant that you dare not show him respect? Since you wish to receive instruction, how can you not humble yourself?" Guṇaprabha (德光) replied, "Venerable one, your words are truly instructive. However, I am a fully ordained bhikṣu and a monastic disciple, while Maitreya Bodhisattva enjoys heavenly bliss and is not a companion of the monastic order; I fear it would be inappropriate for me to pay him homage." The Bodhisattva, knowing that his pride was deeply rooted and that he was not a vessel for hearing the Dharma, did not resolve his doubts even after he had traveled back and forth three times. He again requested the heavenly host to allow him to pay homage, but the heavenly host, disgusted by his pride, ignored him and did not respond. Since Guṇaprabha did not have his wish fulfilled, he harbored resentment and immediately went into the mountain forests to practice and develop supernatural powers and meditative concentration; however, because his pride was not eliminated, he did not realize the fruits of the Path.  Three or four li to the north of the Guṇaprabha Monastery (德光伽藍) is a large monastery with over two hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). This is the place where the master Saṃghabhadra (眾賢論師) passed away. The master was a native of the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國). He was intelligent, learned, and widely known for his reputation since his youth, and he studied the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (說一切有部毘婆沙論) of the Sarvāstivāda school with particular depth. At that time, there was the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (世親菩薩), who was single-mindedly devoted to the profound Path and sought to understand the meaning beyond the words. He refuted the positions held by the masters of the *Vibhāṣā* and composed the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* (阿毘達磨俱舍論), which was skillful in its phrasing and meaning, and lofty in its reasoning. Saṃghabhadra read and examined it, and consequently, he became deeply concerned. Thereupon, he delved deeply into his studies with the utmost rigor for twelve years, composing the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (俱舍雹論) in twenty-five thousand verses, totaling eight hundred thousand words. It was said that his words were profound and far-reaching, exhausting the hidden and penetrating the subtle. He told his disciples, "With my outstanding talent and by upholding my correct arguments, go and refute Vasubandhu (世親) to blunt his sharp edge, so that the old man may no longer enjoy a monopoly on pre-eminent fame." Thereupon, three or four of his most talented disciples took the treatise he had written and went to seek out Vasubandhu. At that time, Vasubandhu was in the city of Sākala (奢羯羅城) in the country of Takka (磔迦國). Word spread from afar that Saṃghabhadra (眾賢) was coming. Upon hearing this, Vasubandhu immediately began to pack his belongings. His disciples, filled with doubt, came forward to remonstrate, saying, "Great Master, your virtue surpasses that of former sages and your fame is unrivaled in the present age; among students near and far, there are none who do not defer to you. Now, upon hearing of Saṃghabhadra, why are you so flustered? If you must lower yourself to him, we shall be deeply ashamed." Vasubandhu replied, "I am traveling far away now, not to avoid this man. It is just that in this country, there are no longer any discerning judges. Saṃghabhadra is a younger scholar whose sophistry flows like a river, while I am old and decrepit, unable to sustain a debate. I wish to defeat his heterodox views with a single word and lead him to Central India to face the eminent and learned scholars, so that they may discern truth from falsehood and examine right and wrong." He immediately summoned his companions, shouldered his book satchel, and set out on his long journey. The Master of Treatises Saṃghabhadra (眾賢) arrived at this monastery one day later, but suddenly felt his vitality failing. He thereupon composed a letter to apologize to Vasubandhu (世親), saying: "Since the Tathāgata entered extinction, the disciples have held to their own sectarian views, transmitting their respective traditions, each specializing in their own field, favoring those of the same path and disparaging those of different schools. In my ignorance and dullness, I rashly received these traditions. Upon reading the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* (阿毘達磨俱舍論) which you composed, I saw that it refuted the great principles of the Vaibhāṣika masters. Without measuring my own strength, I spent many years in deep study and composed this treatise to uphold the orthodox tradition. My wisdom was small but my ambition was great, and now death is approaching. You, Bodhisattva, expound the subtle words and propagate the supreme truth; if you do not disparage my convictions and allow my writings to be preserved, I shall be fortunate indeed, and what regret could I have in death?"  He then carefully selected a disciple who possessed eloquence and told him: "I am truly a junior scholar who has rashly insulted a senior master; such is my fate! I am about to pass away. You must take this letter and the treatise I have composed, apologize to that Bodhisattva, and repent on my behalf." As soon as he finished giving these instructions, he suddenly passed away. The disciple took the letter to Vasubandhu and delivered the message, saying: "My master Saṃghabhadra has already abandoned his life. He left a final letter to reproach himself and apologize for his faults. That his name not be forgotten is not something we would dare to hope for."  Bodhisattva Vasubandhu read the letter and examined the treatise. After pondering for a long time, he said to the disciple: "The Master of Treatises Saṃghabhadra was a clever junior scholar; although his reasoning was insufficient, his eloquence was abundant. I now wish to refute the treatise of Saṃghabhadra, and it will be as easy as pointing to the palm of my hand." "However, considering his dying request and valuing his challenging words, if it serves the great principles, I shall preserve his original intention; how much more so when this treatise clarifies my own school?" He then changed the title to the *Abhidharma-nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (順正理論). His disciples remonstrated, saying: "Saṃghabhadra is not yet dead, and the Master has traveled far away; having obtained his treatise, to then change its title—how can all the students face the shame of this?" The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, wishing to dispel their doubts, spoke a verse: "Like a lion king, avoiding a pig and traveling far away, the wise should know the victory or defeat of the two powers." After Saṃghabhadra died, his body was cremated and his bones collected. In the mango grove (āmra-vana) two hundred paces to the northwest of the monastery, a stūpa was erected, which still exists today. Beside the mango grove is a stūpa containing the remains of the master Vimalamitra (毘末羅蜜多羅). The master was a man from the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國), who had renounced the world in the Sarvāstivāda school. He was widely versed in the various scriptures and studied heterodox treatises. He traveled through the five Indias, studied the profound texts of the Tripiṭaka, and having established his reputation and completed his work, he was about to return to his home country. Passing by the stūpa of the master Saṃghabhadra, he patted it and sighed, saying: "The master possessed such noble magnanimity and refined character, expounding the great principles; just as he was about to defeat the heterodox sects and establish the legacy of his own school, how is it that his life was not prolonged! I, Vimalamitra, though a humble student of later generations, have long admired his righteousness and for ages have cherished his virtue." "Although Vasubandhu (世親) has passed away, his school's teachings are still transmitted. I shall exhaust all my knowledge to compose various treatises, causing the scholars of Jambudvīpa (贍部洲) to abandon the name of the Mahāyāna and to efface the fame of Vasubandhu; this shall be my immortal achievement, fulfilling my long-held ambition." Having spoken these words, his mind became deranged, five tongues emerged from his mouth, and hot blood gushed forth. Knowing that his life was surely coming to an end, he composed a letter of repentance, saying: "The Mahāyāna teachings are the ultimate discourse within the Buddha-dharma. Their names and meanings are profound and absolute, and their principles are subtle and mysterious. Because of my ignorance, I lightly refuted the masters of the past; the karmic retribution is clear, and it is fitting that my body should be destroyed. I dare to warn all students: take this as a mirror, be cautious in your intentions, and do not harbor doubts." The great earth shook, and his life then ended. At the place where he died, the ground sank into a pit. His traveling companions cremated his corpse, collected the remains, and built a memorial over them. At that time, an Arhat saw this and sighed, saying: "Alas! How painful! This master of treatises, indulging in his own biased views, slandered the Mahāyāna and has fallen into the Avīci (無間) hell."

From the crystal lion’s mouth on the north side of the lake flows the Sītā River, which circles the lake once and enters the northeast sea; or it is said that it flows underground and emerges at Jishi Mountain, being the current of the Sītā River and the source of the river of China.

Thirty-some *li* southeast of the city, one arrives at the city of Haḍḍa (醯羅城). It is four or five *li* in circumference, with steep and rugged defenses, and flower groves and ponds that are bright, fresh, and clear as mirrors. The people living in the city are honest, simple, and possess upright faith. There is a multi-storied pavilion with painted beams and vermilion pillars. In the second story of the pavilion is a small stupa made of the seven precious substances, in which the crown bone of the Tathāgata is placed. The bone is one foot and two inches in circumference, with distinct hair pores, and its color is yellowish-white; it is contained in a precious casket and placed inside the stupa. Those who wish to know the signs of their good or evil karma mix incense powder with clay and press it onto the crown bone; according to the response of their merit, the patterns appear clearly. There is another small stupa made of the seven precious substances to store the Tathāgata’s skull bone, which is shaped like a lotus leaf and is the same color as the crown bone; it is also kept sealed within a precious casket. There is another small stupa made of the seven precious substances containing the Tathāgata’s eyeball, which is as large as a *nā* (crabapple) fruit, brilliant and transparent, shining through from inside to out; it is also kept sealed within a precious casket. The Tathāgata’s *saṃghāṭī* (monastic robe) is made of fine *nü* (a type of fine cotton or wool fabric), its color is yellowish-red, and it is kept in a precious casket; as the years have been long, it is slightly damaged. The Tathāgata’s *khakkhara* (monk’s staff) has rings made of white iron and a shaft made of sandalwood; it is kept in a precious tube. Recently, a king heard that all these objects were things the Tathāgata had personally used in the past, and relying on his power, he forcibly took them away. Once they arrived in his own country, he placed them in the palace where he resided, but before even twelve days had passed, when he sought them, they were already lost; upon further searching, they had already returned to their original place. These five sacred sites possess many spiritual wonders, and the king of Kapiśa (迦畢試國) has appointed five pure-practitioners (brahmacārins) to provide incense and flowers in service to them. Pilgrims coming to pay their respects arrive in an unbroken succession. The pure-practitioners, desiring to pursue emptiness and tranquility, and considering that wealth is something people value, have provisionally established a schedule of fees to put an end to the clamor and confusion. The general outline is as follows: those who wish to see the Tathāgata’s skull bone must pay a tax of one gold coin; if they wish to take an impression, they must pay a tax of five gold coins; for the remaining items, there is a graded schedule of fees. Although the fees are heavy, the number of those coming to pay their respects only increases. To the northwest of the multi-storied pavilion is a stūpa, which is also very tall and displays many spiritual wonders; if a person touches it with a finger, it immediately begins to shake, its very foundations tilt and move, and its bells ring in harmony.

In the northwest territory of the kingdom, on the east bank of the Ganges (gaṅgā) River, lies the city of Mayūra (摩裕羅城), which is over twenty li in circuit. The inhabitants are prosperous, and the city is encircled by clear streams; it produces brass, rock crystal, and precious vessels. Not far from the city, bordering the Ganges River, there is a great deva temple with many miraculous manifestations. Within it is a pond with stone-lined banks, replenished by water diverted from the Ganges; the people of the five Indias call it the Gate of the Ganges (Gaṅgādvāra), a place for generating merit and expiating sins. Constantly, hundreds of thousands of people from distant regions gather here to bathe. Benevolent kings have established charitable hostels here, stocked with fine food and stored with medicines, to bestow gifts upon the widowed and solitary, and to provide for the orphaned and destitute.

The central region of the continent of Jambudvīpa is the Anavatapta Lake (阿那婆答多池). It is situated to the south of the Fragrant Mountain (香山; Skt. Gandhamādana-giri) and to the north of the Great Snow Mountain (大雪山; Skt. Himavat), with a circumference of eight hundred li.

From here, traveling southeast through mountain valleys for more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Gandhāra (健馱邏國). The country of Gandhāra is over one thousand *li* from east to west and eight hundred *li* from north to south. To the east, it borders the Sindhu River (信度河). The great capital city of the country is called Puruṣapura (布路沙布邏), which is over forty *li* in circumference. The royal lineage has become extinct, and it is subject to the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國). The towns and villages are desolate, and the inhabitants are few; in one corner of the palace city, there are over a thousand households. The grain crops are abundant, flowers and fruits are lush, there is much sugarcane, and it produces rock honey. The climate is warm and hot, with almost no frost or snow. The people are timid and cowardly; they are fond of studying the arts and classics, and they mostly revere heterodox paths, having little faith in the True Dharma. Since ancient times, this has been the birthplace of various masters in the regions of India who composed treatises, such as Nārāyaṇa-deva (那羅延天), the Bodhisattva Asaṅga (無著菩薩), the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (世親菩薩), Dharmatrāta (法救), Manoratha (如意), and the Venerable Pārśva (脇尊者). There are over a thousand *saṃghārāmas*, which are ruined, desolate, overgrown, and bleak; many of the *stūpas* have collapsed. There are one hundred *deva* temples, where heterodox practitioners live together.

From here, traveling north for more than three hundred li, one arrives at the country of Brahmapura (婆羅吸摩補羅國). The country of Brahmapura is over four thousand li in circuit, and mountains surround its four borders. The capital city of the country is more than twenty li in circuit. The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous, and the households are wealthy. The soil is fertile, crops are sown in their proper seasons, and the land produces brass and rock crystal. The climate is slightly cold, and the customs are fierce and unyielding. There is little interest in the arts, and many pursue profit. The nature of the people is wild and violent, and they believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are five sanghārāmas (伽藍) with few monks, and more than ten deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.
Some say that it flows underground and emerges at Jishi Mountain (積石山), being the current of the Sītā River (徙多河) and the source of the river of China.
The great capital city of the country is called Puruṣapura (布路沙布邏), and it is over forty li in circuit.

In the midst of the Great Snowy Mountains to the north of the borders of this country lies the country of Suvarṇagotra (蘇伐剌拏瞿呾羅國). It produces superior gold, and is named accordingly. It is long from east to west and narrow from north to south; this is the Eastern Women’s Kingdom (東女國). For generations, it has been ruled by women, and thus it is called the Women’s Kingdom. The husband is also a king, but he does not manage state affairs; the men’s only duties are warfare and farming. The soil is suitable for winter wheat, and there is an abundance of sheep and horses. The climate is cold and severe, and the people are impetuous and violent. To the east it borders the kingdom of Tubo (吐蕃國), to the north it borders the kingdom of Khotan (于闐國), and to the west it borders the kingdom of Sampaha (三波訶國).

From the Black Ridge (Heiling) onwards, all are customs of the Hu. Although they are grouped with the Rong peoples, they are divided into distinct tribes with demarcated borders, and for the most part, they are settled inhabitants. They build walled cities and devote themselves to agriculture and animal husbandry. By nature, they value wealth and property, while their customs hold benevolence and righteousness in low regard. There is no ritual in marriage, and no order of precedence between the noble and the base; the words of women are heeded, while men occupy a subordinate position. Upon death, they cremate the remains, and there is no fixed period for mourning. They scarify their faces and mutilate their ears, cut their hair and rend their garments, and slaughter herds of livestock to sacrifice to the spirits of the dead. On auspicious occasions they wear white garments, while for mourning they dress in black. These are the general customs and practices, briefly outlined here; their differing administrations and unique regulations will be described separately according to each region. The customs of India are discussed in the final record.

Inside the royal city, to the northeast, there is an old foundation; it was formerly the precious pedestal of the Buddha’s alms bowl. After the Tathāgata entered nirvana, the bowl drifted to this country, where it was formally worshipped for several hundred years; it then circulated through various countries and is now in Persia (Pārśva). Eight or nine li to the southeast of the city, there is a Pippala tree (卑鉢羅樹) over a hundred feet high, with wide-spreading branches and leaves that provide a dense shade. The four Buddhas of the past have already sat beneath it, and images of these four Buddhas still exist there today. During the Bhadrakalpa, the nine hundred and ninety-six Buddhas will all sit there as well. Deities guard and protect it, and its spiritual influence is secretly bestowed. The Śākya Tathāgata once sat under this tree facing south and told Ānanda: "Four hundred years after I pass away, a king will appear in the world named Kaniṣka; not far to the south of this spot, he will erect a stūpa, and a great portion of the relics of my bones and flesh will be gathered within it."
Departing from the former territory of Gaochang (高昌), I begin with the nearest land, which is called the country of Agni (阿耆尼國).

Traveling southeast from Matipura (末底補羅國) for more than four hundred li, one arrives at the country of Goviṣāṇa (瞿毘霜那國). The country of Goviṣāṇa is more than two thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is fourteen or fifteen li in circuit; it is high, precipitous, and strategically secure, with a dense and prosperous population, and flowery groves and ponds are interspersed throughout. The climate and soil conditions are the same as those of the country of Matipura. The customs of the people are simple and honest; they are diligent in learning and fond of merit. Many believe in non-Buddhist paths and seek present-day happiness. There are two saṃghārāmas with over one hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Hīnayāna. There are more than thirty Deva temples, where followers of various paths dwell together. Beside the old saṃghārāma near the great city, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, which is over two hundred feet high. In the past, the Tathāgata stayed here for one month to preach the essential teachings of the Dharma; nearby are the seats and walking-paths of the four past Buddhas. Beside these are two stūpas containing the hair and nail clippings of the Tathāgata, each over one chang high.

The kingdom of Agni (阿耆尼國) is over six hundred *li* from east to west and over four hundred *li* from south to north. The kingdom’s capital city is six or seven *li* in circumference. It is backed by mountains on all four sides, and the roads are perilous and easy to defend. Streams flow around it, and water is diverted to irrigate the fields. The soil is suitable for growing non-glutinous millet, broomcorn millet, winter wheat, fragrant jujubes, grapes, pears, crabapples, and various other fruits. The climate is mild and pleasant, and the customs of the people are simple and honest. Their writing system is modeled on that of India, with slight modifications. Their clothing is made of felt and coarse wool; they cut their hair short and do not wear headcloths. For currency, they use gold coins, silver coins, and small copper coins. The king is a native of the country; he is brave but lacks strategy, and he is fond of boasting of his own achievements. The country lacks a strict code of conduct, and the laws are not well-regulated. There are more than ten monasteries with over two thousand monks, who study the Sarvāstivāda (說一切有部) school of the Hīnayāna. Since their scriptural teachings and Vinaya discipline follow those of India, the students study them using the original texts. Their conduct and adherence to the Vinaya are pure, clean, and diligent. However, they consume the three kinds of "pure meat," remaining attached to the gradual teachings.

From here, traveling southeast for more than four hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Ahicchatrā (堊醯掣呾邏國). The country of Ahicchatrā is more than three thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city is seventeen or eighteen *li* in circuit; it is situated in a secure and rugged location, is suitable for grain and wheat, and has many forests and springs. The climate is temperate and pleasant, and the customs of the people are honest and simple. They delight in the Way and are diligent in their studies, being talented and widely learned. There are more than ten *saṃghārāmas* (monasteries) and over one thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Sammatiya school of the Lesser Vehicle. There are nine *deva* temples, and more than three hundred followers of heterodox paths who serve Īśvara (自在天) and are companions who smear themselves with ash. Outside the city, beside a dragon pool, there is a *stūpa* built by King Aśoka (無憂王). It was here that the Tathāgata, in a former life when he was a dragon king, preached the Dharma for seven days. Beside it are four small *stūpas*, which are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas.

From here, traveling east for two hundred sixty or seventy li, one crosses the Ganges (Gaṅgā) River and arrives south at the country of Vilaśāṇa (毘羅那拏國). The country of Vilaśāṇa is over two thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is over ten li in circuit. The climate and soil conditions are the same as those of the country of Ahicchatrā (堊醯掣呾邏國). The customs are fierce and violent, yet the people value learning and the arts. They revere and believe in non-Buddhist paths and have little respect for the Buddhadharma. There are two monasteries with three hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Mahāyāna. There are five Deva temples where followers of various paths live together. Inside an old monastery in the great city, there is the base of a stūpa which, although dilapidated, is still over one hundred feet high; it was built by King Aśoka (無憂王). This is the place where the Tathāgata in the past spent seven days preaching the *Skandhadhātvāyatana-sūtra* (蘊界處經). Beside it are the seats of the four past Buddhas and the traces of their walking meditation.
The capital city of the country of Agni (阿耆尼國) is six or seven li in circuit. It is backed by mountains on all four sides, and the roads are precipitous and easy to defend.

From here, traveling southeast for more than two hundred li, one arrives at the country of Kapitha (劫比他國). The country of Kapitha is more than two thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than twenty li in circuit. The climate and soil conditions are the same as those of the country of Viraṇāṇa (毘羅那拏國). The customs are honest and harmonious, and the people are generally devoted to the arts. There are four saṃghārāmas with more than one thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Hīnayāna Saṃmitīya school. There are ten deva temples where followers of different paths live together, all of whom jointly worship Maheśvara.

Traveling southwest from here for over two hundred li, crossing a small mountain and two large rivers, I reached a plain to the west; after traveling seven hundred li, I arrived at the country of Kuci (屈支國). The country of Kuci is over one thousand li from east to west and over six hundred li from south to north. The capital city is seventeen or eighteen li in circuit. The soil is suitable for millet and wheat, yields round-grained rice, produces grapes and pomegranates, and abounds in pears, crabapples, peaches, and apricots. The land produces gold, copper, iron, lead, and tin. The climate is temperate and the customs are honest. Their writing system is modeled on that of India, with slight modifications. In the arts of string and wind instruments, they are exceptionally skilled compared to other countries. Their clothing is made of brocade and felt, and they cut their hair and wear turbans. For currency, they use gold coins, silver coins, and small copper coins. The king is of Kuci stock; he is of limited wisdom and is constrained by powerful ministers. It is their custom when a child is born to press its head with a wooden board, wishing for it to be flat. There are over one hundred monasteries with more than five thousand monks, who study the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teachings of the Sarvāstivāda school. Their scriptural teachings and monastic regulations are modeled on those of India, and those who study them read the original texts. They still adhere to the gradual teachings and consume the three kinds of pure meat. They are devoted to purity and cleanliness, and the people compete in performing meritorious deeds.

In front of a divine shrine (devalaya) north of a city on the eastern border of the kingdom, there is a large dragon pond. The various dragons change their forms to mate with mares, and thus produce dragon-colts that are fierce and difficult to tame. It is only the offspring of these dragon-colts that can be broken and ridden, which is why this country produces many fine horses. According to the accounts of the ancients, in recent times there was a king named Golden Flower (Suvarṇapuṣpa), whose administration and teachings were enlightened and discerning, and he moved a dragon to serve as his mount. When the king was about to pass away, he touched the dragon’s ear with his whip, whereupon it submerged and disappeared, remaining hidden to this day. There are no wells in the city, so the people draw water from that pond. The dragons transform into men and mate with the women; the children born of this are brave and swift, able to outrun galloping horses. Through this gradual intermingling, the people have all become of dragon lineage, relying on their strength to act tyrannically and refusing to obey the king’s commands. The king then colluded with the Turks to slaughter the people of this city, executing both young and old until not a single soul remained. The city is now desolate, and human habitation has ceased.

To the south of the Pippala tree is a stupa built by King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王). Four hundred years after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, King Kaniṣka ascended the throne and ruled over Jambudvīpa. He did not believe in merit or demerit and slighted the Buddha’s Dharma. While hunting in the marshes, he encountered a white rabbit; the king personally gave chase, but it suddenly vanished at this spot. He saw a young cowherd among the trees making a small stupa three feet in height. The king asked, "What are you doing?" The cowherd replied, "Long ago, the holy wisdom of Śākya Buddha prophesied: 'A king will appear who shall build a stupa on this excellent site, and many of my bodily relics will be gathered within it.' Your Majesty’s holy virtues were cultivated in the past, your name matches the ancient prophecy, and your divine merit and superior fortune are destined for this very moment; therefore, I have come ahead to alert and inspire you." Having said this, he suddenly disappeared. Hearing these words, the king was filled with joy and reverence. Reflecting on his name and the Great Sage’s prior prophecy, he developed true faith and deeply respected the Buddha’s Dharma. Around the small stupa, he built a stone stupa, wishing to use his power to cover it completely. Yet, as he increased the height, the small stupa always emerged three feet above it. Only when the height exceeded four hundred feet—with the base standing one and a half li in circumference and a five-tiered foundation one hundred and fifty feet high—was he finally able to cover the small stupa. The king, rejoicing at this auspicious event, further erected twenty-five tiers of gilded copper rings above it, and placing one hu of the Tathāgata’s relics within them, he performed offerings in this manner. No sooner was the construction finished than he saw the small stupa protruding halfway out from beneath the southeast corner of the great foundation. The king was displeased and cast it away; it then lodged halfway within the stone base under the second tier of the stupa, while another small stupa emerged once more at its original location. The king then withdrew and sighed, saying: "Alas, human efforts are easily misguided, but divine merit is difficult to conceal. When supported by the holy and spiritual, what can anger achieve?" Having felt shame and fear, he confessed his fault and returned. Those two stupas are still present today; those who are afflicted with illness and wish to pray for recovery apply incense and scatter flowers, and with sincere devotion take refuge, most of them obtaining a cure. To the south of the stone steps on the eastern face of the great stupa, two stupas are carved, one three feet high and the other five feet high, their design and shape modeled after the great stupa. Two Buddha images are also fashioned, one four feet high and the other six feet high, imitating the seated image with crossed legs under the Mahā-bodhi tree; when the sunlight shines upon them, the golden color glitters brilliantly, and as the shadows gradually shift, the stone patterns appear dark blue. I have heard from the elders that several hundred years ago, there were golden ants in the crevices of the stone base, the large ones like fingers and the small ones like grains of wheat, which followed one another to gnaw at the stone wall, the patterns appearing as if carved and inlaid with gold sand, forming these images, which are still present today. On the southern side of the stone steps of the great stūpa (大窣堵波) there is a painted Buddha image sixteen feet high; from the chest upward it appears as two bodies, but from the chest downward it is joined into one. I have heard from the elders that in the beginning, there was a poor man who supported himself by manual labor and, having obtained one gold coin, wished to have a Buddha image made. He went to the place of the stūpa and said to a painter, "I now wish to depict the exquisite features of the Tathāgata (如來), but I have only one gold coin, which is insufficient to reward your labor; I have long cherished this desire but am burdened by worry, being constrained by my poverty." At that time, the painter, perceiving his utmost sincerity, did not speak of the price but promised to complete the work. Later, there was another man whose circumstances were the same as the former; he brought a gold coin and requested that an image of the Buddha be painted. The painter then accepted the money from both men, sought out excellent pigments, and painted a single image for them both. When the two men came on the same day to pay their respects, the painter pointed to the one image, showed it to them, and said, "This is the Buddha image you commissioned." The two men looked at each other, as if they had some misgivings. The painter, knowing their doubts in his heart, said to the two men, "Why are you so long in thought? Whatever I have received, I have not diminished by even a hair's breadth. If these words are not false, the image will surely manifest a divine transformation." Before his voice had ceased, the image manifested a miracle: the bodies separated and their shadows intertwined, and the light of the image shone brilliantly. The two men were convinced and filled with faith and joy. More than a hundred paces to the southwest of the great stupa (mahāstūpa), there is a white stone Buddha image eighteen feet high, standing and facing north; it possesses many divine signs and frequently emits light. At times, people have seen the image go out at night to walk, circumambulating the great stupa. Recently, a group of thieves intended to enter and commit theft, but the image went out to meet them; the band of thieves was terrified and retreated, and the image returned to its original place, standing as before. Because of this, the group of thieves reformed and renewed themselves, traveling through the towns and villages to tell everyone, far and near. To the left and right of the great stupa, there are hundreds of small stupas arranged like fish scales. The Buddha images are adorned with the utmost craftsmanship, and extraordinary fragrances and strange sounds are sometimes heard; divine immortals and sages are occasionally seen circumambulating them. Regarding this stupa, the Tathāgata prophesied that it would be burned seven times and rebuilt seven times, at which point the Buddhadharma would come to an end. The records of the ancients state that it has already been built and destroyed three times. When I first arrived in this country, I happened to encounter a great fire, and I saw it being constructed, though it was not yet completed.

More than twenty *li* west of the city is a large monastery, its construction magnificent and its craftsmanship exquisite; the sacred forms and venerable images are adorned with the utmost solemnity. There are several hundred monks who study the teachings of the Saṃmitīya school, and tens of thousands of laypeople reside in its vicinity. Within the great wall of the monastery are the Devāvatāra (三寶階), arranged from north to south and facing east, where the Tathāgata returned from the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
