In the past, the Tathāgata rose from the Jetavana (勝林) and ascended to the heavenly palace, where he resided in the Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā-sabhā) to preach the Dharma for his mother. After three months had passed, he intended to descend. Śakra, the Lord of Devas, then exercised his divine power to establish a precious stairway: the middle step was of gold, the left of crystal, and the right of silver. The Tathāgata rose from the Hall of Good Dharma and, followed by a host of deities, stepped down the middle stairway; the Great Brahmā King, holding a white whisk, walked on the silver stairway to attend on the right; Śakra, the Lord of Devas, holding a precious canopy, stepped on the crystal stairway to attend on the left; the heavenly host hovered in the void, scattering flowers and praising his virtues. Several hundred years ago, the stairs still existed, but by the present time, they have completely sunk into the earth. The kings of various countries, lamenting that they could not see them, stacked bricks and stones and decorated them with precious gems upon the original foundation to imitate the ancient precious stairway. It is over seventy feet high, and a *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍) is built upon it. Inside is a stone Buddha image, and on the stairs to the left and right are images of Śakra and Brahmā, modeled after the original appearance, still in a descending posture. Beside it is a stone pillar, over seventy feet high, erected by King Aśoka (無憂王). Its color is dark blue and lustrous, its substance hard and its texture dense. At the top is a lion, crouching and facing the stairway, with strange forms carved and engraved around its four sides; according to the merits or sins of the person, shadows appear within the pillar. Not far from the side of the precious stairway is a stūpa, which is the site of the traces where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation. Beside it is a stūpa where the Tathāgata formerly bathed. Beside that is a *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍), which is the place where the Tathāgata entered into meditation. Beside the *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* is a large stone with a base fifty paces long and seven feet high, which is the place where the Tathāgata performed walking meditation. The footprints he trod upon all have lotus flower patterns. To the left and right of the base are small stūpas, which were built by Śakra (帝釋) and Brahmā (梵王). In front of the stūpas of Śakra and Brahmā is the place where the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā (蓮華色苾芻尼), wishing to be the first to see the Buddha, transformed herself into a Cakravartin king. When the Tathāgata returned to Jambudvīpa from the heavenly palace, Subhūti (蘇部底) was sitting in meditation in a stone chamber and thought to himself: "Now that the Buddha is returning and descending, guided and followed by humans and devas, what is appropriate for someone like me to do? I have heard the Buddha say that to know all phenomena are empty and to realize the nature of all phenomena is to behold the Dharma-kāya with the eye of wisdom." At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, wishing to be the first to see the Buddha, transformed herself into a Cakravartin king, guided and followed by the seven treasures and guarded by the fourfold army, and arrived at the place of the World-Honored One, where she returned to her form as a bhikṣuṇī. The Tathāgata said to her: "You are not the first to see me. For one who is well-manifested, to contemplate that all phenomena are empty is to see the Dharma-kāya." Within the enclosure of the holy traces, miraculous manifestations occur one after another. To the southeast of the great stūpa, there is a dragon pond; the dragon constantly protects the holy traces. Since there is this unseen protection, they are difficult to violate lightly; although they have decayed naturally over the long years, no human could destroy them. Traveling southeast from here for less than two hundred li, one arrives at the country of Kanyākubja (羯若鞠闍國).

More than forty *li* to the north of the deserted city, nestled against a mountain slope and separated by a river, are two monasteries; both are named Cakuri (昭怙釐), distinguished as the Eastern and Western respectively. The ornamentation of the Buddha statues almost surpasses human craftsmanship. The monks are pure and austere, truly diligent and earnest. In the Buddha hall of the Eastern Cakuri Monastery, there is a jade stone over two feet wide, yellowish-white in color and shaped like a sea clam. Upon it is a footprint left by the Buddha, measuring one foot eight inches in length and over six inches in width. On some fast days, it emits a brilliant light. Outside the west gate of the great city, on both sides of the road, there are standing statues of the Buddha, each over ninety feet tall. In front of these statues is the site where a great assembly is held every five years. Every year, during the several tens of days around the autumnal equinox, the monks of the entire country gather here. From the king down to the officials and commoners, all set aside worldly affairs to observe fasts and precepts, receive scriptures, and listen to the Dharma, forgetting their fatigue throughout the day. The various monasteries adorn their Buddha statues, polishing them with precious gems and decorating them with brocades and silks, then loading them onto palanquins; these are called "processional images." Numbering in the thousands, they gather like clouds at the assembly site. On the fifteenth and the last day of every month, the king and his ministers deliberate on state affairs, consulting with eminent monks before making proclamations.

Northwest of the assembly hall, one crosses a river and arrives at the Āścarya monastery (阿奢理貳伽藍). The courtyards and buildings are spacious and bright, and the Buddha images are skillfully adorned. The community of monks is solemn and respectful, diligent and untiring; they are all elders of great virtue, profound learning, and high talent, as well as outstanding individuals from distant regions who have arrived here out of admiration for the teachings. The king, ministers, officials, commoners, and the wealthy and influential provide the four requisites of support, and their reverence only increases with time.  I have heard from the records of former times that a previous king of this country, who deeply revered the Triple Gem, wished to travel abroad to pay homage to holy sites, so he commanded his younger brother by the same mother to act as regent and oversee state affairs. Upon receiving this command, the younger brother secretly castrated himself to prevent any future suspicion. He sealed the organ in a golden casket and presented it to the king. The king asked, "What is the meaning of this?" He replied, "You may open it on the day you return from your journey." The king then entrusted it to an attendant to be kept safe with the royal baggage.  Upon the king’s return, there were indeed those who slandered him, saying, "While the king ordered him to oversee the state, he committed adultery within the inner palace." Hearing this, the king was enraged and wished to impose a severe punishment. The brother said, "I dare not evade the charge, but I ask that you open the golden casket." The king then opened it and looked inside, finding only the severed organ. The king asked, "What is this strange object? What are you trying to demonstrate?" He replied, "When Your Majesty went on a tour in the past and ordered me to handle affairs in your absence, I feared the disaster of slander, so I castrated myself to prove my innocence. Now that the evidence has indeed appeared, I ask that you examine it." The king was deeply astonished and moved, and his affection for him grew even greater; he was permitted to enter and leave the inner palace without any restrictions. Later, the king’s younger brother was traveling when he encountered a man driving five hundred bulls, intending to have them castrated. Seeing this, he reflected on their shared plight and his heart was filled with emotion: "That I am now physically deformed, is it not due to my past karma?" He immediately used his wealth and treasures to redeem this herd of bulls. Through the power of his compassion, his male form was gradually restored. Because his masculinity had been restored, he would no longer enter the inner palace. The king was puzzled and asked him why, whereupon he explained the whole story from beginning to end. The king regarded this as a marvelous event and subsequently built a monastery (saṃghārāma) to commemorate this noble deed and transmit his fame to future generations.

From here, traveling westward for more than six hundred li and passing through a small desert, I arrived at the kingdom of Bālukā (跋祿迦國). The kingdom of Bālukā measures over six hundred li from east to west and more than three hundred li from south to north. The kingdom’s great capital city is five or six li in circumference. The soil, climate, human temperament, customs, and system of writing are the same as those of the kingdom of Kuci (屈支國), though the language differs slightly. Fine felt and fine woolen cloth are highly valued by neighboring countries. There are several dozen sanghārāmas (伽藍) with over one thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle according to the Sarvāstivāda school (說一切有部).

The country of Īraṇaparvata (伊爛拏鉢伐多國) is more than three thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country borders the Ganges River (殑伽河) to the north and is more than twenty li in circuit. The crops are lush and the flowers and fruits are abundant. The climate is mild and pleasant, and the customs are simple and honest. There are more than ten monasteries with over four thousand monks, most of whom study the teachings of the Hīnayāna Sāmmitīya school. There are more than twenty deva temples, where followers of various heterodox paths live together. Recently, a neighboring king deposed the ruler of this country and bestowed the capital city upon the community of monks. Within this city, he built two monasteries, each housing nearly one thousand monks, both of which study the Hīnayāna teachings of the Sarvāstivāda school.  Beside the great city, overlooking the Ganges River, is Mount Īraṇa (伊爛拏山), which exhales mists and clouds that obscure the sun and moon. Throughout the ages, immortals and sages have followed one another to dwell here in meditation, and there is now a deva temple that still observes the traditional rites. In the past, the Tathāgata also resided here and preached the profound Dharma extensively for devas and humans. To the south of the great city is a stūpa where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for three months. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the three past Buddhas. Not far to the west of the walking paths of the three Buddhas is a stūpa, which is the birthplace of the bhikṣu Śrotaviṃśatikoṭi (室縷多頻設底拘胝). In the past, there was a wealthy and noble elder in this city who had a child late in life. Whenever a messenger brought him news, he would bestow two hundred koṭis of gold coins, and thus he named his son "He who heard of the two hundred koṭis" (Śrotaviṃśatikoṭi). By the time he reached adulthood, he had never walked upon the ground, and therefore the hair on the soles of his feet was over a foot long, lustrous, fine, and soft, and the color of yellow gold. Cherishing this son, the elder provided him with every kind of luxury; from his residence all the way to the Snow Mountains, post-stations were linked together and servants lined the roads, so that whenever a rare medicine was required, the word was passed along and the item delivered in succession, arriving in no time at all—such was the extent of his great wealth. The World-Honored One, knowing that his roots of goodness were about to sprout, commanded Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅子) to go and convert him. Upon arriving at the gate, he had no way to announce himself. The elder’s family worshipped the Sun Deity, and every morning they would face east to bow. At that time, the Venerable One, using his supernatural powers, descended from the solar disc and stood before them. The elder’s son, suspecting he was the Sun Deity, offered him fragrant rice; the Venerable One then returned, and the aroma of the rice filled the entire city of Rājagṛha (王舍城). At that time, King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王) was astonished by the extraordinary fragrance and ordered a messenger to investigate; it was discovered that Maudgalyāyana of the Bamboo Grove Monastery (竹林精舍) had brought the rice from the elder’s house, and thus, knowing the elder’s son possessed such a wonder, the king summoned him. The elder accepted the command, but pondered how to travel safely. To travel by boat and row with oars carried the danger of wind and waves; to ride in a carriage or on an elephant brought the fear of stumbling or falling. Thereupon, from his residence to the city of Rājagṛha, he excavated a canal for transport and filled it with mustard seeds, so that the boat could rest securely and be towed along by a long rope. Upon arriving at the city of Rājagṛha, he first paid homage to the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One said to him, "King Bimbisāra has sent a messenger to summon you for no other reason than to see the hair on the soles of your feet. If the King wishes to view them, you should sit in the cross-legged position. To extend your feet toward the King is, by the laws of the country, a capital offense." The son of the elder received this instruction and went forth, and was led into the court to have an audience. When the king wished to view the hair, he sat in the cross-legged position; the king appreciated his politeness and came to cherish him deeply. Having been permitted to return, he went back to the place of the Buddha. At that time, the Tathāgata (如來) preached the Dharma and provided instruction; upon hearing this, he was moved to realization and immediately renounced the household life. Thereupon, he practiced with diligent effort, seeking to realize the fruits of enlightenment; he engaged in walking meditation without rest until his feet began to bleed. The World-Honored One said to him, "Good man, when you were at home as a layman, did you know how to play the lute?" He replied, "I did." "If that is so, take this as an analogy. If the strings are too tight, the sound will not be in harmony; if the strings are too loose, the melody will not be refined. Neither too tight nor too loose, the sound is then harmonious. The practitioner of the path is also like this. If one is too urgent, the body becomes exhausted and the mind weary; if one is too lax, the passions expand and the will becomes dissipated." Having received the Buddha's instruction, he followed it faithfully, and before long, he attained the realization of the fruit.

Traveling northwest from the country for more than three hundred li, one crosses a stony desert and reaches the Ice Mountains (凌山, *Língshān*). This is the northern plateau of the Pamir Range (葱嶺, *Cōnglǐng*), where the waters mostly flow eastward. Snow accumulates in the mountain valleys, remaining frozen throughout the spring and summer; although it occasionally thaws, it soon freezes over again. The path is dangerous and obstructed, and the cold winds are bitter and fierce. There are many disasters caused by violent dragons that harass travelers. Those who travel this road must not wear reddish-brown clothing, carry calabashes, or shout loudly. If there is the slightest violation, disaster is witnessed immediately. Violent winds erupt, blowing sand and raining stones; those who encounter them perish, and it is difficult to survive.

Beside the great city, overlooking the Ganges (殑伽河) River, is Mount Īraṇa (伊爛拏山), which breathes forth mists and clouds that obscure the sun and moon. From ancient times to the present, immortals and sages have followed one another to dwell here in meditation, and there is now a deva temple that still observes the traditional rites. In the past, the Tathāgata also resided here, extensively expounding the wonderful Dharma for the sake of devas and humans.

At the western border of the country, south of the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) river, one reaches the Small Isolated Mountain (小孤山; Skt. asura), where the peaks are layered and precipitous. In the past, the Buddha spent three months of the rainy season retreat here, subduing the yakṣa Bakula (薄句羅). On a large rock below the southeastern cliff of the mountain, there is a trace of where the Buddha sat, which is more than an inch deep into the stone, five feet two inches long, and two feet one inch wide; a stūpa has been built upon it. To the south, on another stone, there is a trace of where the Buddha placed his kuṇḍikā (捃稚迦), which is more than an inch deep and shaped like an eight-petaled flower. Not far to the southeast of the Buddha’s sitting trace is the footprint of the yakṣa Bakula, which is one foot five or six inches long, seven or eight inches wide, and slightly less than two inches deep. Behind the yakṣa’s footprint is a stone statue of the seated Buddha, six or seven feet high. Not far to the west is a place where the Buddha walked in meditation. On the summit of the mountain is the former dwelling of the yakṣa. To the north is a footprint of the Buddha, one foot eight inches long, over six inches wide, and about half an inch deep, with a stūpa built over the trace. In the past, the Tathāgata subdued the yakṣa, causing him to cease killing people and eating meat; he respectfully received the Buddha’s precepts and was later reborn in the heavens. To the west of this are six or seven hot springs, the water of which is extremely hot. In the great mountain forests at the southern border of the country, there are many wild elephants, which are immense in size.

Traveling over four hundred li through the mountains, I reached the Great Pure Lake (Daqing chi). It is over one thousand li in circumference, long from east to west and narrow from north to south. Surrounded by mountains on all sides, it is the confluence of many streams; its color is a dark greenish-black, its taste is both salty and bitter, and its vast waves surge and billow with a tumultuous roar. Dragons and fish dwell together therein, and supernatural monsters occasionally appear; therefore, passing travelers pray to them for blessings, and though aquatic life is abundant, no one dares to fish for them.

Traveling northwest from the Clear Lake (Qingchi) for over five hundred li, one arrives at the city of the Suyab River (素葉水城). The city is six or seven li in circumference, where merchants from various Hu countries live together. The soil is suitable for millet, wheat, and grapes, though trees are sparse. The climate is windy and cold, and the people wear garments of felt and coarse wool. To the west of Suyab, there are several dozen isolated cities, each with its own established leader; although they do not take orders from one another, they are all subject to the Turks (突厥).

From here, following the southern bank of the Ganges (gaṅgā) river and traveling east for more than three hundred li, one arrives at the country of Campā (瞻波國). The country of Campā is more than four thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country has the Ganges river at its back to the north and is more than forty li in circuit. The land is low and damp, and the crops are lush and abundant. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are simple and honest. There are several dozen saṃghārāmas, most of which are in ruins, with over two hundred monks who study the teachings of the Hīnayāna. There are more than twenty deva temples, where followers of various heterodox paths live together. The capital city is built of brick; its height is several zhang, its foundations are lofty and steep, and its parapets are high and dangerous. In the past, at the beginning of the kalpa, when human beings first appeared, they lived in the wild and dwelt in caves, not yet knowing of palaces or houses. Later, a celestial maiden descended among humans and, while wandering by the Ganges and bathing in its currents to please herself, she was spiritually moved and became pregnant, eventually giving birth to four sons. They divided Jambudvīpa among themselves, each ruling over a region, building capitals and constructing towns, and marking out borders and boundaries; this was the capital of one of those sons, and the beginning of all the cities in Jambudvīpa.

One hundred forty or fifty li to the east of the city, south of the Ganges (gaṅgā), water surrounds a solitary islet with lofty and precipitous cliffs; atop it stands a deva temple where the deity manifests many miracles. Chambers have been carved into the cliffs and water channeled to form ponds; with its flowery groves, exotic trees, massive rocks, and perilous peaks, it is an abode for the benevolent and wise, so beautiful that visitors forget to return. In the mountains and forests of the country's southern border, wild elephants and fierce beasts roam in herds numbering in the thousands.

From the city of the Suyab River (素葉水城) to the kingdom of Kesh (羯霜那國), the region is named Sogdiana (窣利), and the people are also called by this name. Their script and language are named accordingly. The origins of their script are simple, consisting of only twenty-odd letters which generate further words through combination; their use has gradually expanded until they possess rudimentary written records. They read their texts vertically and pass them down from teacher to pupil without interruption. They wear garments of felt and coarse wool, and dress in furs and fine cotton, with narrow and tight-fitting clothing. They trim their hair to expose the crown or shave it off entirely, and bind their foreheads with colored silk. They are tall and imposing in stature but timid in disposition. Their customs are frivolous and deceitful; they often act with guile and are generally avaricious. Fathers and sons calculate profit against each other, regarding wealth as the measure of nobility and making no distinction between the virtuous and the base. Although some possess vast wealth, their clothing and food are coarse and simple. Those who labor in the fields and those who pursue profit are mixed in roughly equal halves.

Traveling east from here for more than four hundred li, one reaches the country of Kajaṅgala (羯朱嗢祇羅國). The country of Kajaṅgala is more than two thousand li in circuit. The land is damp and marshy, the crops are abundant, the climate is temperate, and the customs are harmonious. The people value high talent and esteem learning and the arts. There are six or seven saṃghārāmas with more than three hundred monks. There are ten deva temples, where followers of various heterodox paths live together. For several hundred years, the royal line has been extinct and the country has been a dependency of neighboring states; for this reason, the cities and towns are in ruins, and the people live mostly in villages. Therefore, when King Śīlāditya (戒日王) traveled to East India, he built a palace here to manage the affairs of the various states; when he arrived, he thatched a building with grass, and when he departed, he set it on fire. In the southern border region of the country, there are many wild elephants.

Traveling more than four hundred *li* westward from the city of Suyab (素葉城), one arrives at the Thousand Springs (千泉). The Thousand Springs is an area over two hundred *li* square, with the Snow Mountains (雪山) to the south and level land on the other three sides. The soil and water are fertile and moist, and the trees are sparse and spreading; in the month of late spring, the various flowers are like brocade. There are a thousand springs and ponds, which is how it earned its name. The Khan of the Turks (突厥可汗) comes here every year to escape the summer heat. Within the area are herds of deer, many of which are adorned with bells and rings; they are tame and familiar with people, and do not easily take fright or run away. The Khan cherishes and admires them, and has issued an order to his subordinates that anyone who dares to kill or harm them shall be executed without pardon. Therefore, these herds of deer are able to live out their natural lives.

In the northern border, not far from the Ganges (殑伽河; gaṅgā) River, there is a large high terrace built of piled bricks and stones. Its foundation is broad and lofty, featuring exquisite carvings, and all around its sides are engraved images of various holy beings, with the forms of the Buddha and the devas distinctly rendered.

Traveling one hundred and forty or fifty li westward from the Thousand Springs (千泉), one arrives at the city of Talas (呾邏私城). The city is eight or nine li in circumference, and Hu merchants from various countries live there together. The suitability of the soil and the sequence of the seasons are much the same as in Suyab (素葉).

Traveling southward for more than ten *li*, there is a small isolated town (小孤城) of over three hundred households. The inhabitants were originally people of the Middle Kingdom (中國人) who were captured by the Turks (突厥) in the past; later, they gathered their compatriots together to jointly defend this town and settled within it. In their clothing and deportment, they have come to resemble the Turks, yet in their speech and manners, they still retain those of their original country.

From here, crossing the Ganges (殑伽河) to the east and traveling more than six hundred li, one arrives at the country of Puṇḍravardhana (奔那伐彈那國). The country of Puṇḍravardhana is more than four thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than thirty li in circuit. The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous, with ponds, pavilions, and flower gardens interspersed throughout. The land is low and damp, and the crops are lush and abundant. The panasa (般核娑) fruit is both plentiful and highly valued; the fruit is as large as a winter melon, and when ripe, it turns yellowish-red. When sliced open, it contains dozens of smaller fruits as large as crane eggs, and when these are further broken, they yield a yellowish-red juice with a sweet and delicious taste. Some grow on the branches like the fruits of other trees, while others grow from the roots, like poria cocos (伏苓) in the soil. The climate is temperate, and the customs favor learning. There are more than twenty saṃghārāmas (伽藍) with over three thousand monks, who study both the Small and Great Vehicles. There are one hundred deva temples, where followers of various heterodox sects dwell together, and the Nirgrantha (尼乾) ascetics who go naked are particularly numerous among their factions.

From here, traveling southwest for more than two hundred li, one arrives at the city of Baishui (White Water). The city is six or seven li in circumference. The produce of the land and the suitability of the climate are even superior to those of Talas (呾邏私).

More than twenty li to the west of the city is the Vāśibhā Monastery (跋始婆僧伽藍). Its courtyards and buildings are spacious and open, and its terraces and pavilions are lofty. There are more than seven hundred monks, all of whom study the Mahayana teachings; most of the eminent scholars and renowned monks of East India reside here. Not far to its side is a stupa (窣堵波) built by King Aśoka. This is the place where, in the past, the Tathāgata spent three months preaching the Dharma for the devas and humans; on fast days, it sometimes emits a brilliant light. To its side are the sites of the sitting and walking meditation paths of the four Buddhas. Not far from here is another shrine (精舍; Skt. mūla-gandha-kuṭī), in which is an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara. Its spiritual insight is all-revealing and its divine responses are manifest, so that people from far and near fast and pray before it.

Traveling southwest for more than two hundred li, one arrives at the city of Gongyu (恭御城). The city is five or six li in circumference. The plains and marshes are rich and fertile, and the forests are lush and luxuriant.

From here, traveling south for forty or fifty li, one arrives at the country of Nujkend (笯赤建國). The country of Nujkend is over one thousand li in circuit. The land is fertile and suitable for sowing and reaping; the vegetation is lush, flowers and fruits are abundant, and grapes are grown in great quantities and are also highly valued. There are hundreds of cities and towns, each with its own separate ruler; in their movements and dealings, they do not take orders from one another. Although the territory is divided into distinct regions, they are collectively known as the country of Nujkend.

From here, traveling west for over two hundred li, one arrives at the country of Chāch (赭時國). The country of Chāch is over one thousand li in circumference. To the west, it borders the Yaxartes River (葉河). It is narrow from east to west and long from north to south. The soil, products, and climate are the same as those of the country of Nūjakath (笯赤建國). There are several dozen cities, each with its own ruler; as there is no overall sovereign, they are subject to the Turks.
To the east, it borders the Yaxartes River (葉河). The Yaxartes River originates from the northern source of the Onion Mountains (葱嶺), flows to the northwest, and is vast, turbid, turbulent, and swift.

From here, traveling east for over nine hundred *li* and crossing a great river, one reaches the country of Kāmarūpa (迦摩縷波國). The country of Kāmarūpa is over ten thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city is over thirty *li* in circuit. The land is low and moist, and crops are sown at the proper seasons. Although there are many *panasa* (jackfruit) and *nārikela* (coconut) trees, they are highly valued. Rivers, lakes, and ponds encircle the cities. The climate is mild and pleasant, and the customs are honest and simple. The people are short in stature and dark in complexion. Their language differs slightly from that of Mid-India. Their nature is very fierce and impetuous, yet they are intent on diligent study. They revere and serve the heavenly deities and do not believe in the Buddha-dharma. Therefore, from the rise of the Buddha until the present day, no monasteries have been established to gather monks. Those who possess pure faith merely cherish their devotion in private. There are several hundred *deva* temples and tens of thousands of non-Buddhists. The current king is a descendant of the god Nārāyaṇa and belongs to the Brāhmaṇa caste; his name is Bhāskaravarman (婆塞羯羅伐摩) and his title is Kumāra (拘摩羅). He has held this territory, with his family reigning in succession for a thousand generations down to the present king. The ruler is fond of learning, and the populace follows his lead; men of high talent from distant lands, admiring his righteousness, come to visit as guests. Although he does not sincerely believe in the Buddha-dharma, he respects learned *śramaṇa*s. Previously, having heard that a *śramaṇa* from the country of Mahācīna was at the Nālandā (那爛陀) Monastery in Magadha, having come from afar to study the profound Dharma of the Buddha, the king sent cordial invitations back and forth three times, but the monk had not yet complied with the request. At that time, the Master of Treatises Śīlabhadra said, "If you wish to repay the Buddha’s kindness, you must propagate the True Dharma; you should go, and do not fear the long journey. The family of King Kumāra (拘摩羅王) has followed non-Buddhist paths for generations, but now he invites a *śramaṇa*; this is a virtuous deed. If he changes his course because of this, the benefits will be vast and far-reaching. You previously aroused a great mind and made a grand vow, wishing to travel alone to foreign lands, casting aside your body to seek the Dharma, and universally saving all sentient beings—how could this be limited to your own country? You should forget about gain and loss, disregard honor and disgrace, propagate the holy teachings, enlighten the deluded, put others before yourself, and forget personal fame to spread the Dharma." Thereupon, being unable to decline, he went with the envoy and met with the king.  King Kumāra said, "Although I am without talent, I have always admired those of high learning; having heard of your fame and noble character, I ventured to invite you."  He replied, "I am of little ability and narrow wisdom, yet I have undeservedly received your attention."  King Kumāra said, "Excellent! You admire the Dharma and love learning, regarding your own body as light as a feather, crossing over heavy dangers to travel far to foreign lands. This is surely the result of your king’s transformation and the scholarly customs of your country. Now, in the various countries of India, there are many who sing the 'Music of the King of Qin Breaking the Enemy Lines' (秦王破陣樂) of the country of Mahācīna (摩訶至那國); I have heard it for a long time—is this not the country of the Great Virtuous One?"  He replied, "Indeed, this song praises the virtue of my sovereign."  King Kumāra said, "I did not realize that you, Great Virtuous One, were a man of this country; I have always admired its refined culture and have long looked toward the East, but as the mountains and rivers block the way, I have had no means to go there myself." I replied, "The sacred virtues of our great monarch extend far and wide, and his benevolent influence reaches distant lands; there are many from foreign regions and strange customs who come to the imperial palace to pay homage and declare themselves subjects." King Kumāra said, "Since his grace covers all like heaven and earth, I have long hoped to send tribute. Now King Śīlāditya (戒日王) is in the country of Kajuṅghira (羯朱嗢祇羅國), where he is about to hold a great almsgiving to cultivate merit and wisdom; all the Śramaṇas and Brahmins of the five Indias who possess learning have been summoned to assemble. He has now sent an envoy to invite me, and I wish for you to travel with me." I then went with him.  In the eastern part of this country, mountains and hills are interconnected, and there are no large capital cities; as its borders adjoin the southwestern barbarians (西南夷), its people resemble the Man (蠻) and Lao (獠) tribes. I inquired in detail about the local customs and learned that one could reach the southwestern borders of Shu (蜀) in about two months' travel; however, the mountains and rivers are treacherous and obstructed, the mountain mists are noxious, and poisonous snakes and herbs cause great harm. In the southeast of the country, wild elephants roam in violent herds, which is why the elephant corps of this country is particularly numerous.

From here, traveling south for one thousand two hundred or one thousand three hundred li, one reaches the country of Samataṭa (三摩呾吒國). The country of Samataṭa is more than three thousand li in circuit. It borders the great sea, and the land is low and damp. The capital city is more than twenty li in circuit. Crops are cultivated in abundance, and flowers and fruits are lush. The climate is temperate, and the customs are harmonious. The people are firm and fierce by nature, short in stature, and dark in complexion; they are diligent in learning and believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are more than thirty saṃghārāmas with over two thousand monks, all of whom follow the study of the Sthavira school. There are one hundred deva temples where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together; the Nirgrantha ascetics who go naked are particularly numerous. Not far from the city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. In the past, the Tathāgata preached the profound and wonderful Dharma here for seven days for the sake of devas and humans. Nearby are the sites of the four past Buddhas’ seats and walking paths. Not far from this, in a saṃghārāma, there is a blue jade Buddha image eight feet high, with all the physical marks perfectly complete, which frequently manifests spiritual responses.  From here, to the northeast in a valley by the shore of the great sea, is the country of Śrīkṣetra (室利差呾羅國). Next, to the southeast at a corner of the great sea, is the country of Kāmalaṅkā (迦摩浪迦國). Next, to the east, is the country of Dvāravatī (墮羅鉢底國). Next, to the east, is the country of Īśānapura (伊賞那補羅國). Next, to the east, is the country of Mahācampā (摩訶瞻波國), which is what is called Linyi (林邑) here. Next, to the southwest, is the country of Yamanadvīpa (閻摩那洲國). Regarding these six countries, the mountains and rivers make the roads difficult, and I did not enter their borders; however, their customs and lands can be known by hearsay.
To the northeast of here, in a valley by the shore of the great sea, is the kingdom of Śrīkṣetra (室利差呾羅國).

From here, traveling southeast for more than one thousand li, one reaches the country of Feihan (㤄捍國). The country of Feihan is over four thousand li in circuit and is surrounded by mountains on all four sides. The land is fertile, crops grow in abundance, flowers and fruits are plentiful, and it is suitable for raising sheep and horses. The climate is cold, the people are fierce and brave by nature, their language differs from that of other countries, and their physical appearance is coarse and unattractive. For several decades, there has been no great ruler; the chieftains compete for power and refuse to submit to one another, occupying strategic points along rivers and mountains to demarcate their territories and divide their capitals.

Traveling westward from here for more than a thousand li, one reaches the country of Sutrūṣṇa (窣堵利瑟那國). The country of Sutrūṣṇa is fourteen or fifteen hundred li in circuit. To the east, it borders the Yaxartes River (葉河). The Yaxartes River originates from the northern source of the Onion Mountains (葱嶺), flows toward the northwest, and is vast, turbid, turbulent, and swift. The products of the soil and the customs of the people are the same as those of the country of Chāch (赭時國). It has its own king and is subject to the Turks (突厥).

From here, going northwest, one enters the Great Sandy Desert (大沙磧), where there is absolutely no water or grass. The roads are vast and indistinct, and the boundaries are difficult to discern; one must look toward the great mountains (pravaragiri) and seek out scattered bones to know the direction and mark the path traveled.

Traveling more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Samarkand (颯秣建國). The country of Samarkand is sixteen or seventeen hundred *li* in circuit, long from east to west and narrow from south to north. The capital city of the country is more than twenty *li* in circuit; it is extremely steep and secure, and densely populated. Precious goods from foreign regions are mostly gathered in this country. The soil is rich and fertile, all kinds of crops are planted, the forest trees are luxuriant, flowers and fruits grow in abundance, and it produces many fine horses. Its mechanical skills are especially superior to those of other countries. The climate is mild and pleasant, and the customs are fierce. Among all the Hu (胡) countries, this one is the center; its deportment in movement and stillness is taken as a model by both near and far. Its king is bold and brave, and neighboring countries obey his commands. His troops and horses are strong and numerous, with many *Cakar* (赭羯). The *Cakar* people are courageous and fierce by nature, viewing death as a return home, and no enemy can stand before them in battle.
The capital city of the country (Samarkand 颯秣建國) is more than twenty li in circuit; it is extremely strategic and secure, and is densely populated.

From here, proceeding southeast, one arrives at the country of Mimohe (弭秣賀國; Maymurgh). The country of Mimohe is four or five hundred li in circuit. It is situated in the middle of a river valley; it is narrow from east to west and long from north to south. Its native products and customs are the same as those of the country of Samarkand (颯秣建國; Samarkand).

From here, proceeding north, one arrives at the country of Kapūtāna (劫布呾那國). The country of Kapūtāna is fourteen or fifteen hundred li in circuit; it is long from east to west and narrow from south to north. The soil, products, and customs are the same as those of the country of Samarkand (颯秣建國).

From this country, traveling west for more than three hundred li, one arrives at the country of Kuṣāṇika (屈霜爾迦國). The country of Kuṣāṇika is fourteen or fifteen hundred li in circuit; it is narrow from east to west and long from south to north. Its soil, products, and customs are the same as those of the country of Samarkand (颯秣建國).

From this country, traveling west for more than two hundred li, one reaches the country of Kharghānkath (喝捍國). The country of Kharghānkath is more than one thousand li in circuit. Its soil, products, and customs are the same as those of the country of Samarkand (颯秣建國).

From this country, traveling west for more than four hundred li, one reaches the country of Buhe (Bukhara). The country of Buhe is sixteen or seventeen hundred li in circuit; it is long from east to west and narrow from south to north. Its soil, products, and customs are the same as those of the country of Samarkand (颯秣建國).

From this country, proceeding westward for more than four hundred li, one reaches the country of Fadi (伐地國). The country of Fadi is more than four hundred li in circuit; its native products and customs are the same as those of the country of Samarkand (颯秣建國).

From here, traveling southwest for over five hundred li, one reaches the country of Chorasmia (貨利習彌伽國). The country of Chorasmia lies along both banks of the Oxus River (縛芻河); it is twenty to thirty li from east to west and over five hundred li from south to north. The agricultural products and customs are the same as those of the country of Vadi (伐地國), though the language differs slightly.

Traveling southwest from the country of Samarkand (颯秣建國) for more than three hundred li, one reaches the country of Kesh (羯霜那國). The country of Kesh is fourteen or fifteen hundred li in circuit. Its soil, products, and customs are the same as those of the country of Samarkand. From here, traveling southwest for more than two hundred li, one enters the mountains. The mountain paths are rugged and the ravine trails are dangerous; they are devoid of human habitation and also lack water and grass.

Traveling southeast through the mountains for more than three hundred *li*, one enters the Iron Gate (Tämir qapïɣ). The Iron Gate is flanked by mountains on both sides that are extremely steep and precipitous; although there is a narrow path, it is fraught with obstructions, and the stone walls on both sides are the color of iron. Gate leaves have been installed and reinforced with iron clamps, and many iron bells are suspended from the door panels; because of its strategic peril and strength, it was given this name.

Exiting the Iron Gate (鐵門), one arrives at the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國). Its territory extends over a thousand *li* from north to south and three thousand *li* from east to west. It is bounded by the Pamirs (葱嶺) in the east, adjoins Persia (波剌斯) in the west, reaches the Great Snow Mountains in the south, and occupies the Iron Gate in the north, with the great Oxus River (縛芻大河) flowing westward through the middle of the region. For several hundred years, the royal lineage has been extinct; powerful chieftains have competed with one another, each ruling as a lord and relying on rivers and natural barriers, dividing the land into twenty-seven states. Although the territory is divided into distinct regions, they are all subject to the Turks (突厥). The climate is warm, and epidemics are frequent. From the end of winter to the beginning of spring, there is continuous rain. Therefore, from the south of this territory to the north of Lampā (濫波), the local climates of these countries are prone to many febrile ailments. Consequently, the monks enter their retreat on the sixteenth day of the twelfth month and end it on the fifteenth day of the third month; this is based on the heavy rainfall and is an example of establishing religious rules according to the seasons. As for their customs, the people are timid and fearful; their appearance is coarse, and they have a rough understanding of faith and righteousness, not being overly deceitful. Their language and manners differ slightly from other countries. Their script consists of twenty-five basic letters which are combined to form words for all things; they write horizontally from left to right, and their records have gradually increased until they exceed those of the Sogdians (窣利) in scope. They wear mostly cotton garments and rarely wear wool. Their currency consists of gold and silver coins, the appearance of which differs from those of other countries.

Following the course of the Vakhsh River (縛芻河) downstream to the north, one arrives at the country of Tirmidh (呾蜜國). The country of Tirmidh is over six hundred *li* from east to west and over four hundred *li* from south to north. The capital city of the country is over twenty *li* in circumference; it is long from east to west and narrow from south to north. There are more than ten monasteries and over one thousand monks. Regarding the various *stūpas*—which are what were formerly called *futu* (浮圖), and also called *tūpa* (鍮婆), *tāpa* (塔婆), *sītūpō* (私鍮簸), or *sǒudǒupō* (藪斗波), all of which are corruptions—as well as the venerable images of the Buddha, they possess many miraculous manifestations and are spiritually responsive.

To the east, one arrives at the country of Cagayāna (赤鄂衍那國). The country of Cagayāna is more than four hundred li from east to west and over five hundred li from south to north. The capital city of the country is more than ten li in circumference. There are five sanghārāmas (伽藍), and the number of monks is very small.

To the east, one reaches the country of Kharūn (忽露摩國). The country of Kharūn is over one hundred *li* from east to west and over three hundred *li* from north to south. The capital city of the country is over ten *li* in circumference. Its king is a Xisu Turk. There are two monasteries and over one hundred monks.

To the east, one reaches the country of Shūmān (愉漫國). The country of Shūmān is more than four hundred li from east to west and over one hundred li from south to north. The capital city of the country is sixteen or seventeen li in circuit. Its king is a Xisu Turk. There are two sanghārāmas (伽藍), and the number of monks is small.

To the southwest, bordering the Vakhsh River (縛芻河), one reaches the country of Kuwayāna (鞠和衍那國). The country of Kuwayāna is more than two hundred *li* from east to west and over three hundred *li* from south to north. The capital city of the country is more than ten *li* in circumference. There are three monasteries and more than one hundred monks.

To the east, one reaches the country of Wakhsh (鑊沙國). The country of Wakhsh is more than three hundred li from east to west and over five hundred li from north to south. The capital city of the country is sixteen or seventeen li in circuit.

To the east, one arrives at the country of Khuttal (珂咄羅國). The country of Khuttal is over one thousand li from east to west and over one thousand li from north to south. The capital city of the country is over twenty li in circumference.

To the east, it borders the Onion Range (葱嶺), reaching the country of Kumēdha (拘謎陀國). The country of Kumēdha is more than two thousand *li* from east to west and two hundred *li* from north to south. It is situated in the midst of the Great Onion Range. The capital city of the country is more than twenty *li* in circumference. To the southwest, it is adjacent to the Vakṣu River (縛芻河), and to the south, it borders the country of Śikini (尸棄尼國). Crossing the Vakṣu River to the south, one reaches the country of Dharmasthiti (達摩悉鐵帝國), the country of Badakšān (鉢鐸創那國), the country of Yambagan (淫薄健國), the country of Kuranna (屈浪拏國), the country of Himatala (呬摩呾羅國), the country of Parighar (鉢利曷國), the country of Kṛṣma (訖栗瑟摩國), the country of Rāgh (曷邏胡國), the country of Alini (阿利尼國), and the country of Mungan (瞢健國). From the country of Hu (活國) southeast to the country of Khasta (闊悉多國) and the country of Antarava (安呾羅縛國), the details are in the return record.

From the country of Hu (*γwar*) to the southeast lie the countries of Khasta (闊悉多國) and Antarava (安呾羅縛國); the accounts of these are recorded in the narrative of the return journey. To the southwest of the country of Hu is the country of Baghlān (縛伽浪國).

To the southwest of the country of Hu (活國) is the country of Baghlān (縛伽浪國). The country of Baghlān is over fifty li from east to west and over two hundred li from south to north. The capital city of the country is over ten li in circumference.
To the south, one reaches the country of Rūb-Simingān (紇露悉泯健國). The country of Rūb-Simingān is over one thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is fourteen or fifteen li in circuit.

To the northwest, one arrives at the country of Khulm (忽懍國). The country of Khulm is over eight hundred li in circuit. The capital city of the country is five or six li in circuit. There are more than ten sanghārāmas (伽藍), and the community of monks numbers more than five hundred.

To the west, one arrives at the country of Bākhl (縛喝國). The country of Bākhl is more than eight hundred *li* from east to west and more than four hundred *li* from north to south. To the north, it borders the Vaxšu River (縛芻河). The capital city of the country is more than twenty *li* in circuit, and people all call it the "Little Rājagṛha." Although the city is fortified, it has very few inhabitants. The produce of the land is extremely abundant, and the various flowers of land and water are difficult to enumerate fully. There are more than one hundred monasteries and over three thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Hīnayāna.

To the southwest of the city is the Nava-saṃghārāma (納縛僧伽藍), which was built by a former king of this country. Among the masters who compose treatises north of the Great Snow Mountains (the Hindukush), only this monastery maintains its excellent traditions without decline. Its Buddha images are polished with famous jewels, and its halls are adorned with rare treasures. For this reason, the rulers of various countries have coveted them and sought to plunder them. This monastery has long possessed a statue of Vaiśravaṇa (毘沙門天), whose spiritual insight is reliable and who provides hidden protection. Recently, the son of the Western Turkic Yabghu Qaghan, Si Yabghu Qaghan (肆葉護可汗), mobilized his tribes and led his troops to launch a surprise attack on the monastery, intending to seize its treasures. He camped his army in the fields not far from here. That night, he dreamed that Vaiśravaṇa said to him, "What power do you possess that you dare to destroy this monastery?" He then pierced the Qaghan’s chest and back with a long halberd. The Qaghan awoke in a fright and immediately suffered severe heart pain. He told his subordinates of the ominous sign he had dreamed and sent messengers in haste to invite the monks, intending to offer a confession and apology; however, before he could receive a reply, he had already died.  In the southern Buddha hall within the monastery, there is a Buddha’s bathing pot with a capacity of over one *dou*; it is of variegated colors and dazzling, made of a substance difficult to classify as metal or stone. There is also a Buddha’s tooth, over one inch long and eight or nine *fen* wide; it is yellowish-white in color, and its texture is bright and pure. There is also a Buddha’s broom made of *kāśa* grass, over two feet long and about seven inches in circumference, with a handle adorned with various precious gems. Whenever the six days of fasting arrive, these three objects are displayed for offerings as the monastic and lay communities gather; moved by their utmost sincerity, the objects sometimes emit light. To the north of the monastery is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, plastered with diamond-like mortar and adorned with various precious gems. Inside are relics that occasionally emit a miraculous light. To the southwest of the monastery is a vihāra (精廬) that has stood for many years since its establishment. People from afar gather here, and men of high talent congregate; those who have attained the four fruits (catur-phala) are too numerous to detail. Therefore, when the various arhats were about to enter nirvāṇa, they manifested supernatural powers and became known to the public, which led to the construction of their stūpas; the foundations of these stūpas stand side by side, numbering more than several hundred. Although there are also thousands who attained the holy fruit but did not manifest supernatural powers, no monuments were erected for them. At present, there are over one hundred monks who are diligent day and night, and it is difficult to distinguish the ordinary from the holy among them.

More than fifty *li* to the northwest of the great city, one arrives at the city of Trapuṣa (提謂城); forty *li* to the north of that city is the city of Bhallika (波利城). In each of these cities, there is a *stūpa* over three *zhang* in height. In the past, when the Tathāgata had first realized the fruit of Buddhahood, he arose from the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) and was on his way to the Deer Park. At that time, two merchants encountered his majestic radiance and, following the provisions they had for their journey, offered him parched grain and honey. The World-Honored One spoke to them of the blessings of humans and gods, and they were the first to hear of the five precepts and the ten virtues. Having heard his Dharma instruction, they requested something to venerate, and the Tathāgata then bestowed upon them his hair and nails. As the two merchants were about to return to their own country, they asked for the ritual of veneration. The Tathāgata took his *saṃghāṭī* (僧伽胝) and folded it square to place on the ground; next he placed his *uttarāsaṅga* (欝多羅僧), then his *saṃkakṣikā* (僧却崎), then inverted his alms bowl, and stood his *khakkhara* (錫杖) upright. In this sequence, he formed a *stūpa*. The two men accepted his command and each returned to his own city, where they modeled their constructions after the holy design and built them accordingly; these were the very first *stūpas* in the Dharma of Śākyamuni. Seventy *li* to the west of the city is a *stūpa* over two *zhang* in height, which was built in the past during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha. From the great city, one goes southwest into the valleys of the Snow Mountains (雪山阿) to reach the country of Udyāna (銳秣陀國).
The country of Jumadha (銳秣陀國) is fifty or sixty li from east to west and over one hundred li from south to north. The capital city of the country is over ten li in circuit.

Proceeding southwest, one reaches the country of Gūzgān (胡寔健國). The country of Gūzgān is more than five hundred *li* from east to west and over one thousand *li* from north to south. The capital city of the country is more than twenty *li* in circumference. There are many mountains and rivers, and it produces excellent horses.

Proceeding northwest, one reaches the country of Ṭālaqān (呾剌健國). The country of Ṭālaqān is over five hundred li from east to west and fifty or sixty li from south to north. The capital city of the country is over ten li in circumference. To the west, it borders on the frontiers of the country of Pārs (波剌斯國).

Traveling south from the country of Bactria (縛喝國) for over one hundred li, one arrives at the country of Gachi (揭職國). The country of Gachi is over five hundred li from east to west and three hundred li from north to south. The capital city is four or five li in circuit; the land is stony and barren, with a succession of hills and mounds. There are few flowers or fruits, but much pulse and wheat. The climate is cold and severe, and the customs of the people are fierce and violent. There are more than ten monasteries and over three hundred monks, all of whom study the Hīnayāna teachings of the Sarvāstivāda school. To the southeast, one enters the Great Snow Mountains (Mahāhimavat), where the valleys are deep and the mountains high, and the peaks and cliffs are treacherous. Wind and snow follow one another, and even in midsummer, it remains frozen; accumulated snow fills the valleys, and the paths are difficult to traverse. Mountain spirits and demons act with violent malice, and bands of robbers roam freely, making murder their occupation.

After traveling more than six hundred li, I left the borders of the country of Tukhāra (都貨邏國) and arrived at the country of Bāmīyāna (梵衍那國). The country of Bāmīyāna is more than two thousand li from east to west and over three hundred li from north to south; it is situated in the midst of the Snow Mountains. The people rely on the mountain valleys and build their settlements according to the terrain. The capital city of the kingdom rests against a cliff and spans a valley, measuring six or seven li in length, with high rocks at its back to the north. There is winter wheat, but few flowers or fruits; it is suitable for animal husbandry, and there are many sheep and horses. The climate is cold and harsh, and the customs are rugged and fierce; the people mostly wear garments of leather and wool, which is appropriate for their environment. Their writing, customs, and use of currency are the same as those of the country of Tukhāra. Their language is slightly different, but their appearance and manners are largely the same. Their sincere faith is especially greater than that of neighboring countries. From the Three Jewels above down to the hundred spirits below, there is none to whom they do not offer their sincerity, exhausting their hearts in reverence. For merchants traveling to and fro, the heavenly spirits manifest auspicious signs or show ominous changes to seek blessings and merit. There are several dozen monasteries and several thousand monks, who follow the Lokottaravāda school (說出世部) of the Lesser Vehicle.

In a mountain nook to the northeast of the royal city, there is a standing stone statue of the Buddha, one hundred and forty or fifty feet high; its golden color is dazzling, and its precious ornaments are brilliant. To the east is a monastery, which was built by a former king of this country.
To the east of the monastery is a standing statue of the Buddha Śākyamuni (釋迦佛) made of brass, over one hundred feet high; its parts were cast separately and then joined together to form the whole.

In a monastery two or three li east of the city, there is a reclining statue of the Buddha entering nirvana, over a thousand feet long. Whenever the king holds a Great Quinquennial Assembly (pañcavārṣika) here, he gives away everything from his wife and children down to the national treasures; once the state treasury is exhausted, he offers himself as a gift, and his officials and subordinates then pay ransom to the monks to redeem him, considering such practices to be their primary duty.

Traveling over two hundred li southeast from the Monastery of the Reclining Image (臥像伽藍), one crosses the Great Snow Mountain and arrives east at a small valley where the springs and ponds are clear as mirrors and the forests and trees are lush and green. There is a monastery containing a tooth of the Buddha and a tooth of a Pratyekabuddha (獨覺) from the beginning of the kalpa, which is over five inches long and slightly less than four inches wide. There is also the tooth of a Cakravartin (金輪王), three inches long and two inches wide, and the iron alms bowl held by the great Arhat Śāṇakavāsa (商諾迦縛娑), with a capacity of about eight or nine sheng. All these relics of the three sages are sealed with gold.  There is also the nine-striped saṃghāṭī robe of Śāṇakavāsa, which is dark red in color and woven from the fibers of the śāṇaka plant. Śāṇakavāsa was a disciple of Ānanda. In a previous life, on the day of the conclusion of the summer retreat, he offered śāṇaka grass robes to the monastic community. By the power of this merit, he wore this robe constantly throughout the intermediate states (antarābhava) and birth states (upapattibhava) of five hundred lifetimes. In his final body, the robe emerged from the womb along with him; as his body gradually grew, the robe expanded accordingly. When Ānanda ordained him, the robe transformed into a dharma robe, and when he received the full precepts, it further transformed into a nine-striped saṃghāṭī. As he was about to realize extinction, he entered the limit-attaining meditation (koṭi-samādhi) and, by the power of his wisdom and vow, left this kaṣāya robe to remain until the end of the Buddha Śākyamuni’s teachings. Only after the teachings have perished will it finally decay. It is now slightly damaged, which is a sign of its authenticity.
From here, traveling east, one enters the Snow Mountains (Himavat), crosses over the Black Range (Kṛṣṇagiri), and reaches the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國).

From here, traveling east, one enters the Snow Mountains (Himālaya), crosses the Black Range (Paropamisos), and arrives at the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國). The country of Kāpiśī is over four thousand li in circuit; it has the Snow Mountains at its back to the north and is bordered on three sides by the Black Range. The capital city of the country is over ten li in circuit. The land is suitable for grain and wheat, and produces many fruits and trees; it yields fine horses and saffron. Rare goods from various regions are mostly gathered in this country. The climate is cold and windy; the people’s nature is violent and rough, their speech is vulgar, and their marriage customs are chaotic. Their writing is largely the same as that of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國), though their customs, language, and manners of instruction are quite different. They wear garments of wool and clothing made of leather and felt. For currency, they use gold coins, silver coins, and small copper coins, the standards and designs of which differ from those of other countries. The king is of the Kṣatriya caste; he is wise and resourceful, brave and fierce by nature, and his might intimidates the neighboring regions, ruling over ten or more countries. He loves and nurtures his subjects and reveres the Triple Gem. Every year, he commissions a silver Buddha image eighteen feet high and holds a Great Quinquennial Assembly (Pañcavārṣika) to provide for the poor and destitute and bestow alms upon widowers and widows. There are over one hundred saṃghārāmas, with more than six thousand monks, who mostly study the teachings of the Mahāyāna. The stūpas and saṃghārāmas are lofty, spacious, vast, and pure. There are several dozen deva temples and over one thousand followers of heterodox paths; some go naked, some smear themselves with ash, and some wear garlands of skulls as crowns.

Three or four li to the east of the great city, at the foot of the northern mountain, there is a large monastery with over three hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). According to the records of former times, King Kaniṣka of the country of Gandhāra (健馱邏國) once extended his prestige to neighboring countries and his influence to distant regions. He mobilized his army to expand his territory as far as the east of the Pamirs (葱嶺), and the vassal states west of the river, fearing his might, sent hostages to him. Having received the hostage princes, King Kaniṣka treated them with special courtesy and provided them with different residences according to the seasons: in winter they stayed in the various states of India, in summer they returned to the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國), and in spring and autumn they resided in the country of Gandhāra. Because the hostage princes had residences for these three seasons, a monastery was built for each; this monastery is the one built for their summer residence. Therefore, on the walls of the various buildings, the hostage princes are depicted, their appearance and attire quite similar to those of the Middle Kingdom (China). After they were able to return to their own countries, they kept their former residences in their hearts, and although separated by mountains and rivers, they did not cease their offerings. Thus, the present community of monks, whenever the time comes for the entry into or the conclusion of the summer retreat, holds grand Dharma assemblies to pray for blessings and cultivate merit for the sake of the hostage princes, a practice that has continued without interruption to the present day. Beneath the right foot of the statue of the Great Spirit King, located to the south of the east gate of the monastery’s Buddha hall, there is treasure buried in the ground, hidden there by the hostage princes. The inscription regarding this says: "When the monastery falls into disrepair, take this to restore it." Recently, a frontier king, greedy and fierce, heard that this monastery contained much hidden treasure and drove out the monks. Just as he was about to begin the excavation, the figure of a parrot on the crown of the Divine King vigorously flapped its wings and cried out in alarm, causing the earth to shake; the king and his soldiers fell back in terror and collapsed, and only after a long time could they rise, whereupon they apologized for their offense and returned home. On the northern ridge of the monastery there are several stone chambers, which are the places where the hostage princes practiced meditation. Within them are hidden many miscellaneous treasures, and beside them is an inscription, guarded by a yakṣa. Whenever anyone wished to open them and take the treasures within, this yakṣa would manifest various forms through supernatural power—appearing as a lion, a python, a fierce beast, or a poisonous insect—showing great wrath in these strange forms, so that no one dared to attempt an excavation. On a great mountain ridge (Skt. pravaragiri) two or three li to the west of the stone chambers, there is a statue of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara; if someone prays with utmost sincerity to see him, the Bodhisattva emerges from the statue in a wondrous physical form to comfort the practitioner.

Thirty-some *li* southeast of the great city, one arrives at the Rāhula (曷邏怙羅) monastery. Beside it is a *stūpa* over one hundred feet high. On days of fasting, it sometimes emits a bright light. From the crevices in the stone of the inverted-bowl structure, black fragrant oil flows out, and in the quiet of the night, sounds of music are sometimes heard. According to ancient records, it was built in the past by Rāhula, a high minister of this country. After the work was completed, someone spoke to him in a dream, saying, "The *stūpa* you have built does not yet contain any relics. Tomorrow morning, someone will offer one; you should request it from the king." At dawn, he entered the court and made his request, saying, "Unaware of my own mediocrity, I dare to make a petition." The king asked, "What is it that you desire?" He replied, "There is someone who will offer something today; I hope for your grace to bestow it upon me." The king said, "Very well." Rāhula stood waiting at the palace gate, watching for the arrival. Soon, a man appeared carrying a relic casket. The minister asked, "What do you intend to offer?" The man replied, "Buddha relics." The minister said, "I will guard them for you; you should first report this to the king." Fearing that the king would prize the relics and regret his previous favor, Rāhula hurried to the monastery and climbed the *stūpa*. Moved by his utmost sincerity, the stone inverted bowl opened of its own accord. He placed the relics inside and rushed out so quickly that his clothes were caught. The king sent men to pursue him, but the stone had already closed. Therefore, black fragrant oil flows from its crevices.

Forty-odd li to the south of the city, one arrives at the city of Śvetavāras (霫蔽多伐剌祠城). Whenever there is a great earthquake and mountain cliffs collapse, nothing within the boundaries of this city is shaken.

More than thirty *li* to the south of the city of the Śvetavāras (霫蔽多伐剌祠城), one arrives at Mount Aruṇa (阿路猱山). Its cliffs and ridges are steep and precipitous, and its rocky valleys are dark and deep. Every year, its peak increases in height by several hundred feet, and as soon as it appears to gaze across toward Mount Śunāhila (䅳那呬羅山) in the country of Jāguḍa (漕矩吒國), it immediately collapses. I have heard from the local people: In the beginning, the deity Śunā (䅳那) came from afar, wishing to dwell on this mountain. The mountain deity was enraged and shook the ravines and valleys. The deity said, "It is because you do not wish to host me that you shake and tilt in this way. If you would show a little hospitality as a host to a guest, you would be filled with wealth and treasures. I am now going to Mount Śunāhila in the country of Jāguḍa; every year, when the time comes for me to receive the sacrifices and offerings of the king and his ministers, you should gaze toward me." Therefore, as soon as Mount Aruṇa has increased in height, it immediately collapses.

Two hundred and more *li* northwest of the royal city, one arrives at the Great Snowy Mountain (Mahāhimavat). On the summit of the mountain is a pool; those who pray for rain or for clear weather have their wishes fulfilled according to their requests. According to ancient records, there was formerly an arhat in the country of Gandhāra (健馱邏國) who regularly received offerings from the nāga king of this pool. Every day at the midday meal, he would use his supernatural powers to sit upon his rope bed and travel through the void. His attendant, a novice (śrāmaṇera), secretly clung to the underside of the rope bed and hid himself. When the time for the meal arrived, the arhat departed; upon reaching the nāga palace, he discovered the novice. The nāga king then invited them both to stay for the meal. The nāga king served the arhat with heavenly nectar, while he served the novice with human food. Once the arhat had finished his meal, he expounded the essential teachings of the Dharma for the nāga king. The novice, as was his custom, washed the bowls for his master. Finding leftover grains in the bowl and being astonished by their fragrance, he immediately gave rise to an evil vow, resenting his master and feeling anger toward the nāga: "May all the power of my merit manifest now, that I may cut off this nāga’s life and become the king myself." At the moment the novice made this vow, the nāga king already felt a headache. The arhat spoke words of instruction and exhortation, and the nāga king apologized for his faults and blamed himself; however, the novice remained resentful and did not follow the instruction to forgive. Once they had returned to the monastery (saṃghārāma), the novice made a vow with utmost sincerity. Due to the power of his merit, he died that very night and was reborn as a great nāga king. Fierce and impetuous, he came to enter the pool, killed the former nāga king, occupied the nāga palace, took possession of his retinue, and assumed control over his life. Because of his former vow, he stirred up violent storms and rain, uprooting trees and intending to destroy the monastery. At that time, King Kaniṣka, feeling puzzled, inquired about the matter, and the arhat explained everything to the king. The king then established a monastery (saṃghārāma) for the nāga at the foot of the Snow Mountains and erected a stupa (stūpa) over one hundred feet high. The nāga, harboring his former resentment, proceeded to stir up wind and rain. The king was intent on universal salvation, while the nāga, fueled by the poison of his anger, committed acts of violence, causing the monastery and the stupa to be destroyed six times and rebuilt seven times. King Kaniṣka, ashamed that his work was not being completed, wished to fill in the nāga’s pool and destroy his dwelling; he immediately mobilized his troops and arrived at the foot of the Snow Mountains. At that time, the nāga king, feeling deep fear, transformed himself into an old brahmin, knocked on the king’s elephant, and remonstrated, saying: "Great King, you have cultivated good roots in the past and planted many superior causes, which has enabled you to become a human king to whom all submit. Why, then, do you contend with a nāga today? A nāga is merely an animal, a base and vile species, yet he possesses great power and cannot be contested by force. Riding the clouds and driving the wind, treading on the void and walking on water—these are things not controlled by human power; how could they be objects of the king’s wrath? If the king now mobilizes the entire nation to fight against a single nāga, then if you win, the king will gain no prestige for subduing a distant foe, and if you lose, the king will suffer the shame of being defeated by an unworthy opponent. For the sake of the king’s own interests, it would be best to withdraw the troops." King Kaniṣka did not follow this advice. The nāga then returned to the pool, and with a sound like rolling thunder, violent winds uprooted trees, sand and stones fell like rain, clouds and fog obscured the light, and the army’s horses were terrified. The king then took refuge in the Triple Gem and prayed for protection, saying, "By virtue of the many blessings I cultivated in past lives, I became a king of men, deterring powerful enemies and ruling over Jambudvīpa; that I am now humiliated by this dragon beast is truly due to my meager merit. May all the power of my merit manifest at this moment." Immediately, great smoke and flames arose from his two shoulders; the dragon retreated, the wind grew still, and the clouds and fog rolled away. The king ordered his army to each carry one stone to fill the dragon pool. The dragon king transformed back into a Brahmin and entreated the king again, saying, "I am the dragon king of that pool; fearing your majesty, I submit to you. May the king have compassion and forgive my past offenses. The king nurtures and protects all living beings; why would you inflict harm upon me alone? If you kill me, both you and I will fall into the evil realms; you will be guilty of taking a life, and I will harbor a heart of resentment and enmity—karmic retribution is clear, and good and evil are manifest." The king then made a clear covenant with the dragon, stating that if there were any further offenses, he would certainly not forgive them. The dragon said, "Because of my evil karma, I have received a body as a dragon. The nature of a dragon is fierce and evil, and I cannot control myself; if a heart of anger arises, I may forget what has been stipulated. Now that the king is establishing a monastery (saṃghārāma), I dare not destroy it. I will send one person to keep watch on the mountain ridge; if black clouds arise, they must strike the ghaṇṭā (gong) urgently. When I hear that sound, my evil heart will cease." The king thereupon renovated the monastery and built a stūpa, and the practice of watching for clouds continues to this day without interruption. According to the records of predecessors, there is more than one *sheng* of the Tathāgata’s bone and flesh relics inside the stūpa, and the miraculous events associated with them are difficult to describe in detail. Once, smoke suddenly rose from within the stūpa, followed shortly by fierce flames. The people of the time thought the stūpa had been reduced to ashes, but after gazing at it for a long while, the fire died down and the smoke vanished. Then, the relics were seen like a banner of white pearls, circling the central pillar and winding upwards to the edge of the clouds before whirling back down.

Inside the Old Royal Monastery (Jiuwang Jialan) on the south bank of the great river to the northwest of the royal city, there is a tooth of the Bodhisattva Śākya from his childhood, over an inch long. To the southeast of this monastery is another monastery, also named Old Royal, which possesses a piece of the Tathāgata’s skull bone over an inch wide; its color is yellowish-white, and the hair pores are distinct. There is also hair of the Tathāgata, the color of which is dark blue, spiraling to the right, drawn out to over a foot in length, and curled to about half an inch. Regarding these three items, whenever the six fast days arrive, the king and his ministers scatter flowers in offering. To the southwest of the Skull Bone Monastery is the Old Queen’s Monastery (Jiuwangfei Jialan), in which there is a gold and copper stūpa over a hundred feet high. According to local tradition, there is more than a *sheng* of the Buddha’s relics inside this stūpa. On the night of the fifteenth day of every month, it emits a circular light that illuminates the dew basin, shining continuously until dawn, at which point the light gradually withdraws into the stūpa.

To the southwest of the city is the mountain of Pīlusāra (比羅娑洛山). The mountain deity takes the form of an elephant, hence it is called "Elephant-Strong" (象堅). Formerly, when the Tathāgata was in the world, the deity Elephant-Strong invited the World-Honored One and twelve hundred great arhats. There was a large flat rock at the mountain peak; the Tathāgata sat upon it and accepted the deity’s offerings. Afterward, King Aśoka (無憂王) built a stūpa upon that flat rock, over one hundred feet high, which people today call the Elephant-Strong Stūpa. It is also said that it contains over a sheng of the Tathāgata’s relics. Below the mountain cliff to the north of the Elephant-Strong Stūpa is a dragon spring (龍泉). This is where the Tathāgata, after receiving the deity’s meal, and the arhats rinsed their mouths and chewed willow twigs, which then took root and became the dense grove that exists today. Later people established a saṃghārāma (伽藍) here, named Viḍhaka (鞞鐸佉). From here, traveling east for over six hundred li, through connected mountain valleys and over steep and precipitous peaks, one crosses the Black Ridge (黑嶺) and enters the borders of North India, arriving at the country of Lampāka (濫波國).

The kingdom of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國) is over four thousand li in circuit; to the north, it has the Snow Mountains at its back, and on three sides, it is bordered by the Black Range (黑嶺). The kingdom’s great capital city is over ten li in circuit.

To the west of the great stūpa is an old monastery (saṃghārāma), which was built by King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王). It has multi-storied pavilions and tiered halls, with layered terraces and open windows; it was built to summon high-ranking monks and to manifest auspicious blessings. Although it is now dilapidated, it is still considered a marvelous work of craftsmanship. The number of monks has decreased, and they all study the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). Since the monastery was built, extraordinary people have appeared there one after another. The masters who composed treatises and those who attained the holy fruits have left behind a pure influence that still circulates, and their supreme virtues have not been extinguished.  On the third story of the pavilion is the room of the Venerable Pārśva (波栗濕縛尊者), which has long since collapsed, though a commemorative marker still stands. Originally, when the Venerable was a teacher of the Brahmins (梵志), he was nearly eighty years old when he left his home and donned the dyed robes. The youths in the city mocked him, saying: "What a foolish, decrepit old man, how shallow his wisdom! Those who leave home have two duties: first, to practice meditation; second, to recite the scriptures. Now, in your senility, you have made no progress; you merely clutter the ranks of the pure and know only how to eat your fill."
