When the Venerable Pārśva heard these reproaches, he took leave of the people of the time and made a vow, saying: "If I do not master the principles of the Tripiṭaka, sever the desires of the three realms, attain the six supernatural powers, and possess the eight liberations, I shall never let my ribs (脇) touch a mat!" From then on, he felt only that the days were insufficient; whether walking, sitting, or standing in contemplation, he studied the doctrines by day and practiced quiet meditation with a concentrated mind by night. After three years had passed, he had mastered the Tripiṭaka, severed the desires of the three realms, and attained the three types of clear wisdom (trividyā). The people of the time respected him and thus called him the Venerable Pārśva (脇尊者). To the east of the room of the Venerable Pārśva (脇尊者) is an old chamber where the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (世親) composed the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* (阿毘達磨俱舍論); people respect it and have sealed it to mark the site. More than fifty paces to the south of Vasubandhu’s room is a second-story pavilion where the master Manoratha (末笯曷剌他) composed the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (毘婆沙論). This master appeared in the world one thousand years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. In his youth, he was fond of learning and possessed talent and eloquence; his reputation reached far and wide, and both the clergy and the laity turned their hearts toward him.  At that time, King Vikramāditya (毘訖羅摩阿迭多) of the country of Śrāvastī (室羅伐悉底國) extended his majestic influence to distant lands and brought all of India under his rule; every day he distributed five hundred million gold coins to provide for the poor, the destitute, the orphaned, and the solitary. The treasurer, fearing that the national resources would be exhausted, offered a remonstrance, saying: "Your Majesty’s awe-inspiring power reaches foreign peoples and your benevolence extends even to insects; I pray you increase the distribution by another five hundred million gold coins to relieve the needy of the four quarters. Once the treasury is empty, we shall have to levy further taxes on the landholders; when heavy taxation continues without end and the cries of resentment spread everywhere, then the sovereign above will enjoy the reputation of being a generous provider, while the ministers below will bear the blame for being disrespectful." The King replied: "I gather the surplus to provide for the insufficient; I do not do this for the sake of personal luxury or the squandering of national resources." He then added another five hundred million to bestow upon the poor and needy.  Later, while hunting, he chased a boar and lost his way. He offered a reward of one hundred million gold coins to anyone who could find and track it. The master Manoratha once had a person shave his head, and the King immediately bestowed one hundred million gold coins upon him, which the state historians recorded accordingly. The King felt ashamed to be outdone and was constantly vexed in his heart, wishing to publicly humiliate the master Manoratha. He then summoned one hundred practitioners of heterodox schools who were of high virtue and profound learning, and issued an order, saying: "Desiring to focus my attention and wander in the true realms, yet finding the heterodox paths to be chaotic and my mind at a loss as to where to turn, I shall now examine their relative merits so that I may focus my devotion on the most excellent." When the time came for the debate, he issued a further order, saying: "The heterodox masters are all men of talent; the assembly of Śramaṇas should be well-versed in their own doctrines. If they win, I shall honor the Buddha-Dharma; if they lose, I shall execute the monks." Thereupon, Manoratha (如意) questioned the various heterodox teachers, and ninety-nine of them had already retreated in defeat. Regarding the one person remaining in the lower seat, he looked upon him with contempt and engaged in a heated debate, which turned to the subject of fire and smoke. The king and the heterodox teacher both shouted out: "Master Manoratha’s words and reasoning are flawed! For smoke to precede fire is the constant principle of things." Although Manoratha wished to explain the difficulty, no one would listen. Ashamed at being publicly humiliated, he bit off his tongue and wrote a warning to his disciple Vasubandhu (世親), saying: "Among a crowd of partisans, do not contend for the great truth; among the confused masses, do not argue for the correct doctrine." Having finished speaking, he died. Not long after, the king Vikramāditya (超日王) lost his kingdom, and a new king rose to power who valued the wise and virtuous. The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, wishing to wash away the previous shame, came and addressed the king, saying: "Great King, you rule with holy virtue and are the master and life-force of all sentient beings. My late teacher Manoratha had mastered the most profound mysteries, yet the former king, harboring an old grudge, humiliated his great reputation before the masses; having received his guidance and instruction, I wish to avenge the grievance done to my predecessor." The king, knowing that Manoratha (如意) was a man of wisdom and admiring the noble character of Vasubandhu (世親), summoned the various non-Buddhists (外道) to debate with Manoratha. Vasubandhu restated the principles of his predecessor, and the non-Buddhists, admitting defeat, withdrew.

Traveling more than fifty *li* northeast from the monastery of King Kaniṣka, one crosses a great river and arrives at the city of Puṣkalāvatī (布色羯邏伐底城). It is fourteen or fifteen *li* in circumference. The inhabitants are prosperous, and the houses are connected in continuous rows. Outside the west gate of the city is a temple to a deva; the image of the deva is majestic, and miraculous manifestations occur there in succession. To the east of the city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王), which marks the place where the four past Buddhas preached the Dharma. In ancient times, many sages and worthies descended from Central India to this land to guide living beings. It was here that the śāstra-master Vasumitra (伐蘇蜜呾羅) composed the *Abhidharma-prakaraṇa-pāda-śāstra* (眾事分阿毘達磨論). Four or five *li* to the north of the city is an old monastery; its courtyards and buildings are desolate, and the number of monks is small, yet they all follow and study the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). It was here that the śāstra-master Dharmatrāta (達磨呾邏多) composed the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* (雜阿毘達磨論). Beside the monastery is a stūpa several hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka. It is fashioned from carved wood and patterned stone, and its craftsmanship is quite extraordinary. This is the place where, in the past, the Buddha Śākyamuni, while acting as a king and practicing the bodhisattva path, followed the wishes of living beings and gave gifts without fatigue, treating the loss of his own body as if it were nothing; in this land, he was king for a thousand lives, and in this very place, he gave away his eyes for a thousand lives. Not far to the east of the place where he gave his eyes are two stone stūpas, each over one hundred feet high. The one on the right was erected by the Brahmā-deva (梵王), and the one on the left was built by the Lord of Devas (Śakra/Indra) (天帝); they were adorned with exquisite jewels. After the Tathāgata attained extinction, the jewels turned into stone; although the bases have collapsed and sunk, they are still considered lofty.

Traveling over fifty li to the northwest of the stūpas of Brahmā and Indra, there is a stūpa where the Śākya Tathāgata converted the Mother of Demon Children (Hārītī) and caused her to cease harming people; therefore, it is the custom of this country to offer sacrifices to her when praying for offspring.

Traveling more than fifty li to the north of the place where the Mother of Demons (Hārītī) was converted, there is a stupa. This is where the Bodhisattva Śyāmaka (商莫迦) was dutifully providing for his blind parents and gathering fruit when he encountered a king out hunting and was accidentally struck by a poisoned arrow. His utmost sincerity moved the spirits; the Lord of Heaven (Śakra) applied medicine, and his virtue stirred the enlightened sages, so that he was immediately restored to life.
Traveling two hundred-odd li southeast from the place where the Bodhisattva Śyāmaka (商莫迦) was harmed, one arrives at the city of Varusa (跋虜沙城).

To the north of the city is a stūpa, which is where Prince Sudāna (蘇達拏) gave his father the king’s great elephant to a Brahmin, and having been rebuked and banished, looked back to thank the people of the country and bid them farewell after passing through the city gate. Beside it is a saṃghārāma with more than fifty monks, all of whom are students of the Hīnayāna. In the past, the logician Īśvara (伊濕伐邏) composed the *Abhidharma-pradīpa-śāstra* (阿毘達磨明燈論) here.

Outside the east gate of the city of Varusa (跋虜沙城), there is a monastery with more than fifty monks, all of whom are students of the Mahāyāna. There is a stūpa that was built by King Aśoka. Formerly, when Prince Sudāna (蘇達拏太子) was exiled to Mount Daṇḍaloka (彈多落迦山), a Brahmin begged for his son and daughter and sold them at this place.

More than twenty *li* to the northeast of the city of Varusa (跋虜沙城), one arrives at the mountain of Daṇḍaloka (彈多落迦山). On the ridge there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, where Prince Sudāna (蘇達拏) once lived in seclusion. Not far to its side is a stūpa where the prince gave his son and daughter as a gift to a brahmin; the brahmin beat the children, and their blood stained the ground, so that even now the plants and trees there still bear a crimson hue. In the crags is a stone chamber, the place where the prince and his consort practiced meditation. In the valley, the branches of the forest trees hang down like curtains; these are all places where the prince used to roam and rest in the past. Not far to its side is a stone hut, which is the dwelling place of an ancient *ṛṣi*.

Traveling over a hundred *li* to the northwest from the rishi’s hut and crossing a small mountain, one reaches the great mountain (Pravaragiri). On the southern side of the mountain is a monastery with few monks, all of whom study the Mahāyāna. Beside it is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. This is the place where the One-Horned Rishi (Ekashṛṅga-ṛṣi) formerly resided. The rishi was seduced and led astray by a courtesan, causing him to lose his supernatural powers, and the courtesan then rode upon his shoulders to return to the city.

Fifty-some *li* to the northeast of the city of Varusa (跋虜沙城), one arrives at Mount Cong (崇山). On the mountain, there is a blue stone image of the wife of Maheśvara (大自在天), who is the goddess Bhīmā (毘摩天女). According to local tradition, this celestial image appeared there naturally. Because it is highly miraculous, there are many who come to pray; people from all the countries of India, whether noble or humble, gather here from far and near to seek blessings and make vows. For those who wish to see the form of the celestial deity, if they are sincere and single-minded and fast for seven days, some may obtain a vision, and most of their prayers are fulfilled. At the foot of the mountain, there is a temple of Maheśvara where ash-smearing heretics (塗灰外道) perform their ritual worship.

Traveling one hundred and fifty li southeast from the Bhīmā temple (毘摩天祠), one reaches the city of Udakahāṇḍa (烏鐸迦漢荼城), which is over twenty li in circuit and borders the Sindhu River (信度河) to the south. The inhabitants are wealthy and happy, precious goods are accumulated in abundance, and rare curiosities from all quarters are mostly gathered here.

Traveling over twenty li northwest from the city of Udakhāṇḍa (烏鐸迦漢荼城), one reaches the town of Śalātura (婆羅覩邏邑), which is the birthplace of the ṛṣi Pāṇini (波爾尼仙), the author of the Śabdavidyā-śāstra (聲明論). At the beginning of remote antiquity, written characters were numerous and extensive, but as time passed through the kalpa of destruction, the world became a void, until the long-lived deities descended to inspire both the sacred and the secular, and from this, literary records were born. Since that time, their sources have proliferated. King Brahmā and Lord Indra created models according to the needs of the times, and the various immortals of heterodox paths each devised their own scripts; people followed their predecessors and vied to practice what was handed down, but students' efforts were in vain, as it was difficult to investigate the systems in detail.  When the human lifespan was one hundred years, there was the ṛṣi Pāṇini, who was born with great wisdom and broad learning. Pitying the decadence of the age, he wished to prune away the superficial and false, and to edit and refine the cumbersome and redundant. He traveled to various regions to inquire after the Way, and upon meeting Maheśvara (自在天), he expressed his intention to compose a work. Maheśvara said, "Excellent! I shall assist you." Having received these instructions, the ṛṣi withdrew and applied his mind to deep reflection, collecting a vast array of words to compose a lexicon consisting of one thousand stanzas, each containing thirty-two syllables. It exhausted the depths of both the present and the past, and summarized the entirety of literary language. He sealed it and presented it to the king, who found it most extraordinary and issued a decree throughout the kingdom to make it universally studied, rewarding anyone who could recite it with mastery with one thousand gold coins. This is why the tradition of teacher and student has been passed down and flourished in the present age. Consequently, the Brahmins in this town are men of great learning and high talent, possessing broad knowledge and excellent memories. In the town of Śalātura (婆羅覩邏邑) there is a stūpa, which is the place where an Arhat converted the later followers of the sage Pāṇini. Five hundred years after the Tathāgata had passed away, a great Arhat traveling from the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國) arrived here and saw a Brahmin beating and scolding a young boy. The Arhat asked the Brahmin, "Why are you tormenting this child?" The Brahmin replied, "I am making him study the *Śabdavidyā-śāstra* (聲明論), but his progress is not timely." The Arhat smiled gently. The old Brahmin said, "The nature of a Śramaṇa is compassion and pity for all living beings. I wish to hear the reason for your laughter." The Arhat said, "It is not easy to speak of this, for I fear it will cause deep doubt. Have you ever heard that the sage Pāṇini composed the *Śabdavidyā-śāstra* and left it as a teaching for the world?" The Brahmin replied, "The children of this town, as later followers, look up to his virtue, and his image is still here." The Arhat said, "This child of yours is that very sage. Because he possessed a powerful memory, he indulged in the study of worldly texts, discussing only heterodox doctrines without investigating the true principles. His spiritual wisdom was wasted in vain, and his transmigration has not yet ceased; it is only by riding on the merit of his remaining good deeds that he has become your beloved son. However, the literary expressions of worldly texts merely exhaust one's efforts; how can they compare to the holy teachings of the Tathāgata, which nourish merit and wisdom in the dark? Formerly, on the shore of the Southern Sea, there was a withered tree where five hundred bats lived in holes." Some merchants stopped under this tree. At that time, it was windy and cold, and everyone was hungry and freezing. They gathered firewood and brush, and kindled a fire beneath it. The smoke and flames gradually intensified, and the withered tree caught fire. Among the merchants, there was one trader who, after the middle of the night, recited the Abhidharma-piṭaka. Although those bats were distressed by the fire, they loved the sound of the Dharma so much that they endured it and did not leave, and thus they met their end there. Following their karma, they were reborn, all obtaining human bodies. They left home to study and practice, and by virtue of having heard the sound of the Dharma, they possessed keen intelligence and wisdom, and all attained the holy fruit, becoming fields of merit for the world. Recently, King Kaniṣka and the Venerable Pārśva (脇尊者) summoned five hundred sages in the kingdom of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國) to compile the Vibhāṣā-śāstra (毘婆沙論); these are the very same five hundred bats from the withered tree. Although I am unworthy, I am one of that number. This shows how the superior and the inferior are truly different, and how the flying and the crawling are vastly distinct. You should now allow your beloved son to leave home; the merit of leaving home is beyond words."  When the Arhat had finished speaking these words, he displayed his supernatural powers and suddenly disappeared. The brahmin was deeply moved by awe and wonder, and after exclaiming his admiration for a long time, he told his neighbors everything. He then allowed his son to leave home to study and practice, and subsequently turned to the faith, honoring the Triple Gem. His fellow villagers followed his example, and their devotion remains strong to this day.  From the city of Udakahāṇḍa (烏鐸迦漢荼城), traveling north, crossing mountains and fording rivers for more than six hundred li, one arrives at the country of Uḍḍiyāna (烏仗那國).

The country of Uḍḍiyāna (烏仗那國) is over five thousand li in circuit. Mountains and valleys are contiguous, and rivers and marshes connect with the plains. Although grain is sown, the land is not very fertile. There are many grapes but little sugarcane; the land produces gold and iron and is suitable for saffron; the forests are lush, and flowers and fruits are abundant. The cold and heat are temperate, and the winds and rains follow their proper seasons. The people are timid and cowardly, and their customs are deceitful. They are fond of learning but do not achieve success, and they make incantations their professional skill. They mostly wear white cotton cloth and have few other types of clothing. Although their language differs, it is largely the same as that of India. Their writing and etiquette are quite similar. They highly esteem the Buddhadharma and revere and believe in the Mahāyāna. Along the banks of the Śubhavastu River (蘇婆伐窣堵河), there were formerly one thousand four hundred monasteries, most of which are now desolate. Formerly there were eighteen thousand monks, but now they have gradually decreased. They all study the Mahāyāna and make silent meditation their occupation; they are skilled at reciting the texts but have not yet fathomed their profound meanings. Their moral conduct is pure, and they are especially skilled in incantations. Regarding the traditions of the Vinaya rules, there are five schools: first, the Dharmaguptaka; second, the Mahīśāsaka; third, the Kāśyapīya; fourth, the Sarvāstivāda; and fifth, the Mahāsāṃghika. There are more than ten deva temples, where followers of different paths live together. There are four or five fortified cities, and their king usually governs from the city of Mangala (瞢揭釐城). The city is sixteen or seventeen li in circuit and is densely populated.
There are four or five fortified cities, and the king mostly governs from the city of Maṅgala (瞢揭釐城). The city is sixteen or seventeen li in circuit, and the inhabitants are numerous and prosperous.
Along the banks of the Śubhavastu River (蘇婆伐窣堵河), there were formerly one thousand four hundred monasteries, most of which are now desolate.

Four or five li to the east of the city of Maṅgala (瞢揭釐城), there is a stūpa that possesses many miraculous signs; it is the place where the Buddha, in a former life as the Kṣāntirṣi (忍辱仙人, Rishi of Patience), had his limbs severed by King Kali (羯利王).

Traveling two hundred and fifty or sixty *li* northeast from the city of Maṅgala (瞢揭釐城), one enters a great mountain and reaches the Apalāla (阿波邏羅) Dragon Spring, which is the source of the Śubhavastu (蘇婆伐窣堵) River. The stream flows to the southwest; it contains ice during the spring and summer, and at dusk, the flying spray resembles snow, with the snowflakes shimmering in five colors and radiating light in all directions.  As for this dragon, in the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he was born in the human realm with the name Gangi (殑祇); he was deeply skilled in sorcery and restrained evil dragons from causing torrential rains, so the people of the country relied on him to store surplus grain. The inhabitants and the masses, feeling gratitude and cherishing his virtue, taxed each household one *dou* of grain to present to him. After many years had passed, there were some who defaulted on their payments. Gangi became angry and vowed to become a poisonous dragon, violently unleashing wind and rain to damage the crops. After his life ended, he became the dragon of this pool. The spring flows with white water, damaging the land's productivity.  The Śākya Tathāgata, governing the world with great compassion, took pity on the people of this country for suffering this unique disaster and descended to this place, desiring to convert the violent dragon. He had the Vajrapāṇi (執金剛神) strike the mountain cliff with his vajra; the Dragon King was terrified and emerged to take refuge. Hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, his mind became pure and he attained faith and enlightenment. The Tathāgata then commanded him not to damage the crops. The dragon said, "Everything I eat depends on the harvest from the people's fields. Now, having received the holy teaching, I fear it will be difficult to sustain myself; I request to collect grain stores once every twelve years." The Tathāgata, in his encompassing compassion, took pity and granted this. Thus, even now, the country suffers the calamity of white water once every twelve years.

More than thirty *li* to the southwest of the Apalāla (阿波邏羅) Dragon Spring, on a large flat rock on the northern bank of the river, there is a footprint trodden by the Tathāgata. Its measured length varies according to the merit of the person, for this is where the Tathāgata left his mark when he departed after subduing this dragon. Later generations piled stones upon it to construct a chamber, and people from far and near gather there to make offerings of flowers and incense.
Going more than thirty li downstream, one reaches the rock where the Tathāgata washed his clothes, where the patterns of the kaṣāya robe are as distinct as if they had been engraved.

More than four hundred li to the south of the city of Maṅgala (瞢揭釐城), one reaches Mount Hiḍḍa (醯羅山). The valley stream branches to the west, but as one ascends eastward against the current, various flowers and strange fruits cover the gullies and line the cliffs. The peaks and crags are perilous, and the streams and valleys wind and meander; one sometimes hears the sound of loud talking, or the strains of music. There are square stones like pagodas, appearing as if fashioned by craftsmen, stretching out in succession and spreading through the cliffs and valleys. This is where the Tathāgata, in a former life, sacrificed his life and body in order to hear half a stanza of the Dharma.

More than two hundred li to the south of the city of Maṅgala (瞢揭釐城), by the side of a great mountain (大山), one reaches the Mahāvana (摩訶伐那) Monastery. This is where the Tathāgata, in a former life when practicing the bodhisattva path as a king named Sarvadatta (薩縛達), having fled his enemies and abandoned his kingdom, traveled in secret to this place and encountered a poor brahmin who had come to beg for alms. Having already lost his royal position and having nothing to give, he ordered the brahmin to bind him and take him captive to the enemy king, hoping that the reward money could be used as a gift of charity in return.

To the northwest of the Mahāvana Monastery (Mahāvana-saṃghārāma), descending the mountain for thirty or forty li, one reaches the Mayū Monastery (Mayū-saṃghārāma). There is a stūpa over one hundred feet high. On a large square stone at its side, there is a footprint of the Tathāgata, left when the Buddha formerly stepped on this stone and emitted a koṭi of rays of light to illuminate the Mahāvana Monastery, while preaching Jātaka stories for the sake of humans and devas. Below the base of this stūpa is a stone, yellowish-white in color, which is always moist and oily. It is said that when the Tathāgata was formerly practicing the bodhisattva path, in order to hear the true Dharma, he broke his bones here to use as a pen for writing down the scriptures.

Sixty or seventy li to the west of the Mayū Monastery (摩愉伽藍), one reaches a stūpa built by King Aśoka. It was here that the Tathāgata, in a former life while practicing the conduct of a Bodhisattva, was known as King Śibi (毘迦王); seeking the fruit of Buddhahood, he cut his own flesh to ransom a dove from a hawk.

Northwest of the country of Kapota (代鴿) for more than two hundred *li*, one enters the Sanirāja (珊尼羅闍) River valley and arrives at the Sarpa-auṣadhi (薩裒殺地) monastery. There is a stūpa here, more than eighty feet high. It was here that the Tathāgata, in a former life as Indra (帝釋), encountered a time of famine and widespread pestilence; medical treatments were of no avail, and deaths followed one after another. Indra, moved by compassion and thinking of how to save them, transformed his body into that of a giant python, lying dead in the valley, and proclaimed to all from the air. Those who heard were moved and rejoiced, rushing to the spot; as they cut pieces from the body, it would grow back, curing their hunger and their illnesses. Not far to the side is a great Soma (蘇摩) stūpa. It was here that the Tathāgata, in a former life as Indra, during a time of pestilence, took pity on all sentient beings and transformed his body into a Soma snake; all who ate of it were restored to health and comfort. Beside the stone cliff to the north of the Sanirāja River, there is a stūpa. Sick people who come here to pray are often cured of their ailments. In the past, when the Tathāgata was a peacock king, he came to this place with his flock; driven by heat and thirst, they sought water but could not find any, so the peacock king pecked the cliff with his beak, causing a spring to gush forth. This has now become a pool, and those who drink from it or bathe in it are cured of their illnesses. Traces of the peacock still remain on the stone.

Not far from its side is the great stūpa of Soma (蘇摩). In the past, when the Tathāgata was Indra (帝釋), there was a time of pestilence in the world. Taking pity on all sentient beings, he transformed his body into a Soma snake; all who ate of it were restored to health and comfort.

Traveling sixty or seventy li southwest of the city of Maṅgala (瞢揭釐城), on the east bank of a great river, there is a stūpa over sixty feet high, which was built by King Uttarasena (上軍王). Formerly, when the Tathāgata was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he told the great assembly: "After my nirvāṇa, King Uttarasena of the country of Uḍḍiyāna (烏仗那國) should be given a share of the relics." When the various kings were about to measure out the shares, King Uttarasena arrived late, and consequently, there was talk of slighting him. At that time, the assembly of devas and men reiterated the words of the Tathāgata’s final charge, so he was allowed to participate in the distribution; he carried them back to his own country and reverently constructed this to honor them.

By the bank of the great river beside the stupa, there is a large rock shaped like an elephant. Formerly, when King Uttarasena (上軍王) was returning with the relics carried by a great white elephant, the elephant suddenly stumbled and fell upon reaching this spot, and consequently died; it then turned into stone, and a stupa was built right beside it.

More than fifty li to the west of the city of Maṅgala (瞢揭釐城), crossing a great river, one arrives at the Rohitaka-stūpa (盧醯呾迦窣堵波; meaning "red"). It is over fifty feet high and was built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, when the Tathāgata was practicing the bodhisattva path, he was a great king named Maitrībala (慈力), who here pierced his body to draw blood to feed five yakṣas (藥叉).

More than thirty li to the northeast of the city of Maṅgala (瞢揭釐城), one reaches the Adbhuta (遏部多; "Miraculous") stone stupa, which is over forty feet high. In the past, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma here to instruct humans and devas. After the Tathāgata departed, it gushed forth from the earth; the common people revere it, and offerings of incense and flowers never cease.

Crossing the great river thirty or forty li to the west of the stone stupa, one arrives at a vihāra (精舍) containing an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (阿縛盧枳低濕伐羅). His majestic spiritual influence is latently bestowed and his divine traces are clearly manifest; both monastics and laity flock there, making offerings without cease.

One hundred and fifty li northwest of the statue of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, one arrives at the mountain of Lamboura (藍勃盧山). On the mountain ridge is a dragon lake, over thirty li in circumference; its green waves are vast and expansive, and its clear waters are as bright as a mirror. In the past, when King Virūḍhaka (毘盧釋迦王) attacked the Śākyas, four men resisted the army; they were expelled by their kinsmen and each fled in a different direction. One of these Śākyas, having left the capital, was exhausted from his travels and stopped midway. At that time, a wild goose flew before him; since it was tame and friendly, he mounted it. The goose flew and landed beside this lake. The Śākya, wandering aimlessly and having traveled far to a foreign land, was lost and did not know the way, so he took a nap in the shade of a tree. The young daughter of the dragon of the lake was wandering along the water's edge when she suddenly saw the Śākya; fearing her appearance was inappropriate, she transformed into human form and approached to stroke him. The Śākya was startled awake and asked, "I am a weary traveler, why do you show me such intimacy?" He then pressed her with great earnestness, forcing himself upon her in the wilderness. The woman said, "I have my parents' instructions, which I respect and do not violate. Although I am honored by your attention, I have not received their command." The Śākya asked, "The mountain valleys are dark and remote; where is your home?" She replied, "I am the dragon daughter of this lake. I respectfully heard that your noble clan was wandering in exile, and as I happened to be out for a stroll, I dared to offer comfort for your fatigue. As for the matter of intimate relations, I have not heard of such an intention. Furthermore, due to accumulated karma, I have received this dragon body; humans and animals follow different paths, and such a thing is unheard of." The Śākya said, "If you grant me this one word, my long-held desire will be fulfilled." The dragon girl said, "I respectfully hear your command; I submit to whatever you decide." The Śākya then made a vow in his heart: "By whatever power of merit I possess, let this dragon girl's entire body be transformed into that of a human." Moved by the power of his merit, the dragon then changed her form; having attained a human body, she was deeply overjoyed. She thanked the Śākya, saying, "Due to my accumulated evil karma, I have been wandering in the lower realms. Fortunately, I have received your kind attention, and through the application of your merit, this wretched body held for vast kalpas has been transformed in an instant. I wish to repay this virtue, but even shattering my body would not be enough. I desire to accompany you, but I am constrained by the opinions of others. I wish to inform my parents, and then prepare the rites."  The dragon girl returned to the pool and told her parents, "Today while out on an excursion, I suddenly met a member of the Śākya clan; moved by the power of his merit, I have been transformed into a human. My heart is set on a happy union, and I venture to state the facts." The Dragon King, pleased with the human realm and holding the holy clan in high regard, acceded to his daughter's request. He then emerged from the pool and thanked the Śākya, saying, "You have not shunned those of a different species, but have lowered your noble status to accommodate the lowly. I wish for you to grace my dwelling, where I dare to offer you service."  The Śākya accepted the Dragon King's invitation and went to his residence. There, within the dragon palace, they prepared the rites for a personal wedding, and in the joy of their new union, they indulged in the utmost pleasure. However, the Śākya, seeing the dragon's form, felt constant fear and disgust, and wished to take his leave. The Dragon King stopped him, saying, "I hope you will not go far away, but reside in this neighborhood. I shall cause you to occupy territory, assume a great title, rule over subjects, and enjoy a long-lasting dynasty." The Śākya declined, saying, "This is not what I desire." The Dragon King placed a precious sword into a box and covered it with a fine white cotton cloth. He said to the Śākya, "I hope you will take this cloth and present it to the king. The king will surely receive this tribute from a man from afar in person, and at that moment, you can slay him. By then seizing his kingdom, would that not be excellent?" The Śākya accepted the dragon's instructions and went to make the offering. As the King of Udyāna (烏仗那) personally lifted the cloth, the Śākya seized his sleeve and stabbed him. The attendant ministers and guards clamored on the palace steps, but the Śākya brandished his sword and declared, "The sword I wield was bestowed upon me by the divine dragon to execute those who resist and to behead those who do not submit." All were awed by his divine martial prowess and pushed him to the throne. He then reformed the corrupt administration, honored the virtuous, and relieved the suffering. Having done this, he mobilized a great assembly and prepared a royal procession to go to the dragon palace to report his success and welcome the dragon girl back to the capital.  The dragon girl’s past karma was not yet exhausted, and as her remaining retribution still persisted, whenever they were in private, nine dragon heads would emerge from her head. The Śākya, fearful and disgusted, did not know what plan to devise, but while she was sleeping, he used a sharp blade to cut them off. The dragon girl, startled from her sleep, said, "This is not to the benefit of our descendants. Not only is my life somewhat injured, but your offspring shall suffer from headaches." Therefore, the people of this royal clan often suffer from this affliction; although it is not continuous, it flares up from time to time. After the Śākya passed away, his son succeeded to the throne; this was King Uttarasena (嗢呾羅犀那王). After King Uttarasena succeeded to the throne, his mother lost her sight. After the Tathāgata had subdued the dragon Apalāla (阿波邏羅), he returned, descending through the air into the palace. King Uttarasena (嗢呾羅犀那王) had just gone out hunting, and the Tathāgata took the opportunity to briefly explain the essentials of the Dharma to his mother. Upon encountering the Holy One and hearing the Dharma, she immediately regained her sight. The Tathāgata asked, "Your son is of my clan; where is he now?" The mother replied, "He went out early this morning to hunt and is now about to return." The Tathāgata and the great assembly were about to depart. The King's mother said, "It is only by my good fortune that I gave birth into this holy clan; the Tathāgata has shown compassion and personally descended here. My son is just now returning, so I pray you stay and wait a moment." The World-Honored One said, "This person is of my clan. He can be awakened to faith by hearing the teachings; he does not require personal instruction to generate the resolve. I must go. When he returns, tell him: 'The Tathāgata is going from here to the śāla trees of the city of Kuśinagara (拘尸城) to enter nirvana; he should take some of the relics for his own worship.'" The Tathāgata and the great assembly then departed, traversing the void. King Uttarasena was hunting when he saw from afar a brilliant light shining in the palace; suspecting a fire, he stopped his hunt and returned. He then saw that his mother had regained her sight, and rejoicing, he asked, "How long was I gone that such an auspicious response occurred, restoring my mother's vision as it was before?" His mother replied, "After you went out, the Tathāgata arrived here; upon hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, I regained my sight. The Tathāgata is going from here to the śāla trees of the city of Kuśinagara to enter nirvana, and he summons you to come quickly to share in the relics." When the king heard this, he wailed with grief and collapsed to the ground. After a long time, he regained consciousness and ordered his carriage to hasten to the site. By the time he arrived among the twin śāla trees, the Buddha had already entered nirvana. At that time, the various kings looked down upon him for being from a remote borderland; they prized the relics highly and did not wish to share them with him. Then, the assembly of devas and men restated the Buddha’s intention, and having heard this, the kings finally granted him an equal share.

Going northeast from the city of Maṅgala (瞢揭釐城), crossing mountains and traversing valleys, and heading upstream along the Indus River (信度河), the path is perilous and the mountain valleys are dark and gloomy. One must tread on rope bridges or cling to iron chains; plank paths are suspended over voids, and bridges are built precariously high, with wooden pegs driven into the rock to serve as steps. After traveling over a thousand li, one reaches the valley of Darada (達麗羅川), which is the old capital of the kingdom of Udyāna (烏仗那國). It produces much gold and saffron.  Beside a great monastery in the Darada valley, there is a carved wooden statue of the Bodhisattva Maitreya (慈氏菩薩). Its golden color shines brightly, and its spiritual efficacy is subtly responsive. It is over a hundred feet tall and was created by the Arhat Madhyāntika (末田底迦). Using his supernatural powers, the Arhat took a craftsman up to the Tuṣita Heaven (覩史多天) to personally observe the exquisite features of the Bodhisattva. After three such visits, the work was finally completed. Ever since this statue came into existence, the Dharma has flowed toward the eastern regions.

Traveling east from here, crossing ridges and traversing valleys, one goes upstream along the Indus River (信度河; Skt. sindhu), crossing flying bridges and plank paths, treading through danger and peril for over five hundred li, until arriving at the country of Balūra (鉢露羅國). The country of Balūra is over four thousand li in circuit, situated amidst the Great Snow Mountains; it is long from east to west and narrow from south to north. There is an abundance of wheat and beans, and it produces gold and silver; relying on the profit from this gold, the national treasury is wealthy and abundant. The climate is consistently cold and harsh. The people are fierce and violent by nature, lacking in benevolence and righteousness, and they have no knowledge of etiquette or propriety. Their appearance is coarse and unrefined, and their clothing is made of wool and felt. Their writing is largely the same as that of India, but their language differs from that of other countries. There are several hundred monasteries and several thousand monks; their studies are not specialized, and their observance of the precepts is largely lax.

From here I returned to the city of Udakhanda (烏鐸迦漢荼城) and crossed the Indus River (信度河) to the south. The river is three or four li wide, flowing southward; it is clear and bright as a mirror, yet surging and rushing along. Poisonous dragons and evil beasts have their dens therein; if those crossing carry precious gems, rare flower or fruit seeds, or relics of the Buddha, their boats are often tossed about and submerged. Crossing the river, I arrived at the country of Takṣaśilā (呾叉始羅國). The country of Takṣaśilā is over two thousand li in circuit. The capital city is over ten li in circuit. The local chieftains contend for power, and the royal lineage has become extinct; in the past, it was subject to the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國), and recently it has become a vassal to the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國). The land is known for its fertile soil, and agriculture is flourishing; there are many springs and streams, and flowers and plants grow luxuriantly. The climate is mild and pleasant, the customs are spirited and brave, and the people revere the Three Jewels. Although there are many monasteries, they are mostly in a state of great ruin, and the number of monks is small; they all study the Mahāyāna.
The capital city of the kingdom is more than ten li in circuit.

More than seventy li to the northwest of the great city is the pond of the Dragon King Elāpattra (醫羅鉢呾羅), which is over a hundred paces in circumference. Its water is clear and pure, and multicolored lotus flowers bloom there together in diverse hues. This dragon is the one who, in the time of the Buddha Kāśyapa, was a bhikṣu that damaged an elāpattra tree. Therefore, when the people of that land now pray for rain or clear weather, they must go to the pond together with a śramaṇa; when he snaps his fingers and offers words of comfort, their wishes are invariably fulfilled.

Traveling over thirty li southeast from the Dragon Pond and entering between two mountains, there is a stupa (stūpa) built by King Aśoka (無憂王), over a hundred feet in height. It is the prediction of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni that when the future World-Honored One Maitreya (慈氏世尊) appears in the world, there will naturally be four great treasure troves, and this sacred site is one of them. According to ancient records, whenever an earthquake occurs and all the mountains shake, the area for a hundred paces around the treasure remains perfectly still without any quivering. Some foolish men once attempted to dig it up recklessly, but the earth shook and they all fell prostrate. Nearby is a monastery (saṃghārāma), which is severely dilapidated and has long been devoid of monks.

Twelve or thirteen li to the north of the city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王). On days of fasting, it sometimes emits a divine light, and divine flowers and celestial music are frequently seen and heard. I have heard from the records of former sages that, recently, a woman afflicted with malignant leprosy came secretly to the stūpa to reproach herself and perform repentance. Seeing that the courtyard was covered in filth, she cleared it away, swept and sprinkled the ground, applied incense, scattered flowers, and gathered blue lotuses to spread over the ground again. Her malignant disease was cured, her appearance became more beautiful, and her body emitted a famous fragrance, as fragrant as the blue lotuses. This is a sacred site; it is where the Tathāgata, in the past, while practicing the bodhisattva path as a great king named Candraprabha (戰達羅鉢剌婆), sought bodhi and sacrificed his head as a gift. He made such sacrifices for a thousand lifetimes. Beside the Head-Sacrifice Stūpa (捨頭窣堵波) is a saṃghārāma with a desolate courtyard and few monks. In the past, the Sautrāntika master Kumāralāta (拘摩羅邏多) composed various treatises here.

To the southeast of the city, on the northern side of the South Hill, there is a stūpa over a hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王) at the place where his son, Prince Kuṇāla (拘浪拏), had his eyes gouged out after being falsely accused by his stepmother. Blind people who pray here often have their sight restored. This prince was the son of the first queen; he was elegant in appearance and had long been renowned for his kindness and benevolence. After the first queen passed away, the stepmother, who was arrogant and lewd, gave free rein to her muddled stupidity and privately attempted to seduce the prince. The prince wept, took the blame upon himself, and withdrew to apologize for his perceived offense. Seeing her advances rejected, the stepmother’s fury intensified. Waiting for a moment when the king was at leisure, she said composedly, "Takṣaśilā (呾叉始羅) is a strategic key to the kingdom; can it be entrusted to anyone other than a close royal scion? Now, the prince is known for his benevolence and filial piety, and because he is both a relative and a man of virtue, public opinion favors him." The king, hearing this, was pleased by the treacherous scheme; he immediately summoned the prince and admonished him, saying, "I have inherited the legacy of my ancestors to continue their rule, and I live in constant fear of losing it and thereby bringing shame upon the late kings. Takṣaśilā is the throat and belt of the kingdom, and I now appoint you to govern that country. The affairs of the state are heavy and complex, and the sentiments of the people are devious and mixed; do not act rashly or carelessly, lest you damage the foundation of our inheritance. Whenever there is a summons, verify it with my tooth-seal. The seal is in my mouth; how could there be any error?" Thereupon, the prince accepted the command and came to govern. As time passed, the stepmother’s anger grew; she forged a royal decree, sealed it with purple clay, and while the king was sleeping, she stole his teeth to make the impression, then dispatched a messenger to deliver the letter of condemnation. The assisting ministers knelt to read it, looking at one another in dismay. The prince asked, "Why are you so sorrowful?" They replied, "The Great King has issued a command, a written decree reprimanding the prince, ordering that your two eyes be gouged out and that you be exiled and abandoned in the mountain valleys, leaving you and your wife to live or die as fate decides. Although this command exists, we have not yet been able to act upon it. We should now request a confirmation, and you should present yourself bound to await your punishment." The prince said, "If a father grants death to his son, how can it be refused? The tooth-seal serves as the signet; truly, there can be no error." He ordered a Caṇḍāla to gouge out his eyes. Once his eyes were blinded, he begged for alms to sustain himself, wandering from place to place until he reached his father’s capital city. His wife said to him, "This is the royal city. Alas, the suffering of hunger and cold is truly bitter! Once a prince, now a beggar! I wish for us to make this known and have the previous charge re-examined." Thereupon, they devised a plan to enter the king’s inner stables. In the final watch of the night, weeping as he faced the clear breeze, he sang out in a long, mournful wail, accompanying himself on the konghou (harp). From his high pavilion, the king heard the elegant singing, the lyrics of which were deeply resentful and sorrowful; wondering at it, he asked, "The sound of the singing to the konghou seems to be that of my son; for what reason has he come here?" He immediately asked the inner stables, "Who is singing and wailing?" They then brought the blind man before the king. Seeing the prince, the king asked with suppressed grief, "Who has harmed your body and brought this calamity upon you? My beloved son has lost his sight, yet I remained unaware; how then can I investigate the affairs of all the common people? O Heaven, O Heaven! How has my virtue declined!" The prince wept piteously and replied apologetically, "It is truly because of my lack of filial piety that I have incurred the blame of Heaven. On a certain day of a certain month, I suddenly received your compassionate edict; having no way to voice my plea, I did not dare to evade my responsibility." The king, knowing in his heart that his second wife had acted improperly, did not investigate further but immediately imposed a severe punishment.  At that time, there was a great Arhat named Ghoṣa (瞿沙) at the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) monastery, who possessed unobstructed eloquence in the four analytical knowledges and was fully endowed with the three insights. The king brought his blind son and explained the situation to him, wishing only for his compassion to restore the boy's sight. After the Arhat accepted the king's request, he announced to the people of the country on that very day, "The day after tomorrow, I wish to preach the sublime truth. Let each person bring a vessel and come here to listen to the Dharma, so as to collect your tears."  Thereupon, people from near and far flocked to the site, and men and women gathered like clouds. At that time, the Arhat preached on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination; among all those who heard the Dharma, there was none who was not moved to deep sorrow, and they used the vessels they carried to collect their falling tears. When the preaching was finished, he collected all the tears and placed them in a golden basin, then made a vow, saying, "All that I have spoken is the ultimate truth of the Buddhas. If this truth is not genuine and my teaching contains errors, then so be it; but if it is not so, I wish to wash these blind eyes with the tears of the multitude, so that his sight may be restored and he may see as clearly as before."  Having spoken these words, he used the tears to wash the eyes, and the eyes were immediately restored to sight. The king then rebuked his ministers and interrogated his officials; some were dismissed or banished, while others were demoted or put to death. The powerful and wealthy families were moved to the sandy desert to the northeast of the Snow Mountains (Himālaya).

From here, traveling southeast across various mountains and valleys for more than seven hundred li, one arrives at the country of Siṃhapura (僧訶補羅國). The country of Siṃhapura is three thousand five or six hundred li in circuit and borders the Indus River (信度河) to the west. The capital city of the country is fourteen or fifteen li in circuit; it rests against the mountains and occupies the ridges, making it solid, steep, and impregnable. There is little labor in agricultural work, yet the land yields abundant harvests. The climate is cold, the people are fierce by nature, their customs prize bravery, and they are also often deceitful. The country has no sovereign ruler of its own and is subject to the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國).
The capital city of the country (Siṃhapura 僧訶補羅國) is fourteen or fifteen li in circuit; it rests against the mountains and occupies the ridges, making it steep, precipitous, and strategically secure.

Not far to the south of the city is a stupa (stūpa), which was built by King Aśoka (無憂王). Its ornamentation is damaged, but miraculous manifestations occur there in succession. Beside it is a monastery (saṃghārāma), which is empty and without monks.

Forty or fifty li to the southeast of the city, one reaches a stone stupa built by King Aśoka, which is over two hundred feet high. There are more than ten ponds surrounding it on the left and right, with banks carved from stone in various shapes and kinds. The clear water surges and flows, gurgling and splashing; dragons, fish, and other aquatic creatures swim deep within their underwater grottoes, while lotus flowers of four colors cover the clear pools. A hundred kinds of fruit trees grow in abundance, flourishing together in different colors; the woods and ponds reflect one another, truly a place for recreation. Beside it is a monastery, long since devoid of monks. Not far from the side of the stupa is the place where the original teacher of the white-robed heretics realized the principles he sought and first preached his doctrine; there is now a memorial mark there, and a deva temple has been built beside it. His followers practice austerities, diligent day and night, without a moment of rest. The doctrine preached by their original teacher largely steals the meaning of the Buddhist sutras, establishing methods according to their own kind and imitating the rules and rituals. The elders are called bhikṣu (苾芻), and the juniors are called śrāmaṇera (沙彌). Their deportment and monastic discipline are quite similar to the Buddhist laws. They differ only in that they retain a small amount of hair, go naked, or, if they do wear clothing, it is white, which serves to distinguish them from other sects. Their image of the heavenly teacher is surreptitiously modeled after the Tathāgata; the clothing is different, but the auspicious marks are no different.

From here, I returned to the northern border of the country of Takṣaśilā (呾叉始羅國), crossed the Indus River (信度河), and traveled southeast for over two hundred li, passing through a great stone gate. This is where, in the past, Prince Mahāsattva sacrificed his body to feed a starving tigress. One hundred and forty or fifty paces to the south of this is a stone stūpa. Pitying the starving beast for its lack of strength, the Mahāsattva walked to this spot, pierced himself with a dry bamboo splinter, and fed it his blood, whereupon the beast devoured him. The soil there, as well as the plants and trees, is slightly reddish in color, as if stained with blood. When people tread upon this ground, they feel as if pricked by thorns; regardless of whether they are skeptical or believing, none can help but feel a sense of profound grief.

To the north of the site of the body-sacrifice, there is a stone stūpa over two hundred feet high, which was built by King Aśoka (無憂王). It is carved with extraordinary craftsmanship and often illuminates with divine light. Small stūpas and various stone niches, numbering in the hundreds, surround this sacred precinct; those who suffer from illnesses are often cured after circumambulating it. To the east of the stone stūpa is a monastery (saṃghārāma) with more than a hundred monks, all of whom study the Mahāyāna teachings.

From here, traveling east for more than fifty li, one reaches the mountain of Vyāsa (孤山). There is a monastery (saṃghārāma) there with over two hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Mahāyāna. Flowers and fruits are abundant, and the springs and ponds are as clear as mirrors. Beside it is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, which marks the spot where the Tathāgata in the past converted an evil yakṣa, commanding him to cease eating meat.

From here, traveling southeast for more than five hundred li, one arrives at the country of Uraśā (烏剌尸國). The country of Uraśā is more than two thousand li in circuit, with mountains and hills connected together and cultivated fields that are narrow and cramped. The capital city of the country is seven or eight li in circuit; it has no great sovereign ruler and is subject to the country of Kaśmīra (迦隰彌羅國). It is suitable for agriculture, but there are few flowers or fruits. The climate is mild, with slight frost and snow. The customs lack propriety and righteousness; the people’s nature is fierce and violent, they frequently practice deceit, and they do not believe in the Buddha’s Dharma. Four or five li to the southwest of the great city, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka. Beside it is a saṃghārāma with few monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Mahāyāna.

From here, traveling southeast, climbing mountains and traversing dangerous paths, crossing an iron bridge, and journeying more than one thousand li, one arrives at the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國). The country of Kaśmīra is over seven thousand li in circumference. Its four borders are backed by mountains; the mountains are extremely steep and precipitous. Although there are gateways and paths, they are narrow and constricted, and since ancient times, neighboring enemies have been unable to invade or conquer it. The capital city of the country faces a great river to the west; it measures twelve or thirteen li from south to north and four or five li from east to west. It is suitable for agriculture, produces many flowers and fruits, and yields dragon-breed horses, saffron (鬱金香), fire-pearls, and medicinal herbs. The climate is cold and harsh, with much snow and little wind. The people wear woolen garments and white cotton (㲲) clothing. The local customs are frivolous, and the people are mostly timid and cowardly. The country is protected by a dragon, and thus it dominates the neighboring regions. The people are beautiful in appearance, but their dispositions are deceitful. They are fond of learning and are well-informed, believing in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are over one hundred saṃghārāmas (伽藍) with more than five thousand monks. There are four stūpas (窣堵波), all built by King Aśoka (無憂王), each containing over a pint (升) of the Tathāgata’s relics. The *Country Records* (國志) state: "The land of this country was originally a dragon lake. In the past, when the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had subdued an evil spirit in the country of Uḍḍiyāna (烏仗那國) and wished to return to the Middle Kingdom, he rode through the air over this country and said to Ānanda: 'After my parinirvāṇa, there will be an arhat named Madhyāntika (末田底迦) who will establish a country here, settle the people, and propagate the Buddha-dharma.'" In the fiftieth year after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the arhat Madhyāntika (末田底迦), a disciple of Ānanda who had attained the six supernatural powers and possessed the eight liberations, heard the Buddha’s prediction and felt great joy in his heart. He then came to this place, sat in meditation within the woods of a great mountain range (大山嶺), and manifested great supernatural transformations. The dragon saw this and, deeply believing, asked what he desired. The arhat said, "I wish for you to grant me enough space within the lake to accommodate my knees." The dragon king then caused the water to recede and offered the space. The arhat used his supernatural power to expand his body, and the dragon king exerted his strength to shrink the water; the lake was emptied and the water exhausted, so the dragon turned and asked for the land back. The arhat left one pool for him to the northwest of this place, measuring over one hundred *li* in circumference; the rest of his kin were to dwell separately in smaller pools. The dragon king said, "The land of the lake has been entirely bestowed; I wish to provide offerings perpetually." Madhyāntika replied, "I shall soon enter parinirvāṇa without remainder; though I wish to accept your invitation, how would that be possible?" The dragon king requested again, "May five hundred arhats always receive my offerings until the Dharma comes to an end; after the Dharma has ended, I shall take back this country to serve as my dwelling lake." Madhyāntika granted his request. Once the arhat had obtained the land, he employed his great supernatural power to establish five hundred monasteries (伽藍). He purchased lowborn people from various foreign countries to serve as laborers and provide for the monastic community. After Madhyāntika entered parinirvāṇa, those lowborn people established their own rulers. The neighboring countries despised them for their lowly origin and would not associate with them, calling them Kṛīta (訖利多). At the present time, the spring water has largely overflowed. In the hundredth year after the Tathāgata’s nirvana, King Aśoka (無憂王) of the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) ascended the throne to rule the world, his majesty extending to distant lands. He deeply believed in the Three Jewels and cherished all living beings. At that time, there were five hundred arhat monks and five hundred ordinary monks, all of whom the king revered and supported without distinction. Among the ordinary monks was one named Mahādeva (摩訶提婆), who was broad-minded and highly intelligent; he sought out both fame and reality, and through profound contemplation, he composed treatises whose principles contradicted the sacred teachings. All who heard of them followed his divergent views. King Aśoka, unable to distinguish between the ordinary and the holy, sympathized with those he favored and sided with those he was close to; he summoned the community of monks to the Ganges River (殑伽河), intending to drown them in the deep current and execute them all. At that time, the arhats, being pressed by the threat to their lives, all exercised their supernatural powers, ascended into the void, and walked through the air, arriving in this country to dwell in the mountains and hide in the valleys. When King Aśoka heard of this, he was afraid; he came in person to apologize and requested them to return to their own country. Those arhats firmly refused to comply. King Aśoka built five hundred monasteries (僧伽藍) for the arhats and offered this entire country as a gift to the community of monks. King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王) of the country of Gandhāra (健馱邏國), in the four-hundredth year after the Tathāgata’s nirvana, responded to the times and assumed the mandate to rule; his royal influence spread far and wide, and people of diverse customs submitted to his authority. In his leisure from state affairs, he frequently studied the Buddhist scriptures and invited one monk each day to enter the palace to explain the Dharma. However, the various schools held different and divergent views, and the king was deeply perplexed, unable to resolve his doubts. At that time, the Venerable Pārśva (脇尊者) said: "Since the Tathāgata passed away, the years have grown distant; the disciples have formed different schools, and teachers have held divergent views, each relying on what they have heard and seen, and all contradicting one another." When the king heard this, he was deeply moved and grieved; after sighing in lamentation for a long while, he said to the Venerable: "By my humble remaining merit, I have followed in the footsteps of my predecessors; though far removed from the Sage, I am still fortunate. I dare not forget my own unworthiness, and I wish to promote and exalt the Dharma, explaining the Tripiṭaka in full according to the tenets of the various schools." The Venerable Pārśva said: "Your Majesty has planted roots of goodness in past lives and is richly endowed with blessings; that you should devote your mind to the Buddha-dharma is exactly what I desire."  The king then issued a decree to near and far, summoning the sages and philosophers. Thereupon, they converged from the four directions, traveling ten thousand *li* like shooting stars; the brilliant and the virtuous all gathered, and the wise and the holy assembled in full. For seven days, he provided the four requisites as offerings. Wishing to hold a council on the Dharma, he feared it would be noisy and chaotic. The king then expressed his intentions to the monks, saying: "Those who have realized the holy fruit may stay; those who are still bound by defilements shall return." Even so, the number remained large. He issued another order: "Those who are 'without learning' (aśaikṣa) may stay; those who are 'still learning' (śaikṣa) shall return." It was still too numerous. He issued yet another order: "Those who possess the three insights (te-vidyā) and are equipped with the six supernatural powers (ṣaḍ-abhijñā) may stay; all others shall return." Yet it was still numerous. He issued a further order: "Those who have internally mastered the Tripiṭaka and externally attained proficiency in the five sciences (pañca-vidyā) may remain; all others shall return." Thereupon, four hundred and ninety-nine men were obtained. The king wished to hold the assembly in his own country, as he suffered from its heat and humidity, and he also wished to go to the stone chamber where Mahākāśyapa (大迦葉波) had held the compilation at Rājagṛha (王舍城). The Venerable Pārśva (脇尊者) and the others deliberated and said: "That is not possible. There are many non-Buddhists there, and their divergent views are tangled and confusing; one would be too busy responding to them to have any energy to compose a treatise. The hearts of the assembly are set on this country. This country is surrounded by solid mountains, guarded by Yakṣas (藥叉), the land is fertile, and its products are abundant; it is a place where sages and saints gather, and where spiritual immortals (靈僊) roam and dwell." The assembly agreed with this, and all said: "This is appropriate." At that time, the king and the Arhats came from there, established a monastery, compiled the Tripiṭaka, and wished to compose the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (毘婆沙論). At that time, the Venerable Vasumitra (世友) was outside the door mending his robes. The Arhats said to Vasumitra: "Your fetters (kleśa) have not yet been eliminated, and your presence would disrupt our pure deliberations; you should depart to a distant place and not remain here." Vasumitra said: "You virtuous ones have no doubts regarding the Dharma and are spreading the teachings on behalf of the Buddha; you are now assembling the great meanings, intending to compose a definitive treatise. Although I am not clever, I have a rough understanding of the subtle words; I have also studied deeply the profound texts of the Tripiṭaka and the ultimate principles of the five sciences (pañca-vidyā), and have grasped their essence." The Arhats said: "One cannot speak like this. You should withdraw, quickly attain the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), and then join us; it will not be too late." Vasumitra said: "I regard the state of no-more-learning as no more than mucus or spittle; my ambition is to seek the fruit of Buddhahood and not to follow the Lesser Path." "I shall throw this ball of thread, and before it falls to the ground, I shall certainly realize the holy fruit of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa)." At that time, the various Arhats rebuked him again, saying, "This is what is called a person of excessive pride (abhimāna). The fruit of no-more-learning is praised by all Buddhas; you should realize it quickly to resolve the doubts of the assembly." Thereupon, Vasumitra (世友) threw the ball of thread, but the devas in the air caught the ball and pleaded, "You are destined to realize the fruit of Buddhahood and will succeed Maitreya (慈氏) as the most honored one in the three realms (traidhātuka) and the one upon whom all beings of the four births (catur-yoni) depend; why do you wish to realize the lesser fruit here?" When the various Arhats saw this event, they apologized for their fault, acknowledged his virtue, and invited him to be the chairman (sthavira), and whenever there were doubts or discussions, they all took his decision as final.  These five hundred sages first composed the *Upadeśa-śāstra* (鄔波第鑠論) of one hundred thousand stanzas to explain the *Sūtra-piṭaka* (素呾纜藏). Next, they composed the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (毘柰耶毘婆沙論) of one hundred thousand stanzas to explain the *Vinaya-piṭaka* (毘奈耶藏). Finally, they composed the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (阿毘達磨毘婆沙論) of one hundred thousand stanzas to explain the *Abhidharma-piṭaka* (阿毘達磨藏). In total, there are three hundred thousand stanzas and nine million six hundred thousand words, providing a complete explanation of the Tripiṭaka to be preserved for all eternity; they exhaustively explore every branch and detail, investigating both the shallow and the deep, so that the great principles are clarified once more, the subtle words are again revealed, and through their wide circulation, later students may rely upon them. King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王) then had the treatises incised on red copper plates, sealed them in stone cases, and erected a stūpa (窣堵波) to store them inside. He commanded the yakṣa (藥叉) spirits to guard the country, not allowing those of other schools to take these treatises out, intending that those who wished to study them should receive instruction within the country. When this work was completed, he returned with his army to his capital. He went out through the western gate of this country, knelt facing the east, and once again bestowed this entire country upon the community of monks. After King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王) had died, the Kṛta (訖利多) tribe again proclaimed themselves kings, expelled the monks, and destroyed the Buddha-dharma. The King of Himatala (呬摩呾羅) in the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國) was a descendant of the Śākya (釋種) clan. Six hundred years after the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa, he came to possess the territory and succeeded to the royal throne; he planted his heart in the Buddha-land and let his feelings flow into the ocean of the Dharma. Hearing that the Kṛta were destroying the Buddha-dharma, he gathered the brave and courageous men of his country, obtaining three thousand people, and disguised them as merchants. Carrying many precious goods and concealing weapons, they came and entered this country. The king of this country treated them with special courtesy. From among the merchants, he further selected five hundred men who were fierce and resourceful; each hid a sharp blade in his sleeve and, all carrying heavy treasures, they personally brought their offerings to present to him. At that moment, the King of Himatala removed his cap and took the throne. The Kṛta king was paralyzed with terror, whereupon he beheaded him and commanded the subordinates, saying: "I am the King of Himatala in the country of Tukhāra. I am angry at this base tribe for practicing tyrannical government, and therefore I have now executed the guilty one. As for all you common people, this is not your crime." However, he relocated the country’s ministers and officials to a foreign land. Having pacified this country, he summoned the monastic community, built monasteries, and settled the people as before. Furthermore, outside the western gate of this country, he knelt facing the east and offered the country to the monastic community. The Kṛta (訖利多) tribe had frequently caused the ruin of clans and the extinction of ancestral sacrifices on account of the monks, and for generations they had accumulated resentment and detested the Buddha-dharma. As time passed, they again proclaimed themselves kings. Therefore, at present, this country does not have much faith, and they pay special attention to the temples of the non-Buddhist devas.
The capital city of the country faces a great river to its west; it measures twelve or thirteen li from north to south and four or five li from east to west.

More than ten *li* southeast of the new city, north of the old city, and on the sunny side of the great mountain (Pravaragiri), there is a monastery with over three hundred monks. In its stupa is a Buddha’s tooth, about an inch and a half long and yellowish-white in color, which sometimes emits light on fast days. In the past, when the Kṛtīya (訖利多) race destroyed the Buddha’s Dharma, the monks dispersed, each living where they found it convenient. There was one śramaṇa who traveled through the various regions of India to observe and pay homage to the sacred sites, expressing his utmost sincerity. Later, hearing that his home country had been pacified, he set out on his return journey. He encountered a herd of elephants moving across the marshes, rushing about and roaring thunderously. Seeing this, the śramaṇa climbed a tree to avoid them. At that time, the elephants rushed together, vied with each other to suck up pond water to soak the roots of the tree, and then collectively pushed and dug at it until the tree finally toppled over. Having captured the śramaṇa, they carried him on their backs into a great forest, where a sick elephant lay suffering from a sore; it led the monk's hand to the afflicted spot, which had been pierced by a piece of withered bamboo. The śramaṇa then pulled out the bamboo, applied medicine, tore his robe, and wrapped the elephant's foot. Another large elephant brought a golden casket and gave it to the sick elephant, who, upon receiving it, passed it to the śramaṇa; when the śramaṇa opened the casket, he found it contained a Buddha’s tooth. The elephants surrounded him, and the monk had no way to leave. The next day at the time of the midday meal, they each brought exotic fruits to serve as his meal. After he had eaten, they carried the monk out of the forest, and only after traveling several hundred *li* did they set him down, whereupon each knelt in worship and departed. The śramaṇa reached the western border of the country and crossed a rapid river; when he reached midstream, the boat was on the verge of capsizing. Those sharing the boat said to one another, "The cause of this boat's impending disaster is this śramaṇa; he must possess a relic of the Tathāgata, and the dragons covet it." The boatman searched and indeed found a Buddha’s tooth. Then the śramaṇa held up the Buddha’s tooth and, looking down, said to the dragon, "I now entrust this to you, and shall return before long to take it back." He did not cross the river, but turned the boat back and departed; looking at the river, he sighed and said, "Because I lack the arts of subdual, I have been deceived by a dragon beast!" He went again to India to learn the methods for subduing dragons. After three years, he returned to his own country; when he reached the riverbank and set up an altar, the dragon then held up the casket of the Buddha’s tooth and presented it to the śramaṇa. The śramaṇa took it back and, at this saṃghārāma (伽藍), performed offerings.
More than ten li to the southeast of the new city, to the north of the old city, and on the southern slope of the great mountain (Pravaragiri), there is a monastery with over three hundred monks.

Fourteen or fifteen li to the south of the monastery, there is a small monastery containing a standing statue of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩). For those who vow to fast until death with the intention of seeing the Bodhisattva, he manifests his marvelous physical body from within the statue.

Traveling over thirty li southeast from the small monastery, one reaches the great mountain (Pravaragiri), where there is an old monastery. Its design was once magnificent, but it is now largely overgrown and in ruins, with only a small multi-storied pavilion remaining in one corner. There are over thirty monks, all of whom study the Mahayana teachings. Formerly, the śāstra-master Saṃghabhadra composed the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (順正理論) here. In the stūpas around the monastery, the relics of great arhats are preserved. Wild beasts and mountain apes gather flowers to offer them, never failing to do so throughout the year, as if following a command. There are many miraculous traces in these mountains, such as stone walls split horizontally or horse tracks left upon the peaks. All such phenomena, with their strange and unusual forms, are said to be the result of arhats and novices playing in groups, pointing and gesturing, or riding horses to and fro. Such traces are too numerous to describe in detail.

More than ten li to the east of the Buddha-tooth monastery, among the cliffs of the northern mountains, there is a small monastery where the great master of shastras Skandhila (索建地羅) once composed the *Abhidharma-prakaraṇa-pāda-śāstra* (眾事分毘婆沙論). In the small monastery there is a stone stūpa over fifty feet high, which contains the bodily relics of an arhat. Previously, there was an arhat whose physical form was immense, and all that he ate was equal to that of an elephant. The people of the time ridiculed him, saying, "You only know how to eat your fill; how could you understand right from wrong?" When the arhat was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he told the people, "I shall soon attain the state of no-remainder; I wish to speak of the wonderful Dharma that I have personally realized." When the people heard this, they mocked one another, yet they all gathered together to observe his success or failure. Then the arhat said to the people, "I will now tell you the original cause and condition. Prior to this life, I received the retribution of an elephant's body in East India, where I lived in the king's inner stable. At that time, there was a śramaṇa in that country who traveled far to India to search for the scriptures and treatises of the holy teachings. The king took me and gave me to the śramaṇa to carry the Buddhist scriptures, and in this way, I arrived here. Not long after, I died. By virtue of the merit accumulated through carrying the scriptures, I was born as a human. Furthermore, blessed with remaining fortune, I donned the dyed robes early and diligently sought liberation, never resting, until I attained the six supernatural powers and severed the desires of the three realms. However, regarding what I eat, the residual habit remains; I always restrain myself, eating only one-third of what I once did." Although there was this account, people still did not believe it. He then ascended into the void, entered the fire-light samādhi (火光定), and smoke and flames issued from his body as he entered parinirvāṇa; his remaining bones fell to the ground, and a stūpa (窣堵波) was erected over them.
Traveling over two hundred li northwest from the royal city, one reaches the Vikrītavana Monastery (商林伽藍), where the śāstra master Pūrṇa (布剌拏) composed the *Exposition of the Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (釋毘婆沙論).

Traveling one hundred forty or fifty li west of the city, to the north of a great river and the south of a mountain, one reaches a Mahāsāṃghika monastery (大眾部伽藍) with over a hundred monks. In the past, the Master of Śāstras Bodhila (佛地羅論師) composed the Mahāsāṃghika work *Tattvasaṃcaya Śāstra* (集真論) here.

From here, traveling southwest across mountains and through dangerous terrain for over seven hundred li, one arrives at the kingdom of Parṇotsa (半笯嗟國). The kingdom of Parṇotsa is over two thousand li in circuit. There are many mountains and rivers, and the arable land is narrow; crops are sown in their proper seasons, and flowers and fruits grow in abundance. There is much sugarcane but no grapes; fruit trees such as the āmra (mango), udumbara (cluster fig), and moca (plantain) are planted in groves by every household, as their flavors are highly prized. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs of the people are fierce and valiant. Regarding their clothing, they mostly wear cotton cloth. The people are honest and straightforward by nature, and they have pure faith in the Three Jewels. There are five monasteries, all of which are mostly dilapidated. There is no great sovereign, and the country is subject to the kingdom of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國). In the monastery to the north of the city, there are few monks. To the north of the monastery is a stone stūpa, which manifests many spiritual miracles.

From here, traveling southeast for more than four hundred li, one reaches the country of Rājapura (曷邏闍補羅國). The country of Rājapura is more than four thousand li in circuit. The capital city is more than ten li in circuit. It is extremely steep and secure, with many mountains and hills; the rivers and plains are narrow and confined, and the land is not fertile. The suitability of the soil and the sequence of the seasons are the same as in the country of Parṇotsa (半笯嗟國). The customs are fierce, and the people are brave and valiant. The country has no sovereign, being subject to the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國). There are ten saṃghārāmas, with few monks. There is one Deva temple, and there are many followers of heterodox paths. From the country of Lampāka (濫波國) to this land, the people’s appearance is coarse and ugly, their nature is vulgar and violent, their language is crude and base, and their sense of courtesy and righteousness is slight; this is not the proper territory of India, but a remote frontier with rustic customs. From here, traveling southeast, descending mountains and crossing rivers for more than seven hundred li, one reaches the country of Ṭakka (磔迦國).
