The country of Kanyakubja (羯若鞠闍國) is over four thousand li in circuit. The capital city borders the Ganges (殑伽河) to the west; it is over twenty li in length and four to five li in breadth. The city walls are solid and steep, with towers and pavilions overlooking one another; flower gardens and ponds are bright and clear as mirrors. Rare goods from distant regions are mostly gathered here. The inhabitants are prosperous and happy, and their households are wealthy. Flowers and fruits are abundant, and crops are sown in their proper seasons. The climate is mild and pleasant, and the customs are honest and simple. The people are refined in appearance and wear bright and elegant clothing. They are devoted to learning and skilled in the arts, and their discussions are clear and profound. Regarding the two paths of the heterodox and the orthodox, the number of believers is about equal. There are over one hundred sanghārāmas and more than ten thousand monks; they study both the Great and Small Vehicles with equal diligence. There are over two hundred deva temples, and several thousand followers of heterodox paths.  In the time when the people of Kanyakubja were long-lived, their old royal capital was called Kusumapura (拘蘇磨補羅). The king was named Brahmadatta (梵授); he possessed the accumulated merits and wisdom of the past, was fully accomplished in both civil and military affairs, his power intimidated Jambudvīpa, and his fame shook neighboring countries. He had a full thousand sons, who were wise, brave, magnanimous, and resolute; he also had one hundred daughters, who were beautiful in appearance and refined in manner.  At that time, there was a rishi living by the side of the Ganges who concentrated his spirit in meditative absorption for tens of thousands of years until his form resembled a withered tree. Migratory birds perched and gathered there, dropping a nyagrodha (尼拘律) fruit upon the rishi's shoulder; as summers went and winters came, it grew to provide shade with a trunk of great girth. After many years had passed, he rose from his meditation and wished to remove the tree, but fearing he might overturn the birds' nests, he desisted. The people of the time praised his virtue and called him the Rishi of the Big Tree (大樹仙人). The rishi cast his eyes along the riverbank and wandered through the thickets, where he saw the king’s daughters playing together. Desire for the realm of the senses arose, and a heart of attachment was born; he then went to the magnificent palace, wishing to make a formal request. When the king heard that the rishi had arrived, he went to welcome him in person and greeted him, saying, "The great rishi dwells in spirit beyond the material world; what has prompted this sudden visit?" The rishi replied, "I have dwelt in the forest and marshes for many years. Emerging from meditation to wander about, I saw the king’s daughters, and a heart of attachment was born; I have come from afar to make this request." Hearing his words, the king was at a loss for a plan and said to the rishi, "Return now to your dwelling; please wait for an auspicious day." The rishi heard this command and returned to the forest and marshes. The king then asked each of his daughters in turn, but none would consent to the marriage. Fearing the rishi’s power, the king became sorrowful and haggard. His youngest daughter, waiting for a break in the king’s affairs, calmly asked, "Father, you have a full thousand sons and ten thousand nations admire your virtue; for what reason are you so sorrowful, as if you are in fear?" The king said, "The Rishi of the Big Tree (大樹仙人) has deigned to seek a marriage alliance, yet none of you sisters are willing to obey. An immortal possesses great power and can bring about either disaster or fortune; if his heart’s desire is not met, he will surely fall into a rage, destroying the kingdom, ending our ancestral sacrifices, and bringing shame upon the late kings. Deeply contemplating this calamity, I am truly afraid." The youngest daughter replied, "To have caused this deep sorrow is our fault. I am willing to offer my humble self to preserve the prosperity of the state." Hearing this, the king was overjoyed and ordered a carriage to send her to him. Upon arriving at the immortal’s hermitage, the king thanked the immortal, saying, "Great Immortal, you possess supramundane sentiments yet deign to show concern for the worldly; I venture to offer my youngest daughter to serve you by sweeping and cleaning." The immortal was displeased upon seeing her and said to the king, "You must despise me as an old man to match me with one so unattractive." The king replied, "I have asked all my daughters, and none were willing to obey. Only this youngest one is willing to serve as a maid." The immortal was filled with rage and cast an evil curse, saying, "May the ninety-nine daughters all become hunchbacked at once; with their forms thus ruined and marred, may they remain unmarried for the rest of their lives." The king sent someone to verify this, and indeed, their backs were already hunched. From that time on, it has been called the City of the Hunchbacked Maidens (Kanyakubja).  The present king is of the Vaiśya caste, and his name is Harṣavardhana (曷利沙伐彈那). He rules over the land, being the third king of the second generation. His father’s name was Prabhākaravardhana (波羅羯羅伐彈那), and his elder brother’s name was Rājyavardhana (曷邏闍伐彈那). King Harṣavardhana succeeded to the throne by seniority and governed with virtue. At that time, King Śaśāṅka (設賞迦) of the country of Karṇasuvarṇa (羯羅拏蘇伐剌那國) in Eastern India often said to his ministers, "A virtuous ruler in a neighboring state is a disaster for one's own kingdom." Thereupon, he lured and invited him, and upon meeting, he killed him. Once the people had lost their ruler, the country fell into chaos. At that time, the high minister Bhaṇi (婆尼), whose position and reputation were of great weight, said to the officials and the populace, "The great plan for the country must be decided today. The son of the former king and younger brother of the deceased monarch is benevolent by nature and filial by heart; he is truly close to the virtuous, and I wish for him to succeed to the throne. What do you think of this matter? Each of you, state your intentions." The masses all looked up to his virtue, and there was never any dissenting opinion. Thereupon, the assistant ministers and officials all exhorted him to take the throne, saying: "May the prince listen to us; the late king accumulated merits and cultivated virtues, gloriously possessing the mandate of the state. The succession passed to the king, and we expected him to live out his full span of years; but his assistants were not good, and he was abandoned to the hands of his enemies. This is a great shame for the country, and it is the fault of us, your humble ministers. Public opinion and the rumors of the time rightly turn toward your brilliant virtue. If you were to preside over the land, recover the country from the enemy, wash away the shame of the nation, and glorify the legacy of your father, what merit could be greater than this? We hope you will not decline!"  The prince said: "The weight of national succession has been a difficult matter from ancient times to the present; the establishment of one in the position of a sovereign must be considered with great prudence. I am truly lacking in virtue, and now that my father and elder brother have passed away, if I were to be pushed to succeed to the great throne, would I be able to succeed in my duties? Although public opinion deems it appropriate, how could I forget my own insignificance? Now, on the bank of the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) river, there is an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩) which is highly responsive; I wish to go there to seek guidance."  He immediately went before the image of the Bodhisattva and, fasting, offered his prayers. The Bodhisattva, moved by his sincerity, manifested his form and asked: "What do you seek, that you are so diligent and earnest?" The prince replied: "I have only accumulated disasters; my compassionate father has passed away, and I have suffered this heavy, cruel punishment, with my benevolent brother being harmed. Considering myself lacking in virtue, yet the people of the country honor me and urge me to succeed to the throne to glorify my father's legacy. I am foolish and ignorant; I dare to hope for your holy instruction!" The Bodhisattva replied: "In a former life, you were an āraṇyaka-bhikṣu (練若苾芻) in this forest, and you were diligent and unremitting." "By the power of this merit, you have become this prince. Since the King of Karṇasuvarṇa (金耳國王) has destroyed the Buddha-dharma, you, in succeeding to the throne, should revive it. Let compassion be your aim and sympathy dwell in your heart, and you will soon be the ruler of the five regions of India. If you wish to extend the royal lineage, you must follow my instructions; you will be secretly aided by auspicious blessings, and there will be no powerful enemies in the neighboring regions. Do not ascend the lion throne, and do not assume the title of Great King." Thereupon, he received the instruction and withdrew. He immediately succeeded to the throne, calling himself Prince, with the title Śīlāditya (尸羅阿迭多). He then said to his ministers: "The vengeance for my brother has not been avenged, and the neighboring countries have not submitted; I shall not have a time to eat with my right hand. All you officials, be of one mind and exert your strength." He then gathered the national troops and trained his soldiers. He had an elephant corps of 5,000, a cavalry of 20,000, and an infantry of 50,000. Moving from the west to the east, he conquered those who would not submit. The elephants were not unsaddled and the men did not remove their armor; within six years, he brought the five regions of India into submission. Having expanded his territory, he further increased his military forces, reaching an elephant corps of 60,000 and a cavalry of 100,000. For nearly thirty years, no weapons were raised in war; the administration and instruction were peaceful. He diligently practiced frugality, seeking merit and cultivating goodness so earnestly that he forgot to sleep or eat. He ordered that no meat be eaten throughout the five regions of India, and if anyone took a life, they would be executed without pardon. Along the banks of the Gaṅgā (殑伽河), he erected several thousand stūpas (窣堵波), each more than one hundred feet high. In the cities, villages, streets, and crossroads of the five regions of India (Pañca-Indu), he established vihāras (精廬) to store food and drink and provide medicine, distributing these to travelers and the poor without ceasing. At every site of a sacred relic, he built a saṃghārāma (伽藍). Every five years, he held a great Pañcavārṣika assembly, emptying the royal treasury to bestow gifts upon all beings, withholding only the weaponry from his charitable offerings. Every year, he gathered śramaṇas (沙門) from various countries for a meeting lasting twenty-one days, during which he provided them with the four requisites, grandly decorated the Dharma seats and discussion halls, and had them engage in debate to assess their relative merits, praise the virtuous and criticize the evil, and demote the ignorant while promoting the enlightened. Those whose observance of the precepts was steadfast and whose moral character was profound were invited to ascend the lion seat, and the king would receive the Dharma from them in person. Those whose precepts were pure but whose learning was not grounded in the ancient texts were merely treated with respect to show them honor. Those who had no discipline and whose corrupt conduct was manifest were driven out of the country, as he did not wish to hear of or see them. If the minor rulers and assistant ministers of neighboring countries cultivated merit without ceasing and sought goodness without weariness, the king would take them by the hand to sit together and call them his "virtuous friends." If they were different from this, he would not meet them face-to-face, and if there were matters to be discussed, he would communicate through envoys. He toured the regions to inspect the customs and did not have a fixed residence, building huts to stay in wherever he arrived. Only during the three months of the rainy season, when there was much rain, did he not travel. At his temporary palaces, he would daily prepare fine food to feed one thousand monks and five hundred Brāhmaṇas of various schools. He divided each day into three periods: one period for managing affairs and governing, and two periods for cultivating merit and practicing virtue. He was diligent and tireless, feeling that the day was never long enough. Initially, I accepted an invitation from King Kumāra to travel from the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) to the country of Kāmarūpa (迦摩縷波國). At that time, King Śīlāditya (戒日王) was on a tour of inspection in the country of Kajuṅghira (羯朱嗢祇羅國) and commanded King Kumāra, saying: "You should come quickly with the guest śramaṇa from Nālandā (那爛陀) to attend the assembly." Thereupon, I went with King Kumāra to meet him. After King Śīlāditya had exchanged greetings, he asked: "From what country have you come, and what do you seek?" I replied: "I have come from the Great Tang (大唐) country to seek the Buddha-dharma." The king asked: "In what direction does the Great Tang country lie? What is the extent of the route, and how far is it from here?" I replied: "It lies more than several tens of thousands of li to the northeast of here; it is what the people of India call the country of Mahācīna (摩訶至那國)." The king said: "I have heard that in the country of Mahācīna there is a Son of Heaven, the Prince of Qin (秦王), who was perceptive and wise in his youth and has become divinely martial in his maturity. In the past, when the previous dynasty fell into chaos, the land was divided and collapsed, weapons and armor rose up in competition, and all living beings were poisoned by suffering. But the Son of Heaven, the Prince of Qin, early on cherished far-reaching strategies, aroused great compassion, rescued and saved all sentient beings, and pacified the world within the seas. His customs and teachings reached far and wide, and his virtuous grace extended to distant places; strange lands and foreign regions admired his transformation and declared themselves his subjects. The common people, bearing the burden of his nurturing, all sing the 'Music of the Prince of Qin Breaking the Battle Lines' (秦王破陣樂). I have heard of this elegant eulogy for a long time. Is the reputation of his magnificent virtue truly as it is said?" 'Is this the country of the Great Tang?' I replied, 'It is. Cīna (至那) was the name of the country under former kings; Great Tang is the title of the country under our current sovereign. Before he ascended the throne, he was known as the Prince of Qin; now that he has assumed the succession, he is called the Son of Heaven. When the destiny of the previous dynasty ended, the masses were without a master; weapons of war arose in chaos, and living beings were cruelly harmed. The Prince of Qin, endowed by Heaven with a broad and magnanimous nature, gave rise to a heart of compassion. His majestic influence stirred and spread, the various violent factions were exterminated, the eight directions were brought to peace and quiet, and ten thousand nations came to pay tribute. He cherished and nurtured the four types of birth, revered and honored the Three Jewels, lightened taxes and levies, and reduced punishments and penalties. Yet, the state’s resources remained in surplus, and the common people had no need for hidden shelters (Original note: meaning they were so prosperous they did not need to hide their wealth). His civilizing influence and great transformation are difficult to fully enumerate.' King Śīlāditya (戒日王) said, 'How magnificent! The living beings of that land are blessed to be moved by such a holy lord.'  At that time, King Śīlāditya was about to return to the city of Kanyākubja (曲女城) to hold a religious assembly, followed by hundreds of thousands of people on the southern bank of the Gaṅgā (殑伽河). King Kumāra (拘摩羅王) followed with tens of thousands of people, residing on the northern bank. They divided the river between them and advanced by both water and land. The two kings led the way, escorted by the four divisions of the army; some sailed in boats, others rode elephants, beating drums, blowing conches, and playing string and wind instruments. After ninety days, they reached the city of Kanyākubja, which is located in a great flower forest to the west of the Gaṅgā. At that time, more than twenty kings from various countries, having previously received the summons, arrived with the eminent śramaṇas, brahmans, officials, and soldiers of their respective kingdoms to gather for the great assembly. The King had previously built a great monastery (saṃghārāma) on the west side of the river. To the east of the monastery, he erected a precious terrace over one hundred feet high, in which was a golden Buddha image equal in size to the King’s own body. To the south of the terrace, he built a precious altar as a place to bathe the Buddha image. Fourteen or fifteen li to the northeast of this, he had separately constructed a temporary palace. It was then the month of mid-spring. From the first day to the twenty-first, he provided delicious food to all the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas. From the temporary palace to the monastery, pavilions were built along the sides of the road, exhausted of all adornments; musicians remained in place, playing elegant music in succession.  The King brought out a golden image from the temporary palace, hollow and embossed, over three feet in height; it was loaded onto a great elephant and covered with a precious canopy. King Śīlāditya (戒日王), dressed in the attire of Indra (帝釋), held a precious canopy and attended on the left, while King Kumāra (拘摩羅王) assumed the guise of Brahmā (梵王), holding a white fly-whisk and attending on the right. Five hundred elephant-mounted soldiers on each side, clad in armor, provided a protective escort, and one hundred great elephants preceded and followed the Buddha image, carrying musicians who played music and beat drums. King Śīlāditya scattered pearls, mixed jewels, and gold and silver flowers as he walked, making offerings to the Three Jewels. First, they proceeded to the precious altar to bathe the image with perfumed water; the King personally carried the image and escorted it up to the western terrace, making offerings of tens of hundreds of thousands of various jewels and kauśeya garments. At that time, only twenty-some śramaṇas were permitted to follow, while the various kings served as guards. Once the meal was finished, he gathered the various heterodox scholars to discuss subtle doctrines and clarify profound principles. As the sun approached dusk, the King returned to his temporary palace. Each day he escorted the golden image, with the procession following as before, until the final day of the assembly. Suddenly, a fire broke out on the great terrace, and smoke and flames began to rage at the gatehouse of the monastery. The King said: "I have exhausted the treasures of the nation to build this monastery in honor of my late father, so as to manifest his magnificent achievements; yet my lack of virtue has left me without protection, resulting in such a disaster—with such an omen of calamity, what is the use of living!" He then burned incense, made a ritual petition, and took a vow, saying: "By the grace of my past good deeds, I have become a king over all India; may the power of my merit extinguish this fire, and if there is no spiritual response, I shall lose my life from this moment forth!" He immediately exerted himself, leaped across the threshold of the gate, and as if he had extinguished it, the fire and smoke vanished. The various kings witnessed this miracle and their awe and fear increased all the more. Afterward, his expression remained unchanged and his speech was as usual; he asked the various kings: "Suddenly this disaster has occurred, and the work of the monastery has been reduced to ashes; what is in your hearts, and what are your thoughts?" The various kings prostrated themselves, weeping, and replied: "This magnificent achievement was hoped to be passed on to future generations; now that it is reduced to ashes in an instant, how could we not be grieved? Moreover, the various heterodox scholars are rejoicing in their hearts!" The King said: "Viewing it in this light, what the Tathāgata said is true. The heterodox scholars and those of different doctrines cling to the view of permanence, whereas only our Great Master teaches impermanence. However, my giving and renunciation have already been completed, and my heart’s wishes have been fulfilled; encountering this destruction, I have come to know once again the truthful teaching of the Tathāgata. This is a great good, and there is no cause for deep sorrow." Thereupon, he followed the various kings to the east, ascended the great stūpa, and looked out over the view. Just as he was descending the steps, a strange man suddenly appeared holding a blade to confront the king. The king, in that moment of peril, retreated up the steps, bent down to seize the man, and handed him over to his officials. At that time, the officials were in a state of panic and did not know how to step forward to assist. The various kings all requested that this man be executed, but King Śīlāditya (戒日王) showed no sign of anger and ordered that he not be killed. The king personally asked, "What have I done to wrong you that you would commit such a violent and evil act?" He replied, "Your Majesty’s virtuous grace is impartial, and both within and without the realm, all are indebted to you. However, I am mad and foolish; without considering the greater consequences, I was moved by a single word from the heretics to become an assassin and plot this treasonous murder." The king asked, "For what reason did the heretics harbor this evil intent?" He replied, "Your Majesty has gathered the various nations and emptied the treasury to provide for the śramaṇas and to cast images of the Buddha, yet the heretics who were summoned from afar have not been granted an audience, and they truly feel ashamed and humiliated. This led me, in my madness and folly, to dare to commit this treacherous act." Thereupon, the king investigated the followers of the heretics. There were five hundred Brahmins, along with other men of high talent, who had assembled by royal command; envious of the śramaṇas receiving the king's respect and honors, they shot fire-arrows to burn the precious terrace, hoping that in the ensuing chaos as people rushed to put out the fire, they could kill the Great King. Having found no other opportunity, they hired this man to rush into the narrow passage and assassinate him. At that time, the various kings and ministers requested the execution of the heretics. The king punished the ringleaders but did not incriminate the remaining partisans, banishing the five hundred Brahmins from the borders of India. Thereupon, he returned to the capital.  To the northwest of the city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata spent seven days here preaching various wonderful Dharmas. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. There are also small stūpas containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata.  To the south of the preaching stūpa, overlooking the Ganges (殑伽河) river, there are three monasteries (saṃghārāma) sharing the same wall but having separate gates. The Buddha images are magnificent and beautiful, the monastic community is solemn and respectful, and they employ over a thousand households of pure servants (karmadāna). In the precious casket of the main temple (mūla-gandha-kuṭī), there is a Buddha tooth, over an inch and a half long, of extraordinary radiance and changing colors, shifting from morning to evening. People from near and far flock there, and scholars and commoners gather in great numbers, daily amounting to a hundred thousand, to pay their respects. The overseers, troubled by the clamor and confusion, temporarily established a heavy tax, announcing to those near and far: "Those who wish to see the Buddha tooth must pay a large sum of gold." Nevertheless, the number of pilgrims remains vast, and they pay the gold tax with joyful hearts. On every fast day, it is brought out and placed on a high seat; hundreds of thousands of people burn incense and scatter flowers. Although the flowers pile up, they do not submerge the tooth casket.  To the left and right in front of the monasteries, there are temples (mūla-gandha-kuṭī) over a hundred feet high, with stone foundations and brick chambers. The Buddha images within are adorned with various jewels, some cast in gold or silver, others smelted from brass (鍮石). In front of each of the two temples, there is a small monastery. Not far to the southeast of the monastery, there is a large temple (mūla-gandha-kuṭī) with stone foundations and brick chambers, over two hundred feet in height. Inside is a standing image of the Tathāgata, over thirty feet high, cast in brass (鍮石) and adorned with various wonderful jewels. On the stone walls surrounding the temple, the deeds experienced by the Tathāgata while practicing the bodhisattva path are carved and painted, fully and exhaustively engraved. Not far to the south of the stone temple, there is a shrine to the Sun God (Āditya-deva). Not far to the south of that shrine, there is a shrine to Maheśvara (大自在天). Both are made of polished blue stone and are equally exquisite in their carvings; their scale and dimensions are the same as the Buddha’s temple. Each has a thousand households assigned to sweep and clean them, with drums, music, and singing continuing day and night without ceasing. Six or seven li to the southeast of the great city, on the south bank of the Ganges (gaṅgā), there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata stayed here for six months, teaching that the body is impermanent, suffering, empty, and impure. Beside it are the sites of the sitting and walking meditation of the four past Buddhas. There are also small stūpas containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata; if people are afflicted with illness, they circumambulate them with utmost sincerity and are sure to be cured, receiving their blessings.

Traveling southeast from the great city for more than one hundred *li*, one arrives at the city of Navadevakula (納縛提婆矩羅城). It is situated on the eastern bank of the Ganges (殑伽河) and measures more than twenty *li* in circumference. Flowery groves and clear ponds reflect one another. To the northwest of the city of Navadevakula, on the east side of the Ganges, there is a temple to a deva, with multi-storied pavilions and terraced platforms, featuring extraordinary workmanship and unique construction. Five *li* to the east of the city, there are three monasteries (saṃghārāma) sharing the same wall but having different gates, with over five hundred monks who all study the Hīnayāna Sarvāstivāda school. Two hundred paces in front of the monasteries, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. Although the base has collapsed and sunk, it is still over one hundred feet high; this is the place where the Tathāgata formerly preached the Dharma for seven days. Inside it are relics that occasionally emit light. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. Three or four *li* to the north of the monasteries, bordering the bank of the Ganges, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka. Formerly, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma here for seven days, at which time five hundred hungry ghosts (preta) came to the Buddha’s presence, heard the Dharma, attained understanding, and, abandoning their ghost bodies, were reborn in heaven. Beside the stūpa of the preaching of the Dharma are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. Beside that, there is also a stūpa containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata.

From here, traveling southeast for more than six hundred li, one crosses the Ganges (gaṅgā) river and arrives south at the country of Ayodhyā (阿踰陀國). The country of Ayodhyā is more than five thousand li in circuit. The capital city is more than twenty li in circuit. The grain crops are abundant, and flowers and fruits are lush. The climate is mild and pleasant, and the customs are virtuous and compliant; the people delight in performing meritorious deeds and are diligent in studying the arts. There are more than one hundred monasteries and over three thousand monks, who study both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings with equal effort. There are ten Deva temples, and those of heterodox sects are few.  Within the great city is an old monastery where the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (伐蘇畔度) spent several decades composing various treatises on the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Beside it are the old foundations of the hall where the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (世親) lectured on the teachings and expounded the Dharma for kings, eminent scholars from the four quarters, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas.  Four or five li to the north of the city, on the bank of the Ganges river, within a large monastery, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka. This is the place where the Tathāgata once preached the various wonderful Dharma teachings for the assembly of gods and men for three months. Beside it is a stūpa marking the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. Four or five li to the west of the monastery, there is a stūpa containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata. To the north of the hair and nail stūpa are the remaining foundations of a monastery where, in the past, the Sautrāntika master Śrīlāta (室利邏多) composed the Sautrāntika *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*. Five or six li to the southwest of the city, in a large mango grove, there is an old monastery; this is the place where the Bodhisattva Asaṅga (阿僧伽) sought instruction to guide the common people. At night, the Bodhisattva Asaṅga would ascend to the heavenly palace and receive the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra-śāstra*, the *Madhyāntavibhāga-śāstra*, and others from the Bodhisattva Maitreya; by day, he would expound their wonderful principles to the great assembly. One hundred or more paces to the northwest of the mango grove, there is a stūpa containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata. Beside it are the old foundations of the place where the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (世親) descended from the Tuṣita heaven to meet the Bodhisattva Asaṅga.  The Bodhisattva Asaṅga was a man from the country of Gandhāra (健馱邏國). One thousand years after the Buddha passed away, he was born, possessing a keen and brilliant mind. Following the tradition, he awakened to the Way, left home to study in the Mahīśāsaka school, and shortly thereafter turned his faith to the Mahāyāna. His younger brother, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, left home and received his training in the Sarvāstivāda school; he was widely learned and possessed a strong memory, having mastered the teachings and investigated their subtle mechanisms. Asaṅga’s disciple, Buddhasiṃha (佛陀僧訶), had a hidden practice that was unfathomable, and he was renowned for his high talent. These two or three sages would often say to one another, "In all our cultivation of religious practice, we aspire to behold Maitreya. If one of us should pass away first and succeed in fulfilling this long-held wish, he must return to report it so that the others may know where he has gone."  Later, Buddhasiṃha passed away first, but three years passed without a report. The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu subsequently passed away as well; six months went by, and there was also no report. At that time, the various heterodox teachers all mocked them, believing that the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu and Buddhasiṃha had transmigrated into evil destinies and thus lacked spiritual insight. Later, in the first watch of the night, as the Bodhisattva Asaṅga was instructing his disciples in the methods of meditation, the lamplight suddenly dimmed and the air became brilliantly illuminated. A celestial being descended through the void, approached the courtyard, and paid homage to Asaṅga. Asaṅga asked, "Why have you come so late? What is your name now?" He replied, "Upon departing from this life, I was reborn within a lotus flower in the inner assembly of Maitreya in the Tuṣita heaven. The lotus had just opened when Maitreya praised me, saying, 'Welcome, Vast-Wisdom! Welcome, Vast-Wisdom!' I had only just finished circling him when I came to report." The Bodhisattva Asaṅga asked, "Where is Buddhasiṃha now?" He replied, "When I was circling, I saw Buddhasiṃha in the outer assembly, indulging in sensual pleasures; he had no time to look at me, so how could he come to report?" The Bodhisattva Asaṅga said, "That matter is finished. What is Maitreya’s appearance like, and what Dharma does he expound?" He replied, "Maitreya’s marks and signs are so excellent that words cannot describe them. The Dharma he expounds is not different in meaning from this, yet the Bodhisattva’s wonderful voice is clear, fluent, harmonious, and elegant; those who hear it forget their fatigue, and those who receive it are never satiated." Forty-odd *li* northwest of the old foundation of Asaṅga’s lecture hall, one arrives at an old monastery facing the Gaṅgā river to the north. In it is a brick stūpa, over one hundred feet high, which is the place where the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu first generated the aspiration for the Great Vehicle. When the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (世親) arrived here from Northern India, the Bodhisattva Asaṅga (無著) instructed his disciples to go and welcome him. Upon arriving at this monastery, they met and held an audience. A disciple of Asaṅga stopped outside the window and, after midnight, recited the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* (十地經). Having heard this, Vasubandhu was enlightened and filled with remorse, realizing that this profound and wonderful Dharma was something he had never heard before; he felt that the sin of his slander originated from his tongue, and since the tongue was the root of his offense, he should now cut it off. He immediately took up a sharp knife, intending to cut out his tongue. Suddenly, he saw Asaṅga standing there, who told him: "The Mahayana teachings are the ultimate truth, praised by all Buddhas and revered by all sages. I intended to instruct you, but you have now attained enlightenment yourself. Since you have attained it at this time, what could be better? According to the holy teachings of the Buddhas, cutting off one's tongue is not true repentance. In the past you used your tongue to revile the Mahayana, so now you should use your tongue to praise the Mahayana; to make amends and start anew is still a virtuous deed, but what benefit is there in remaining silent and speechless?" Having spoken these words, he suddenly disappeared. Vasubandhu followed his instructions and did not cut off his tongue. At dawn, he went to see Asaṅga to receive instruction in the Mahayana. Thereupon, he applied himself to intensive study and profound reflection, composing more than a hundred Mahayana treatises, all of which were widely circulated and promoted.

From here, traveling eastward for more than three hundred li, one crosses the Ganges (gaṅgā) river and arrives at the country of Ayamukha (阿耶穆佉國). The country of Ayamukha is two thousand four or five hundred li in circuit. The capital city of the country borders the Ganges river and is more than twenty li in circuit. Its climate and soil conditions are the same as those of the country of Ayodhyā (阿踰陀國). The people are honest and their customs are simple; they are diligent in study and fond of merit. There are five monasteries with over one thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Sāmmitīya school of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). There are more than ten Deva temples, where followers of different paths live together. Not far to the southeast of the city, on the bank of the Ganges river, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, which is over two hundred feet high; it is the place where the Tathāgata once preached the Dharma for three months. Beside it are the sites of the sitting and walking-meditation traces of the four past Buddhas. There is also a stūpa of blue stone containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata. Beside it is a monastery with over two hundred monks; the Buddha images are adorned and majestic, as if he were still present. The pavilions and towers are magnificent, with unique structures rising up; this is where the master of treatises Buddhadeva (佛陀馱婆) once composed the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (大毘婆沙論) of the Sarvāstivāda school.

From here, traveling southeast for more than seven hundred *li*, crossing to the south of the Gaṅgā River and the north of the Yamunā River, one arrives at the country of Prayāga (鉢邏耶伽國). The country of Prayāga is more than five thousand *li* in circuit. The great capital city of the country is situated at the confluence of the two rivers and is more than twenty *li* in circuit. The crops are abundant and flourishing, and the fruit trees are lush and spreading. The climate is mild and pleasant, and the customs are virtuous and compliant. The people are fond of learning the arts and believe in the heterodox paths. There are two *saṃghārāmas* (monasteries), with few monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Hīnayāna. There are several hundred *deva* temples, and the heterodox sects are truly numerous.  To the southwest of the great city, in a grove of Campaka flowers, there is a *stūpa* built by King Aśoka. Although the base has collapsed and fallen into ruin, it still stands over one hundred feet high. In the past, the Tathāgata subdued the heterodox here. Beside it are *stūpas* containing hair and nail relics, as well as traces of where he walked. Beside the hair and nail *stūpas* is an old *saṃghārāma*, which is the place where the Bodhisattva Deva composed the *Śataśāstra-vaipulya* (廣百論) to defeat the Hīnayāna and subdue the heterodox.   Formerly, when the Bodhisattva Deva arrived at this *saṃghārāma* from South India, there was a heterodox Brahmin in the city who was renowned for his lofty arguments and possessed unimpeded eloquence; he would scrutinize names to demand reality and use counter-interrogations to exhaust his opponents' words. Knowing that Deva was widely versed in the profound and mysterious, and wishing to blunt his edge, he followed the logic of names and asked, "What is your name?" Deva replied, "My name is Deva (Heaven)." The heterodox one asked, "Who is Deva?" Deva replied, "I am." The heterodox one asked, "Who am I?" Deva replied, "A dog." The heterodox one asked, "Who is the dog?" Deva replied, "You." The heterodox one asked, "Who are you?" Deva replied, "Heaven." The heterodox one asked, "Who is Heaven?" Deva replied, "I." The heterodox one asked, "Who am I?" Deva replied, "A dog." The heterodox one asked, "Who is the dog?" Deva replied, "You." The heterodox one asked, "Who are you?" Deva replied, "Heaven." Through this cycle, the heterodox one finally awakened. From that time thereafter, he deeply respected his noble influence.

In the city there is a temple to a deity, adorned and resplendent, with many varied manifestations of spiritual power. According to its scriptures, this place is a supreme site for sentient beings to cultivate merit; to donate a single coin at this temple yields merit exceeding a gift of a thousand gold pieces elsewhere. Furthermore, those who treat life lightly and end their existence within the temple receive heavenly bliss and joy, eternal and inexhaustible. In front of the temple hall stands a large tree with luxuriant branches and dense foliage, where a man-eating ghost (piśāca) has made its home; consequently, many skeletal remains lie scattered around it. When people come to this temple, they invariably throw away their lives, being both intimidated by perverse doctrines and enticed by the deity; from antiquity to the present, this erroneous practice has continued without change. Recently, there was a Brahmin, a son of a noble clan, who was magnanimous, wise, perceptive, and highly talented; he came to the temple and said to the crowd: "It is difficult to guide and transform those with crooked customs and base minds; I shall first join them in their actions and then lead them to conversion." Having ascended the tree, he looked down and said to his friends: "I am about to die. What I once considered a deception is now proven true; heavenly beings and celestial music are in the sky to receive me, and I shall abandon this base form to follow them to a superior realm." He immediately sought to cast himself down to end his life, and though his friends remonstrated with him, his resolve did not waver. He spread out his clothes all around beneath the tree, and when he threw himself down, he remained unharmed and his body was preserved. After a long while he regained consciousness and said: "I only saw various deities in the sky summoning me; this was the lure of evil spirits, not the attainment of heavenly bliss."

To the east of the great city, where two rivers meet, the area is over ten *li* wide; the land is high and dry, covered with fine sand. From ancient times to the present, whenever kings and noble families have wished to perform acts of charity, they have all come to this place to distribute gifts without measure, and thus it is called the Grand Arena of Almsgiving (Mahādānapīṭha). The current King Śīlāditya (戒日王) continues the traditions of his predecessors and is devoted to the practice of charity; he accumulates wealth for five years and then, in a single day, empties his stores, gathering a vast quantity of precious goods at this arena. On the first day, a large statue of the Buddha is installed and adorned with various gems, and the most exquisite and rare treasures are offered to it. Next, offerings are made to the resident monks; then to the assembly present; then to those of high talent and profound learning, and those of broad knowledge and many skills; then to the disciples of non-Buddhist sects and those who live in seclusion; and finally to the widowed, the orphaned, the solitary, and the poor and destitute. Every kind of precious object is prepared and the finest foods are exhausted; in this graded order, everyone is provided for. Once the treasury is emptied and all clothing and ornaments are exhausted, he gives away the lustrous pearl in his topknot and the various necklaces on his body one after another, without the slightest regret. Having completed the distribution, he declares: "How joyful! All that I possessed has now been deposited into the indestructible treasury of the Vajra." Following this, the kings of various countries each offer him precious garments, and within ten days, his treasury is filled once again. At the confluence of the rivers to the east of the Grand Arena of Almsgiving, several hundred people drown themselves every day. The local custom holds that those who wish to be reborn in heaven should abstain from food and drown themselves at this spot, for by bathing in the middle of the current, their sins and defilements will be eradicated. For this reason, people from distant foreign lands flock here, fasting for seven days before ending their lives. As for the mountain apes and wild deer, they roam in groups along the riverbank; some return after washing in the current, while others fast until they die. During the great almsgiving of King Śīlāditya (戒日王), there was a macaque that lived by the riverbank, remaining alone under a tree, isolating itself and fasting, until it died of starvation after several days. Therefore, the various non-Buddhist ascetics (外道) who practice austerities plant tall pillars in the river. At the approach of dawn, they climb them, grasping the top of the pillar with one hand and one foot while stepping on a side peg, with the other hand and foot suspended and stretched out into the void, held straight without bending. They crane their necks and stare with wide eyes, watching the sun as it rotates to the right, and only when dusk falls do they descend. There are dozens of such followers who, hoping through this diligent suffering to escape the cycle of birth and death, have never slackened for several decades.

From here, traveling southwest into a great forest, one encounters fierce beasts and wild elephants that frequently attack travelers; unless one has a large retinue, it is difficult to pass through. Traveling more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Kauśāmbī (憍賞彌國). The country of Kauśāmbī is more than six thousand *li* in circumference. The capital city is over thirty *li* in circumference. The soil is described as fertile, the land is rich in produce, and there is much non-glutinous rice and abundant sugarcane. The climate is hot, and the customs of the people are fierce and impetuous. They are fond of learning and the arts, and they esteem and cultivate merit and goodness. There are more than ten *saṃghārāmas*, which are dilapidated and overgrown, with over three hundred monks who study the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). There are more than fifty *deva* temples, and the non-Buddhists are very numerous.  Within the old palace in the city, there is a large *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍) over sixty feet high, housing a sandalwood Buddha image with a stone canopy suspended above it, which was made by King Udayana (鄔陀衍那王). Miraculous signs appear from time to time, and divine light shines forth occasionally. Kings of various countries, relying on their strength, have wished to carry it away, but although they brought many people, none could move it. Consequently, they have sought to make offerings to it, all claiming to have obtained the true image; speaking of its origin and traces, this is indeed that very image.  Formerly, after the Tathāgata had attained perfect enlightenment, he ascended to the heavenly palace to preach the Dharma for his mother, remaining there for three months without returning. The king, longing for him, wished to have his likeness made. He then requested the Venerable Maudgalyāyana to use his supernatural powers to transport an artisan to the heavenly palace to personally observe the Buddha's marvelous features and carve an image from sandalwood. When the Tathāgata returned from the heavenly palace, the sandalwood image rose to greet the World-Honored One, and the World-Honored One consoled it, saying: "Have you been weary from the work of converting and guiding others?" "To guide and lead those in the final age, this is truly the hope." More than one hundred paces to the east of the *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍), there are sites containing the traces of where the four past Buddhas sat and walked. Not far to the side are a well and a bathhouse used by the Tathāgata; the well still provides water for drawing, but the bathhouse has fallen into ruin.

In the southeast corner of the city are the remaining foundations of an old residence, which was the former home of the elder Ghoṣila (具史羅長者). Within it are a Buddhist temple (精舍) and a stupa containing hair and nail relics. There is also an old foundation that was the bathroom of the Tathāgata. Not far to the southeast of the city is an old monastery, which was the former garden of the elder Ghoṣila. Within it is a stupa built by King Aśoka, over two hundred feet high. The Tathāgata preached the Dharma here for several years. Beside it are the seats of the four past Buddhas and the sites of their walking meditation, as well as another stupa containing the hair and nail relics of the Tathāgata. In a brick chamber on an upper story to the southeast of the monastery, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu once resided and composed the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (唯識論) to refute the Lesser Vehicle and challenge various non-Buddhist schools. In an Āmra (mango) grove to the east of the monastery is an old foundation where the Bodhisattva Asaṅga composed the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* (顯揚聖教論).  Eight or nine *li* to the southwest of the city is the stone cavern of the poisonous dragon. In the past, the Tathāgata subdued this poisonous dragon and left his shadow within it; although this is recorded in the chronicles, nothing can be seen there today. Beside it is a stupa built by King Aśoka, over two hundred feet high. Nearby are the sites of the Tathāgata’s walking meditation and a stupa containing his hair and nail relics; those suffering from illnesses who pray there are often healed. When the Dharma of Śākyamuni reaches its end, this country will be the last to remain; therefore, from the sovereign down to the common people, all who enter the borders of this country are naturally moved to sorrow, and there are none who do not weep and sigh before returning.

Traveling over seven hundred li through a great forest to the northeast of the dragon cave and crossing the Ganges (gaṅgā) River, one arrives at the city of Kāśapura (迦奢布羅城), which is over ten li in circuit and whose inhabitants are wealthy and happy. Beside the city is an old monastery of which only the foundations remain; this is the place where the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla once subdued the heretics. A former king of this country supported heterodox views and wished to destroy the Buddha-dharma while venerating the heretics. From among the heretics, he summoned a master of treatises who was intelligent, brilliant, and well-versed in subtle mysteries to compose a fallacious and heterodox work of one thousand stanzas, totaling thirty-two thousand words, to slander the Buddha-dharma and establish his own sect as the orthodox one. Thereupon, he summoned the assembly of monks and ordered them to engage in a debate. If the heretics were victorious, the Buddha-dharma was to be destroyed; if the assembly of monks were not defeated, they were to cut out their tongues in atonement. At that time, the monks, fearing defeat, gathered and discussed the matter, saying, "The sun of wisdom has already set, and the bridge of the Dharma is about to be destroyed. The king sides with the heretics; how can we oppose them? With the situation as it is, what plan can we devise?" The assembly was silent, and no one could offer a suggestion. The Bodhisattva Dharmapāla, though young in years, was eloquent, wise, and widely learned, with a character of great breadth. He spoke out in the midst of the assembly, saying, "Although I am not clever, I ask to present a brief proposal. It is truly appropriate that I should quickly respond to the king's command. If I win the high debate, it will be a spiritual blessing; if I am defeated in the inquiry, it will be attributed to my tender age. In this way, there will be an explanation whether I advance or retreat, and the Dharma and the Sangha will be without fault." Everyone said, "This is acceptable." He followed his plan, immediately responded to the king's command, and ascended the debate seat. The non-Buddhist (tīrthika) then laid out his main points, modulating his tone and meaning, and recited his own tenets, waiting for the opponent to raise objections. The Bodhisattva Dharmapāla (護法) accepted his words and laughed, saying, "I have already won! Will you recite them in reverse order? Or will you recite them in a confused manner?" The non-Buddhist was taken aback and said to him, "Do not be arrogant. If you can repeat the words in their entirety, that will be victory; accept the text as it is, and then explain its meaning." Dharmapāla then followed his intonation and recited the text and its meaning; his phrasing and logic were not in error, and his tone and rhythm were without discrepancy. Upon hearing this, the non-Buddhist wanted to cut out his own tongue. Dharmapāla said, "Cutting the tongue is not an apology; changing one's views is repentance." He then preached the Dharma for him, and his heart became faithful and his mind enlightened. The king abandoned his heterodox path and followed and honored the true Dharma. Beside the place where Dharmapāla subdued the non-Buddhist, there is a stupa (窣堵波) built by King Aśoka (無憂王); although its foundation has subsided, it is still over two hundred feet high. This is where the Tathāgata formerly preached the Dharma for six months. Nearby are the traces of his walking meditation (caṅkrama) and a stupa containing his hair and nails.

From here, traveling north for one hundred seventy or eighty li, one arrives at the country of Viśākha (鞞索迦國). The country of Viśākha is over four thousand li in circuit. The capital city is sixteen li in circuit. The crops are abundant, and flowers and fruits are plentiful. The climate is mild and pleasant, and the customs are honest and simple. The people are fond of learning without fatigue and are unswerving in their pursuit of merit. There are more than twenty monasteries and over three thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Sāmmitīya school of the Lesser Vehicle. There are more than fifty deva temples, and the followers of non-Buddhist paths are very numerous.  To the left of the road south of the city, there is a large monastery. In the past, the arhat Devaśarman composed the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra* (識身論) here, which argues that there is no self or person; the arhat Gopa composed the *Śāstra on the Essential Truth of the Holy Teaching* (聖教要實論), which argues that there is a self and a person. Because of this attachment to their respective doctrines, they engaged in deep debate. Furthermore, it was here that the bodhisattva Dharmapāla defeated one hundred masters of the Lesser Vehicle in seven days.  Beside the monastery is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka. In the past, the Tathāgata spent six years here preaching the Dharma and guiding the people. Beside the place where he preached is a marvelous tree, six or seven feet high; as spring and autumn succeed one another, it neither increases nor decreases. It is said that the Tathāgata once cleaned his teeth here and discarded the twig, which then took root and has remained lush to this day. Many people of wrong views and followers of non-Buddhist paths have vied to cut and destroy it, but it immediately grows back as it was before. Not far from there is the site of the seats and walking paths of the four past buddhas. There are also stūpas containing the hair and nail clippings of the Tathāgata. The sacred foundations are connected at the corners, and the forests and ponds reflect one another. Traveling northeast from here for more than five hundred li, one arrives at the country of Śrāvastī (室羅伐悉底國).

The country of Śrāvastī (室羅伐悉底國) is over 6,000 li in circuit. The capital city is desolate and ruined, and its boundaries are not clearly defined. The old foundations of the palace city are over 20 li in circuit; although it is largely ruined and overgrown, there are still inhabitants. The grain crops are abundant, and the climate is temperate. The customs are simple and honest, and the people are devoted to learning and fond of performing meritorious deeds. There are several hundred saṃghārāmas, most of which are in ruins, and the number of monks is small; they study the Sammatiya school (正量部). There are one hundred deva temples, and non-Buddhists are very numerous. This was the capital city governed by King Prasenajit (鉢邏犀那恃多王) during the time the Tathāgata was in the world. Therefore, within the old palace city, there are old foundations which are the remaining traces of the palace of King Prasenajit (勝軍王). Not far to the east, there is an old foundation upon which a small stūpa is built; this was the Great Dharma Hall that King Prasenajit built for the Tathāgata in the past. Not far from the side of the Dharma Hall, there is a stūpa on an old foundation; this is the site of the nunnery (精舍) of the Buddha’s maternal aunt, Mahāprajāpatī (鉢邏闍鉢底), which was established by King Prasenajit. To the east of this stūpa is the old residence of Sudatta (蘇達多). Beside the residence of the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada (善施長者) is a large stūpa; this is the place where Aṅgulimāla (鴦窶利摩羅) lived. Aṅgulimāla was a violent man of Śrāvastī. He harmed living beings and terrorized the city and the country, killing people to take their fingers to make a garland for his head. He was about to kill his mother to complete the count of fingers. The World-Honored One, out of compassion, set out to guide and transform him. Seeing the World-Honored One from afar, he secretly rejoiced and said, "I shall now certainly be reborn in heaven." "My former teacher gave me instructions, and his final words were these: 'If one harms a Buddha and kills his mother, he shall be reborn in the Brahma Heaven.'" He said to his mother, "Old lady, stay here for now; I must first kill that great śramaṇa." He immediately took up his sword and went to intercept the World-Honored One. The Tathāgata then retreated at a slow pace, yet the wicked Aṅgulimāla (指鬘) could not catch up even though he ran fast. The World-Honored One said to him, "Why do you cling to such ignoble intentions, abandoning the root of goodness and stirring up the source of evil?" At that time, Aṅgulimāla heard this instruction and realized that his actions were wrong; he then surrendered his life, sought to enter the Dharma, practiced with diligence and without sloth, and attained the fruit of an Arhat.

Five or six li to the south of the city is the Jetavana (逝多林), which is the Anāthapiṇḍada-ārāma (給孤獨園). The minister Sudatta (善施) of King Prasenajit (勝軍王) built a vihāra (精舍) for the Buddha; it was formerly a monastery (saṃghārāma), but now it lies in ruins. To the left and right of the east gate stand stone pillars over seventy feet high; the left pillar is topped with a carved wheel, and the right pillar is surmounted by the figure of a bull, both of which were erected by King Aśoka (無憂王). The buildings have collapsed, leaving only the old foundations, save for a single brick chamber that stands alone and imposing, within which is an image of the Buddha. Formerly, after the Tathāgata had ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to preach the Dharma for his mother, King Prasenajit heard that King Udayana (出愛王) had carved a sandalwood image of the Buddha, and he thereupon had this image made. The Elder Sudatta was benevolent and intelligent; he was able to distribute what he had accumulated, helping the needy and relieving the poor, and showing compassion to the orphaned and the elderly. People of the time praised his virtues and called him Anāthapiṇḍada (給孤獨, "the giver to the lonely and solitary"). Having heard of the Buddha’s merits, he developed a deep sense of respect and wished to build a vihāra, inviting the Buddha to descend and visit. The World-Honored One commanded Śāriputra to accompany him to survey the land, and they found that only the garden of Prince Jeta (逝多) was high and dry. He immediately went to the prince and explained his intentions in full. The prince said in jest, "If you cover it with gold, I will sell it." Upon hearing this, Sudatta’s heart was filled with joy; he immediately brought out his hidden gold and covered the ground as he had promised. There was a small portion left uncovered, which the prince asked to keep, saying, "The Buddha is truly a fertile field; it is fitting to plant good seeds." Thereupon, on the vacant land, they built the vihāra. The World-Honored One went there and said to Ānanda, "The garden ground was purchased by Sudatta (善施), and the trees were donated by Jeta (逝多); the two men, being of one mind, have together established this meritorious work. From now on, this place shall be called the Jetavana-anāthapiṇḍikārāma (逝多林給孤獨園)."  To the northeast of the Anāthapiṇḍikārāma is a stūpa, which is the place where the Tathāgata washed a sick bhikṣu. Formerly, when the Tathāgata was in the world, there was a sick bhikṣu who, enduring suffering, lived alone. The World-Honored One saw him and asked, "What is your suffering? Why do you live alone?" He replied, "My nature is lazy and slothful, and I cannot bear to look after the sick; therefore, I am now afflicted with illness, and there is no one to attend to me." At that time, the Tathāgata, feeling compassion, said to him, "Good man, I will now look after you." He stroked him with his hand, and his illness and suffering were all healed. He helped him out of the room, changed his bedding, personally washed him, and put new clothes on him. The Buddha said to the bhikṣu, "You should be diligent yourself." Hearing this instruction, he felt gratitude, and his heart was joyful and his body at ease.  To the northwest of the Anāthapiṇḍikārāma is a small stūpa, which is the place where Maudgalyāyanaputra (沒特伽羅子) exerted his supernatural power to lift Śāriputra’s (舍利子) robe and belt, but could not move them. Formerly, when the Buddha was at Lake Anavatapta (無熱惱池), humans and devas had all gathered, but only Śāriputra did not arrive at the assembly in time. The Buddha ordered Maudgalyāyana to go and summon him to join the assembly. Maudgalyāyana accepted the command and went; Śāriputra was mending his dharma-robe. Maudgalyāyana said, "The World-Honored One is now at Lake Anavatapta and has ordered me to summon you." Śāriputra (舍利子) said, "Wait a moment; I must finish mending this, and then I will go with you." Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅) said, "If you do not go quickly, I shall use my supernatural power to lift your stone chamber and take it to the great assembly." Śāriputra then untied his robe and belt, placed them on the ground, and said, "If you can lift this belt, my body might move." At that time, Maudgalyāyana exerted his great supernatural power, but he could not lift the belt; instead, the earth shook. He then used his supernatural foot-power to return to the place of the Buddha, where he saw that Śāriputra was already seated in the assembly. Maudgalyāyana bowed his head and sighed, saying, "Only now do I know that the power of supernatural abilities is not equal to the power of wisdom."  Not far from the side of the stupa (窣堵波) where the belt was lifted, there is a well. When the Tathāgata (如來) was in the world, water was drawn from it for the Buddha’s use. Beside it is a stupa built by King Aśoka (無憂王), which contains the relics of the Tathāgata. The sites of his walking meditation and the places where he preached the Dharma are all marked with banners and have had stupas built upon them. Deities and spirits stand guard, and miraculous signs appear from time to time; sometimes celestial music is played, and at other times divine incense is smelled. These auspicious blessings are difficult to describe in full.  Not far behind the monastery (伽藍) is the place where the non-Buddhist ascetics (外道梵志) murdered a courtesan to slander the Buddha. The Tathāgata possesses the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and omniscience; he is revered by humans and devas, and honored by sages and worthies. At that time, the various non-Buddhists consulted together, saying, "We should employ deceit and slander him in the midst of the crowd." They then enticed and hired a courtesan, pretending she was coming to listen to the Dharma, and once this was known to the public, they secretly murdered her, buried her corpse beside a tree, and lodged a complaint with the king. The king ordered a search, and her body was discovered in the Jetavana (逝多園). At that time, the non-Buddhists loudly proclaimed: "The great śramaṇa Gautama (喬答摩) constantly praises precepts and patience; yet now he has had illicit relations with this woman and murdered her to silence her. Having both fornicated and murdered, where are his precepts and where is his patience?" The devas in the sky followed their voices and proclaimed: "The wicked non-Buddhists have made this slander."  More than one hundred paces to the east of the monastery (伽藍) is a large, deep pit; this is the place where Devadatta (提婆達多), intending to harm the Buddha with poison, fell alive into hell. Devadatta was the son of King Droṇodana (斛飯王). He practiced diligently for twelve years and had already memorized the eighty thousand sections of the Dharma-store. Later, for the sake of profit, he sought to learn supernatural powers and associated with evil friends, consulting with them and saying: "My physical marks are thirty, not much less than the Buddha's; surrounded by the great assembly, how am I different from the Tathāgata?" Having thought this, he proceeded to cause a schism in the Sangha. Śāriputra (舍利子) and Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅子), following the Buddha’s instructions and relying on the Buddha’s spiritual power, preached the Dharma and offered exhortations, and the Sangha was restored to harmony. Devadatta did not relinquish his evil intentions; he placed a deadly poison under his fingernails, intending to harm the Buddha while performing an act of homage. As he was carrying out this plot, coming from afar and arriving at this spot, the earth suddenly split open, and he fell alive into hell. To the south of this, there is another large pit where the bhikṣu Kokālika (瞿伽梨) fell alive into hell for slandering the Tathāgata. More than eight hundred paces to the south of the pit of Kokālika, there is a large, deep pit, which is the place where the Brahmin woman Ciñcā (戰遮) fell alive into hell for slandering the Tathāgata.  When the Buddha was preaching the essential Dharma to humans and devas, a disciple of an externalist sect saw from afar the great assembly paying homage to the World-Honored One and thought to herself, "I must humiliate Gautama today and ruin his good reputation, so that my own teacher may alone possess a fragrant name." She then concealed a wooden basin tied to her belly and went to the Jetavana (給孤獨園), where she cried out in a loud voice before the great assembly, "This preacher has had illicit relations with me, and the child in my womb is of the Śākya clan." Those with wrong views all believed her, while those who were steadfast and firm knew it was a slanderous accusation.  At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, wishing to dispel the doubt, transformed himself into a white mouse and gnawed through the cord holding the basin. The sound of the cord snapping startled the great assembly, and all who saw and heard it felt a deep sense of joy. One person in the assembly stood up, held the wooden basin, and showed it to the woman, saying, "Is this your child?" At that moment, the earth split open of its own accord, and she fell in, her whole body sinking into the Avīci hell to suffer the full consequences of her actions.  These three pits are bottomless; during the heavy rains of autumn and summer, when ditches and pools overflow, no water ever remains in these deep hollows. Sixty or seventy paces to the east of the monastery, there is a *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍) more than sixty feet high, in which there is an image of the Buddha seated facing east. In the past, the Tathāgata debated with various heretics here. To the east of this is a deva temple, equal in size to the *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍). When the sun rises and sheds its light, the shadow of the deva temple does not cover the *mūla-gandha-kuṭī*; when the sun is about to set, the shadow of the *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* covers the deva temple. Three or four *li* to the east of the place where the shadow falls, there is a stūpa, which is the place where the Venerable Śāriputra debated with the heretics.  Initially, the elder Sudatta (善施長者) purchased the garden of Prince Jeta (逝多太子) and wished to build a *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* for the Tathāgata. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra accompanied the elder to survey the site. The teachers of the six heretical schools sought to compete in supernatural powers, but Śāriputra converted them according to the circumstances and subdued them in response to their challenges. Beside this, in front of the *mūla-gandha-kuṭī*, a stūpa was built; it was here that the Tathāgata defeated the various heretics and also accepted the invitation of Mother Viśākhā (毘舍佉母).  To the south of the stūpa where he accepted the invitation is the place where King Virūḍhaka (毘盧釋迦王) mobilized his army to slaughter the Śākya clan, and where he saw the Buddha and turned his army back. After King Virūḍhaka ascended the throne, he pursued his resentment over a previous humiliation, mobilized his army, and moved his great host. Once the deployment was complete and the orders were issued, he set out. At that time, a bhikṣu heard of this and reported it to the Buddha. The World-Honored One then sat beneath a withered tree. King Virūḍhaka saw the World-Honored One from afar, dismounted to pay his respects, and standing to the side, said, "Lush trees are spreading and thick; why do you not sit beneath them? Why do you dwell by a withered, rotten stump?" The World-Honored One replied, "One's kinsmen are like the branches and leaves. When the branches and leaves are in danger, where is the shade?" The King said, "The World-Honored One does this for the sake of his kinsmen; you may return." Thereupon, seeing the Holy One, he was moved with emotion, turned his army back, and returned to his country. Beside the place where the army turned back, there is a stūpa, which is the place where the Śākya women were slaughtered. When King Virūḍhaka had conquered the Śākyas, he selected five hundred women to fill his palace. The Śākya women were resentful and angry, and spoke insolent words of complaint, reviling the King, saying, "You are the son of a domestic servant." When the King heard this, he became enraged and ordered them to be slaughtered. The executioners obeyed the King’s command, severed their hands and feet, and threw them into a pit. At that time, the Śākya women, enduring their suffering, called upon the Buddha. The World-Honored One, with his holy insight, perceived their bitter agony and commanded the bhikṣus to gather their robes and go there to preach the subtle Dharma to the Śākya women, namely, that they were bound by the five desires, wandering through the three evil paths, suffering the separation of loved ones, and that birth and death are long and far-reaching. When the Śākya women heard the Buddha’s instruction, they distanced themselves from dust and removed their stains, attained the pure Dharma-eye, and at the same time passed away, all being reborn in the heavens. At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra transformed himself into a brāhmaṇa, collected their remains, and cremated them; later generations have marked the spot. Not far from the stūpa of the slaughtered Śākyas, there is a large dried-up pond, which is the place where King Virūḍhaka sank into hell. After the World-Honored One had observed the Śākya women, he returned to the Jetavana (逝多林給孤獨園) and told the bhikṣus, "Seven days from now, King Virūḍhaka will be consumed by fire." When the King heard the Buddha’s prophecy, he was filled with great fear and trepidation. When the seventh day arrived, he was peaceful and in no danger. The king, feeling jubilant, ordered the palace maidens to go to the riverside to enjoy themselves with music and wine. Still fearing that a fire might break out, he rowed upon the clear currents and drifted along with the waves. Suddenly, a blazing fire erupted, consuming the light boat; the king’s body fell, and he entered the Avīci Hell to undergo all manner of suffering.

Three or four li to the northwest of the monastery, one reaches the Wood of Regained Sight (Andhavana). There are traces of the Tathāgata’s walking meditation and places where various sages practiced concentration, all marked by trees and designated by stūpas. In the past, there was a band of five hundred bandits in this country who ran amok in the villages and acted lawlessly throughout the cities and states. King Prasenajit (勝軍王) captured them, gouged out their eyes, and abandoned them in the deep forest. The bandits, tormented by suffering, cried out in supplication to the Buddha. At that time, the Tathāgata was in the Jetavana Monastery (逝多精舍); hearing their cries of grief, he felt great compassion, and a gentle, cooling breeze blew medicinal herbs from the Snow Mountains into their eyes, whereupon their sight was immediately restored. Upon seeing the World-Honored One standing before them, they conceived the resolve for enlightenment, bowed in joyful worship, and departed after casting down their staves, which then took root there.

More than sixty li to the northwest of the great city, there is an ancient city; this was the birthplace of the Buddha Kāśyapa (迦葉波佛) during the Bhadrakalpa, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years. To the south of the city is a stūpa, which marks the place where he first met his father after attaining perfect enlightenment. To the north of the city is a stūpa containing the entire-body relics of the Buddha Kāśyapa. Both were built by King Aśoka (無憂王).

From here, traveling southeast for more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Kapilavastu (劫比羅伐窣堵國). The country of Kapilavastu is over four thousand *li* in circuit. There are more than ten empty cities, which are extremely desolate and overgrown. The royal city is in ruins, and its exact circuit is unknown. The inner palace city is fourteen or fifteen *li* in circuit; it was built of piled bricks, and its foundations remain steep and solid. Having been desolate for a long time, the inhabited villages are sparse and wide apart. There is no great monarch; each city has its own ruler. The land is fertile and rich, and crops are sown in their proper seasons. The climate is regular, and the customs are harmonious and pleasant. There are more than a thousand old foundations of *saṃghārāmas*. Beside the palace city, there is one *saṃghārāma* with more than three thousand monks who study the teachings of the Sammatiya school of the Lesser Vehicle. There are two temples to the gods, where followers of different paths live together.  Inside the palace city are the old foundations of the main hall of King Śuddhodana (淨飯王). A *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍) has been built upon it, containing a statue of the king. Not far to its side are the old foundations of the bedchamber of Queen Mahāmāyā (摩訶摩耶夫人). A *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* has been built upon it, containing a statue of the queen. The *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* beside it marks the place where the Bodhisattva Śākya descended into his mother’s womb, and inside is a representation of the Bodhisattva’s descent. The Sthavira school holds that the Bodhisattva descended into his mother’s womb on the night of the thirtieth day of the month of Uttarāṣāḍhā, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the fifth month here; the various other schools hold that he descended into his mother’s womb on the night of the twenty-third day of that month, which corresponds to the eighth day of the fifth month here. To the northeast of the place where the Bodhisattva descended, there is a *stūpa* marking the place where the sage Asita examined the prince. On the day the Bodhisattva was born, auspicious signs converged. At that time, King Śuddhodana (淨飯王) summoned the physiognomists and said to them, "This child has been born; what is his fortune, good or evil? You must examine him thoroughly and speak clearly in your reply." They said, "According to the records of the ancient sages and examining the auspicious omens, if he remains in household life, he will become a Cakravartin king; if he renounces the household, he will attain Samyak-saṃbuddha." At that time, the sage Asita (阿私多仙) arrived from afar and knocked at the gate to request an audience. The King was very joyful, personally welcomed and paid homage to him, and invited him to take a precious seat, saying, "I did not expect the Great Sage to visit today." The sage said, "While I was dwelling in peace and sitting at ease in the heavenly palace, I suddenly saw hosts of devas dancing. I then asked them, 'Why are you so extremely joyful?' They replied, 'Great Sage, you should know that the first lady of King Śuddhodana of the Śākya clan in Jambudvīpa has now given birth to a prince, who shall realize Samyak-saṃbodhi and perfectly illuminate all-encompassing wisdom.' Having heard these words, I came to pay my respects. What I lament is my decrepit old age, which will not allow me to encounter his holy transformation."  At the south gate of the city is a *stūpa* marking the place where the Prince competed in feats of strength with the other Śākyas and threw an elephant. The Prince was highly skilled in many arts, standing alone and peerless. King Śuddhodana, feeling joyful, was about to return, and a servant was driving an elephant, just about to exit the city. Devadatta (提婆達多), who had always prided himself on his great strength, came in from the outside and asked the driver, "You have prepared this elephant; who is going to ride it?" He replied, "The Prince is about to return, so I am going to serve as his driver." Devadatta, in a fit of anger, pulled the elephant, struck its forehead, and kicked its chest, causing it to fall dead and block the road, obstructing the path so that no one could move it, and the crowds were jammed. Nanda arrived later and asked, "Who killed this elephant?" They replied, "Devadatta." He immediately dragged it aside to clear the road. The Prince arrived and also asked, "Who did this evil deed and killed this elephant?" They replied, "Devadatta killed it to block the gate, and Nanda dragged it to open the path." The Prince then lifted the elephant and threw it high, over the city moat. Where the elephant fell to the ground, it formed a large, deep pit, which local tradition calls the Pit of the Fallen Elephant. In a *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍) beside it, a statue of the Prince has been made. Beside that is another *mūla-gandha-kuṭī*, which was the bedchamber of the Prince’s consort; inside are statues of Yaśodharā and Rāhula. In the *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* beside the palace, a statue is made in the posture of receiving instruction; this is the original site of the Prince’s schoolroom. At the southeast corner of the city is a *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* containing a statue of the Prince riding a white horse through the air, marking the spot where he leaped over the city wall. Outside the four gates of the city, there is a *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* at each, containing statues of an old man, a sick man, a dead man, and a *śramaṇa* (沙門). These represent the Prince’s excursions, where, upon seeing these signs, his concern deepened, he felt a profound weariness with the mundane world, became enlightened at these sights, and ordered his servant to turn the carriage back.

Traveling over fifty *li* south of the city, one reaches an ancient city containing a *stūpa*; this was the birthplace of the Buddha Krakucchanda (迦羅迦村馱佛) during the Bhadrakalpa, when the human lifespan was sixty thousand years. Not far to the south of the city is a *stūpa* marking the place where he met his father after attaining full enlightenment. To the southeast of the city is a *stūpa* containing the relics of that Tathāgata’s remains. In front of it stands a stone pillar over thirty feet high, on top of which is carved the image of a lion, with an inscription on the side recording the events of his *parinirvāṇa*; it was erected by King Aśoka (無憂王).

Traveling more than thirty li northeast from the city of Krakucchanda Buddha (迦羅迦村馱佛), one reaches an ancient great city.
