Traveling fifty or sixty li to the northwest of the great city, one reaches a great stūpa at the place where the Licchavis (栗呫婆子) bade farewell to the Tathāgata. When the Tathāgata was proceeding from the city of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐城) toward the country of Kuśinagara (拘尸那國), the Licchavis, hearing that the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, followed him, wailing and lamenting as they saw him off. Seeing that their sorrow and longing were so deep as to be beyond words, the World-honored One used his supernatural powers to create a great river with steep, precipitous banks and a rapid current; the Licchavis stopped there in bitter grief, and the Tathāgata left his almsbowl as a memento for them.

Less than two hundred li to the northwest of the city of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐城), there is an old city that has been desolate for a long time and has few inhabitants. Within it is a stūpa, which is where the Buddha in the past, for the sake of an assembly of bodhisattvas, humans, and devas, recounted his former births and his cultivation of bodhisattva deeds, having once been a wheel-turning king in this city named Mahādeva (摩訶提婆). Possessing the seven treasures, he ruled over the four continents. Upon observing the signs of decay and realizing the principle of impermanence, he became deeply contemplative and sought a higher path; he renounced his attachment to his exalted position, abandoned his kingdom to go forth into homelessness, and donned the dyed robes to cultivate and study.

Traveling fourteen or fifteen *li* to the southeast of the city, one reaches a great stūpa, which is the place where the seven hundred sages and saints performed the second council. One hundred and ten years after the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*, there were *bhikṣus* in the city of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐國) who had strayed from the Buddha-dharma and were practicing the disciplinary rules erroneously. At that time, the Elder Yaśoda was residing in the kingdom of Kosala (憍薩羅國), the Elder Sambhūta was residing in the kingdom of Mathurā (秣兔羅國), the Elder Revata was residing in the kingdom of Sahajāti (韓若國), the Elder Sālha was residing in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, and the Elder Kubjashobhita was residing in the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra (娑羅梨弗國). These great *arhats* had attained mastery of mind, were keepers of the *tripiṭaka*, had attained the three knowledges, possessed great renown, were known to the masses, and were all disciples of the Venerable Ānanda. At that time, Yaśoda sent messengers to inform the various noble sages that they should all assemble in the city of Vaiśālī. There was still one person missing, and the number of seven hundred was not yet complete. At that time, Kubjashobhita, using his heavenly eye, saw the great noble sages gathering to discuss matters of the Dharma and employed his spiritual foot-power to arrive at the assembly. Then Sambhūta, in the midst of the great assembly, bared his right shoulder, knelt on one knee, and proclaimed aloud: "Let the assembly be silent! Listen with reverence, attend with care! Long ago, the Great Sage, the Dharma King, skillfully and expediently entered *nirvāṇa*; although much time has passed, his verbal teachings still remain. The negligent *bhikṣus* of the city of Vaiśālī have erred regarding the disciplinary rules; ten matters have arisen that violate the teachings of Him who possesses the Ten Powers. Now, you noble ones, who deeply understand what is to be upheld and what is to be avoided, all having received the instructions of the great virtuous Ānanda, remember to repay the Buddha’s kindness and once again proclaim the holy decree." At that time, the great assembly was moved with grief; they immediately summoned the *bhikṣus* and, in accordance with the *Vinaya* (毘柰耶), reproached and restrained them, eliminated the erroneous practices, and clarified the holy teachings.

At that time, the Elder Yaśoda (耶舍陀) was residing in the country of Kosala (憍薩羅國), the Elder Sambhūta (三菩伽) was residing in the country of Mathurā (秣兔羅國), the Elder Revata (釐波多) was residing in the country of Sahajāti (韓若國), the Elder Sālha (沙羅) was residing in the country of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐國), and the Elder Kubjashobhita (富闍蘇彌羅) was residing in the country of Pāṭaliputra (娑羅梨弗國).

Traveling eighty or ninety li south from the place where the seven hundred sages and saints held their assembly, one arrives at the Śvetapura Monastery (濕吠多補羅僧伽藍), where the tiered terraces are magnificent and the multi-storied pavilions soar like birds in flight; the community of monks is pure and solemn, and they all study the Mahayana. Beside it are the sites of the traces where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation. Next to these is a stupa built by King Aśoka. This is the site where the Tathāgata, in the past, stopped to rest while traveling south to the kingdom of Magadha (摩揭陀國) and looking back north toward the city of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐城).

Traveling more than thirty li southeast from the Śvetapura (濕吠多補羅) Monastery, there is a stūpa on both the north and south banks of the Gaṅgā (殑伽) River; these are the places where the Venerable Ānanda divided his body between the two countries. Ānanda was the paternal cousin of the Tathāgata; he was learned and possessed of total retention, broad in his knowledge and strong in his memory. After the Buddha passed away, he succeeded Mahākāśyapa in upholding the True Dharma and guiding those who were advancing in their studies. While in the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國), he was walking in a forest when he saw a novice monk reciting a Buddhist scripture with erroneous chapters and sentences, and confused wording. Upon hearing this, Ānanda felt a growing sense of sympathy and longing; he slowly approached the novice and offered to correct and instruct him. The novice laughed and said, "The Great Virtuous one is senile; what you say is wrong! My teacher is brilliant and in the prime of his life; having received his instructions personally, there is certainly no error." Ānanda remained silent, withdrew, and sighed, saying, "Although I am aged, I have wished to remain in the world for a long time for the sake of all sentient beings, to uphold the True Dharma. However, the defilements of sentient beings are heavy, and it is difficult to instruct them with words; remaining for a long time is of no benefit, so I may as well quickly enter parinirvāṇa." Thereupon, he left the country of Magadha and headed for the city of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐城), crossing the Gaṅgā River and sailing in a boat midstream. When the King of Magadha heard that Ānanda was departing, his heart was filled with deep attachment to his virtue; he immediately prepared his military carriages and drove rapidly in pursuit to invite him back, with hundreds of thousands of people camping as an army on the southern bank. When the King of Vaiśālī heard that Ānanda was coming, his heart was filled with both grief and joy; he also mobilized his troops and raced to welcome him, with hundreds of thousands of people stationed as an army on the northern bank. The two armies faced each other, their banners and flags obscuring the sun. Ānanda, fearing that their troops would clash and kill one another, rose from the boat and ascended into the void. He manifested supernatural transformations and immediately entered into extinction (parinirvāṇa); he transformed into fire to consume his remains, and the remains then split in two, one part falling on the southern bank and one part falling on the northern bank. Thereupon, the two kings each obtained a portion; their entire armies wailed in grief, and they both returned to their respective countries to erect stūpas and perform offerings.

From here, traveling northeast for over five hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Vṛji (弗栗恃國). The country of Vṛji is over four thousand *li* in circuit, long from east to west and narrow from south to north. The land is fertile and rich, with abundant flowers and fruits. The climate is slightly cold, and the people are impetuous and hasty; they mostly revere non-Buddhist sects and have little faith in the Buddha’s Dharma. There are more than ten monasteries with fewer than one thousand monks, who study both the Great and Small Vehicles. There are several dozen *deva* temples, and the non-Buddhists are very numerous. The capital city of the country is called Zhan-shu-na (占戍挐), which is mostly in ruins. Within the old palace city, there are still over three thousand households, resembling a village or a town. To the northeast of the great river, there is a monastery where the monks are few but their academic standards are lofty.  Traveling west from here along the bank of the river, there is a *stūpa* over thirty feet high, bordered to the south by a long flowing stream; this is the place where the Great Compassionate World-Honored One converted the fishermen. In the time of the Buddha, five hundred fishermen had formed a group and joined forces to catch aquatic creatures. In this river, they caught a large fish that had eighteen heads, each with two eyes. Just as the fishermen were about to kill it, the Tathāgata, who was in the country of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐國), saw this with his divine eye and felt great compassion. Seizing the moment to transform and guide them, and using this opportunity to awaken them, he told the great assembly: "In the country of Vṛji there is a large fish; I wish to lead it to salvation in order to enlighten the fishermen, so you should know that the time has come." Thereupon, the great assembly surrounded him, and using their supernatural powers, they traversed the void and arrived at the riverbank, where they spread their seats as usual. He then told the fishermen, "Do not kill the fish." By his supernatural power, he opened a door of expedient means and extended his majesty to the great fish, enabling it to know its past lives, speak human language, and understand human sentiments. At that time, the Tathāgata, knowing the answer but asking anyway, said, "What sins did you commit in your previous life that caused you to wander through evil realms and receive this wretched body?" The fish replied, "In the past, by virtue of accumulated blessings, I was born into a noble family; I was the great Brahmin known as Kapittha (劫比他). Relying on my clan and lineage, I looked down upon and insulted others; relying on my extensive learning, I held the scriptures and the Dharma in contempt. With a haughty mind, I slandered the Buddhas, and with foul language, I abused the community of monks, comparing them to animals such as camels, donkeys, elephants, and horses, and other ugly forms. Because of these evil deeds, I received this wretched body. Yet, relying on my past roots of goodness, I have been born during the time of a Buddha, have witnessed his holy transformation, and have personally received his holy teaching." Thereupon, it repented and apologized, regretting its former deeds. The Tathāgata gathered and transformed it according to its capacity, guiding it as was appropriate. Having heard the Dharma, the fish then passed away. By the power of these blessings, it was reborn in the heavenly palace. There, it observed its own body and wondered, "For what reason was I born here?" Once it knew its past lives, it thought of repaying the Buddha's kindness and arrived with a host of heavenly beings. After completing its prostrations, it circumambulated the Buddha to the right, stood aside, and made offerings of heavenly gems, incense, and flowers. The World-Honored One pointed and spoke to the fishermen, preaching the wonderful Dharma to them. They were immediately awakened, expressed their sincerity in repentance, tore up their nets, burned their boats, returned to the truth, and accepted the Dharma. Having donned the dyed robes and heard the supreme teachings, they all emerged from the dust of defilement and together attained the fruits of sainthood.
The capital city of the country is called Cañśuma (占戍挐), and it is mostly in ruins. Within the old palace city, there are still over three thousand households, living as if in a village or a town.

To the northeast of the great river there is a monastery (saṃghārāma) with few monks, whose academic pursuits are pure and lofty. Proceeding west from here along the riverbank, there is a stūpa over three *zhang* high; to its south flows a long stream, and this is the place where the Great Compassionate World-Honored One converted the fishermen.

Traveling more than one hundred *li* to the northeast of the Duyu (Fisherman) country, to the west of an old city, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王), over one hundred feet high. It is the place where the Buddha in the past dwelt for six months, preaching the Dharma to save various gods and humans. One hundred forty or fifty paces to the north of this is a small stūpa where the Tathāgata in the past established the precepts for the bhikṣus. Not far to the west of this is a stūpa containing the hair and nail relics of the Tathāgata. At this place, in the past, people from near and far towns would gather together, burning incense, scattering flowers, and keeping lamps and torches burning without interruption.

From here, traveling northwest for one thousand four or five hundred li, crossing mountains and entering valleys, one reaches the country of Nepāla (尼波羅國). The country of Nepāla is over four thousand li in circumference and is situated within the snowy mountains. The capital city of the country is over twenty li in circumference. The mountains and rivers are connected; the land is suitable for grain and crops, and there are many flowers and fruits. It produces red copper, yaks, and jīvañjīvaka birds (命命鳥). For currency, they use red copper coins. The climate is cold and severe. The customs are treacherous and devious; the people are stubborn and fierce, and they hold faith and righteousness in low regard. They lack formal learning and arts, but they possess craftsmanship. Their physical appearance is ugly and wretched, and they believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. Buddhist monasteries (saṅghārāma) and Deva temples stand side by side. There are more than two thousand monks, who study both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings. The number of followers of non-Buddhist sects is unknown. The king is of the Kṣatriya Licchavi (栗呫婆) clan. His aspirations for learning are noble and lofty, and he has pure faith in the Buddha-dharma. In recent times, there was a king named Aṃśuvarman (鴦輸伐摩). He was a man of great learning and intelligence who authored the *Śabdavidyā-śāstra* (聲明論). He valued learning and respected virtue, and his fame was known both far and near. To the southeast of the capital city, there is a small pool of water; when a person throws fire into it, the water immediately bursts into flames, and if other objects are thrown in, they also turn into fire. From here, one returns to the country of Vaiśālī (吠舍釐國), crosses the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) to the south, and arrives in the country of Magadha.

The country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) is over five thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city has few inhabitants, but the towns have many registered households. The land is rich and fertile, nourishing crops; there is a unique variety of rice with large grains, an extraordinary fragrance, and a remarkable luster, which the local people call "rice for great personages." The land is low and damp, so the towns are built on high ground; from the end of early summer to the middle of autumn, the plains are covered with flowing water, allowing for the use of boats. The customs are honest and simple, and the climate is warm and hot. The people highly value the pursuit of learning and respect the Buddha-Dharma. There are over fifty monasteries and more than ten thousand monks, most of whom study the Mahayana teachings. There are several dozen *deva* temples, and followers of non-Buddhist paths are numerous.

To the south of the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) River is an old city, over seventy li in circuit; although it has long been deserted, its foundations still remain. In the past, when the human life span was immeasurable, it was called the city of Kusumapura (拘蘇摩補羅). Because there were many flowers in the royal palace, it was named accordingly. When the human life span reached several thousand years, the name was changed to Pāṭaliputra (波吒釐子城).  Initially, there was a Brahmin of high talent and broad learning who had several thousand disciples receiving instruction from him. As the students were traveling together for sightseeing, there was one young scholar who paced back and forth, looking melancholy. His companions asked him, "Why are you so worried?" He replied, "My prime of life is in its vigor, yet I am a traveler following my own shadow; years and months have accumulated, but my arts and studies have achieved nothing. Reflecting on this, my heart is filled with even greater sorrow."  Thereupon, the students jokingly said to him, "We shall now seek a marriage match for you." They then designated two people to act as the groom's parents and two as the bride's parents, and seated him under a Pāṭalī tree, saying, "This is the marriage tree." They gathered seasonal fruits, drew from the clear stream, set forth the sequence of the marriage rites, and requested a date for the happy union. At that time, the man acting as the bride's father plucked a flowering branch and handed it to the scholar, saying, "This is your fine spouse; I hope you will not decline."  The scholar’s heart was joyful and self-satisfied. At dusk, when it was time to return, he remained behind, filled with longing. The students said, "Our previous words were only a joke! You should come back with us. We fear that wild beasts in the forest might harm you." The scholar, however, remained and kept walking back and forth beside the tree. After the sun had set, a strange light illuminated the wilderness, and the sounds of strings and pipes were elegant and refined, with curtains and canopies set out in array. Presently, an old man was seen approaching with a staff to offer greetings, followed by an old woman leading a young maiden, with the road filled with attendants in splendid attire playing music. The old man then pointed to the maiden and said, "This is your wife." They indulged in singing and feasting for seven days. The students, suspecting that he had been harmed by wild beasts, went to search for him and found him sitting alone in the shade of the tree as if entertaining an honored guest. They urged him to return with them, but he declined and would not follow their instructions. Later, he entered the city himself, paid visits to his relatives and friends, and recounted the whole story from beginning to end. Those who heard this were astonished and went with his friends into the forest, where they all saw that the flowering tree had become a grand mansion, with servants and attendants hurrying to and fro, while the old man received them with composure, laying out a feast and playing music, with all the etiquette between host and guests fully observed. His friends returned to the city and reported the details to everyone, both near and far. After one year, a son was born. The scholar said to his wife, "I now wish to return home, yet I cannot bear to be separated from you; but if I continue to stay here, I am merely lodging in the open, exposed to the elements." When his wife heard this, she reported it all to her father. The old man said to the scholar, "In human life, one seeks pleasure; why must it be in one's native village? I shall now build a house for you; you should have no other intentions." Thereupon, a host of laborers was put to work, and the task was completed in no time. The capital was moved from the old city of Kusumapura (拘蘇摩補羅) to this town. Because of that son, the spirits built the city, and from then on, it was named the city of Pāṭaliputra (波吒釐子城). To the north of the old palace of the king is a stone pillar, several tens of feet high, which is the place where King Aśoka (無憂王) established a hell. One hundred years after the Nirvāṇa of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, there was a king named Aśoka, the great-grandson of King Bimbisāra (頻毘婆羅王), who moved the capital from Rājagṛha (王舍城) to Pāṭali (波吒釐) and built an outer wall encircling the old city. As the years have grown distant, only the old foundations remain. Of the monasteries, deva temples, and stūpas, there are several hundred remaining sites, but only two or three still exist. Only to the north of the old palace, bordering the Ganges (殑伽河), is a small city containing over a thousand families.  Initially, after King Aśoka succeeded to the throne, his conduct was harsh and tyrannical; he established a hell to harm living beings. Lofty walls rose steeply on all sides, with watchtowers standing tall at the corners; there were furnaces of fierce fire and sharp-edged weapons, with all manner of torture instruments prepared in imitation of the underworld, and a savage man was recruited to be the jailer. At first, those in the country who broke the law were all cast into this pit of fire, regardless of whether their offenses were light or heavy. Later, anyone who happened to pass by the prison was seized and executed; all who arrived there died, and thus the evidence was destroyed.  At that time, there was a śramaṇa who had newly joined the monastic order; while making his rounds in the neighborhood to beg for food, he happened upon the gate of the prison, and the cruel jailer seized him, intending to do him harm. The śramaṇa was terrified and requested permission to perform repentance. Suddenly, he saw a man who was bound and brought into the prison, where his hands and feet were cut off and his body was torn apart; in the blink of an eye, his limbs and torso were ground to pieces. Having seen this, the śramaṇa’s grief and sorrow deepened; he attained the contemplation of impermanence and realized the fruit of an arhat (無學果). The jailer said, "You may die now." The śramaṇa, having already realized the fruit of the holy (無學果), viewed life and death with equanimity. Although he entered the boiling cauldron, it was as if he were in a clear pond, with a great lotus flower serving as his seat. The warden of the prison was terrified and sent a messenger to inform the King. The King then came in person to observe and deeply praised this miraculous protection. The warden said, "Your Majesty must die." The King asked, "Why?" He replied, "Your Majesty previously issued a decree ordering me to oversee the prison, stating that all who reach the prison walls are to be executed; it did not say that if the King enters, he alone should be exempt from death." The King said, "The law has already been fixed, and in principle, it cannot be changed again. Since I issued the order first, how could I exclude you? That you have lived in excess for so long is my fault." He immediately ordered the jailers to throw him into a great furnace. Once the warden was dead, the King was able to leave. Thereupon, he tore down the walls, filled in the moats, abolished the prison, and relaxed the punishments.

Not far to the south of the hell is a stūpa. Its foundation is collapsed and sunken, leaving only the shape of an inverted bowl; it is adorned with precious substances and has stone railings. This is one of the eighty-four thousand. King Aśoka (無憂王) built it within the palace using human labor. Inside, there is one *dou* of the Tathāgata’s relics, and miraculous manifestations occasionally arise, with divine light shining from time to time.  After King Aśoka abolished the prison, he met the great arhat Upagupta (近護), who skillfully guided and transformed him according to his capacity. The king said to the arhat, "Fortunately, due to past merit, I occupy the position of the most honored among men, yet I lament these karmic obstructions that prevented me from encountering the Buddha’s teaching. Now, as the Tathāgata has left behind bodily relics, I wish to rebuild many stūpas." The arhat replied, "Great King, by the power of your merit, you can command all spirits, and with a heart of great vows, you protect the Three Jewels. This is a worthy wish, and now is the time." He then spoke extensively on the causes of offering earth and the Tathāgata’s prophecy regarding the merit of this construction.  Upon hearing this, King Aśoka was delighted. He summoned the spirits and commanded them, saying, "The Dharma King guides and benefits, and all sentient beings are fortunate. Relying on my past virtues, I have reached the pinnacle of honor among men. To honor the Tathāgata’s bodily relics, I am now rebuilding them for worship. You spirits must exert your strength and work with one heart! Throughout the borders of Jambudvīpa (贍部), wherever there are households numbering in the *koṭi*, you shall build stūpas using the Buddha’s relics. The intention originates with me, but the work is accomplished by you. I do not wish to possess the benefit of this supreme merit alone. You should each begin construction and await further orders." The spirits and deities received the command and set to work; once the work was completed, they all came to request further instructions. After King Aśoka (無憂王) had opened the various stūpas built by the eight kingdoms, divided their relics, and entrusted them to the spirits and deities, he said to the Arhat, "My desire is that the relics be enshrined in all these places at the same time. Although this is my wish, the matter has not yet gone according to my desire." The Arhat said, "Your Majesty should command the spirits and deities that on the appointed day, when the sun is obscured by a shape like a hand, that is the moment to enshrine the relics." The King accepted this instruction and proclaimed it to the spirits and deities. When the appointed day arrived, King Aśoka observed the sunlight; at high noon, the Arhat used his supernatural power to stretch out his hand and block the sun, which was witnessed by all at the construction sites, and at this very moment, the works were all completed.  Not far from the side of the stūpa, there is a large stone within a *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍) where the Tathāgata once stepped, and his twin footprints still remain; they are one foot eight inches long and over six inches wide. Both footprints possess the mark of a wheel, all ten toes are adorned with floral patterns, and the shape of a fish is clearly visible, emitting light from time to time. In the past, when the Tathāgata was about to attain extinction, he proceeded north toward the city of Kuśinagara (拘尸那城) and looked back south at the kingdom of Magadha (摩揭陀國); standing upon this stone, he told Ānanda, "I now leave these last footprints here as I am about to enter extinction, looking back at Magadha. One hundred years after my passing, there will be a King Aśoka who will rule the world, establish his capital in this land, protect the Three Jewels, and command the hundred spirits." When King Aśoka (無憂王) succeeded to the throne, he moved the capital and built a city, enclosing the stone with the footprints of the Buddha (周迹石) within it. As it was near the palace city, he constantly made offerings to it in person. Later, various kings competed to carry it away, but although the stone was not large, no one could move it. Recently, King Śaśāṅka (設賞迦王) destroyed the Buddha-dharma and went to the site of the stone, intending to obliterate the holy relic; however, after he chiseled it, the surface became smooth again and the patterns remained as before, so he threw it into the Ganges River (殑伽河), but it soon returned to its original place. The stupa (窣堵波) beside it is the site of the traces where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation.

Not far from the side of the Vihara of the Buddha’s Footprints (佛迹精舍), there is a large stone pillar over thirty feet high. The inscription is incomplete, but its general meaning is: "King Aśoka’s (無憂王) roots of faith were firm and solid; he thrice offered Jambudvīpa (贍部洲) to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and thrice redeemed it with various precious treasures." The text says that this is the general meaning. To the north of the old palace is a large rock chamber; from the outside it appears like a high mountain, and inside it is several zhang wide. It was built by King Aśoka for his younger brother who had left home to become a monk, by employing spirits and ghosts.  Originally, King Aśoka had a younger brother by the same mother named Mahendra (摩醯因陀羅). Born into the nobility, he wore clothing that usurped royal regulations and was extravagant and violent, causing the populace to harbor resentment. An old minister who assisted the state remonstrated with the King, saying: "Your arrogant brother’s abuse of power has already become too excessive. When government is equitable, the state is well-governed; when the people are harmonious, the ruler is secure. This is an ancient teaching that has existed for a long time. I hope you will uphold the state laws and hand him over to the law enforcement officials."  King Aśoka wept and said to his brother: "I have inherited the foundation of the ancestors and provide shelter to all living beings; how could I forget the affection for you, my own flesh and blood? Yet, because I did not guide you earlier, you have already fallen into the trap of the penal code. Above, I fear the spirits of my ancestors; below, I am pressured by the public outcry."  Mahendra bowed his head and apologized, saying: "I did not conduct myself with prudence and dared to violate the national laws. I pray you grant me a new lease on life by allowing a seven-day respite." Thereupon, he was placed in a secluded chamber and guarded strictly, with fine delicacies and superior food served to him without fail. The guard would call out: "One day has passed; six days remain." By the end of the sixth day, having felt deep anxiety and fear, he further exerted his body and mind, whereupon he attained the fruit of enlightenment, ascended into the void, and manifested divine miracles; soon after, he left the secular world to dwell far away in a rocky valley. King Aśoka (無憂王) went to him in person and said: "Previously, I was constrained by the laws of the state and intended to inflict a severe punishment upon you. Who would have thought that you would transcend the mundane, attain the holy fruit, and, being now free from all attachments, be able to return to the kingdom?" The younger brother replied: "Formerly, I was bound by the net of desire, my mind racing after sounds and forms; now that I have escaped the city of danger, my will finds joy in the mountain valleys. I wish to abandon the human world and dwell forever among the hills and ravines." The King said: "If you wish to quiet your thoughts and reflections, why must it be in a secluded cliff? I shall follow your will and build a retreat for you." He then summoned the spirits and deities and told them: "The day after tomorrow, I shall prepare a grand feast of delicacies; you shall lead one another to gather at my assembly, each bringing a large stone to serve as your own seat." The spirits and deities accepted the command and, when the time arrived, they all gathered. When the assembly had ended, the King said to the spirits: "The stone seats are scattered about; you should stack them up yourselves. Without the labor of construction, pile them into a chamber." The spirits and deities accepted the command and completed it in less than a day. King Aśoka went in person to invite him to stay in this mountain hut. North of the old palace and south of the hell, there is a large stone trough; it was through the divine labor of King Aśoka’s craftsmen that this vessel was created to store food when providing meals for the monks. To the southwest of the old palace is a small rocky mountain, and among its surrounding cliffs and valleys are several dozen stone chambers, which King Aśoka (無憂王) had built by employing spirits and deities for the sake of the arhat Upagupta (近護) and others. Beside them is an old terrace with remaining foundations of piled stone; there is a pond with rippling water, clear and limpid like a mirror, which people from neighboring countries and distant lands call the "holy water," believing that if one drinks from or washes in it, one’s sins and defilements will be eradicated. To the southwest of the mountain are five stupas; their lofty foundations have already subsided, yet the remaining sites are still high, and when viewed from afar, they appear as lush as mountain mounds, with each side measuring several hundred paces. People of later generations have rebuilt small stupas atop them. The *Record of India* (印度記) states: "In the past, after King Aśoka had built eighty-four thousand stupas, there still remained five *dou* of relics; therefore, he specially constructed these five stupas, with a design surpassing all other places, where miracles occur from time to time to represent the fivefold Dharma-body (五分法身) of the Tathāgata. Those of shallow faith secretly speculated and discussed among themselves, saying that it was King Nanda (難陀王) who had built this treasury to store his seven treasures. Later, there was a king who was not very sincere in his faith; hearing these earlier rumors, he gave free rein to his greed and desire, mobilized his army and generals, and came in person to excavate them. The earth shook and the mountains tilted, clouds darkened and the sun was obscured, and a great sound like thunder shook from within the stupas; the soldiers fell down stiff, and the elephants and horses fled in terror. From that time on, no one has dared to covet them." Some say: "Although there are many public opinions, none are definitive conclusions; by following the ancient records, one can obtain the truth."

To the southeast of the old city is the Kukkutārāma Monastery (屈吒阿濫摩僧伽藍), built by King Aśoka (無憂王). When King Aśoka first gained faith in the Buddha-dharma, he followed the teachings to build this monastery and cultivate the seeds of merit; he summoned a thousand monks, both ordinary and holy, providing them with the four requisites and a complete supply of daily necessities. Though it has long been in ruins, the foundation remains. Beside the monastery is a large stūpa named Āmalaka (阿摩落伽). This is the name of an Indian medicinal fruit. When King Aśoka fell ill and was on the verge of death, knowing his life could not be saved, he wished to renounce his treasures to cultivate a field of merit. However, powerful ministers held the reins of government and warned him not to follow his desires. Later, during a meal, he kept an āmalaka fruit and toyed with it until it was half-rotten; then, clutching the fruit and sighing deeply, he asked his ministers, "Who is now the lord of Jambudvīpa (贍部洲)?" The ministers replied, "Only the Great King." The King said, "That is not so. I am no longer the lord. Only this half-fruit is under my control. Alas! Worldly wealth and honor are more precarious than a candle in the wind. Though I held dominion over the realm and possessed the highest of titles, I am destitute at my deathbed, coerced by powerful ministers; the world is no longer mine, and all that remains is this half a fruit!" He then commanded an attendant, saying: "Take this half a fruit to the Kukkutārāma (雞園), offer it to the assembly of monks, and speak these words: 'The former lord of Jambudvīpa, now the king of half an āmalaka fruit, bows his head before the monks of great virtue and prays that you will accept his final offering.'" 'All that I possessed has been lost; only this half-fruit remains, over which I have a little freedom. May you have compassion for the destitute and increase the seeds of merit.'" The senior monk of the assembly spoke thus: "King Aśoka (無憂大王) long cherished the vow of universal salvation, but now he is afflicted by illness, treacherous ministers have usurped his authority, his accumulated treasures are no longer his own, and he offers this half-fruit as alms. We have received the King’s final command to distribute it to the entire assembly of monks." He then summoned the steward to boil it all in a soup. They collected the fruit’s pit and erected a stupa. Having received this great kindness, they commemorated his final instructions.  To the northwest of the Āmalaka Stupa (阿摩落伽窣堵波), in an old monastery, there is a stupa called "Sound of Striking the Ghaṇṭā (揵稚)." Originally, there were hundreds of monasteries within this city; the monks were solemn and respectful, their academic pursuits were lofty, and the non-Buddhist scholars kept silent and held their tongues. Later, the monks passed away one after another, and the younger generation failed to continue the practices of their predecessors. The non-Buddhist teachers and their disciples passed down their training until they had mastered their arts; they then summoned their companions by the thousands and tens of thousands to assemble at the monastery, shouting aloud: "Strike the ghaṇṭā and summon your scholars!" The ignorant crowd gathered together and mistakenly struck it. They then reported to the King, requesting a debate to determine who was superior. The non-Buddhist masters were of high talent and great learning, while the monks, though numerous, were shallow in their rhetoric and arguments. The non-Buddhists said: "Our arguments have prevailed. From this day forward, no monastery shall strike the ghaṇṭā to assemble its members." The King granted their request and enforced the rule based on the previous debate. The community of monks accepted the shame, endured the insults, and withdrew; for twelve years, they did not strike the ghaṇṭā. At that time, the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna (那伽閼剌樹那) of South India, who had been renowned for his elegance since childhood and had attained great fame in his maturity, renounced sensual desires, left home to study, delved deeply into the subtle principles, and attained the first bhūmi. He had a great disciple named Deva (提婆), who was wise, bright, and quick-witted; he said to his teacher, "The scholars of the city of Pāṭaliputra (波吒釐城) have been defeated in rhetoric by the non-Buddhists and have not struck the ghaṇṭā; time has passed swiftly, and it has been twelve years. I dare to wish to crush the mountain of wrong views and light the torch of the true Dharma." Nāgārjuna said, "The non-Buddhists of Pāṭaliputra are erudite, and you are no match for them; I shall go myself." Deva said, "To crush rotten grass, why must one overturn a mountain? I dare to accept your instruction to expel these heterodox scholars. May the Master establish the non-Buddhist doctrines, and I shall refute them point by point; after we have examined their strengths and weaknesses, I will then plan my journey." Nāgārjuna then upheld the non-Buddhist doctrines, and Deva refuted his logic accordingly; after seven days, Nāgārjuna lost his position and sighed, saying, "Fallacious words are easily defeated, and false doctrines are difficult to maintain. You may go now; you will surely crush them!" Bodhisattva Deva had long enjoyed a great reputation; when the non-Buddhists of Pāṭaliputra heard of this, they immediately assembled and hurried to inform the King, saying, "Your Majesty previously condescended to listen to us and prohibited the śramaṇas from striking the ghaṇṭā. We request that you issue a decree." "Order the gatekeepers not to allow any strange monks from neighboring territories to enter the city, for fear that they might form a faction and recklessly overturn the previous regulation." The King agreed to their words and strictly increased the watch. When Deva (提婆) arrived, he was unable to enter the city. Hearing of the restrictive order, he changed his clothes, folded his saṃghāṭī (僧加胝) robe and placed it inside a bundle of straw, then lifting his skirts and hurrying along, he entered while carrying the bundle on his head. Once inside the city, he discarded the straw and put on his robe, then came to this monastery (saṃghārāma) seeking a place to rest. As there were few people who knew him and no one to offer him lodging, he spent the night on the ghaṇṭā (揵稚) platform. At dawn, he struck it loudly. The crowd heard it and investigated, finding it was a traveling bhikṣu. All the monasteries echoed the sound in response. When the King heard of it and made inquiries, he could not find the originator until he reached this monastery, where everyone pointed to Deva. Deva said, "The ghaṇṭā is struck to assemble the community. If one has it but does not use it, why hang it up?" The King’s men replied, "Previously, the monastic community lost a debate, and it was decreed that it should not be struck; it has been twelve years." Deva said, "Is that so? Today, I shall sound the Dharma-drum once more." He sent word to the King, saying, "A strange śramaṇa wishes to wash away the previous shame." The King then summoned the scholars and established a rule, saying, "Whoever loses the debate and abandons their original school shall forfeit their life in atonement." Thereupon, the non-Buddhists vied to display their banners and drums, clamoring with heterodox doctrines, each showing off the sharpness of their rhetoric. Once the Bodhisattva Deva (提婆菩薩) had ascended the debate seat, he listened to their initial arguments and, following the logic of their points, dismantled them; in less than half a day, he had crushed all the heterodox schools. The king and his ministers were filled with joy and built this spiritual foundation to commemorate his supreme virtue. To the north of the Stupa of the Striking of the Ghaṇṭā (擊揵稚窣堵波) is an old foundation, which was the former dwelling place of the "Demon-Eloquent Brahman."  Formerly, there was a Brahman in this city who built a hut in a desolate thicket, withdrew from the world, worshipped ghosts to seek blessings, and consorted with demons. He engaged in profound discussions and intense debates, his elegant words responding to all inquiries; when people challenged him, he would answer from behind a lowered curtain. Among the scholars and men of talent of that time, none could surpass him, and the gentry and commoners alike looked up to him as if he were a sage.  There was a Bodhisattva named Aśvaghoṣa (阿濕縛窶沙), whose wisdom encompassed all things and whose path spread the Three Vehicles. He often said to others, "This Brahman has not received his learning from a teacher, nor does his art rely on ancient precedents; he lives in seclusion and solitude, yet he alone enjoys a high reputation. If he is not reliant on ghosts and spirits or possessed by demons, how could he be like this? His eloquence is derived from demonic instruction; he does not speak face-to-face with people, and once his words are heard, no one can repeat them. I shall now go to him and observe his conduct."  He then approached the Brahman’s hut and said to him, "I have long admired your great virtue. I hope you will be willing to raise the curtain, as I dare to express a long-held wish." However, the Brahman remained arrogant and haughty, responding from behind the lowered curtain and refusing to speak face-to-face. Aśvaghoṣa (馬鳴) knew in his heart that it was a demonic influence, yet he was very confident. After taking his leave and withdrawing, he said to the people, "I already know him; I shall certainly defeat him." He then went to inform the king, "I only hope you will grant me permission to engage that layman in a rigorous debate." Upon hearing this, the king was alarmed and said, "Who is this man! If one has not realized the three knowledges (三明) and possesses the six supernatural powers (六通), how can one debate with him?" The king ordered his carriage and went in person to observe the debate. At that time, Aśvaghoṣa discussed the subtle words of the Tripitaka (三藏) and expounded the great principles of the five sciences (五明); his marvelous eloquence was unrestrained, and his lofty arguments were clear and profound. After the Brahman had finished stating his case, Aśvaghoṣa spoke again, saying, "You have missed the gist of my argument; you should state it again." At that time, the Brahman remained silent and kept his mouth shut. Aśvaghoṣa scolded him, saying, "Why do you not resolve the difficulty? The demon you serve should quickly provide you with words!" He then swiftly lifted the curtain to observe the strange creature. The Brahman was terrified and said, "Stop! Stop!" Aśvaghoṣa withdrew and said, "This fellow’s reputation has collapsed this morning; empty fame does not last long—this is what is meant by that." The king said, "If not for a man of great virtue, who could discern the heterodox path? Such wisdom in knowing men is unparalleled in the past and future. The state has established customs; we should honor such genuine achievement."

More than two hundred *li* to the southwest of the city, there are the remains of a monastery. Beside it is a *stūpa* where divine light occasionally shines and miraculous signs appear from time to time; the masses, both near and far, never fail to offer their prayers there, for it is the site of the traces where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation.

Traveling southwest from the aforementioned monastery for more than one hundred *li*, one arrives at the Tiladha-vihāra (鞮羅釋迦伽藍). Its courtyards comprise four precincts, with pavilions and towers of three stories; the elevated terraces rise to a height of many *ren*, and the heavy gates open wide. It was built by a descendant of King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王). It summons those of high talent and extends a broad invitation to those of eminent virtue; scholars from foreign lands and elites from distant regions, being of the same inclination, flock together, arriving one after another. The community of monks numbers in the thousands, all of whom study the Great Vehicle. Facing the path at the middle gate are three *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍), topped with wheel-symbols and hung with bells that sway in the air. Below, they are built on tiered foundations with railings surrounding them, while the doors, windows, beams, pillars, walls, and steps are all adorned with inlaid gold and copper reliefs. In the middle *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* is a standing statue of the Buddha thirty feet high, with a statue of Tārā Bodhisattva to the left and a statue of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva to the right. All three of these statues are cast from brass; their majestic presence is awe-inspiring, and their spiritual insight reaches far. In each of the *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* there is one *sheng* of relics, which sometimes emit spiritual light and occasionally manifest miraculous omens.

More than ninety *li* southwest of the Tiladhaka Monastery (鞮羅釋迦伽藍), one reaches the great mountain of Pravaragiri (大山), where the clouds and rocks are dense and secluded, a dwelling place for spirits and immortals; venomous snakes and violent dragons nest in its marshes, and fierce beasts and birds of prey lurk in its forests. On the summit of the mountain is a large flat rock upon which a stūpa over ten feet high is built; this is the place where the Buddha entered into samādhi. In the past, the Tathāgata descended and stayed here, sitting upon this flat rock to enter the cessation samādhi (nirodha-samāpatti) for the duration of one night. The heavenly beings and holy spirits made offerings to the Tathāgata, playing heavenly music and raining down heavenly flowers. When the Tathāgata emerged from samādhi, the heavenly beings, moved by admiration, built a stūpa out of precious gems, gold, and silver. As the time since the Sage’s passing has grown more distant, the precious materials have turned into stone. From ancient times until the present, no human has ever reached it. Looking at the high mountain from afar, one sees strange phenomena: long snakes and fierce beasts moving in groups to the right, and heavenly immortals and holy spirits following shoulder to shoulder in praise and worship. On a ridge to the east of the mountain is a stūpa, marking the spot where the Tathāgata once stood to gaze at the land of Magadha (摩揭陀國) through which he had traveled.

More than thirty *li* to the northwest of the mountain, in a mountain recess, there is a monastery (saṃghārāma) with a lofty foundation backed against a ridge, and pavilions standing upon sparse cliffs. There are more than fifty monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna). This is the place where the Bodhisattva Guṇamati (德慧) subdued a non-Buddhist.  Formerly, there was a non-Buddhist in this mountain named Mādhava (摩沓婆), who took the Sāṃkhya (僧佉) school as his ancestor and practiced its path. His learning exhausted both internal and external doctrines, his words reached the limits of emptiness and existence, his reputation stood above his contemporaries, and his virtue was esteemed at the time. The king cherished and respected him, calling him the treasure of the country, while the ministers and commoners revered him, all calling him their master. Scholars from neighboring countries, hearing of his influence and admiring his virtue, ranked him among the foremost, truly a man of broad attainment. He was supported by the revenues of two cities, which surrounded his residence as a fief.  At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇamati of South India was quick-witted from his youth; he excelled early in subtle and profound matters, his learning mastered the Three Baskets (Tripiṭaka), and his reasoning exhausted the Four Noble Truths. Hearing that Mādhava’s theories were extremely profound and subtle, he harbored the intent to blunt his sharp edge, and ordered a disciple to write a letter saying: "I respectfully inquire whether Mādhava is well and at peace. You should set aside your weariness and toil to refine your old studies, for after three years, I shall destroy your fine reputation."  In this manner, during the second and third years, he sent a messenger to notify him each time. When he was about to set out, he wrote another letter saying: "The time limit has expired; how are your studies? I am arriving now; you should be aware of this." Mādhava was filled with great fear and warned his disciples and the inhabitants of his town: "From this day forward, you must not provide lodging to any śramaṇas or followers of heterodox paths; spread this word among yourselves and do not violate this command." At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇamati (德慧) came carrying his staff and reached the town of Mādhava (摩沓婆邑). The people kept their agreement, and no one would offer him lodging. The Brahmins further reviled him, saying: "With your shaven head and strange attire, how are you different from a non-human? You should leave quickly; do not stop here!" The Bodhisattva Guṇamati, wishing to defeat the heterodox paths and hoping to lodge in the town, spoke with a compassionate heart and humble words, saying: "You all practice the pure conduct of worldly truth, while I practice the pure conduct of ultimate truth; since our pure conduct is the same, why do you reject me?" The Brahmins would not speak to him, but only busied themselves with driving him away. They drove him out of the town and into a great forest. In the forest, packs of fierce beasts acted with violence. A man of pure faith, fearing he might be harmed by the beasts, bound together a torch and took up a staff, saying to the Bodhisattva: "There is a Bodhisattva Guṇamati of South India whose reputation has spread far and wide, and who intends to come here for a debate; therefore, the lord of this town, fearing the loss of his good name, has strictly decreed that no śramaṇa be allowed to stay. Fearing you might be harmed by the creatures, I have come to assist you. Go now and be at peace; have no other worries." Guṇamati said: "I must tell you, pure believer, that I am Guṇamati." Having heard this, the pure believer showed even deeper respect and said to Guṇamati: "Since it is as you say, you should depart quickly." He then left the deep forest and rested in an empty marsh. The pure believer lit a fire and held his bow, patrolling around him. When the night had ended, he said to Guṇamati: "You may go now, for I fear people may hear of this and come to harm you." Guṇamati thanked him, saying, "I shall not forget your kindness." He then departed. Upon arriving at the royal palace, he said to the gatekeeper, "There is a śramaṇa who has come from afar; he requests the king’s gracious permission to debate with Mādhava (摩沓婆)." Hearing this, the king was startled and said, "This is but a deluded man." He immediately ordered an envoy to go to Mādhava’s residence to proclaim the royal decree, saying, "An extraordinary śramaṇa has come seeking a debate. The debate hall has now been cleansed and prepared, and an announcement has been sent out far and near; we await your arrival and hope you will grace us with your presence."  Mādhava asked the king’s envoy, "Is it not the Śāstra Master Guṇamati (德慧論師) of South India?" The envoy replied, "It is." Upon hearing this, Mādhava was very displeased, but as the matter was difficult to decline, he proceeded to the debate hall. The king, ministers, scholars, commoners, and the nobility all gathered to listen to the profound discourse. Guṇamati first established his thesis. By the time the sun had set, Mādhava excused himself on the grounds of his advanced age and the dullness of his wit in responding quickly, requesting to return home to reflect in silence so that he might respond to the challenges the next day. Every matter was deferred until the next day, but when he ascended the seat at dawn, he ultimately offered no different arguments. On the sixth day, he vomited blood and died. As he was about to expire, he looked at his wife and commanded, "You possess great talent; do not forget this shame!"  After Mādhava died, his death was concealed and not announced. His wife changed into fresh, elegant attire and came to the debate hall. The crowd broke into a hubbub, saying to one another, "Mādhava is conceited about his own talent and is ashamed to face Guṇamati, so he has sent his wife instead; the difference in their caliber is now clear." Guṇamati Bodhisattva (德慧菩薩) said to his wife, "The one who could control you, I have already subdued." Mādhava’s wife, realizing the difficulty, withdrew. The King asked, "What was said in such secrecy that she then fell silent?" Guṇamati replied, "Alas, Mādhava is dead! His wife intended to come and debate with me." The King asked, "How did you know this? I wish you would explain it to me." Guṇamati said, "When his wife came, her face bore the look of mourning and her voice was filled with grief and resentment; therefore, I knew that Mādhava was dead. By 'the one who could control you,' I meant her husband." The King ordered an envoy to go and observe, and it was indeed as he had discussed. The King then apologized, saying, "The Buddha-Dharma is profound and mysterious; brilliant sages follow in succession. By practicing non-action and guarding the Way, all sentient beings are moistened by its transformation. According to the ancient laws of the state, virtue is always rewarded." Guṇamati said, "Though I am ignorant, I embody the Way and dwell in purity. If one maintains integrity and seeks to benefit others, then to promote and guide them, one must first crush their arrogance. As for using expedient means to gather and transform them, now is the time. I only wish that Your Majesty would assign the descendants of the households in Mādhava’s fief to serve the monastery for a thousand generations, so as to leave a warning for future ages and spread this fame boundlessly. May those with pure faith who provide protection have their merit extended throughout the world, and may their food and provisions be the same as the monks', so as to encourage the pure-hearted and praise great virtue." Thereupon, this monastery was built to commemorate this remarkable event. Initially, after Mādhava was defeated in debate, more than ten Brahmacārins (淨行) fled to a neighboring country to escape the disgrace, where they informed the various non-Buddhists of their humiliation and recruited talented individuals to come and wash away their former shame. Since the king esteemed and respected Guṇamati (德慧), he went in person to request him, saying: "Now these non-Buddhists, overestimating their own strength, have formed a clique and dared to sound the drum of debate; I only wish that the Great Master would crush these heterodox sects." Guṇamati replied: "It is appropriate to assemble the debaters." Thereupon, the non-Buddhist scholars comforted one another with joy, saying: "Today, we are certain to be victorious over him!" When the non-Buddhists began to expound their doctrines, Guṇamati Bodhisattva said: "These non-Buddhists have fled from afar to take refuge here; according to the king's prior decree, they are all outcasts, so how can I engage in a debate with them?" Guṇamati had a seat-carrier (負座竪) who had long listened to various debates and was quite familiar with the subtle principles; he stood by his side, listening to their lofty discourse. Guṇamati patted his seat and said: "Seat, you may debate with them." The assembly was entirely shocked and surprised by his command. At that time, the seat-carrier immediately initiated the challenge; profound meanings gushed forth like a spring, and his clear eloquence responded to every point. After three rounds of debate, the non-Buddhists lost their tenets; their sharpness was severely blunted, and their wings were broken. Ever since they were defeated in debate, they have been established as the monastery’s village households.

More than twenty *li* southwest of the Guṇamati (德慧) monastery, one arrives at the Vyāsa (孤山) mountain. There is a monastery here that the master of treatises Śīlabhadra (尸羅跋陀羅) built after winning a debate, donating his village for its construction. A single precipitous peak rises up like a stūpa, where Buddha relics are enshrined. The master of treatises was of the royal lineage of the country of Samataṭa (三摩呾吒國) and of the Brāhmaṇa caste. In his youth, he was fond of learning and possessed noble character; he traveled throughout the various Indias, inquiring after the wise and sagacious. Upon arriving at the Nālandā (那爛陀) monastery in this country, he met the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla (護法), and upon hearing the Dharma, he gained faith and awakening. He requested to don the dyed robes, consulted him on the ultimate goal, and asked about the path to liberation. Having exhausted the highest truths and investigated the subtle words, his fame dominated the era and his reputation was high in foreign lands.  In South India, there was a non-Buddhist who explored the obscure and searched for the hidden, exhausting the profound and penetrating the subtle. Hearing of Dharmapāla’s high fame, he conceived deep arrogance and jealousy, and undeterred by mountains or rivers, he beat the drum to demand a debate, saying: "I am a man of South India. I have heard that there is a great master of treatises within this kingdom; although I am not clever, I wish to discuss matters with him in detail." The king said: "It is so; it is truly as you say." He then ordered an envoy to invite Dharmapāla, saying: "A non-Buddhist from South India has come from a distance of a thousand *li* to seek a debate; I only hope you will condescend to attend the assembly at the debate ground." Having heard this, Dharmapāla gathered his robes and prepared to go. His disciple Śīlabhadra (戒賢), who was the most outstanding among the younger generation, stepped forward and requested: "Why must you go so hastily?" Dharmapāla said: "Since the Sun of Wisdom has hidden its radiance and the Lamp of the Dharma has ceased its illumination, non-Buddhists have gathered like ants and heterodox schools have swarmed like wasps; therefore, I now intend to demolish their arguments." Śīlabhadra (戒賢) said: "I humbly request to hear the remaining arguments and dare to demolish the heterodox path." Dharmapāla knew that he was a man of outstanding talent and therefore granted his consent. At that time, Śīlabhadra was just thirty years old, and the assembly slighted his youth, fearing he would be unable to shoulder the task alone. Dharmapāla, knowing the dissatisfaction of the assembly, explained to them: "What is valued is brilliance and wisdom, not one's age; judging by the present, he will certainly defeat them." When the day of the debate arrived, people from far and near flocked to the scene, and both young and old gathered together. The non-Buddhist expounded his great principles, exhausting their profound subtleties; Śīlabhadra followed reason to demand the truth, reaching the depths of the abstruse. The non-Buddhist’s arguments were exhausted, and he retreated in shame. The king, wishing to reward his virtue, bestowed this city upon him. The Master of Shastras declined, saying: "A man in dyed robes finds his support in contentment and maintains himself in purity; what use has he for a city?" The king said: "The Dharma King has hidden his traces and the Boat of Wisdom has sunk; if there is no recognition, there is no way to encourage future students. For the sake of propagating the True Dharma, I hope you will compassionately accept." The Master of Shastras, unable to refuse, accepted this city. He then built a monastery (伽藍), exhausting all the rules of construction, and donated the households of the city to provide for its maintenance.

Traveling forty or fifty li southwest from the Śīlabhadra Monastery (戒賢伽藍), one crosses the Nairañjanā River (尼連禪河) and reaches the city of Gayā (伽耶城). It is very rugged and well-fortified, but has few inhabitants, except for over a thousand families of Brahmins who are the descendants of a great rishi; the king does not treat them as subjects, and everyone holds them in high esteem. More than thirty li to the north of the city, there is a clear spring which Indian tradition calls holy water; for all who drink from or wash in it, the defilements of sin are eliminated.

Five or six li southwest of the city, one arrives at Mount Gayā (伽耶山; Skt. Gayā-śīrṣa). Its valleys are deep and dark, and its peaks and crags are perilous. In the customs of the country of India, it is popularly called the Spiritual Mountain. Since ancient times, sovereigns who have governed the world and succeeded to the throne, whose civilizing influence has reached distant peoples and whose virtue has surpassed that of previous eras, have all ascended this mountain to perform the rites and announce their success. On the summit of the mountain is a stone stūpa over one hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). Its spiritual efficacy is secretly bestowed, and divine light occasionally illuminates it; in the past, the Tathāgata (如來) expounded the *Ratnamegha-sūtra* (寶雲經) and other scriptures here. To the southeast of Mount Gayā is a stūpa, which is the native village of Kāśyapa (迦葉波). To its south are two stūpas, which are the places where Gayā-Kāśyapa (伽耶迦葉波) and Nadī-Kāśyapa (捺地迦葉波) practiced fire worship.

East of the place where Gayā-Kāśyapa practiced fire worship, one crosses a great river and arrives at the mountain of Prāgbodhi (鉢羅笈菩提山). The Tathāgata had sought diligently for six years without attaining perfect enlightenment; later, he abandoned his austerities and accepted milk gruel. Traveling from the northeast, he gazed upon this mountain and, cherishing its secluded tranquility, desired to realize perfect enlightenment there. He ascended from the northeast ridge to the summit, whereupon the earth quaked and the mountain shook. The mountain god was terrified and said to the Bodhisattva, "This mountain is not a blessed place for attaining perfect enlightenment. If you remain here to enter the vajra-samādhi, the earth will quake and collapse, and the mountain will overturn." The Bodhisattva descended to the southwest; halfway down the mountain cliff, with his back to the crags and facing a ravine, there was a large stone chamber. The Bodhisattva entered it and sat down cross-legged, whereupon the earth quaked again and the mountain shook once more. At that time, the Śuddhāvāsa devas (淨居天) proclaimed from the sky, "This is not the place where the Tathāgata will attain perfect enlightenment. Fourteen or fifteen li to the southwest of here, not far from the place of your austerities, there is a Pippala tree (卑鉢羅樹) with a Diamond Throne (金剛座) beneath it. All Buddhas of the past and future attain perfect enlightenment upon this seat; we pray you proceed there." Just as the Bodhisattva rose, the dragon in the chamber said, "This chamber is pure and excellent; it is suitable for realizing the holy state. I only pray that out of compassion, you will not abandon it." Knowing that this was not the place for attaining enlightenment, the Bodhisattva left his shadow behind to fulfill the dragon's wish and departed. The devas led the way, and he went to the Bodhi tree (菩提樹). When King Aśoka (無憂王) rose to power, he erected markers and built stūpas at every spot where the Bodhisattva had ascended or descended the mountain. Although these monuments differ in size, their spiritual manifestations are equally remarkable; sometimes celestial flowers rain from the sky, and at other times light illuminates the deep valleys. Every year, on the day the summer retreat ends, monks and laypeople from various regions climb the mountain to perform offerings, staying for two nights before returning.

Traveling fourteen or fifteen *li* southwest from the mountain of the Previous Enlightenment (Pūrvaśilā), one arrives at the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹). A surrounding wall of piled bricks is high, steep, and secure. It is long from east to west and narrow from north to south, measuring over five hundred paces in circumference. Rare trees and famous flowers interweave their shade and shadows; fine sand and exotic grasses form a lush, spreading carpet. The main gate opens to the east, facing the Nairañjanā River; the south gate connects to a large flower pond; the west side is narrow and secure; and the north gate leads to a great monastery. Within the enclosure, sacred sites are adjacent to one another, some being stūpas and others being *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍). Kings, ministers, and noble families from all the countries of Jambudvīpa, reverently upholding the Buddha’s legacy, have built them as memorials.  In the center of the Mahā-bodhi enclosure is the Vajra Seat (金剛座). Long ago, when the Bhadrakalpa was first formed, it arose together with the great earth. It is situated in the center of the three-thousand great chiliocosm, reaching down to the golden wheel and up to the surface of the ground. It is composed of diamond and measures over a hundred paces in circumference. Because the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa sit upon it to enter the diamond samādhi, it is called the Vajra Seat. It is the place where the holy path is realized, also called the *bodhimaṇḍa* (道場). When the great earth shakes, this place alone does not tremble or sway. For this reason, when the Tathāgata was about to realize perfect enlightenment, he traversed these four corners, and the ground shook everywhere; but when he later arrived at this spot, it was peaceful and did not tilt. Since entering the final age, the True Dharma has gradually faded, and it has become covered with sand and earth, no longer to be seen. After the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*, kings of various countries, having heard of the dimensions of the Vajra Seat as described by the Buddha, used two statues of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva to mark the northern and southern boundaries, facing toward the east. I have heard from the elders: "When the bodies of these Bodhisattva statues sink and disappear, the Buddha-Dharma will come to an end." Today, the Bodhisattva at the southern corner has sunk past its chest. The Mahā-bodhi tree (菩提樹) on the Vajra Seat is the pippala tree. When the Buddha was in the world, it was several hundred feet high; though it has been repeatedly cut down, it is still four or five zhang high. The Buddha sat beneath it and attained Perfect Enlightenment, and for this reason, it is called the Bodhi tree. Its trunk is yellowish-white, and its branches and leaves are emerald green; they do not wither in winter or summer, and their luster remains unchanged. Every year on the day of the Tathāgata’s *nirvāṇa*, the leaves all wither and fall, but after a short while, they return to their former state. On that day, the monarchs of various countries, along with monks and laypeople of different traditions, numbering in the tens of millions, gather without being summoned to water and wash the tree with scented water and milk; they then play music, arrange fragrant flowers, and keep lamps and torches burning day and night, vying with one another to present offerings.  After the Tathāgata’s *nirvāṇa*, when King Aśoka (無憂王) first ascended the throne, he believed in heretical doctrines and destroyed the sacred sites left by the Buddha, mobilizing troops and coming in person to cut the tree down. The roots, stems, branches, and leaves were chopped into small pieces and piled up several dozen paces to the west, where fire-worshiping Brahmins were ordered to burn them as a sacrifice to heaven; yet before the smoke and flames had subsided, two trees suddenly grew out from the midst of the fierce fire with luxuriant, verdant leaves, and were thus called the "Ash Bodhi Trees." King Aśoka witnessed this miracle and repented; he watered the remaining roots with scented milk, and by the time dawn approached, the tree had grown back as it was before. The king, seeing this spiritual marvel, was deeply overjoyed; he personally performed offerings and was so delighted that he forgot to return home. The queen, who had long believed in heretical teachings, secretly dispatched messengers after midnight to cut down the tree again. When King Aśoka (無憂王) went to pay his respects at dawn, he saw only a stump; deeply moved by grief, he prayed with utmost sincerity and irrigated it with fragrant milk, and within a few days it grew back to life. The king, deeply respecting this marvel, built a stone wall around it over ten feet high, which can still be seen today.  Recently, King Śaśāṅka (設賞迦王), a believer in heretical teachings who slandered and envied the Buddha-dharma, destroyed monasteries and cut down the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) tree; he dug down to the springs but could not exhaust the roots, so he set it on fire and soaked it with sugarcane juice, wishing to rot it and utterly destroy any remaining sprouts. Several months later, King Pūrṇavarman (補剌拏伐摩王) of the kingdom of Magadha (摩揭陀國), a descendant of King Aśoka, heard of this and sighed, saying: "The sun of wisdom has already set, and only the Buddha-tree remains; now that it has been destroyed again, what will living beings behold!" He threw his whole body to the ground, his sorrow moving all who saw him. He had thousands of cows milked to irrigate the tree, and within a night the tree grew back, reaching a height of over one zhang. Fearing it might be cut down again in the future, he surrounded it with a stone wall twenty-four feet high. Therefore, the Mahā-bodhi tree is now hidden within a stone wall, with only a portion over one zhang in height visible above it.

To the east of the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) tree is a vihara (精舍), one hundred and sixty or seventy feet high, with a base more than twenty paces wide, built of blue bricks and plastered with lime. The tiered niches all contain golden images, and the four walls are carved with exquisite designs, some in the form of linked pearls, others as celestial beings, with a golden-copper āmalaka fruit placed on top. To the east, it connects to a multi-storied pavilion with eaves and roofs rising in three distinct tiers; the rafters, pillars, beams, doors, and windows are all decorated with gold and silver carvings and inlaid with pearls and jade. The inner chambers and deep halls have three sets of connecting doors. On the left and right of the outer gate, there are niche chambers; the one on the left contains an image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva (觀自在菩薩), and the one on the right contains an image of Maitreya Bodhisattva (慈氏菩薩), both cast in white silver and standing over ten feet high. On the original site of this vihara, King Aśoka (無憂王) first built a small vihara, which was later expanded by a Brahmin.   Originally, there was a Brahmin who did not believe in the Buddha’s teachings and worshipped Maheśvara (大自在天). Hearing that the deity resided in the Snow Mountains, he went there with his younger brother to seek the fulfillment of his vows. The deity said, "All wishes and prayers are only fulfilled if one has merit. What you seek is not something I can grant." The Brahmin asked, "What merit must I cultivate to have my heart’s desire fulfilled?" The deity replied, "If you wish to plant good seeds and seek a superior field of merit, the Mahā-bodhi tree is the place where the Buddha attained the fruit of enlightenment. You should return quickly, go to the Mahā-bodhi tree, build a great vihara, dig a large water pond, and perform various offerings; then your wishes shall be fulfilled." The Brahmin, having received the divine command, conceived great faith and returned together; the elder brother built a vihara (精舍) and the younger brother excavated a water pond. Thereupon, they performed grand offerings and diligently sought the fulfillment of their wishes, which were eventually realized as they became high ministers to the king, and all the emoluments and rewards they received were given away as alms. Once the vihara was completed, they sought to recruit craftsmen to fashion an image of the Tathāgata as he first attained Buddhahood. A long time passed, and no one responded to the call. After a while, a Brahmin came and told the assembly, "I am skilled at depicting the wondrous form of the Tathāgata." The assembly asked, "Now that we are to create the image, what do you require?" He replied, "Only scented clay. It should be placed inside the vihara, along with a single lamp for illumination. Once I have entered, seal the door tightly; it may only be opened after six months." The monastic assembly followed his instructions. With four days still remaining before the six months were up, the assembly became alarmed and curious, and they opened the door to look inside. They saw the Buddha image inside the vihara looking majestic, sitting cross-legged with the right foot on top, the left hand withdrawn, and the right hand hanging down, facing east and appearing as solemn as if it were alive. The pedestal was four feet two inches high and twelve feet five inches wide; the image was eleven feet five inches tall, with a distance of eight feet eight inches between the knees and six feet two inches between the shoulders. Its auspicious marks were complete and its compassionate face seemed real, except that the polishing above the right breast was not yet finished. Since the man was nowhere to be seen, they realized it was a divine manifestation, and the assembly sighed in sorrow and earnestly prayed to understand. There was a śramaṇa of simple and honest character who had a dream in which the former brahmin appeared and said to him, "I am Maitreya Bodhisattva (慈氏菩薩); fearing that the thoughts of craftsmen could not fathom the holy countenance, I came in person to depict the Buddha's image. As for the lowered right hand, formerly when the Tathāgata was about to realize the fruit of Buddhahood, the celestial Māra came to harass him, and the earth deities announced their arrival. One of them emerged first to help the Buddha subjugate the demon, but the Tathāgata told him, 'Do not be worried or afraid; I shall surely subjugate him through the power of forbearance.' The demon king asked, 'Who will be the clear witness?' The Tathāgata then lowered his hand and pointed to the ground, saying, 'This is the witness.' At that time, the second earth deity emerged to bear witness; therefore, the hand of the present image imitates that former posture of lowering." The assembly, realizing this spiritual manifestation, was filled with sorrow and reverence. Consequently, where the area above the breast was not yet finished, they filled it with various precious substances, and adorned it with pearl necklaces, jeweled crowns, and rare treasures.  After King Śaśāṅka (設賞迦王) had felled the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) tree, he wished to destroy this image; however, once he beheld its compassionate countenance, his heart could not bear it, and as he turned his carriage to return, he commanded a high minister, saying: "You should remove this Buddha image and install a figure of Maheśvara (大自在天)." Having received the decree, the minister was afraid and sighed, saying: "If I destroy the Buddha image, I shall incur calamity for kalpas to come; yet if I disobey the King's command, I shall lose my life and have my clan exterminated—in such a dilemma, what is the proper course of action!" He then summoned men of faith to serve as laborers and built a brick wall across the front of the image; feeling ashamed that it would be in total darkness, he also placed a bright lamp inside, and on the front of the brick wall, he painted a picture of Maheśvara. When the work was completed, he reported back to the King. Upon hearing this, the King was seized with fear; his entire body broke out in pustules, his skin and flesh cracked and split, and before long, he died. The minister hastened back to destroy the wall and remove the barrier. Although many days had passed, the lamp was still not extinguished. The image remains to this day, and the divine craftsmanship is unimpaired. Because it is situated in a secluded chamber where lamps are kept burning in succession, one cannot clearly observe the compassionate countenance. One must take a large, bright mirror in the morning and direct the light inside to behold the sacred image. Those who see it are naturally filled with sorrow and longing.  The Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment on the eighth day of the second half of the Indian month of Vaiśākha, which corresponds to the eighth day of the third month in our calendar. According to the Sthavira school, however, he attained perfect enlightenment on the fifteenth day of the second half of the month of Vaiśākha, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the third month in our calendar. At that time, the Tathāgata was thirty years old; others say he was thirty-five.  To the north of the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) is the place where the Buddha walked in meditation. After the Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment, he did not rise from his seat for seven days, remaining in silent meditation. When he arose, he went to the north of the Mahā-bodhi and walked in meditation for seven days, pacing back and forth over a distance of more than ten paces. Extraordinary flowers appeared in his footsteps, numbering eighteen in total. Later generations built a brick foundation here, more than three feet high. I have heard from ancient records that this sacred foundation indicates the length of a person's life: if one first makes a sincere vow and then measures it, the number will increase or decrease according to the length of one's lifespan. To the north of this meditation path, on the right side of the road, upon a large rock, there is a great Mūla-gandha-kuṭī (精舍) containing a Buddha image that gazes upward. In the past, the Tathāgata spent seven days here gazing at the Mahā-bodhi tree (菩提樹), his eyes not turning away for even a moment. To repay the kindness of the tree, he gazed upon it in this way.
