To the north of the Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva vihara is a great vihara, over three hundred feet high, built by King Bālāditya (婆羅阿迭多王); its ornamentation, dimensions, and the Buddha image within are the same as those of the great vihara under the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) tree. To its northeast is a stūpa where the Tathāgata in the past expounded the wonderful Dharma for seven days. To the northwest is the place where the four past Buddhas sat. To its south is a brass vihara built by King Śīlāditya (戒日王); although the work is not yet finished, according to its plans and measurements, it will be one hundred feet high when completed. To the east, two hundred and some paces outside the enclosure, is a standing copper Buddha image, over eighty feet high, which required a six-story pavilion to cover it; it was made in the past by King Pūrṇavarman (滿胄王). Two or three li north of the copper Buddha image of King Pūrṇavarman, inside a brick vihara, is an image of the Bodhisattva Tārā (多羅菩薩). Its stature is lofty, and its spiritual efficacy is very manifest. Every year on the first day of the year, grand offerings are made; kings of neighboring regions, ministers, and noble families bring wonderful incense and flowers, hold precious banners and canopies, play metal and stone instruments in succession, and harmonize them with string and bamboo instruments, holding this Dharma assembly for seven days. Inside the south gate of the enclosure, there is a large well. Formerly, in the time of the Buddha, a large company of merchants, pressed by heat and thirst, came to where the Buddha was. The World-Honored One pointed to the ground, indicating that water could be obtained there. The leader of the merchants then struck the ground with a cart axle; once the ground was indented, water gushed forth like a spring. Having drunk and heard the Dharma, they all realized the holy fruit.

Traveling eight or nine li southwest from the monastery, one reaches the town of Kolika (拘理迦邑), where there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka; this is the native village of the Venerable Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅子). Beside it is a stūpa marking the place where the Venerable One entered the nirvana without remainder (anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa), and it contains his bodily relics. The Venerable One was of a great Brahmin lineage and had been a close friend of Śāriputra since youth. Śāriputra was esteemed for his brilliant talent, while the Venerable One was renowned for his profound discernment; they were equals in wisdom, always together in their movements, bound by a lifelong pact to share the same path, and together they grew weary of the secular world and sought to leave the householder's life, eventually taking Sañjaya as their teacher. Śāriputra encountered the arhat Aśvajit, heard the Dharma, and attained realization; he returned and recounted it to the Venerable One, who, upon hearing and realizing the Dharma, attained the first fruit. Together with his two hundred and fifty disciples, he went to the place of the Buddha. The World-Honored One saw them from afar and, pointing them out to the assembly, said: "Those who are coming are the foremost in supernatural powers among my disciples." Upon arriving at the place of the Buddha, they requested to enter the Dharma. The World-Honored One said: "Welcome, monks; practice the holy life purely to reach the end of suffering." Upon hearing these words, their hair and beards fell away, their secular garments changed, their precepts became pure, and their deportment became harmonious. After seven days, their defilements were exhausted, they attained the fruit of arhatship, and they gained supernatural powers. Three or four li to the east of the native village of Maudgalyāyana, there is a stūpa at the place where King Bimbisāra went to meet and see the Buddha. When the Tathāgata first realized the fruit of buddhahood, he knew that the hearts of the people in the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) were thirsting with longing. He accepted the invitation of King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王) and, in the early morning, donned his robes and took up his alms bowl. Surrounded on all sides by a thousand bhikṣus—all of whom were elder brahmans with shell-shaped topknots who had donned dyed robes out of admiration for the Dharma, following him in his retinue—he entered the city of Rājagṛha (王舍城). At that time, the heavenly king Śakra (帝釋天王) transformed himself into a māṇava (摩那婆) with a shell-shaped topknot on his head. Holding a golden vase in his left hand and a precious staff in his right, his feet treading on empty space four finger-widths above the ground, he led the way for the Buddha amidst the assembly. Then King Bimbisāra of the country of Magadha, together with the various brahmans, elders, and laypeople of his kingdom—a multitude of hundreds of thousands—came out of the city of Rājagṛha in a procession to welcome the holy assembly.

King Bimbisāra went to meet the Buddha and traveled more than twenty *li* to the southeast, arriving at the town of Kālapināka (迦羅臂拏迦邑). In it is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. This is the native village of the Venerable Śāriputra, and the well still exists today. Beside it is a stūpa where the Venerable entered into extinction, which contains his bodily relics. The Venerable was of a great Brahmin lineage. His father was highly talented and broadly learned, with a deep insight into the subtle and profound; there was no classic or treatise that he had not thoroughly studied. His wife had a dream and told her husband in detail, saying: "Last night in my sleep, I dreamt of a strange man clad in armor and holding a vajra, who demolished all the mountains and then stood back beneath a single mountain." Her husband said: "This is a very auspicious dream. You will give birth to a son who will be learned and peerless in the world, who will defeat all the masters of debate and shatter their doctrines, but who will be inferior to only one person, to whom he will become a disciple." She was indeed pregnant, and the mother suddenly became intelligent, engaging in high-level discussions and debates with speech that was never obstructed. When the Venerable was eight years old, his fame spread to the four quarters; his nature was pure and simple, his heart was compassionate, he destroyed the bonds of defilement, and he attained wisdom. He and Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅子) were friends from youth and deeply loathed the dusty world, yet they had not found a place to turn. Thereupon, he and Maudgalyāyana went to the place of the non-Buddhist Sañjaya (珊闍耶) to study. They then said to each other: "This is not the ultimate truth, and it cannot exhaust the limits of suffering. Let us each seek a clear guide; whoever tastes the nectar first must share the flavor with the other." At that time, the great arhat Aśvajit (馬勝) held his alms bowl and entered the city to beg for food. Śāriputra (舍利子) saw his dignified and graceful demeanor and immediately asked him, "Who is your teacher?" He replied, "The prince of the Śākya clan, who grew weary of the world, renounced household life, and attained equal and perfect enlightenment—he is my teacher." Śāriputra said, "What dharma does he teach? May I hear it?" He replied, "I have only recently received his instruction and have not yet grasped the profound meaning." Śāriputra said, "I wish to hear what you have learned." Aśvajit then expounded it according to the occasion, and upon hearing it, Śāriputra immediately attained the first fruit. He then went with his two hundred and fifty disciples to the place of the Buddha. The World-Honored One saw them from afar, pointed them out, and told the assembly, "Among my disciples, he is the foremost in wisdom." Upon arriving, he prostrated and requested to follow the Buddha's dharma. The World-Honored One said, "Welcome, bhikṣu." Upon hearing these words, his precepts were fully perfected. More than half a month later, he heard the Buddha teaching the dharma to the Long-nailed Ascetic (長爪梵志), and upon hearing the remaining discourse, he was enlightened and attained the fruit of an arhat. Later, when Ānanda (阿難) received the Buddha's announcement of the time of his extinction, the news was passed from one to another, and all were filled with sorrow. Śāriputra’s deep longing and reverence increased, and he could not bear to see the Buddha enter parinirvāṇa, so he requested the World-Honored One to let him enter extinction first. The World-Honored One said, "You should know the time." He took leave of his disciples and went to his native village, where his attendant novice informed the entire city. King Ajātaśatru (未生怨王) and his subjects, without exception, rushed like the wind and gathered like clouds. Śāriputra spoke extensively on the Dharma, and having heard him, they departed. During the last watch of the night, he focused his mind and entered the samādhi of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti); upon arising from that meditation, he attained extinction. Four or five li to the southeast of the town of Kālapināka (迦羅臂挐迦邑), there is a stūpa at the place where the disciples of the Venerable Śāriputra entered nirvāṇa. Some say that when Kāśyapa Buddha was in the world, three koṭis of great arhats entered nirvāṇa without remainder at this same place.

Traveling more than thirty *li* to the east of the stupa of the disciples of Śāriputra (舍利子), one arrives at the mountain of Indraśailaguhā (因陀羅勢羅窶訶山). The mountain’s cliffs and valleys are deep and secluded, and its flowering forests are lush and dense. On the ridge, two peaks rise prominently. Between the southern cliffs of the western peak is a large stone chamber, wide but not high, where the Tathāgata once stayed. From time to time, Śakra Devānām Indra (天帝釋) would carve forty-two questions of doubt onto the stone to ask the Buddha, and the Buddha would explain them; those traces still remain. Today, an image has been made there to emulate the sacred appearance of the past, and those who enter to pay their respects are invariably filled with awe and trepidation. On the mountain cliffs are the sites where the four past Buddhas sat and walked in meditation. On the eastern peak is a monastery; according to local tradition, the monks there sometimes see, in the middle of the night, lamps and torches shining as constant illumination before the Buddha image in the stone chamber of the western peak. In front of the monastery on the eastern peak of Indraśailaguhā Mountain is a stupa called Haṃsa (亘娑) (Original note: In the language of Tang, this means "goose"). Formerly, this monastery practiced the Hīnayāna, which is a gradual teaching; therefore, it permitted the consumption of the three kinds of pure meat, a practice which this monastery followed without fail. Later, the three kinds of pure meat could not be obtained in time. A monk who was walking in meditation suddenly saw a flock of geese flying by and jokingly said, "Today the monks' midday meal is insufficient; a Mahāsattva should know the time." Before his words had ceased, one goose flew back, landed before the monk, and cast itself down to die. The bhikṣu, having seen this, reported it fully to the assembly of monks. Those who heard were moved with grief and said to one another, "The Tathāgata established the Dharma to guide and entice according to the capacity of the individual; we, clinging to our ignorance, have followed the gradual teaching. The Mahāyāna is the true principle; we should change our former attachments and strive to follow the holy will. This goose has handed down a warning and is truly a bright guide; we should commemorate its great virtue and transmit this record for all eternity." Thereupon, they built a stūpa to manifest its heroic legacy, burying the dead goose beneath it.

Traveling northeast from the Indraśaila-guhā (因陀羅勢羅窶訶) mountain for one hundred and fifty or sixty li, one reaches the Kapotaka (迦布德迦) Monastery, where there are over two hundred monks who study the teachings of the Sarvāstivāda school. To the east of the monastery is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. In the past, the Buddha stayed here for one night to preach the Dharma to a great assembly. At that time, a fowler was netting birds in this forest; having caught nothing all day, he said, "I have but little merit and am always met with misfortune." He came to where the Buddha was and cried out, "Today the Tathāgata is preaching the Dharma here, causing me to catch nothing in my nets; my wife and children are starving, so what plan can I devise?" The Tathāgata said to him, "You should kindle a fire, and I shall provide you with food." The Tathāgata then transformed himself into a large pigeon and threw himself into the fire to die; the fowler took it home, and he and his wife and children ate it together. Afterward, he returned to the Buddha, who used skillful means to guide and transform him. Upon hearing the Dharma, the fowler repented of his faults and renewed himself; he left home to cultivate the path and subsequently attained the holy fruit. Because of this, the monastery that was built there was named the Pigeon (Kapotaka) Monastery.

Two or three li south of the Kapotaka monastery (迦布德迦伽藍), one arrives at the mountain of Vyāsa (孤山). The mountain is lofty and steep, with lush forests, famous flowers, and clear streams covering the cliffs and lining the ravines. Above, there are many vihāras (精舍) and sacred temples, which are extremely refined in their craftsmanship. In the central vihāra is a statue of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩); although small in size, its spiritual majesty inspires awe, as it holds a lotus in its hand and bears a Buddha figure upon its crown. There are often people who fast and focus their minds, seeking a vision of the Bodhisattva for seven days, fourteen days, or even a full month; those who receive a response see the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, in all his solemn and wondrous beauty and brilliant radiance, emerge from the statue to comfort and exhort them. Long ago, the king of Siṃhala (僧伽羅國) in the South Sea looked into a mirror at dawn and saw not his own reflection, but rather this Bodhisattva statue atop a small hill in the Tāla forest of Magadha (摩揭陀國) in Jambudvīpa (贍部洲); the king, deeply moved and joyful, sought to find it. When he arrived at this hill, he found the statue to be exactly as he had seen, so he built a vihāra and established various offerings. Since then, subsequent kings, admiring this legacy, have built vihāras and sacred temples alongside it, and offerings of incense, flowers, and music have never ceased.

Traveling southeast for more than forty li from the statue of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩) on the isolated hill (Vyāsa 孤山), one reaches a monastery where there are more than fifty monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Hīnayāna. In front of the monastery is a great stūpa, which possesses many miraculous qualities; it is the place where the Buddha formerly preached the Dharma for seven days to the Brahmadeva-rāja and others. Beside it are the sites of the traces of the sitting and walking meditation of the three past Buddhas.

Traveling northeast from the monastery for more than seventy li, to the south of the Ganges (Gaṅgā) River, one arrives at a large settlement where the population is dense and prosperous. There are several deva temples, all of which are exquisitely carved and adorned. Not far to the southeast is a great stupa (stūpa), where the Buddha once stayed for one night and preached the Dharma.

From here, traveling east into the mountains and forests for more than one hundred li, one reaches the village of Lāvaṇīla (落般膩羅聚落). In front of the monastery is a great stūpa built by King Aśoka, where the Buddha once preached the Dharma for three months. Two or three li to the north of this place is a large pond, more than thirty li in circumference, where four-colored lotus flowers bloom in all four seasons. From here, traveling east into the great mountains and forests for more than two hundred li, one reaches the country of Hiraṇyaparvata (伊爛拏鉢伐多國).
Further to the southeast, at a corner of the great sea, is the country of Kāmalaṅkā (迦摩浪迦國).
Next, to the east, is the country of Dvāravatī (墮羅鉢底國).
To the east of this is the country of Īśānapura (伊賞那補羅國).
Further to the east is the country of Mahācampā (摩訶瞻波國), which is what is called Linyi (林邑) here.

To the southwest is the country of Yamanadvīpa (閻摩那洲國). Regarding these six countries, the routes are obstructed by mountains and rivers, and I did not enter their territories; however, their customs, lands, and boundaries are known through report.

Traveling west from the country of Samataṭa (三摩呾吒國) for over nine hundred li, one reaches the country of Tāmraliptī (耽摩栗底國). The country of Tāmraliptī is about one thousand four or five hundred li in circuit. The capital city is over ten li in circuit. It is situated near the edge of the sea, and the land is low and damp. Crops are sown in their proper seasons, and flowers and fruits are abundant. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are impetuous and fierce. The people are brave and courageous, and they believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are more than ten saṃghārāmas (伽藍) with over one thousand monks. There are more than fifty deva temples (天祠), where followers of various heterodox paths live together. As the country is situated on a sea corner where water and land routes meet, rare and precious treasures are gathered here in abundance; therefore, the people of this country are generally wealthy. Beside the city is a stūpa (窣堵波) built by King Aśoka (無憂王). Nearby are the sites where the four past Buddhas sat and walked in meditation.

From here, traveling northwest for over seven hundred li, one reaches the country of Karṇasuvarṇa (羯羅拏蘇伐剌那國). The country of Karṇasuvarṇa is four thousand four or five hundred li in circuit. The capital city of the country is over twenty li in circuit. The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous, and the households are wealthy. The land is low and damp; crops are sown in their proper seasons, and various flowers grow luxuriantly, with precious fruits flourishing in abundance. The climate is temperate, and the customs are honest and harmonious. The people value learning and the arts, and they believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are more than ten monasteries with over two thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Sāmmitīya school of the Hīnayāna. There are more than fifty Deva temples, and the number of non-Buddhists is very large. Separately, there are three monasteries where the monks do not consume milk or cream, following the legacy of Devadatta.

Beside the great city is the Raktamṛttika-saṃghārāma (絡多末知僧伽藍). Its courtyards and buildings are spacious and open, and its towers and pavilions are lofty and steep. The highly talented and profoundly learned scholars of the country, as well as those of renowned intelligence, all assemble therein to assist one another through mutual admonition and to cultivate their morality and virtue.  Formerly, before this country believed in the Buddha-dharma, there was a heretic from South India who bound his belly with copper plates, wore a bright torch upon his head, and, leaning on a staff, walked with proud strides into this city, where he struck the drum of debate and sought to engage in discussion. Someone asked him, "Why do you wear a torch on your head and copper plates on your belly?" He replied, "I have studied so many arts and possess such great ability that I fear my belly might burst; I feel compassion for the ignorant and dark-minded, and that is why I carry a light."  Ten days passed, and no one in the city came forward to question him. The king inquired among the eminent and wise, but there was no one who could match him. The king said, "Within the borders of this realm, can there really be no one of wisdom and clarity? To leave a guest's challenge unanswered is a deep shame for the country. We must search further and inquire among those living in seclusion."  Someone said, "In the great forest there is an extraordinary man who calls himself a śramaṇa; he is dedicated to arduous study and has lived here in quiet seclusion for a long time. Were he not one who embodies the Dharma and accords with virtue, how could he live like this?"  Upon hearing this, the king went in person to invite him. The śramaṇa replied, "I am a man of South India staying here as a traveler; my learning is superficial, and I fear I may fall short of what you have heard. However, I dare to accept your command and will no longer firmly decline. If I am not defeated in the debate, I request that you build a saṃghārāma, gather a community of monks, and glorify and praise the Buddha-dharma." The king said, "I respectfully hear your request and will not dare to forget this virtue." The śramaṇa accepted the invitation and went to the site of the debate. The non-Buddhist then recited his tenets, totaling more than thirty thousand words. Their meaning was profound and their phrasing concise; they encompassed all names and characteristics, capturing the sight and hearing of the audience. Upon hearing and examining them once, the śramaṇa found no errors in the logic or terminology, and with a few hundred words, he debated and refuted them, then questioned the non-Buddhist on his tenets. The non-Buddhist, his arguments exhausted and his logic defeated, remained silent and could not respond. Having been defeated in his reputation, he retreated in shame. The king deeply respected the śramaṇa’s virtue and built this saṃghārāma; from that time forward, the Buddha-dharma was widely propagated.  Not far from the side of the saṃghārāma is a stūpa, which was built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata stayed here for seven days to preach the Dharma and provide guidance. Beside it is a mūla-gandha-kuṭī (精舍), the place where the past four Buddhas sat and walked in meditation, leaving behind traces. There are several stūpas, all of which are places where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma, and they were built by King Aśoka.

From here, traveling southwest for more than seven hundred li, one arrives at the country of Uḍra (烏荼國). The country of Uḍra is more than seven thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is over twenty li in circuit. The land is rich and fertile, and the crops and grains are lush and abundant; all kinds of fruits are quite large compared to other countries, and the exotic grasses and famous flowers are difficult to describe. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are fierce and unyielding. The people are tall and robust in appearance, with dark complexions. Their speech and mannerisms differ from those of Mid-India. They are diligent in learning and mostly believe in the Buddhadharma; there are more than one hundred saṃghārāmas (伽藍) and more than ten thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Mahāyāna. There are fifty deva temples (天祠), where followers of various heterodox paths live together. There are more than ten stūpas (窣堵波), all of which are places where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma, and were built by King Aśoka (無憂王).

In the great mountains on the southwestern border of the kingdom is the Puṣpagiri (補澁波祇釐) monastery. Its stone stūpa possesses many spiritual anomalies; sometimes, on fast days, it emits a bright light. Therefore, the pure-hearted faithful, from both near and far, all gather there, holding exquisite flower canopies and vying to perform offerings. Below the dew-receiving basin and above the inverted-bowl structure, if one places the handle of a flower canopy, it remains fixed there as if a magnet were attracting a needle.

In the monastery in the mountains to the northwest, there is a stūpa whose miraculous properties are the same as the former. These two stūpas were built by spirits and deities, and their spiritual wonders are of such a nature.

On the southeastern border of the country, facing the shore of the great sea, is the city of Caritra (折利呾羅城; meaning "Departure"). It is over twenty *li* in circuit and serves as a thoroughfare and stopping place for seagoing merchants and travelers from distant lands. The city is solid and steep, and contains many rare treasures. Outside the city, five monasteries stand in a row; their terraces and pavilions are lofty, and the sacred images are exquisitely crafted. To the south, the country of Siṃhala (僧伽羅國) is over twenty thousand *li* away; gazing into the distance on a quiet night, one can see the light of the precious pearl atop the Buddha-tooth stūpa of that land, shining clearly like a torch suspended in the air.

From here, traveling southwest through a great forest for more than one thousand two hundred li, one reaches the country of Koṅgoda (恭御陀國). The country of Koṅgoda is more than one thousand li in circuit. The capital city is more than twenty li in circuit. It borders the corner of the sea; the mountains and hills are rugged and undulating, the land is low and damp, and crops are sown in their proper seasons. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs of the people are bold and fierce. Their stature is large, and their complexion is black. They possess a rough sense of propriety and righteousness, and are not very deceitful. As for their writing, it is the same as that of Central India, but their language and tone differ considerably. They revere non-Buddhist paths and do not believe in the Buddha-Dharma. There are more than one hundred Deva temples and more than ten thousand followers of non-Buddhist paths. Within the borders of the country, there are several dozen small towns situated near mountain ranges and occupying the junctions of sea routes. The cities are strong and steep, and the soldiers are brave and daring; their power dominates the neighboring regions, so they have no formidable enemies. The country borders the seashore and possesses many rare treasures; conch shells, pearls, and precious stones are used as currency. They produce large dark-colored elephants, which are capable of traveling long distances when ridden.

From here, traveling southwest into a vast wilderness with deep forests and giant trees that reached the sky and obscured the sun, I went one thousand four or five hundred li and arrived at the country of Kaliṅga (羯𩜁伽國). The country of Kaliṅga is more than five thousand li in circuit. The capital city is over twenty li in circuit. Crops are sown in their proper seasons, and flowers and fruits are abundant; forests and marshes stretch continuously for hundreds of li. It produces dark wild elephants, which are prized by neighboring countries. The climate is hot, and the customs are impetuous and violent; the people are by nature impatient and fierce, yet they value faith and righteousness. Their speech is rapid and agile, their tone is plain and direct, and their diction and style are quite different from those of Central India. Few believe in the true Dharma, and most follow non-Buddhist paths. There are more than ten monasteries with over five hundred monks, who study the teachings of the Mahāyāna Sthavira school. There are more than one hundred Deva temples, and the number of non-Buddhists is very great, most of whom are followers of the Nirgrantha (尼乾).  In former times, the country of Kaliṅga was prosperous and densely populated; shoulders rubbed and wheel hubs clashed, and when the people raised their sleeves, they formed a curtain. A sage possessing the five supernatural powers lived in the rocks and cultivated purity; because people insulted and provoked him, he lost his supernatural powers and used evil spells to slaughter the people of the country, leaving neither young nor old, and destroying both the wise and the foolish. Human habitation was cut off for many years. Although people have gradually moved back, it is still not fully populated, and therefore the number of households in this country is currently small. Not far to the south of the city is a stūpa over one hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas.

On the northern frontier of the country, atop the great mountain ridge (Pravaragiri), there is a stone stupa over a hundred feet high. It is the place where, at the beginning of the kalpa when the human lifespan was immeasurable, a Pratyekabuddha entered into extinction.

From here, traveling northwest through mountains and forests for more than 1,800 li, one reaches the country of Kosala (憍薩羅國). The country of Kosala is more than 6,000 li in circumference; its borders are surrounded by mountain ranges, and forests and marshes are interconnected. The capital city of the country is over 40 li in circumference. The soil is rich and fertile, and the land is highly productive. Villages and towns are within sight of one another, and the households are prosperous and substantial. The people are large in stature and dark in complexion. Their customs are fierce and impetuous, and their nature is brave and violent. They believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings, and they are highly skilled in the arts. The king is a Kṣatriya. He deeply reveres the Buddhadharma and is profound in his benevolence and compassion. There are more than one hundred saṃghārāmas, with fewer than ten thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Mahāyāna. There are more than seventy Deva temples, where followers of various heterodox paths live together. Not far to the south of the city is an old saṃghārāma, and beside it is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata once manifested great supernatural powers at this place to subdue heterodox practitioners. Later, the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna (龍猛) resided in this saṃghārāma. At that time, the king of this country was named Sātavāhana (娑多婆訶). He cherished and respected Nāgārjuna, and he guarded the gates of his dwelling. At that time, the Bodhisattva Deva (提婆) came from the country of Siṃhala (執師子國) to seek a debate, and he said to the gatekeeper, "Please announce my visit." The gatekeeper then went to report this. Nāgārjuna, already well aware of his reputation, filled a bowl to the brim with water and instructed a disciple, saying, "Take this water and show it to that Deva." When Deva saw the water, he silently dropped a needle into it. The disciple took the bowl and returned, feeling puzzled. Nāgārjuna said, "What did he say?" The disciple replied, "He said nothing, but merely dropped a needle into the water." Nāgārjuna said, "How wise he is, this man! His knowledge of the subtle is divine, and his perception of the minute is second only to a sage. With such magnificent virtue, he should be invited in immediately." The disciple asked, "What do you mean? Is this what you call silent, marvelous eloquence?" Nāgārjuna said, "Water takes the shape of its container, whether square or round; it adapts to the purity or turbidity of its surroundings; it permeates everywhere without gaps, and its clarity is unfathomable. By showing him the full bowl, I compared it to the all-encompassing nature of my own learning; he, in turn, dropped a needle into it, thereby exhausting its depths. This is no ordinary person; he should be summoned at once."  Nāgārjuna’s demeanor was so awe-inspiring that it commanded respect from all, and those who spoke with him would bow their heads in submission. Deva had long admired his reputation and had long hoped to request his instruction. Before he began his studies, he wished to display his own mental acuity, yet he was also deeply intimidated by the master's majesty. He ascended the hall and sat in a secluded spot, discussing the profound mysteries throughout the day with language and logic of the highest clarity. Nāgārjuna said, "Your scholarship surpasses the world and your brilliant eloquence outshines your predecessors. I am but a feeble old man, and meeting such a talented youth truly allows me to pour the contents of my vessel into another and keep the lamp of transmission burning without end; the propagation of the Dharma depends on such a person. I hope you will move to the front seat so that we may discuss the profound mysteries."  Deva, having heard this command, felt a sense of self-assurance. He prepared to open the storehouse of his doctrines and first wandered through the garden of debate, raising the points of his argument and looking up to challenge the master's principles. But suddenly beholding the master's majestic countenance, he was struck speechless and fell silent; he moved from his seat to acknowledge his faults and then requested to become a disciple. Nāgārjuna (龍猛) said: "Sit down again; I shall now bestow upon you the most perfect and wonderful truth, the authentic teachings of the Dharma King." Deva (提婆) prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, single-mindedly took refuge, and said: "From this moment forward, I dare to follow your instructions." Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva was well-versed in the arts of medicine; by consuming elixirs to nourish his life, he lived for several hundred years, his spirit and appearance showing no signs of decline. The king, known as Yin-zheng (引正 - Sadvaha), having obtained the wonderful medicine, also lived for several hundred years. The king had a young son who said to his mother: "At this rate, when will I ever be able to succeed to the throne?" His mother replied: "Judging by the present situation, there is no prospect of it. Your father the king has already lived for several hundred years, and many of his descendants have already grown old and died. This is all due to the power of Nāgārjuna’s merit and the efficacy of his medical arts. If the Bodhisattva were to pass away, the king would surely perish. Now, Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva possesses vast wisdom and profound compassion; he provides for all living beings and regards his own life as something to be cast aside. You should go to him and try to beg for his head; if you can fulfill this intention, your wish will be granted." The prince respectfully obeyed his mother's command and came to the monastery (saṃghārāma); the gatekeepers were awestruck and fearful, so he was able to enter. At that time, Nāgārjuna Bodhisattva was reciting scriptures while walking in meditation. Suddenly seeing the prince, he stood still and said to him: "For what reason have you come to this monastery this evening, appearing as if in danger and fear, and rushing here so quickly?" He replied: "I have received the words of my compassionate mother, who spoke of those who practice renunciation. I have thought that for all living beings, their precious life is the most important thing, and in the authoritative words of the scriptures, there has never been anyone who lightly cast aside their physical body to bestow it upon those who seek it." My compassionate mother said: "It is not so. The Sugatas of the ten directions and the Tathāgatas of the three ages, from the time they first resolved their minds until they attained the fruit of enlightenment, diligently sought the Buddha-way and practiced precepts and forbearance. Some threw their bodies to feed hungry beasts, some cut their flesh to save a dove; King Candraprabha gave his head to a Brahmin, and King Maitrībala gave his blood to satisfy hungry Yakṣas; examples such as these are truly difficult to enumerate fully. Among the sages of the past, what age was without such people?" Now, Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna (龍猛菩薩), you are firm in your noble ambitions; I have a request for a human head to use, but though I have sought one for many years, no one has yet offered theirs. To commit a violent robbery and murder would result in many accumulated sins, and to cruelly harm the innocent would make one's defiled virtue manifest. But you, Bodhisattva, practice the holy path and look toward the distant fruit of Buddhahood; your compassion moistens all sentient beings, and your kindness reaches the boundless. You treat life as lightly as a floating thing and consider your body as cheap as rotten wood; do not violate your original vow, but grant what I seek!"  Nāgārjuna said: "Yes, these words are true! I seek the holy fruit of Buddhahood and I learn from the Buddha the ability to renounce; this body is like an echo, this body is like a bubble, circulating through the four types of birth and coming and going through the six realms, bound by a long-standing great vow never to oppose the desires of living beings. However, Prince! There is one thing that is not possible; what shall be done about it? Once my body is finished, your father will also perish; considering this, who will be able to provide for him?" Nāgārjuna paced about and looked around, seeking a way to end his life; he cut his own throat with a blade of dry cogon grass as if with a sharp sword, and his head was severed from his body. The prince, having seen this, fled in terror. The gatekeeper went up and reported, detailing the beginning and the end; the king, upon hearing this, was moved by grief and indeed also passed away.

Three hundred or more *li* southwest of the country, one arrives at the mountain of Bhramaragiri (跋邏末羅耆釐山). It rises abruptly and loftily, with precipitous peaks and cliffs; having neither slopes nor valleys, it appears to be a single solid rock. King Śātavāha (引正王) excavated this mountain for the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna (龍猛菩薩) to establish a monastery. Ten or more *li* away from the mountain, a tunnel was excavated; directly beneath the mountain, they chiseled upward to clear the stone. Within it are long corridors and eaves, lofty terraces and multi-storied pavilions; the pavilions have five tiers, and each tier has four courtyards, all containing shrines (*mūla-gandha-kuṭī* 精舍) where golden images of the Buddha's size have been cast with exquisite craftsmanship, while the remaining decorations consist entirely of gold and jewels. From the high peaks of the mountain, a waterfall pours down, flowing around the multi-storied pavilions and winding through the corridors and halls. The outer openings of the isolated cells illuminate the interior spaces.  Initially, when King Śātavāha was building this monastery, the labor force was exhausted and the treasury was empty; with the work not yet half finished, his heart was filled with deep sorrow. Nāgārjuna said to him, "Great King, why are you so burdened with worry?" The king replied, "I have given rise to a great aspiration and ventured to establish a supreme field of merit, hoping it would remain firm forever until the coming of Maitreya (慈氏). With the work not yet finished and the financial resources exhausted, I am constantly filled with this regret, sitting and waiting for the dawn." Nāgārjuna said, "Do not worry. The merit of cultivating such supreme goodness is inexhaustible; if one has raised a vast vow, there is no worry that it will not be fulfilled. Return to the palace today and enjoy yourself to the fullest; tomorrow morning, go out for an excursion to observe the mountains and fields, and then come here to discuss the construction." Having received this instruction, the king followed it and acted accordingly. The Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna (龍猛) used a miraculous elixir, dripping it onto various large rocks, which all turned into gold. When the king went on an excursion and saw the gold, he rejoiced in his heart and words; he returned with his carriage to the place of Nāgārjuna and said, "During my hunting excursion today, I was deluded by spirits and ghosts, for in the mountains and forests I repeatedly saw heaps of gold." Nāgārjuna said, "It was not a delusion by ghosts. It was the response to your utmost sincerity; that is why this gold appeared. You should take and use it in time to complete your supreme undertaking." He then used it for the construction, and after the work was finished, there was still a surplus. Thereupon, in each of the five tiers, he cast four large golden statues, and the remainder was still so abundant that it filled the treasuries. He summoned and gathered one thousand monks to reside within and perform rites and chanting. The Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna collected and classified the teachings proclaimed by the Buddha Śākyamuni and the treatises expounded by the various Bodhisattvas, storing them within. Thus, the first tier at the top housed only Buddha images and various scriptures and treatises; the fifth tier at the bottom was for the residence of lay servants (淨人), property, and miscellaneous goods; and the three middle tiers were the lodgings for the monks. I have heard from the records of former sages that after King Śātavāha (引正王) had completed the construction, the cost of the salt consumed by the workers was calculated to be nine koṭis of gold coins. Later, the monks fell into disputes and went to the king to seek a settlement. At that time, the lay servants said to one another, "Since a quarrel has arisen among the monks and their arguments are contradictory, evil men will watch for an opening to destroy the monastery." Consequently, they barred the multi-storied pavilion and expelled the monks. Since that time, there has been no monastic community. Looking at the mountain cliffs from afar, one cannot discern any gate or path. At that time, they would bring in those skilled in medical arts to treat illnesses, but they were blindfolded upon entering and exiting, so they did not know the route.

From this great forest, traveling south for more than nine hundred li, one reaches the country of Āndhra (案達羅國). The country of Āndhra is more than three thousand li in circumference. The capital city of the country is more than twenty li in circumference and is named Vengīpura (瓶耆羅). The land is fertile and rich, and the crops are abundant. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs of the people are fierce and violent. Their language and tone of speech differ from those of Mid-India, but as for their written characters, the rules are largely the same. There are more than twenty sanghārāmas (伽藍) with more than three thousand monks. There are more than thirty deva temples, and the followers of heterodox paths are very numerous. Not far from the side of Vengīpura city is a large sanghārāma with multi-storied pavilions and layered terraces, the craftsmanship of which exhausts the possibilities of carving; the sacred images of the Buddha are of exquisite and ingenious design. In front of the sanghārāma is a stone stūpa, several hundred feet high, which was built by the arhat Acala (阿折羅). Not far to the southwest of the sanghārāma of the aforementioned arhat is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王); in the past, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma here, manifested great supernatural powers, and saved immeasurable multitudes.

Traveling more than twenty li southwest from the monastery of the Arhat Ācāra, one reaches the solitary hill (Vyāsa). On the mountain ridge is a stone stūpa where the Bodhisattva Dignāga composed the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* (Treatise on Logic). This Bodhisattva Dignāga, after the Buddha had passed away, followed the tradition and donned the dyed robes. His wisdom and vows were vast and great, his power of discernment deep and firm; pitying the world for having no refuge, he contemplated propagating the sacred teachings. Thinking that the theories of *hetuvidyā* were profound in language and extensive in reasoning, such that students labored in vain and found it difficult to achieve success, he hid his traces among secluded cliffs and settled his spirit in silent meditation, examining the merits and demerits of past works and scrutinizing the verbosity and conciseness of their meanings. At that time, the cliffs and valleys shook and echoed, the mist and clouds changed color, and a mountain god lifted the Bodhisattva up several hundred feet, proclaiming: "In the past, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, guided sentient beings through skillful means and, with a compassionate heart, preached the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra*, encompassing wonderful principles and investigating subtle words to their depths. Since the Tathāgata entered extinction, the great meaning has been cut off. Now, the Bodhisattva Dignāga, whose merit and wisdom are vast and far-reaching, and who deeply understands the sacred intent, shall once again propagate the *Hetuvidyā-śāstra* on this day." The Bodhisattva then emitted a great light, illuminating the darkness. At that time, the king of this country felt deep respect; seeing this radiant appearance, he suspected the Bodhisattva had entered the diamond samādhi and therefore requested him to realize the fruit of birthlessness. Dignāga said: "I have entered samādhi to observe and wish to explain the profound scriptures; my heart is set on perfect enlightenment, not on the fruit of birthlessness." The king said: "The fruit of birthlessness is something all sages admire; it severs the desires of the three realms and provides mastery of the three types of supernormal knowledge—this is a magnificent achievement, and I hope you will realize it quickly." At that time, Dignāga was pleased by the king’s request and was about to realize and accept the holy fruit of the non-learner (aśaikṣa). At that moment, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī (妙吉祥菩薩) knew of this and felt it was a pity; wishing to warn him, he snapped his fingers to awaken him and said: "What a pity! How can you abandon your vast and great mind for a narrow and inferior aspiration, following a desire for solitary perfection while discarding your vow to benefit others? If you wish to perform a virtuous benefit, you should widely propagate the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (瑜伽師地論) composed by the Bodhisattva Maitreya (慈氏菩薩) to guide and encourage later students; the benefit of this is truly great." The Bodhisattva Dignāga respectfully accepted this instruction and followed it accordingly. Thereupon, he pondered deeply and researched extensively the treatises on logic (hetuvidyā). Fearing that students might be intimidated by the subtlety of the text and the conciseness of the language, he extracted the essential meanings and synthesized the subtle words to compose the *Nyāyamukha-śāstra* (因門論) in order to guide those who would come after. From this time forward, he propagated the *Yogācāra*, and his flourishing work and disciples were known throughout the world.

From this forest and wilderness, traveling south for more than a thousand li, one arrives at the country of Dhānyakaṭaka (馱那羯磔迦國). The country of Dhānyakaṭaka is more than six thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than forty li in circuit. The land is fertile and rich, and the crops are abundant. There is much wilderness and few settlements. The climate is warm and hot, and the people are dark in complexion. Their nature is fierce and impetuous, and they are fond of learning the arts. The monasteries are arranged like the scales of a fish, but they are extremely desolate; those that remain number more than twenty, with over a thousand monks, all of whom mostly study the teachings of the Mahāsāṃghika school. There are more than a hundred Deva temples, and there are many followers of heterodox paths.

To the east of the city, resting on a mountain, is the Pūrvaśaila (弗婆勢羅) Monastery; to the west of the city, resting on a mountain, is the Avaraśaila (阿伐羅勢羅) Monastery. These were built for the Buddha by a former king of this country. They are situated along the river and connected by paths, with pavilions erected on cleared cliffs, long corridors, and covered walkways, resting against the rocks and joining the mountain peaks. Divine spirits guard and protect them, and sages and saints have frequented them for rest. Within the millennium following the Buddha’s nirvana, a thousand ordinary monks would gather each year to enter the summer retreat; on the day the retreat concluded, they would all attain arhatship and depart by rising into the void through their supernatural powers. After the millennium, ordinary people and sages lived there together. For the past hundred years or so, there have been no more monks, and the mountain spirits have changed their forms—sometimes appearing as jackals and wolves, other times as apes and monkeys—to terrify travelers. For this reason, the place is desolate and devoid of any monastic community.

To the west of the city, resting against a mountain, is the Avaraśaila monastery (阿伐羅勢羅僧伽藍), which a former king of this country built for the Buddha. It is situated above a river with paths leading through it, and its pavilions are built upon carved cliffs; its long corridors and covered eaves rest against the crags and connect with the mountain peaks. Divine spirits guard and protect it, and sages and worthies have wandered and rested there. Within the first millennium after the Buddha’s extinction, a thousand ordinary monks would enter the summer retreat there each year; on the day the retreat concluded, they would all attain arhatship and depart by rising into the void through the power of their supernatural faculties. After the first millennium, ordinary people and holy beings lived there together. For the past hundred years or so, there have been no more monks, and the mountain spirits have changed their forms—sometimes appearing as jackals or wolves, other times as apes or monkeys—to terrify travelers. For this reason, the place is desolate and empty, devoid of any monastic community.

Not far to the south of the city is a great mountain crag, the place where the master of treatises Bhāviveka (婆毘吠伽) dwelt in the Asura Palace (阿素洛宮), awaiting the time when the Bodhisattva Maitreya (慈氏菩薩) attains Buddhahood. The master of treatises possessed a refined character that was vast and far-reaching, and his ultimate virtue was profound and deep; outwardly he displayed the attire of the Sāṃkhya (僧佉), while inwardly he promoted the teachings of Nāgārjuna (龍猛). Hearing that the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla (護法菩薩) in the kingdom of Magadha (摩揭陀國) was propagating the Dharma teachings to thousands of students, he felt a desire to engage in discussion, so he took up his staff and set out. Upon arriving at the city of Pāṭaliputra (波吒釐城), he learned that the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla was at the Bodhi Tree (菩提樹), and the master of treatises instructed his disciple, saying: "Go to the place of the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla at the Bodhi Tree and convey my words as follows: 'The Bodhisattva propagates the bequeathed teachings and guides the deluded; I have long looked up to your virtue with a humble mind. However, because my past vow has not yet been fulfilled, I have been unable to pay my respects. As for the Bodhi Tree, I vow not to see it in vain; when I see it, there must be a realization, and I shall proclaim him the Teacher of Gods and Men.'" The Bodhisattva Dharmapāla said to his messenger: "The human world is like an illusion, and life is like a bubble; my days are consumed with diligent sincerity, and I have no leisure for discussion." Messengers went back and forth, but they never met. After the master of treatises returned to his native land, he sat quietly and thought: "If it is not Maitreya who attains Buddhahood, who can resolve my doubts?" Before an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩), he recited the *Hṛdaya-dhāraṇī* (隨心陀羅尼), abstaining from grain and consuming only water for a period of three years. The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara then manifested a wondrous physical form and said to the master of treatises: "What is your aspiration?" He replied: "I wish to preserve this body to await the sight of Maitreya." The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩) said: "Human life is precarious and fragile, and the world is a floating illusion. It is better to cultivate superior and virtuous vows to be reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven (覩史多天), where you may pay homage and meet him more quickly." The master of treatises replied: "My aspiration cannot be diverted, and my heart cannot be divided." The Bodhisattva said: "If that is so, you should go to the mountain cliff south of the capital of the country of Dhānakaṭaka (馱那羯磔迦國) to the abode of the deity Vajrapāṇi (執金剛神). If you recite the *Vajrapāṇi-dhāraṇī* (執金剛陀羅尼) with utmost sincerity, your wish shall be fulfilled." The master of treatises then went there and recited it. After three years, the deity asked him: "What is your wish, that you are so diligent and earnest?" The master of treatises replied: "I wish to preserve this body to await the sight of Maitreya (慈氏). The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara directed me to come and request this; is it not in your power to fulfill my wish?" The deity then bestowed a secret method upon him and said: "Inside this rock is the palace of the Asuras (阿素洛宮). If you perform the ritual according to the Dharma and make your request, the stone wall shall open. Once it opens, you may enter and wait there to see him." The master of treatises said: "If I dwell in seclusion and see nothing, how will I know when the Buddha has arisen?" Vajrapāṇi replied: "When Maitreya appears in the world, I shall inform you." The master of treatises accepted the command and recited with focused concentration. After another three years had passed, without a single stray thought, he enchanted mustard seeds and struck the rock with them; the stone wall parted and opened wide. At that time, hundreds of thousands of people watched, unable to turn away. The master of treatises (śāstra-master) stepped across the threshold and announced to the crowd: "I have long prayed, waiting to see Maitreya (慈氏). Through the protection of the holy spirits, my great vow is now fulfilled. You should all enter here to witness the arising of the Buddha together." Those who heard this were terrified and none dared to step across the threshold, claiming it was a den of venomous snakes and fearing they would lose their lives. After he exhorted them repeatedly, only six people followed him inside. The master of treatises looked back to bid farewell to the crowd and entered with composure. Once he had entered, the stone wall closed back up. The crowd all lamented and sighed, regretting their previous words.

From here, traveling southwest for more than a thousand li, one reaches the country of Cuḷya (珠利耶國). The country of Cuḷya is two thousand four or five hundred li in circuit. The capital city is more than ten li in circuit. The land is wild and empty, and the marshes and swamps are overgrown and desolate. The households are few, and groups of bandits operate openly. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are treacherous and deceitful. The people are fierce and violent by nature, and they revere and believe in non-Buddhist paths. The monasteries are dilapidated, with only a few monks. There are several dozen Deva temples, mostly belonging to the naked ascetics. Not far to the southeast of the city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. In the past, the Tathāgata displayed great supernatural powers at this place, preached the profound and subtle Dharma, subdued the non-Buddhists, and saved many heavenly beings and humans. Not far to the west of the city is an old monastery, the place where the Bodhisattva Deva (提婆菩薩) debated with an Arhat. Initially, the Bodhisattva Deva heard that there was an Arhat named Uttara (嗢呾羅) in this monastery who had attained the six supernatural powers and possessed the eight liberations, so he came from afar to seek him out and observe his demeanor. Upon arriving at the monastery, he requested to stay with the Arhat. The Arhat was of few desires and knew contentment, possessing only one bed. Since Deva had arrived and there was no other seat, the Arhat gathered fallen leaves and directed him to sit there. The Arhat entered into meditation and only emerged at midnight. Deva then presented his doubts and requested resolutions, and the Arhat explained each difficulty accordingly. However, as Deva followed his words with repeated interrogations, by the seventh round, the Arhat remained silent and could not answer, so he secretly exercised his supernatural powers to go to the Tuṣita Heaven to consult Maitreya (慈氏). Maitreya (慈氏) provided the explanation and then told him, "That Deva (提婆) has practiced for vast kalpas and shall succeed to the Buddha's throne during the Bhadrakalpa; this is beyond your knowledge, and you should pay him deep respect." In the space of a finger-snap, he returned to his original seat, whereupon he again expounded the wonderful meanings and analyzed the subtle words. Deva said to him, "This is the explanation from the holy wisdom of Maitreya Bodhisattva; how could it be something you have investigated thoroughly on your own?" The Arhat replied, "Indeed, it is the intent of the Tathāgata." Thereupon, he left his seat to pay respects and offer thanks, deeply expressing his reverence and admiration.

From here, traveling south into the forests and wilderness for one thousand five hundred or one thousand six hundred li, one arrives at the country of Draviḍa (達羅毘荼國). The country of Draviḍa is over six thousand li in circuit, and its capital city is called Kāñcīpura (逮志補羅), which is over thirty li in circuit. The land is fertile and rich, with abundant crops, many flowers and fruits, and it produces precious goods. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs of the people are brave and fierce. They are deeply devoted to faith and righteousness, and are noble and learned, though their language and script differ slightly from those of Central India. There are more than one hundred monasteries and over ten thousand monks, all of whom follow the teachings of the Sthavira school. There are more than eighty deva temples, mostly belonging to the naked ascetics (Nirgrantha). When the Tathāgata was in the world, he frequently traveled to this country to preach the Dharma and save people; therefore, King Aśoka (無憂王) built stūpas at all these sacred sites. The city of Kāñcīpura is the birthplace of the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla (達磨波羅). The Bodhisattva was the eldest son of a high minister of this country. In his youth, he possessed an elegant character, and as he grew, his aspirations became vast. When he reached the age of twenty, a princess was betrothed to him. On the evening of the wedding ceremony, he felt miserable and distressed, and he prayed earnestly before an image of the Buddha. Moved by his utmost sincerity, a deity carried him far away to a mountain monastery several hundred li from there, where he sat in the Buddha hall. A monk opened the door and, seeing this youth, suspected him of being a thief and questioned him further. The Bodhisattva explained his situation in full and requested to leave the household life. The assembly was astonished and granted his wish. The king then issued a decree to search far and near, and only then did he learn that the Bodhisattva had been carried away by a deity to a distant place. When the king learned of this, his respect and wonder deepened. From the time he donned the dyed robes, he studied with earnest diligence, and his fine reputation and exemplary conduct are described in the preceding record. Not far to the south of the city is a large monastery (saṃghārāma), where the intelligent and learned of the country gather and reside. There is a stupa (stūpa) over a hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata (如來) preached the Dharma here, subdued the followers of non-Buddhist paths, and extensively saved humans and devas. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas.

From here, traveling south more than 3,000 li, one arrives at the country of Malakuṭa (秣羅矩吒國). The country of Malakuṭa is more than 5,000 li in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than 40 li in circuit. The soil is saline and barren, and the land is not productive. Many precious items from the islands of the sea are gathered in this country. The climate is hot, and the people are mostly dark-skinned. Their temperament is fierce and unyielding, and they revere both heterodox and orthodox paths. They do not value the arts, but are only skilled in pursuing profit. There are many ruins of old monasteries, but few remain standing, and the number of monks is also small. There are several hundred Deva temples, and the number of non-Buddhists is very great, many of whom are ascetics who go naked. Not far to the east of the city is an old monastery; its courtyards and buildings are desolate, but the foundations still remain, having been built by the Great King (Mahendra), the younger brother of King Aśoka (無憂王). To its east is a stūpa; its high foundation has sunk, but the inverted-bowl dome still exists, established by King Aśoka. In the past, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma here, manifested great supernatural powers, and saved immeasurable multitudes; this was built to mark these sacred traces. As time has passed, it has become increasingly miraculous, and prayers are sometimes fulfilled.

To the south of the country, bordering the sea, is Mount Malaya (秣剌耶山), with its lofty cliffs, steep ridges, deep caverns, and mountain torrents. Among them are white sandalwood trees and candaneva trees (栴檀儞婆樹). The latter resemble white sandalwood and cannot be distinguished from them, except in the height of summer, when one climbs to a high place and looks out from afar; those entwined by large snakes are known to be such. Because the nature of this wood is cool and cold, the snakes coil around it. Once they have been sighted, arrows are shot to mark them, and only after the snakes have hibernated in winter are the trees harvested. The camphor tree (羯布羅香樹; Skt. karpūra) has a trunk like a pine but different leaves, and its flowers and fruits are also distinct. When first harvested and still moist, it has no fragrance, but after the wood dries, it is split along the grain to reveal a fragrant substance within, shaped like mica and colored like ice or snow; this is what is called camphor (龍腦香).

To the east of the Malaya (秣剌耶) Mountains is Mount Potalaka (布呾洛迦山). The mountain paths are perilous, and the cliffs and valleys are precipitous. On the summit of the mountain is a lake with water as clear as a mirror, from which flows a great river that circles the mountain twenty times before entering the South Sea. Beside the lake is a stone celestial palace where the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩) comes and goes to dwell. Those who wish to see the Bodhisattva disregard their own lives, wading through waters and climbing the mountain, forgetting all hardships and dangers; yet those who are able to reach it are few indeed. As for the inhabitants at the foot of the mountain who pray with a sincere heart to see him, the Bodhisattva may appear in the form of Maheśvara (自在天) or as an ash-smearing ascetic (塗灰外道) to console them and fulfill their wishes.

To the northeast of this mountain, by the seaside, there is a city which is the route to the country of Siṃhala (僧伽羅國) in the South Sea. I have heard from the local people that if one enters the sea from here and travels southeast for more than three thousand li, one reaches the country of Siṃhala.

The country of Siṃhala (僧伽羅國) is over 7,000 li in circumference. The capital city is over 40 li in circumference. The land is fertile, the climate is warm and hot, crops are sown in their proper seasons, and flowers and fruits are abundant. The population is prosperous, and the households are wealthy. The people are short and dark-skinned, and their temperaments are fierce and impetuous. They are fond of learning and value virtue, honoring goodness and diligently cultivating merit. This country was originally an island of gems; it contains many precious treasures and is inhabited by ghosts and spirits.  Later, there was a king in South India whose daughter was betrothed to a neighboring country. On an auspicious day, as she was being escorted there, they encountered a lion on the road. Her attendants abandoned the girl and fled to escape the danger, but the girl remained in her carriage, resigned to losing her life. At that time, the lion king carried the girl away, entering deep mountains and dwelling in secluded valleys. He hunted deer and gathered fruit to provide for her in due season. After many years had passed, she gave birth to a son and a daughter; their appearance was that of humans, but their nature was that of beasts.   As the son gradually grew up, he had the strength to wrestle with wild beasts. When he reached the age of twenty, his human intelligence began to manifest, and he said to his mother, "What am I? My father is a wild beast, and my mother is a human. Since we are not of the same species, how can we be mates?" His mother then recounted the past to her son, saying, "Humans and beasts follow different paths; we should flee at once." The mother said, "I tried to escape before, but I could not succeed on my own." The son subsequently followed his lion father, climbing mountains and crossing ridges to observe his movements so that they might escape the danger. Once he had waited for his father to leave, he carried his mother and sister on his back and descended toward human settlements. The mother said, "We must each be cautious and secretive; do not speak of the origin of these events, for if people should hear of them, they may look down upon us." Thereupon, they arrived at the father’s native country, but the country was not that of their kin, and their ancestral line had already been extinguished. They sought shelter with the townspeople, who asked them, "From what country are you?" They replied, "We are originally from this country, but we were scattered in foreign lands; mother and son have traveled together to return to our old home." The people all felt pity and compassion, and together they provided them with supplies.  When the lion king returned and saw nothing, he pined for his children. His fury erupted, and he left the mountain valleys to roam among the villages and towns, roaring and thundering, violently harming people and animals, and cruelly destroying living beings. Whenever the townspeople came out, he would seize and kill them. They beat drums and blew conch shells, shouldered crossbows and held spears, and followed in groups like an army; only then could they avoid harm.  The king, fearing that his benevolent influence was not reaching the people, released hunters, hoping to capture the beast. The king personally led the four divisions of the army, numbering in the tens of thousands, to surround the forests and thickets, spanning across the mountains and valleys. The lion roared, and both men and beasts fled in terror. Since he could not be captured, the king subsequently issued a recruitment call: whoever could seize the lion and rid the country of this menace would be rewarded with a great prize to honor their distinguished achievement.  Upon hearing the king’s order, the son said to his mother, "Our hunger and cold have become extreme; I should respond to the recruitment, for perhaps I may gain something with which to support you." The mother said, "You must not speak like this! Although he is a beast, he is still called your father; how could you, because of hardship, commit such an act of rebellion and harm?" The son replied, "Humans and beasts are of different species; where then is the place for ritual and righteousness? Since we are already obstructed and hindered, what hope is there for this heart?" He then hid a small knife in his sleeve and went out to answer the recruitment. At that time, thousands of people and ten thousand cavalry gathered like clouds and mist, but the lion sat in the forest, and no one dared to approach. The son went directly before him, and the father became tame and submissive. Thus, out of affection, he forgot his anger; the son then stabbed his blade into the father’s belly. The father still harbored loving kindness and remained without resentment or malice, even as his belly was ripped open, and he died enduring the pain. The king asked, "What kind of person is this, that he is so extraordinary?" He tempted him with benefits and threatened him with punishment, after which the son fully explained the beginning and the end, detailing the entire situation. The king said, "How rebellious! If he would even harm his own father, how much more so would he harm those who are not his kin? The beast species is difficult to tame, and their violent nature is easily stirred. To remove a menace to the people is a great merit, but to sever the life of one's father is a rebellious heart. I shall provide a heavy reward to compensate for his merit, but I shall banish him far away to punish his rebellion. In this way, the laws of the country will not be compromised, and the king’s word will not be inconsistent." Thereupon, he fitted out two large ships and stored them with plenty of provisions. The mother was left in the country and provided for with the reward for the merit, while the son and daughter were each placed on a ship and left to drift with the waves. The son’s ship drifted across the sea until it reached this island of treasures; seeing an abundance of precious gems, he settled there. Later, when merchants came to the island to collect treasures, he killed the merchant leader and kept his children. In this way they multiplied, and their descendants were numerous. They then established a ruler and ministers, assigned ranks of high and low, built a capital and cities, and occupied the territory. Because their ancestor had captured a lion (siṃha), they cited this original achievement to name the country. As for the ship carrying the daughter, it drifted to the west of Persia (Pārasī), where she was bewitched by spirits and gave birth to a group of daughters; this is the origin of the present-day Western Kingdom of Women. Therefore, the people of the country of the Lion (Siṃhala) have a base and dark appearance, with square chins and broad foreheads; their temperament is fierce and violent, and they are cruel and prone to poisoning. This is because they are the descendants of a wild beast, and thus the people are mostly brave and robust. This is one account.  What the Buddha’s teaching records is as follows: In the past, in the great iron city of this precious island, there dwelt five hundred rākṣasīs. Atop the city towers, two tall banners were erected to signify signs of good or ill fortune; the auspicious banner would move when there was a lucky event, and the inauspicious banner would move when there was a calamity. They would constantly lie in wait for merchants arriving at the precious island, whereupon they would transform into beautiful women, carrying fragrant flowers and playing music to welcome and console them, luring them into the iron city. After the festivities and banquets were over, they would place the merchants in an iron prison and gradually devour them.  At that time, in the continent of Jambudvīpa, there was a great merchant leader named Saṃgha; his son was named Saṃghala. His father being old, he took over the family business and set out with five hundred merchants to enter the sea to collect treasures. Blown about by wind and waves, they happened to reach the precious island. When the rākṣasīs saw the auspicious banner move, they brought fragrant flowers and played music, coming together to welcome the merchants and entice them into the iron city. The merchant leader then engaged in joyful entertainment with the rākṣasī queen, and the remaining merchants each paired off with one, and as the years passed, they all fathered children. The rākṣasīs, their affections for their old partners having grown distant, wished to imprison them in an iron jail to wait for other merchants. At that time, Saṃghala had a nightmare during the night and, knowing it was not an auspicious sign, secretly sought a path home. He happened upon the iron jail and heard the sound of piteous wailing, so he climbed a tall tree and asked, "Who is it that is bound and suffering such grief?" They replied, "Do you not know? The women in the city are all rākṣasīs. In the past, they enticed us into the city for entertainment. Once you had arrived, they imprisoned us and gradually consumed us as food; now more than half are gone, and before long, you too will suffer this same calamity." Saṃghala asked, "What plan can be devised to escape this danger?" They replied, "We have heard that there is a heavenly horse on the seashore; if one prays with utmost sincerity, it will surely ferry one across to safety." Having heard this, Saṃghala secretly informed the other merchants, and together they looked toward the seashore, focusing their minds on seeking salvation. At that time, the heavenly horse came and told the men, "If each of you grasps my mane and does not look back, I will ferry you across the sea to escape this peril and reach the continent of Jambudvīpa, returning to your home country." The merchants followed these instructions with single-minded devotion and gripped its mane; the heavenly horse then soared into the clouds and galloped across the seacoast. The rākṣasīs (羅剎女) suddenly realized their husbands had fled; they told one another, wondering where they had gone, and each carrying her young child, they flew through the air in search of them. Knowing the merchants were about to reach the seashore, they called out to one another and flew off to find them. Before long, they encountered the company of merchants; with mixed feelings of grief and joy, their tears flowed freely as they covered their faces, sobbing and saying: "I am grateful for our meeting and fortunate to have wed such a fine man; our home was full of joy and we have long shared deep affection, yet now you abandon us to go far away, leaving your wife and child desolate—how can anyone endure such a heart-wrenching fate? We pray you, look back and return with us to the city."  The hearts of the merchants remained unmoved. The rākṣasīs, finding their entreaties of no avail, resorted to their demonic charms and employed every manner of deception. The merchants, overcome by love and unable to bear the separation, felt their resolve waver, and they all fell back. The rākṣasīs congratulated one another and went away, holding the merchants by the hand.  Siṃhala (僧伽羅), however, possessed deep and firm wisdom; his mind was free from attachments, and he succeeded in crossing the great sea, escaping this peril. Meanwhile, the queen of the rākṣasīs returned alone to the Iron City. The other rākṣasīs said to her, "You lack wisdom and strategy, having been abandoned by your husband; since you are devoid of skill and ability, you should no longer dwell here."  The queen of the rākṣasīs then took the child she had borne, flew before Siṃhala, and, exerting her utmost charms, enticed and pleaded with him to return. Siṃhala recited a mantra and, brandishing his sharp sword, rebuked her, saying: "You are a rākṣasī, and I am a human; humans and ghosts follow different paths, and we are not a match." If you continue to harass me with your suffering, I shall end your life." The rākṣasī, knowing that her seduction had failed, flew through the air and arrived at the home of Siṃhala (僧伽羅). She deceived his father, Siṃha (僧伽), saying: "I am the daughter of a certain king. Siṃhala took me as his wife and we bore a son. We were carrying precious goods to return to his native country, but while crossing the sea, we encountered a storm and our ship was wrecked. Only my son, myself, and Siṃhala managed to survive. The mountains and rivers were difficult to traverse, and we suffered from cold, hunger, and hardship. Because of one word that displeased him, I was abandoned and cast aside, insulted with improper language, and reviled as a rākṣasī. To return home is to face a vast distance, and to stay here is to be a lonely, stranded traveler. With nowhere to turn, I dare to present my situation."  Siṃha said, "It is truly as you say; you should enter the house at once." Not long after, Siṃhala arrived. His father said to him, "Why do you value wealth and treasure while slighting your wife and child?" Siṃhala replied, "This is a rākṣasī." He then explained the previous events in detail to his parents, and his relatives and kin all joined in driving her away.  The rākṣasī then complained to the king, and the king wished to punish Siṃhala. Siṃhala said, "She is a rākṣasī, and her nature is full of seductive bewitchment." The king believed this was untrue, and being charmed by her beauty, he said to Siṃhala, "If you must abandon this woman, I shall keep her in my harem." Siṃhala replied, "I fear it will bring disaster. Since she is a rākṣasī, her only food is blood and flesh." The king did not listen to the words of Siṃhala and proceeded to take her as his wife. Later, in the middle of the night, she flew back to the precious island (Ratnadvīpa) and summoned the other five hundred rākṣasī demonesses to come together to the royal palace. Using poisonous incantations, they ravaged the palace; they ate the flesh and drank the blood of all the people and animals, then took the remaining corpses and returned to the precious island. At daybreak, the ministers and officials gathered for court, but the palace gates were closed and would not open. They waited and listened for a long time, but heard no human voices. Thereupon, they pushed against the doors and opened the gates, following one another as they hurried inside. When they reached the palace courtyard, it was silent and empty of people; there were only skeletons. The officials and aides looked at one another in dismay, wailing and weeping, unable to fathom the source of the disaster. Siṃhala recounted the entire story from beginning to end, and the ministers and subjects believed him, realizing that the king had brought this disaster upon himself.  Thereupon, the state assistants, veteran ministers, various officials, and senior generals inquired after those of illustrious virtue and sought out those of sublime character; all admired the merit and wisdom of Siṃhala, and they consulted together, saying: "How can the one who rules the people be chosen haphazardly? He must first possess merit and wisdom, and secondly embody sagacity and discernment; for without merit and wisdom, one cannot enjoy the precious throne, and without sagacity and discernment, how can one manage the affairs of state? Siṃhala is the very man. He perceived the hidden danger in a dream, was moved by the response of the heavenly horse, was loyal in remonstrating with his lord, and was wise enough to protect himself. The mandate of history is here; let us compose a new song of praise." The masses were happy to support him and honored him by establishing him as king. Siṃhala, unable to decline the offer, agreed to hold to the middle path, and after bowing respectfully to the assembled officials, he ascended the throne. Thereupon, he reformed the previous abuses and set an example of virtue. He then issued an order, saying: "Our former merchant companions are in the land of the Rākṣasas; their life or death is uncertain, and good and evil are indistinguishable. Now, to rescue them from their plight, we should prepare our arms and armor; to save those in peril and show compassion to those in distress is a blessing to the state; to recover precious goods and store up treasures is a benefit to the state." Thereupon, he organized his troops and traveled across the sea. At that time, the banners of ill omen atop the iron city began to shake; the Rākṣasīs, seeing this, were struck with terror and immediately unleashed their seductive charms, coming out to meet the men to entice and deceive them.
