The king, having long known of their deceit, ordered his soldiers to recite mantras with their mouths and exert their martial might with their bodies. The Rākṣasīs stumbled, fell, and were defeated; some fled to hide on isolated islands, while others drowned in the surging currents. Thereupon, he destroyed the iron city, broke the iron prisons, rescued the merchants, and obtained many jewels. He recruited the common people to move and settle on the treasure island, established a capital, built towns, and thus a kingdom was formed. He then used the king’s name as the name of the country.  Siṃhala (僧伽羅) is a matter from a previous life of Śākya Tathāgata. In earlier times, the kingdom of Siṃhala only honored licentious sacrifices. In the hundredth year after the Buddha passed away, Mahendra (摩醯因陀羅), the younger brother of King Aśoka (無憂王), abandoned worldly desires to seek the fruits of sainthood; having attained the six supernatural powers and the eight liberations, he traveled through the air to this country to propagate the true Dharma and spread the bequeathed teachings. From that time onward, the customs have been pure and faithful. There are several hundred saṃghārāmas and over twenty thousand monks, who follow the teachings of the Mahāyāna Sthavira school. More than two hundred years after the arrival of Buddhism, each [group] specialized in its own field, dividing into two schools: the first is the Mahāvihāra (摩訶毘訶羅) school, which rejects the Mahāyāna and studies the Lesser Vehicle; the second is the Abhayagiri (阿跋耶祇釐) school, which studies both vehicles and propagates the Tripiṭaka. The monks are pure in their moral conduct, their concentration and wisdom are clear and bright, their deportment is exemplary, and they are numerous and flourishing.  Beside the royal palace is the Temple of the Buddha’s Tooth (mūla-gandha-kuṭī), several hundred feet high, shimmering with pearls and adorned with rare gems. A signal post is erected atop the temple, upon which is placed a large padmarāga jewel; its brilliant light shines resplendently, and when viewed from afar, it glitters like a bright star by day or night. Three times a day, the king bathes the Buddha’s tooth with scented water and powdered incense, either washing it or burning the incense, striving for the utmost rarity and splendor in his offerings.  Beside the Temple of the Buddha’s Tooth is a small temple, which is also adorned and polished with various precious gems. Inside is a golden Buddha statue, cast by a former king of this country to be of equal stature to himself, with the uṣṇīṣa adorned with precious jewels. Later, there was a thief who waited for an opportunity to steal it, but the heavy doors and surrounding railings were guarded with strict vigilance. The thief then dug a tunnel to enter the temple through a hole; when he attempted to take the jewel, the statue gradually grew taller and higher. Having failed in his quest, the thief retreated and sighed, saying: "In the past, the Tathāgata practiced the bodhisattva path, aroused a vast mind, and made great vows, offering up his own life and body, down to his cities and kingdoms, out of compassion for the four types of birth, bestowing everything upon all beings. Now, how could his bequeathed image be stingy with a jewel?" "Reflecting on this, I do not understand the past conduct." The image then bowed its head and bestowed the jewel. Having obtained it, the thief immediately took it to sell. Those who saw it all said to him, "This treasure is the jewel from the *uṣṇīṣa* (頂髻) of the golden Buddha image of the former king. Where did you obtain it to come here and sell it?" They then seized him and reported it to the king. The king asked where he had obtained it, and the thief said, "The Buddha gave it to me himself; I am not a thief." The king, thinking he was not being truthful, ordered an envoy to go and verify it, and the image was still bowing its head. Witnessing this sacred miracle, the king’s faith became pure and firm; he did not punish the man, but instead redeemed the jewel at a high price, adorned the image’s *uṣṇīṣa*, and replaced it on the crown. Because of this, the image has remained with its head bowed until the present day.  Beside the royal palace, a great kitchen was built, preparing food for eighteen thousand monks daily. When the time for the meal arrived, the assembly of monks would hold their alms bowls to receive the provisions, and having received their food, each would return to his own residence. Since the time the Buddha’s teaching spread to this land, this offering was established, and descendants inherited the succession, continuing the practice until the present. For the past ten or more years, the country has been in political turmoil without a stable ruler, and this practice has been abandoned. The country is situated on the edge of the sea and the land produces precious gems. When the king personally performs sacrifices, the spirits present rare treasures. The city’s inhabitants and scholars travel back and forth to seek and collect them, and according to their karmic rewards, what they obtain differs. Depending on the pearls and gems they acquire, there is a set tax.

More than two hundred years after the arrival of Buddhism, each [group] specialized in its own field, and they divided into two schools: the first is called the Mahāvihāra school (摩訶毘訶羅住部), which rejects the Mahāyāna and studies the Hīnayāna teachings.
The second is the Abhayagiri-vihāra school (阿跋耶祇釐住部), which studies both vehicles and propagates the Tripiṭaka.

Sailing several thousand li across the sea to the south of the country, one reaches the island of Nārikela (那羅稽羅洲). The inhabitants of the island are diminutive, being just over three feet tall; they have human bodies and bird-like beaks, and as they do not cultivate grain or crops, they subsist solely on coconuts.

Sailing several thousand *li* west across the sea from the country of Nārikela (那羅稽羅洲), on the eastern cliff of a solitary island, there is a stone Buddha statue over a hundred feet high, seated facing east. It has a moonstone (*candrakānta*) as its *uṣṇīṣa*; when the moon shines upon it, water flows down, drenching the cliffs and ridges and pouring into the mountain ravines. At one time, a group of merchants, having encountered a storm and drifted with the waves, arrived at this solitary island. The sea water was salty and undrinkable, and they suffered from thirst for a long time. It happened to be the fifteenth day of the month, and water flowed from the top of the statue, by which the entire group was saved; they believed that their utmost sincerity had moved the divine sage to rescue them. They remained there for several days, but whenever the moon was hidden behind the high cliffs, the water would not flow. The leader of the merchants then said, "It is not necessarily the case that it flows to save us. I have heard that when moonlight shines upon a moonstone, water will flow; could it be that there is such a gem atop the head of the Buddha statue?" They then climbed the cliff to look at it and found that the *uṣṇīṣa* of the image was indeed made of moonstone. When they met the people there, they told them the whole story from beginning to end.

To the west of the country, sailing several thousand li across the sea, one reaches the Great Treasure Island (Mahāratnadvīpa), which is uninhabited by humans and serves only as an abode for deities. In the quiet of the night, looking from afar, its light illuminates the mountains and waters. Many merchants have traveled there, but all have returned without obtaining anything.

In the southeast corner of the country is Mount Laṅkā (䮚迦山), with its steep cliffs and deep valleys where spirits and ghosts dwell; it is here that the Tathāgata formerly preached the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra (䮚迦經).

From the country of Draviḍa (達羅毘荼國), traveling north into the forests and wilderness, passing isolated cities and small towns—where bands of brigands harm travelers—one travels over two thousand *li* to reach the country of Konkaṇapura (荼建那補羅國). The country of Konkaṇapura is over five thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city is over thirty *li* in circuit. The land is fertile and the crops are abundant. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are impetuous and fierce. The people are dark-complexioned and their dispositions are wild and violent. They are fond of learning and value virtue and the arts. There are over one hundred monasteries and more than ten thousand monks, who study both the Great and Lesser Vehicles with equal diligence. There are several hundred *deva* temples, where followers of various heterodox sects live together. Beside the royal palace is a great monastery with over three hundred monks, who are truly outstanding men. In the great *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍) of this monastery, which is over one hundred feet high, is the precious crown of Prince Sarvārthasiddha (一切義成太子). It is nearly two feet high, adorned with precious jewels, and kept in a precious casket. Every fast day, it is brought out and placed on a high seat to be worshipped with incense and flowers, at which times it emits light. Beside the city is a great monastery containing a *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* over fifty feet high, in which is a sandalwood statue of Maitreya Bodhisattva (慈氏菩薩) over ten feet high. On some fast days, it shines with divine light; it is said to have been made by the Arhat Śrotaviṃśatikoṭi (二百億羅漢). Not far to the north of the city is a forest of *tāla* trees, thirty *li* in circuit; its leaves are long and broad, and their color is glossy and smooth. In all the various countries, these are used for writing. In the forest is a stūpa, which is the site of the traces of the sitting and walking meditation of the four past Buddhas. Beside it is a stūpa said to contain the relics of the body of the Arhat Śrotaviṃśatikoṭi (二百億羅漢). Not far to the east of the city is a stūpa; its base has already collapsed and sunk, and it remains three *zhang* high. I have heard from the records of predecessors that it contains relics of the Tathāgata, and on fast days it sometimes emits a divine light. In the past, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma here and manifested his supernatural powers to save the multitudes of living beings. Not far to the southwest of the city is a stūpa over one hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). It is said that the Arhat Śrotaviṃśatikoṭi manifested great supernatural powers here to transform and save living beings. Beside it is a saṃghārāma, of which only the foundation remains; it was built by that Arhat.

From here, traveling northwest into a great forest and wilderness, one encounters ferocious beasts and cruel bands of robbers. After traveling two thousand four or five hundred li, one reaches the country of Mahārāṣṭra (摩訶剌侘國). The country of Mahārāṣṭra is over six thousand li in circumference. The capital city of the country borders a great river to the west and is over thirty li in circumference. The soil is fertile and rich, and the crops are abundant. The climate is warm and hot, and the customs are simple and honest. The people are tall and sturdy in stature, and their nature is proud and carefree. They never fail to repay a kindness or avenge a grievance; if someone insults them, they will risk their lives to take vengeance, and if someone in desperate straits seeks their aid, they will forget their own safety to assist them. When they are about to take revenge, they first notify their opponent, and only after both sides have donned sturdy armor do they engage in battle. When pursuing a defeated enemy on the battlefield, they do not kill those who have surrendered. If a general or soldier suffers a defeat, he is not punished; instead, he is presented with women’s clothing, and, feeling ashamed, he will take his own life. The state maintains several hundred brave warriors. Whenever they are about to engage in a decisive battle, they drink wine until they are intoxicated; then, a single man will charge the vanguard, causing ten thousand men to lose their edge. If they happen to harm someone, the state does not impose punishment, and whenever they go out on excursions, they have drums beaten to lead the way. Furthermore, they keep several hundred ferocious elephants. Whenever they are about to engage in battle, these elephants are also given wine to drink; they then charge in a group, trampling everything, and no enemy can stand firm before them. The king relies on these men and elephants to look down upon neighboring countries. The king is of the Kṣatriya (剎帝利) caste and is named Pulakeśin (補羅稽舍). His strategies are far-reaching, his benevolence is widely extended, and his subjects serve him with the utmost loyalty. Currently, the great King Śīlāditya (戒日大王) campaigns from the east to the west, bringing distant lands to submission and near lands to order, yet only the people of this country refuse to acknowledge his suzerainty. Although he has repeatedly led the armored troops of the Five Indias and summoned the heroic generals of many nations to personally lead an invasion, he has yet to achieve victory. Such is the nature of their military, and such are their customs. The people are known for their love of learning, and they revere both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are over one hundred saṃghārāmas (伽藍) and more than five thousand monks; they study both the Great and Lesser Vehicles, mastering them with equal diligence. There are hundreds of Deva temples, and the heterodox sects are very numerous. Inside and outside the great city, there are five stūpas (窣堵波) built by King Aśoka (無憂王) at the sites where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditations. As for the other stūpas made of stone or brick, their number is so great that it is difficult to enumerate them all. Not far to the south of the city is an old saṃghārāma, in which there is a stone image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩); its spiritual efficacy is secretly felt, and those who pray for wishes often see them fulfilled.

On the eastern border of the country there is a great mountain (Pravaragiri), with overlapping ridges and connected barriers, and layered peaks with sheer cliffs. Here there is a monastery situated in a secluded valley, with lofty halls and deep chambers, built against the cliffs and resting upon the peaks; its multi-storied pavilions and tiered terraces lean against the rock and face the gully. It was built by the Arhat Achara (阿折羅). The Arhat was a man from Western India. After his mother passed away, he observed into which realm she had been reborn and saw that she had taken a woman’s body in this country. The Arhat then came to this place, intending to guide and transform her, accepting her according to her capacity. He entered the village to beg for food and arrived at the house where his mother had been reborn. When the young woman brought food to offer, her milk began to flow; when her relatives saw this, they considered it an ill omen. The Arhat explained the original karmic causes, and the woman then attained the holy fruit. Feeling gratitude for the grace of his birth and mindful of the workings of karmic conditions, the Arhat built this monastery to repay her profound virtue.  The great vihara (mūla-gandha-kuṭī) of the monastery is over one hundred feet high, and within it is a stone Buddha statue seventy feet tall. Above it are seven stone canopies, suspended in the void without any supports, with a space of more than three feet between each canopy. I have heard from the records of predecessors that this is sustained by the power of the Arhat’s vows; others say it is the power of supernatural faculties; still others say it is the work of medicinal arts. Upon examining the actual records, the cause remains unclear. The four walls of the vihara are carved with stone reliefs depicting the various causal deeds of the Tathāgata when he was formerly practicing the Bodhisattva path. The auspicious signs of his attainment of the holy fruit and the spiritual responses of his entry into extinction are all carved in detail, with nothing, great or small, left out. Outside the monastery gate, to the south, north, left, and right, there is one stone elephant on each side. I have heard from the local people that these elephants occasionally roar loudly, causing the earth to tremble. In the past, the Bodhisattva Dignāga (陳那) frequently resided in this monastery.

From here, traveling west for more than a thousand li and crossing the Narmadā River (耐秣陀河), one reaches the country of Bharukacchapa (跋祿羯呫婆國). The country of Bharukacchapa is two thousand four or five hundred li in circuit. The capital city is over twenty li in circuit. The land is saline and barren, with sparse vegetation. The people boil seawater to make salt and rely on the sea for their livelihood. The climate is hot, and swirling winds rise frequently. The local customs are shallow, and the people are deceitful by nature. They do not value learning or the arts, and they believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are more than ten monasteries (saṃghārāma) with over three hundred monks, who study the teachings of the Mahāyāna Sthavira school. There are more than ten Deva temples, where followers of various heterodox paths live together.

From here, traveling northwest for more than two thousand *li*, one arrives at the country of Mālava (摩臘婆國). The country of Mālava is more than six thousand *li* in circumference. The capital city is more than thirty *li* in circumference and is situated to the southeast of the Mahī River. The land is fertile and rich, agriculture is flourishing, and the vegetation is lush and dense, with abundant flowers and fruits. It is especially suitable for winter wheat, and the people mostly eat cakes and parched grain. The nature of the people is gentle and compliant; they are generally intelligent and quick-witted, their speech is elegant and clear, and their learning and arts are profound. Within the borders of the five Indies, two countries place great importance on learning: the country of Mālava in the southwest and the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) in the northeast; they value virtue, honor benevolence, and are brilliant and diligent in their studies. However, in this country, both heterodox and orthodox beliefs are practiced. There are several hundred *saṃghārāmas* with more than twenty thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Sāmmitīya school of the Lesser Vehicle. There are several hundred *deva* temples, and the number of heterodox followers is truly great, most of whom are the sect that smears themselves with ashes. The national records state: sixty years ago, there was a king named Śīlāditya (尸羅阿迭多). His ingenuity and wisdom were brilliant, his talent and learning were vast and sharp, he cherished and nurtured the four types of birth, and he revered and honored the Three Jewels. From his birth until his death, his countenance never showed a look of anger, and his hands never harmed a living being. When elephants and horses drank water, he would have it filtered first, fearing that he might injure the life-force of the water. His benevolence and compassion were such as this. During his reign of more than fifty years, wild beasts became familiar with humans, and the entire populace of the country refrained from killing. Beside his palace, he established a *mūla-gandha-kuṭī* (精舍), exhausting all craftsmanship and preparing it with complete adornment, and within it, he had images of the seven Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, made. Every year, he regularly held a Great Pañcavārṣika Assembly (無遮大會), summoning monks from the four directions to provide them with the four monastic requisites, whether in the form of the three robes and religious implements, or rare treasures of the seven precious gems. This tradition has been passed down through successive generations, and this noble practice has never ceased.

More than twenty *li* northwest of the great city, one arrives at the Brahmin village (Brāhmaṇagrāma). Nearby is a deep pit; during the autumn and summer, despite heavy and persistent rains that last for ten days, and although it receives many streams, the water never accumulates. Beside it, a small stūpa has been built. According to ancient records, this is the place where a highly arrogant Brahmin fell into hell while still alive.  Formerly, in this village, there was a Brahmin who was naturally wise and widely learned, his scholarship surpassing that of the eminent men of his time. He had thoroughly investigated the profound mysteries of both internal and external scriptures, and the abstruse texts of astronomy and mathematics were as clear to him as if he were looking at the palm of his own hand. His character was noble and refined, and his reputation spread far and wide. The king held him in great esteem and respect, and the people of the country honored him. He had thousands of disciples who admired his way and were drawn to his influence.  He would often say, "I have appeared in this world to expound the sacred and guide the ordinary; neither the sages of the past nor the philosophers of the future can compare to me. People are all swept up in following Maheśvara, Vāsudeva, Nārāyaṇa, and the World-Honored Buddha; they propagate their doctrines, paint their images, and vie with one another to offer them worship. Now, since my virtue exceeds theirs and my fame dominates the age, if I do not do something different, how can I manifest my greatness?"  He then used red sandalwood to carve images of Maheśvara, Vāsudeva, Nārāyaṇa, and the World-Honored Buddha. He made a four-legged seat for them, and wherever he went, he carried them with him. Such was his arrogance. At that time, in Western India, there was a bhikṣu named Bhadraruci (跋陀羅縷支) who had attained the pinnacle of skill in logic (hetuvidyā) and had deeply exhausted the study of heterodox doctrines. His moral conduct was pure and refined, and the fragrance of his precepts was intense. He had few desires and was content, seeking nothing from the world. Upon hearing of this, he sighed and said, "Alas! There is no one left in this age, allowing that foolish man to dare to practice such wicked deeds." Thereupon, he shouldered his khakkhara staff and traveled from afar, arriving in this country, where he fully explained his long-held intention to the king. When the king saw his tattered robes, he did not feel any respect in his heart, yet he esteemed his ambition and reluctantly accorded him the proper courtesies. He then set up a debate seat and informed the Brahmin. The Brahmin heard this and laughed, saying, "Who is that person who dares to harbor such an ambition?" He ordered his followers to come to the debate grounds, and several hundred thousand people gathered to listen. Bhadraruci wore his tattered, old robes and spread grass upon which to sit. The Brahmin sat perched upon the seat he had brought, denouncing the true Dharma and expounding his heterodox doctrines. The bhikṣu’s clear eloquence flowed like a stream, arguing back and forth. After a long time, the Brahmin admitted defeat. The king then said to him, "You have long abused a false reputation, deceiving your superiors and confusing the masses. The ancient canons record that those who lose a debate should be executed." He intended to use a red-hot iron seat to make him sit upon it. The Brahmin, in dire straits, surrendered and begged for his life. Bhadraruci took pity on him and petitioned the king, saying, "Great King, your benevolence and propriety are known far and wide, and your praises fill the roads; you should spread compassionate nurturance rather than practicing cruelty. Forgive his inadequacies and let him go as he pleases." The king ordered him to ride a donkey and travel around to proclaim his defeat to the cities. The Brahmin, ashamed of this humiliation, became enraged and vomited blood. A bhikṣu, having heard of this, went to comfort him, saying, "Your learning encompasses both internal and external doctrines, and your reputation is known far and wide; you should clearly understand the nature of honor and disgrace, and when to advance or retreat. As for fame, what reality does it possess?" The Brahmin, filled with resentment, bitterly reviled the bhikṣu, slandered the Mahāyāna, and spoke with contempt of the ancient sages. Before his words had even died away, the earth split asunder, and he fell alive into the pit; the traces of this event still remain.

From here, traveling southwest into a maritime bay and then proceeding northwest for two thousand four or five hundred li, one reaches the country of Aṭali (阿吒釐國). The country of Aṭali is over six thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is over twenty li in circuit. The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous, and precious treasures are accumulated in abundance. Although agricultural crops are available, the people make trade their occupation. The land is sandy and saline, and flowers and fruits are scarce. It produces the pepper tree, the leaves of which are like those of the Sichuan pepper. It produces the frankincense tree, the leaves of which are like those of the flowering pear. The climate is hot, and there is much wind and dust. The nature of the people is shallow and base; they value wealth and despise virtue. Their writing, language, appearance, and customs are for the most part the same as those of the country of Mālava (摩臘婆國). Most do not believe in merit, and even among those who do, they revere and serve the heavenly deities. There are more than ten temples, where followers of various heterodox paths dwell together.

Traveling northwest from the country of Mālava (摩臘婆國) for three days, one reaches the country of Kiṭa (契吒國). The country of Kiṭa is more than three thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than twenty *li* in circuit. The population is dense and the households are wealthy. There is no great sovereign, and it is subject to the country of Mālava; its climate, soil, and products are consequently the same as those customs. There are more than ten monasteries with over a thousand monks, who study both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings. There are several dozen *deva* temples, and the non-Buddhists are numerous.

From here, traveling north more than one thousand *li*, one arrives at the country of Valabhī (伐臘毘國). The country of Valabhī is more than six thousand *li* in circumference. The capital city is more than thirty *li* in circumference. The produce of the land, the suitability of the climate, and the customs and human nature of the people are the same as in the country of Mālava (摩臘婆國). The inhabitants are prosperous and the households are wealthy; there are more than one hundred families who have accumulated wealth of one hundred *yuta* (hundreds of millions). Rare goods from distant regions are mostly gathered in this country. There are more than one hundred *saṃghārāma*s, with more than six thousand monks, who mostly study the teachings of the Hīnayāna Saṃmitīya school. There are several hundred *deva* temples, and the heterodox sects are very numerous. When the Tathāgata was in the world, he frequently traveled to this country; therefore, King Aśoka (無憂王) erected markers and built *stūpa*s at all the places where the Buddha stayed. The sites where the three past Buddhas sat, walked, and preached the Dharma are interspersed among them. The current king is of the Kṣatriya caste; he is the nephew of the former King Śīlāditya of the country of Mālava and the son-in-law of the current King Śīlāditya of the country of Kanyākubja (羯若鞠闍國), and his name is Dhruvabhaṭa. His temperament is impetuous and his wisdom and strategy are shallow. However, he has pure faith in the Three Jewels. Every year he holds a great assembly for seven days, offering rare treasures and superior delicacies to the community of monks. The cost of the three robes and medicines, as well as rare and precious items of the seven jewels, are all offered in total, and then redeemed at double their value. He values virtue and esteems the worthy, follows the path and respects learning, and he shows special respect and reverence to high-ranking monks from distant regions. Not far from the city is a great monastery, which was established by the Arhat Ācāra (阿折羅); it is the place where the Bodhisattvas Guṇamati (德慧) and Sthiramati (堅慧) resided and composed treatises, which are both widely circulated.

From here, traveling northwest for more than seven hundred li, one arrives at the country of Ānandapura (阿難陀補羅國). The country of Ānandapura is over two thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the kingdom is over twenty li in circuit. The population is dense and prosperous, and the households are wealthy. There is no great sovereign, and it is subject to the country of Mālava (摩臘婆國). The agricultural products, climate, and the rules of writing are all the same as those there. There are more than ten saṃghārāmas, with fewer than one thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Hīnayāna Sāmmitīya school. There are several dozen Deva temples, where followers of various heterodox paths live together.

Traveling westward from the kingdom of Valabhī (伐臘毘國) for over five hundred li, one reaches the kingdom of Suraṭṭha (蘇剌侘國). The kingdom of Suraṭṭha is over four thousand li in circuit. The capital city is over thirty li in circuit and borders the Mahī River (莫醯河) to the west. The population is dense and the households are wealthy. It is subject to the kingdom of Valabhī. The soil is saline and alkaline, and flowers and fruits are scarce. Although the cold and heat are balanced, the winds are gusty and restless. The local customs are shallow and thin, and the people’s temperament is impulsive and restless. They do not care for learning arts, and they believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are more than fifty saṃghārāmas with over three thousand monks, who mostly study the teachings of the Mahāyāna Sthavira school. There are more than one hundred Deva temples, where various heterodox sects dwell together. The country lies on the route to the Western Sea, and the people all rely on the benefits of the sea, making trade their occupation and exchanging what they have for what they lack.

Not far from the city is Mount Ujjanta (郁鄯多山). On its summit is a monastery, with rooms and corridors mostly carved out of the cliffs and ridges. The forests and trees are lush and dense, and streams flow across the landscape; it is a place where sages and saints wander and dwell, and where spirits and immortals gather.

Traveling north from the country of Valabhī (伐臘毘國) for more than 1,800 li, one reaches the country of Gurjara (瞿折羅國). The country of Gurjara is more than 5,000 li in circuit. The capital city is named Bhīlamāla (毘羅摩羅), and it is more than 30 li in circuit. The soil, climate, and customs are the same as those of the country of Surāṣṭra (蘇剌侘國). The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous, and their households are wealthy. They mostly serve non-Buddhist paths and have little faith in the Buddha’s teachings. There is one saṃghārāma with more than 100 monks, who study the teachings of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) according to the Sarvāstivāda school. There are several dozen deva temples where followers of various non-Buddhist paths live together. The king is of the Kṣatriya caste; he is in the prime of his youth, his wisdom and courage are far-reaching, he deeply believes in the Buddha’s teachings, and he holds noble and extraordinary abilities in high regard.

Traveling southeast from here for over 2,800 li, one reaches the country of Ujjayinī (鄔闍衍那國). The country of Ujjayinī is over 6,000 li in circuit. The capital city is over 30 li in circuit. The soil, climate, and customs are the same as those of the country of Surāṣṭra (蘇剌侘國). The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous, and the households are wealthy. There are several dozen saṃghārāmas, most of which are dilapidated, with only three or five remaining in use. There are over 300 monks, who study both the Great and Lesser Vehicles. There are several dozen Deva temples, where followers of various heterodox sects live together. The king is of the Brāhmaṇa caste; he is widely read in heterodox texts and does not believe in the true Dharma. Not far from the city is a stūpa, which is the place where King Aśoka (無憂王) established a hell.

From here, traveling northeast for more than one thousand li, one arrives at the country of Zhizhituo (擲枳陀國). The country of Zhizhituo is more than four thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is fifteen or sixteen li in circuit. The soil is described as fertile, and crops are cultivated in abundance; it is suitable for pulses and wheat, and there are many flowers and fruits. The climate is temperate and pleasant, and the people are gentle and compliant by nature. They mostly believe in non-Buddhist paths and have little respect for the Buddhadharma. There are several dozen sanghārāmas, but few monks. There are more than ten deva temples and over one thousand followers of non-Buddhist paths. The king is of the Brahmin caste; he is a devout believer in the Three Jewels and respects those who possess virtue, so scholars of broad learning from various regions often gather in this country.

From here, traveling northward for more than nine hundred li, one reaches the country of Maheśvarapura (摩醯濕伐羅補羅國). The country of Maheśvarapura is more than three thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than twenty li in circuit. The soil, products, and customs are the same as those of the country of Ujjayanī (鄔闍衍那國). They revere and honor non-Buddhist paths and do not believe in the Buddha-dharma. There are several dozen Deva temples, and most of the inhabitants are followers who smear themselves with ashes. The king is of the Brahmin caste and does not have much faith or respect for the Buddha-dharma.

From here I returned to the country of Gurjara (瞿折羅國), then traveled north through wild wastes and dangerous deserts for over one thousand nine hundred li, crossed the great Sindhu River, and arrived at the country of Sindhu (信度國). The country of Sindhu is over seven thousand li in circuit. The capital city is named Vīṣanbhavapura (毘苫婆補羅), and it is over thirty li in circuit. The land is suitable for grain and crops, and is abundant in winter wheat. It produces gold, silver, and brass, and is suitable for cattle, sheep, camels, mules, and similar livestock. The camels are small and have only one hump. It produces much red salt, the color of which is like red stone, as well as white salt, black salt, and white rock salt; people in distant foreign lands use these as medicine. The people are fierce and straightforward by nature, frequently quarrel, and are prone to slander. They are not broadly learned, but they have deep faith in the Buddhadharma. There are several hundred monasteries with over ten thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Sammitīya school of the Hīnayāna; for the most part, they are indolent, and their character and conduct are corrupt. However, there are those who are diligent, virtuous, and good, who live alone in quiet seclusion, keeping their traces far from the mountains and forests, and who, without flagging day or night, often realize the holy fruits. There are over thirty Deva temples, where followers of different paths live together. The king is of the Śūdra caste; he is pure and simple by nature and respects the Buddhadharma. In the past, the Tathāgata frequently traveled through this country, and therefore King Aśoka built several dozen stūpas at the sacred sites. The great arhat Upagupta also frequently traveled through this country to preach the Dharma and guide the people; at every place where he stayed, he marked the remains, either by building a monastery or erecting a stūpa, which rise here and there and can be briefly described. Along the marshes and lowlands extending for over a thousand li beside the Indus River (信度河; Skt. sindhu), there are several hundred thousand households residing there. Their nature is fierce and violent, and they occupy themselves solely with killing. They herd cattle to sustain their lives, having no other means of livelihood. Whether male or female, noble or base, they shave their hair and beards and wear monastic robes, appearing like bhikṣus while engaging in secular affairs; they stubbornly cling to Lesser Vehicle (小見; Skt. hīnayāna) views and slander the Great Vehicle (大乘; Skt. mahāyāna). I have heard from the records of the ancients: in the past, the people of this land were hardened and cruel, devoted only to violence. At that time, an Arhat took pity on their fallen state and, in order to transform them, came flying through the air, manifesting great supernatural powers and performing rare wonders to lead the multitude to believe and accept his gradual teachings. The people were respectful and pleased, wishing to follow his instructions. The Arhat, knowing that their hearts were compliant, administered the Three Refuges to them, calmed their ferocity, caused them to cease all killing of living beings, and had them shave their hair, dye their garments, and respectfully practice the teachings of the Dharma. As the ages passed and the world changed, their commitment to goodness wavered and their old habits persisted; though they wear religious robes, they have never possessed the precepts or virtue. Their descendants, generation after generation, have made this their custom.

From here, traveling eastward more than nine hundred li and crossing to the eastern bank of the Indus River (信度河), one arrives at the country of Mūlasthānapura (茂羅三部盧國). The country of Mūlasthānapura is more than four thousand li in circuit. The capital city is more than thirty li in circuit. The inhabitants are numerous and the families are wealthy. It is subject to the country of Takka (磔迦國). The soil is fertile and productive, and the climate is temperate and regular. The customs are honest and straightforward; the people love learning and value virtue. They mostly serve the heavenly deities and have little faith in the Buddha-dharma. There are more than ten monasteries, most of which are dilapidated, with few monks and no specialized studies. There are eight temples of the heavenly deities, where various heterodox sects dwell together. There is a Temple of the Sun God (Aditya), which is extremely magnificent and adorned. The image of the Sun God is cast in gold and decorated with rare jewels. Its spiritual influence is profound and mysterious, and its divine efficacy is secretly bestowed. Female musicians play in rotation, bright torches burn continuously day and night, and offerings of incense and flowers are never interrupted. The kings and noble families of the five Indias never fail to donate precious treasures here and establish charitable houses to provide food, drink, and medicine to the poor and the sick. People from various countries come here to offer prayers, often numbering in the thousands. Around the temple, the ponds and flowery woods are most pleasant for sightseeing.

From here, traveling northeast for more than seven hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Parvata (鉢伐多國). The country of Parvata is over five thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city of the country is over twenty *li* in circuit. The inhabitants are prosperous and numerous. It is subject to the country of Takka (磔迦國). There is much early-ripening rice, and it is suitable for *śāli* (宿) and wheat. The climate is temperate, the customs are simple and honest, the people’s temperament is impetuous and hasty, and their speech contains vulgar expressions. They are deeply learned in the arts and sciences, and they believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are more than ten monasteries with over a thousand monks, who study both the Mahayana and Hinayana teachings. There are four *stūpas* built by King Aśoka. There are twenty *deva* temples, where followers of various heterodox paths live together. Beside the city is a large monastery with over a hundred monks, all of whom study the Mahayana teachings; this is where the former śāstra master Jinaputra (慎那弗呾羅) composed the *Yogācārabhūmi-vyākhyā* (瑜伽師地釋論), and it is also the place where the śāstra masters Bhadraruci (賢愛) and Guṇaprabha (德光) originally entered the monastic order. This large monastery was burned by celestial fire and is now ruined and desolate.

Traveling southwest from the country of Sindhu (信度國) for fifteen or sixteen hundred li, one reaches the country of Audumbatira (阿點婆翅羅國). The country of Audumbatira is over five thousand li in circuit. The great capital city is named Khāḍeśvara (朅䶩濕伐羅), and it is over thirty li in circuit. It is situated in a remote area on the western border, overlooking the Sindhu River and adjacent to the shore of the great ocean. The buildings are magnificent and contain many precious treasures. Recently, there has been no sovereign, and it is under the jurisdiction of the country of Sindhu. The ground is damp, the soil is saline, and foul weeds grow in abundance; the fields are little cultivated. Although all types of grain are available, the *śali* rice and wheat are particularly abundant. The climate is slightly cold, and the winds are fierce and strong. It is suitable for cattle, sheep, camels, mules, and similar livestock. The people are impetuous and do not like to study. Their language differs slightly from that of Mid-India. Their customs are simple and honest, and they revere the Three Jewels. There are more than eighty saṃghārāmas with over five thousand monks, most of whom study the teachings of the Sthavira school’s Saṃmitīya sect (小乘正量部). There are ten deva temples, mostly inhabited by ash-smearing heterodox ascetics. Inside the city is a temple of Maheśvara (大自在天). The temple is carved and decorated, the image of the deity is spiritually responsive, and ash-smearing heterodox ascetics reside within it. In the past, the Tathāgata traveled extensively in this country, preaching the Dharma to save people and guiding the commoners to benefit the world; therefore, King Aśoka (無憂王) built six stūpas at the sites of these sacred traces.

From here, traveling west for less than two thousand li, one reaches the country of Laṅgala (狼揭羅國). The country of Laṅgala measures several thousand li in each of the four directions. The capital city of the country is over thirty li in circuit and is called Sthūlīśvara (窣菟黎濕伐羅). The land is fertile and moist, and the crops are abundant. The climate and customs are the same as those of the country of Adhyavakila (阿點婆翅羅國). The inhabitants are prosperous and possess many precious treasures. It borders the great ocean and is the route to the country of the Western Women (西女國). There is no great sovereign; they occupy the rivers and establish themselves independently, not submitting to one another’s commands, and are subject to the country of Pārsi (波剌斯國). Their writing is largely the same as that of India, though their spoken language differs slightly. They believe in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are over one hundred monasteries with more than six thousand monks, who study and practice the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. There are several hundred deva temples, and the ash-smearing heretics are extremely numerous. Inside the city is a temple of Maheśvara, magnificent and grand, which is the place of worship for the ash-smearing heretics.

From here, going northwest, one reaches the country of Persia (波剌斯國, Pārsi). The country of Persia is several tens of thousands of *li* in circuit. The great capital city is named Surasthāna (蘇剌薩儻那), which is over forty *li* in circuit. The terrain is vast and the climate varies, though it is generally warm. Water is diverted for irrigation, and the households are wealthy and prosperous. The land produces gold, brass, quartz, crystal, and various rare treasures. The people are skilled at weaving large brocades, fine woolens, and rugs (㲲毺), and there are many fine horses and camels. For currency, they use large silver coins. The people are impetuous and violent by nature, and their customs lack propriety and righteousness. Their script and language differ from those of other countries. They have no interest in academic arts but are skilled in crafts; all their manufactures are highly valued by neighboring regions. Their marriage customs are promiscuous, and when people die, they are often abandoned (to be exposed). Their physical stature is large; they cut their hair and go bareheaded, wearing leather and wool garments or brocaded robes. Regarding household taxes and levies, each person pays four silver coins. There are many temples of the devas, and the followers of the Dinabha (提那跋) heretics are those who revere them. There are two or three *saṃghārāmas* (伽藍) with several hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Hīnayāna according to the Sarvāstivāda school. The alms bowl of Śākyamuni Buddha is in the king’s palace here.

On the eastern border of the country is the city of Hūma (鶴秣城); the inner city is not extensive, but the outer wall is more than sixty li in circuit. The inhabitants are numerous, and their households are wealthy.

To the northwest it borders the country of Hrom (拂懍國); its territory and customs are the same as those of Persia (波剌斯). Its physical appearance and language are slightly different; it possesses many rare treasures and is also very wealthy.

On an island in the sea to the southwest of the country of Fulin (拂懍國), there is the Western Women’s Country. It is inhabited entirely by women, and there are virtually no men. It possesses many precious goods and is a dependency of the country of Fulin; therefore, the King of Fulin sends men there every year to mate with them, and it is their custom not to raise any male children who are born.

Traveling north from the country of Adhyavakila (阿點婆翅羅國) for more than seven hundred li, one arrives at the country of Piṭaśilā (臂多縶羅國). The country of Piṭaśilā is more than three thousand li in circuit. The capital city is more than twenty li in circuit. The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous; they have no great sovereign but are subject to the country of Sindhu (信度國). The land is sandy and saline, and the cold winds are biting and severe. There is much wheat and barley, but few flowers or fruits. The customs of the people are fierce and violent. Their language differs from that of Mid-India. They do not care for the arts or learning, yet they are sincere in their faith. There are more than fifty monasteries with over three thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Sammatiya school (正量部) of the Lesser Vehicle. There are more than twenty Deva temples, all belonging to the ash-smearing heretics. In a great forest fifteen or sixteen li north of the city, there is a stūpa several hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). It contains relics that occasionally emit light. This is the place where the Tathāgata, in a former life as a rishi, was harmed by a king. Not far to the east of this is an old monastery, which was established by the great arhat Mahākātyāyana (大迦多延那). Beside it are the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas, where stūpas have been built to mark the sites.

From here, traveling northeast for three hundred li, one arrives at the country of Avaṇḍa (阿軬荼國). The country of Avaṇḍa is two thousand four or five hundred li in circumference. The capital city is over twenty li in circumference. There is no great monarch; it is subject to the country of Sindhu (信度國). The soil is suitable for agriculture; millet and wheat are especially abundant, while flowers and fruits are scarce, and trees and vegetation are sparse. The climate is windy and cold, and the people’s temperament is fierce and impetuous. Their speech is simple and plain, and they do not value academic pursuits, yet they are pure and faithful in their devotion to the Three Jewels. There are over twenty saṃghārāmas with more than two thousand monks, who mostly study the teachings of the Hīnayāna Saṃmitīya school. There are five Deva temples, all belonging to the ash-smearing heretics.  Not far to the northeast of the city, in a large bamboo forest, are the remains of a saṃghārāma; this is where the Tathāgata once listened to the bhikṣus wearing sandals (亟縛屣). Beside it is a stūpa built by King Aśoka; although the base has collapsed, it is still over one hundred feet high. In the adjacent mūla-gandha-kuṭī (精舍), there is a standing Buddha image made of blue stone, which often emits a divine light on fast days.  Eight hundred paces further south, in the forest, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. The Tathāgata once stayed here; because the night was cold, he covered himself with his three robes, and the next morning, he permitted the bhikṣus to wear quilted garments. In this forest, there is a place where the Buddha walked for exercise. There are also several stūpas, arranged like the scales of a fish, which are the places where the four past Buddhas sat. Inside these stūpas are the hair and nails of the Tathāgata, which often emit light on fast days.

From here, traveling northeast for more than nine hundred li, one reaches the country of Varaṇa (伐剌拏國). The country of Varaṇa is more than four thousand li in circuit. The capital city is more than twenty li in circuit. The inhabitants are numerous and prosperous, and they are subject to the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國). The land has many mountains and forests, and crops are sown in their proper seasons. The climate is slightly cold, and the customs are fierce and violent. The people are impetuous and irritable, and their dispositions are base and corrupt. Their language is somewhat similar to that of Mid-India. They revere both heterodox and orthodox teachings, and they do not care for learning or the arts. There are several dozen monasteries, most of which are ruined and desolate; there are over three hundred monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Great Vehicle. There are five Deva temples, mostly occupied by the ash-smearing ascetics. Not far to the south of the city is an old monastery where the Tathāgata in the past preached the Dharma, demonstrating, teaching, benefiting, and rejoicing, and enlightening sentient beings. Beside it are the seats of the four past Buddhas and the sites of their walking meditation. According to local accounts, this country borders the country of Kaikanāna (稽畺那國) to the west; situated among the valleys of great mountains, it has separate local chieftains but no sovereign ruler. There are many sheep and horses; those that are fine horses are large and beautiful in form, a rare breed among the various countries, and are treasured by neighboring regions. Traveling northwest from here again, crossing great mountains, traversing wide rivers, and passing through small towns and cities, one travels over two thousand li, leaves the borders of India, and reaches the country of Jāguḍa (漕矩吒國).

According to local accounts, to the west of this country one reaches the country of Kaikanan (稽畺那國); it is situated among the valleys of the great mountains (Pravaragiri), and it has separate local chieftains but no sovereign ruler. It abounds in sheep and horses, and among the horses are those of excellent quality, whose forms are remarkably large; they are a rare breed among the nations and are prized by neighboring regions.

The country of Jaguḍa (漕矩吒國) is over seven thousand li in circuit. The great capital city of the country is named Ghasna (鶴悉那), which is over thirty li in circuit; sometimes the capital is at the city of Ghasala (鶴薩羅城), which is also over thirty li in circuit. Both are steep, rugged, and well-fortified. The mountains and rivers are undulating, and the fields and ridges are high and dry. Grain crops are sown in their proper seasons, winter wheat is abundant, the vegetation is lush, and flowers and fruits are flourishing. It is suitable for the cultivation of saffron (欝金香), and it produces the hingu herb (興瞿草), which grows in the Rāmēndu River (羅摩印度川) valley. In the city of Ghasala, there is a gushing spring that flows in various channels, which the people of the country utilize to irrigate their fields. The climate is cold and severe, with frequent frost and snow. The nature of the people is impulsive, and their dispositions are often deceitful. They are fond of learning arts and possess many technical skills; they listen but do not understand, yet they can recite tens of thousands of words a day. Their script and language differ from those of other countries. They often embellish empty talk and accomplish little in reality. Although they sacrifice to the hundred gods, they also revere and honor the Three Jewels. There are several hundred saṃghārāmas and more than ten thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Mahāyāna. The present king is pure in faith, having inherited the throne through successive generations; he is diligent in performing meritorious deeds, and is quick-witted and fond of learning. There are more than ten stūpas built by King Aśoka (無憂王). There are several dozen deva temples, where followers of different paths dwell together. There are many non-Buddhists, and their followers are extremely numerous; they revere and serve the god Śuna (䅳那天). This deity formerly moved from Mount Aruṇa in the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國) to reside in Mount Śunāśīra (䅳那呬羅山) on the southern border of this country, where he displays his power, bestows blessings, and commits acts of violence and evil; those who believe and pray to him have their wishes fulfilled, while those who despise him incur calamity. Thus, those far and near revere him, and those high and low stand in awe of him. The rulers, ministers, officials, and commoners of neighboring countries with different customs gather without appointment on auspicious days each year; they bring gold, silver, and rare treasures, or offer cattle, horses, and domestic animals, competing to present offerings to express their sincerity. Consequently, gold and silver are spread upon the ground and sheep and horses fill the valleys, yet no one dares to covet them, as all are intent only on making offerings. Those who follow non-Buddhist paths (外道) practice asceticism with a disciplined heart, and the celestial deity imparts incantations to them; the non-Buddhists who practice these find them highly effective, and those treated for illnesses are often healed.

The great capital city of the country is called Ghasna (鶴悉那), which is over thirty li in circuit; sometimes the capital is at the city of Ghasala (鶴薩羅), which is also over thirty li in circuit, and both are steep, rugged, and well-fortified.

Or the capital is the city of Ghasala (鶴薩羅城), the city circuit is over thirty *li*, and it is both steep, rugged, and well-fortified. The mountains and rivers are undulating, and the fields and ridges are high and dry. Grain crops are sown in their proper seasons, winter wheat grows in abundance, vegetation is lush, and flowers and fruits are flourishing. It is suitable for turmeric (*kuṅkuma*), and produces the *hingu* herb; this herb grows in the Rāmēndu (羅摩印度) river valley. In the city of Ghasala, gushing springs flow in various directions, and the people of the country benefit from them to irrigate their fields.

Crops are sown in their proper seasons, winter wheat grows in abundance, vegetation is lush, and flowers and fruits are flourishing. The land is suitable for turmeric (kuṅkuma) and produces the hingu herb; this herb grows in the Rāmēndu (羅摩印度川) valley.

From here, traveling northward for more than five hundred li, one arrives at the country of Vṛjiṣṭhāna (弗栗恃薩儻那國). The country of Vṛjiṣṭhāna is more than two thousand li from east to west and over one thousand li from north to south. The capital city of the country is named Hūbīnā (護苾那), and it is more than twenty li in circuit. The soil, products, and customs are the same as those of the country of Jaguḍa (漕矩吒國), though the language is different. The climate is cold and harsh, and the temperament of the people is fierce and impetuous. The king is of Turkic lineage; he has deep faith in the Three Jewels, values learning, and adheres to virtue.
The capital city of the country is called Hubina (護苾那), and it is over twenty li in circuit.

Proceeding northeast from this country, crossing mountains and fording rivers, and passing through several dozen small frontier towns of the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國), one reaches the Varasena (婆羅犀那) great range of the Great Snow Mountains. The range is extremely high and steep, with dangerous, precipitous slopes; the paths are winding and the cliffs and peaks interlock. Sometimes one enters deep valleys, and sometimes one ascends high precipices; even in the height of summer it is frozen over, and one must hack through the ice to cross. After traveling for three days, one finally reaches the top of the range. The cold wind is bitter and fierce, and accumulated snow fills the valleys; travelers passing through cannot find a place to stand. Soaring falcons cannot fly across it; they must walk on their feet before taking flight again. Looking down at the various mountains, they appear like small anthills. In the Jambudvīpa (贍部洲), this range is exceptionally high. Its summit has no trees, but only many stone peaks, clustered and leaning against one another, standing dense like a forest.

After traveling for three more days, I finally descended from the mountain range and reached the country of Antarava (安呾羅縛國). The country of Antarava is the former territory of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國). It is over three thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is fourteen or fifteen li in circuit. There is no great sovereign or leader, and it is subject to the Turks. The mountains and hills are connected, and the river valleys and fields are narrow and confined. The climate is cold and severe, and the wind and snow are biting and harsh. It is abundant in crops and suitable for flowers and fruits. The nature of the people is fierce and violent, and their customs lack order and discipline. They do not understand the concepts of sin or merit, and they do not value learning; they only maintain shrines to deities and have little faith in the Buddha-dharma. There are three monasteries with several dozen monks, all of whom follow the teachings of the Mahāsāṃghika school. There is one stūpa, which was built by King Aśoka.

From here, traveling northwest, entering valleys and crossing ridges, and passing through various small towns for over four hundred li, one reaches the country of Khost (闊悉多國). The country of Khost is the former territory of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國). It is less than one thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is over ten li in circuit. There is no great monarch, and it is subject to the Turks (突厥). The mountains are numerous and the rivers narrow; it is windy and cold. The grain crops are abundant, and flowers and fruits are plentiful. The nature of the people is fierce and violent, and their customs lack laws and regulations. There are three saṃghārāmas (伽藍), and the number of monks is very small.

From here, going northwest across mountains and valleys and passing through various towns for over three hundred li, one arrives at the country of Huoh (活國). The country of Huoh is the ancient territory of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國). It is over two thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is over twenty li in circuit. It has no separate ruler, being subject to the Turks (突厥). The land is level and flat; grain is sown in its season, vegetation is lush and flourishing, and flowers and fruits are abundant. The climate is mild and pleasant, and the customs are simple and honest. The people are impetuous and fierce by nature, and they wear garments of felt and coarse wool. They mostly believe in the Three Jewels and rarely worship other gods. There are more than ten monasteries and several hundred monks, who study both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings. Their king is a Turk who governs the various small countries south of the Iron Gate (鐵門); he moves about like a bird and has no permanent seat of government.

From here, traveling east, one enters the Congling (Onion Mountains). The Congling are situated in the center of Jambudvīpa; they connect to the Great Snow Mountains (Mahāhimavat) in the south, reach the Hot Sea (Rēgistan/Issyk-Kul) and the Thousand Springs (Bing-gyul) in the north, border the country of Huo (Kunduz) in the west, and adjoin the country of Wusha (Usha) in the east. They extend for several thousand li in every direction. There are hundreds of layers of cliffs and ridges, with deep, precipitous valleys where ice and snow accumulate permanently and cold winds blow with great intensity. Because they produce many onions, they are called the Congling; furthermore, because the mountain cliffs are of an onion-green color, they are named accordingly.

Traveling east for more than a hundred li, one reaches the country of Mungan (瞢健國). The country of Mungan is the former territory of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國). It is more than four hundred li in circuit. The capital city of the country is fifteen or sixteen li in circuit. The soil, products, and customs are much the same as those of the country of Hu (活國). There is no great sovereign, and it is subject to the Turks.

To the north, one reaches the country of Alini (阿利尼國). The country of Alini is the former territory of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國). It borders both banks of the Vaxšu River (縛芻河) and is over three hundred li in circuit. The capital city of the country is fourteen or fifteen li in circuit. The suitability of the soil and the customs are much the same as those of the country of Hu (活國).

To the east, one reaches the country of Rāhu (曷邏胡國). The country of Rāhu is the former territory of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國). To the north, it borders the Vaxšu River (縛芻河), and it is more than two hundred li in circuit. The capital city of the country is fourteen or fifteen li in circuit. The soil, products, and customs are much the same as those of the country of Hu (活國).

Going east from the country of Mungān (瞢健國), crossing steep mountain ranges, traversing deep valleys, and passing through several river cities for more than three hundred *li*, one reaches the country of Kṛṣma (訖栗瑟摩國). The country of Kṛṣma is the former territory of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國). It is more than ten *li* from east to west and three hundred *li* from north to south. The capital city of the country is fifteen or sixteen *li* in circumference. The native products and social customs are generally the same as those of the country of Mungān, but the people differ in being violent, foolish, and malicious in disposition.

To the north lies the country of Parighar (鉢利曷國). The country of Parighar is the former territory of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國). It is over one hundred li from east to west and over three hundred li from south to north. The capital city of the country is over twenty li in circumference. The soil, products, and customs are much the same as those of the country of Kṛṣma (訖栗瑟摩國).

Going east from the country of Kṛṣma (訖栗瑟摩國), crossing mountains and traversing rivers for over three hundred li, one reaches the country of Himatala (呬摩呾羅國). The country of Himatala is the former territory of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國). It is over three thousand li in circumference. The mountains and rivers are winding and rugged, but the soil is fertile. It is suitable for grain crops, with an abundance of winter wheat; all kinds of plants grow luxuriantly, and various fruits are plentiful. The climate is cold and harsh. The people are violent and impetuous by nature, do not understand merit or sin, and their appearance is coarse and ugly. Their deportment and manners, as well as their clothing of felt and leather, are quite similar to those of the Turks. Their women wear wooden horns on their heads, over three feet high, with two branches in front representing their husband’s parents; the upper branch represents the father-in-law, and the lower branch represents the mother-in-law. As each passes away, the corresponding branch is removed; when both parents-in-law are deceased, the horn headdress is discarded entirely. In the past, this was a powerful kingdom, and the king was of the Śākya clan (釋種); to the west of the Onion Range (葱嶺), many states were subject to them. Because their borders neighbor the Turks, they have gradually adopted their customs; furthermore, due to being subjected to invasions and raids, they have had to defend their own territory. Consequently, the people of this country have been scattered into foreign lands, with dozens of fortified cities each having its own independent ruler, living in domed felt tents and moving about in search of pasture. To the west, it borders the country of Kṛṣma.

Traveling east through the valley for more than two hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Badakhshān (鉢鐸創那國). The country of Badakhshān is the former territory of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國). It is more than two thousand *li* in circuit. The capital city of the country is situated upon a mountain cliff and is six or seven *li* in circuit. The mountains and rivers are winding and rugged, and the land is filled with sand and stone. The soil is suitable for pulse and wheat, and there is an abundance of fruits such as grapes, walnuts, pears, and crabapples. The climate is cold and harsh, and the people are fierce and impetuous by nature. Their customs lack propriety and law, and they have no knowledge of the arts. Their appearance is coarse and ugly, and they mostly wear garments of felt and coarse wool. There are three or four *saṃghārāmas* (monasteries), with very few monks. The king is simple and honest by nature and has deep faith in the Three Jewels.
The capital city of the country (Bada-chuangna 鉢鐸創那國; Skt. Badakhshān) is situated upon a mountain cliff and is six or seven li in circuit.

From here, traveling southeast through a mountain valley for more than two hundred li, one reaches the country of Yambagan (淫薄健國). The country of Yambagan is the former territory of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國). It is more than one thousand li in circumference. The capital city of the country is more than ten li in circumference. The mountain ranges are connected, and the river valleys and fields are narrow and confined. The native products, the climate, and the character of the people are the same as those of Badakshān (鉢鐸創那), though the language is slightly different. The king is harsh and violent by nature, and he does not distinguish between good and evil.

From here, traveling southeast, crossing ridges and traversing valleys along dangerous canyon paths for more than three hundred li, one reaches the country of Kuraṇa (屈浪拏國). The country of Kuraṇa is an old territory of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國). It is more than two thousand li in circumference. The land, topography, and climate are the same as those of the country of Yambagan (淫薄健國). The customs lack laws and regulations, and the people’s nature is base and violent. Most do not cultivate merit, and few believe in the Buddha-Dharma. Their appearance is ugly and wretched, and they mostly wear felt and coarse wool. There are rocky mountains that produce much gold essence; one must chisel and break the stones to obtain it. The monasteries are few, and the monks are also sparse. Their king is simple and sincere, and he reveres and honors the Three Jewels.

From here, traveling northeast, climbing mountains and entering valleys along a difficult and dangerous path for over five hundred li, one arrives at the country of Dharmasthiti (達摩悉鐵帝國). The country of Dharmasthiti lies between two mountains and is the former territory of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國). It is over one thousand five or six hundred li from east to west, and four to five li wide from north to south, while at its narrowest it does not exceed one li. It borders the Oxus River (縛芻河), the land winding and twisting with uneven mounds and hillocks; sand and stones drift and spread, and the cold winds are harsh and piercing. They only cultivate wheat and beans; there are few forests and a lack of flowers and fruits. They produce many fine horses; although the horses are small in stature, they are enduring in travel and wading. The customs lack propriety and righteousness, and the people’s nature is fierce and violent. Their appearance is coarse and ugly, and they wear garments of felt and coarse wool. Their eyes are mostly green, which is different from other countries. There are more than ten saṃghārāmas, but the number of monks is small.

The city of Khaṇḍata (昏馱多城) is the capital of the country. Within it is a monastery established by a former king of this country, who hollowed out the cliffs and filled the valleys to construct its halls and chambers. In earlier times, this country had not been reached by Buddhism and only worshipped heretical deities; it was only a few hundred years ago that the transformation of the Dharma began to spread.  Initially, the king’s beloved son fell ill. He exhausted all medical arts, but the illness only worsened without any sign of recovery. The king then went in person to a temple of the gods to offer rites and pray for salvation. At that time, the priest of the temple spoke on behalf of the deity: "He will certainly recover; there is truly no cause for concern." The king, hearing this, was joyful and comforted, and turned his carriage to return home. On the road, he encountered a śramaṇa whose demeanor was remarkable. Struck by his appearance and attire, the king asked where he had come from. This śramaṇa had already attained the holy fruit and, wishing to propagate the Buddha’s Dharma, had assumed this form. He replied to the king, "I am a disciple of the Tathāgata, what is known as a bhikṣu."  The king, being full of anxiety, immediately asked, "My son is afflicted with illness, and it is not yet certain whether he will live or die." The śramaṇa said, "The king’s ancestors may be raised, but your beloved son is difficult to save." The king said, "The heavenly deity said he would not die, yet this śramaṇa says he shall perish; how can the words of such a deceptive and vulgar man be trusted?"  Upon arriving at the palace, he found his beloved son had already died. He concealed the death and did not hold a funeral, instead asking the priest of the deity again, who still said, "He will not die; the illness will surely be cured." The king then flew into a rage, bound the priest, and rebuked him, saying, "You and your kind live together to foster evil, wantonly exercising power and claiming blessings." "My son is already dead, yet you still claim he will recover; such deceit and delusion are truly unbearable! It is fitting to execute the spirit-master and destroy the spirit-temple." Thereupon, he killed the spirit-master, removed the spirit-images, and cast them into the Vaxšu River (縛芻河). As he turned his carriage to return, he encountered a śramaṇa. Seeing him, he felt respect and joy, bowed his head, and apologized, saying, "In the past, I lacked a bright guide and lingered on evil paths. Although the corruption has lasted long, the reform begins here. I hope you will deign to look upon me and descend to my residence." The śramaṇa accepted the invitation and followed him to the inner palace. Once the son had been buried, the king said to the śramaṇa, "The human world is full of entanglement, and birth and death are in constant flux. When my son fell ill, I asked the spirit whether he would stay or depart, and the spirit spoke falsely, saying he would surely recover. Having previously received your instructions, which indeed proved not to be false, I see that your Dharma is worthy of devotion; I only pray that you will show compassion and guide this deluded follower." He then requested the śramaṇa to survey the site for a monastery (伽藍) and establish it according to the proper rules. From that time on, the Buddha's teaching flourished. Therefore, the main hall (精舍; Skt. mūla-gandha-kuṭī) in the monastery was built for an arhat. In the great main hall of the monastery, there is a stone Buddha image, above which hangs a circular canopy of gilt bronze, adorned with various jewels. When people circumambulate, the canopy also rotates accordingly; when the people stop, the canopy stops. No one can fathom this spiritual manifestation. I heard from the elders that some say it is sustained by the power of a holy person's vow, while others say it is caused by secret mechanical arts. Observing the building, the stone walls are solid and steep. Examining all these opinions, no one knows the true account.

Crossing the great mountain (pravaragiri) of this country, one arrives north at the country of Šikni (尸棄尼國). The country of Šikni is over two thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is five or six li in circuit. The mountains and rivers are connected, and the fields are covered with sand and stone. There is much pulse and wheat, but few cereal crops; trees are sparse, and flowers and fruits are scarce. The climate is bitterly cold. The customs of the people are fierce and brave; they are hardened to slaughter and devoted to theft. They do not know ritual or righteousness, and they do not distinguish between good and evil. They are confused about future misfortune or blessings, yet they fear the calamities of the present life. Their appearance is coarse and unsightly, and they wear skins and coarse wool for clothing. Their writing is the same as that of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨羅國), but their spoken language is different.
The country of Śiknī (尸棄尼國) is over two thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is five or six li in circuit.

Crossing to the south of the great mountains of the country of Dharmasthiti (達摩悉鐵帝國), one arrives at the country of Śami (商彌國). The country of Śami is two thousand five or six hundred li in circumference. Mountains and rivers alternate, with high and low hills interspersed. All kinds of grain are planted, with pulse and wheat being particularly abundant; there are many grapes, and the land produces orpiment, which is obtained by splitting the rocks hewn from the cliffs. The mountain gods are fierce and malicious, repeatedly causing calamities; only after offering sacrifices can one enter, and then travel back and forth in safety. If one does not pray, winds and hail break out. The climate is cold, and the customs are impetuous. The people are simple and honest in disposition, but their customs lack etiquette and righteousness; their wisdom is limited, and their skills are superficial. Their script is the same as that of the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國), but their spoken language is different. They mostly wear felt and coarse wool garments. Their king is of the Śākya clan and deeply reveres the Buddha's teachings; the people follow his example, and all are pure in their faith. There are two saṃghārāmas, with few monks.

To the northeast of the country, crossing mountains and traversing valleys, passing through dangerous terrain and treading over perilous paths for over seven hundred li, one arrives at the Pamir Valley (波謎羅川). It extends over one thousand li from east to west and over one hundred li from south to north, while at its narrowest point it is no more than ten li wide. It is situated between two snowy mountains, and therefore the cold winds are piercingly strong; snow falls during the spring and summer, and winds swirl day and night. The soil is saline and alkaline, with much gravel and stone; crops do not flourish, and vegetation is sparse, which leads to it being a desolate wilderness, entirely devoid of human habitation.

In the Pamir (波謎羅) Valley lies the Great Dragon Lake, extending over three hundred *li* from east to west and over fifty *li* from north to south. It is situated within the Great Onion Range (大葱嶺), lies at the center of Jambudvīpa (贍部洲), and occupies the highest elevation. The water is clear and bright as a mirror, its depth unfathomable, its color a dark blue-black, and its taste extremely sweet. Submerged within it dwell sharks, *chi*-dragons, fish, dragons, soft-shelled turtles, alligators, tortoises, and turtles. Floating and swimming upon it are mandarin ducks, wild geese, *jia*-geese, *su*-birds, and *hu*-birds. These birds lay large eggs, leaving their shells in the wilderness, either among the grassy marshes or upon the sandy islets. A large stream flows out from the west of the lake, running west to the eastern boundary of the Dharmasthiti (達摩悉鐵帝) country, where it joins the Vakṣu (縛芻) River and flows westward; therefore, to the right of this point, all waters flow to the west. A large stream flows out from the east of the lake, running northeast to the western boundary of the Khāsa (佉沙) country, where it joins the Sītā (徙多) River and flows eastward; therefore, to the left of this point, all waters flow to the east. South of the Pamir Valley, crossing the mountains, is the Balūra (鉢露羅) country, which abounds in gold and silver; the color of the gold is like fire.

From this valley, traveling southeast, one climbs mountains and traverses dangerous paths where there are no human habitations, only much ice and snow. After traveling more than five hundred li, one reaches the country of Kharbanda (朅盤陀國). The country of Kharbanda is over two thousand li in circuit. The capital city is built upon a large rocky ridge, with the Sītā River (徙多河) at its back, and it is over twenty li in circuit. The mountain ranges are connected, and the valleys and plains are narrow. Grain crops are scarce, but beans and wheat are abundant; trees are sparse, and there is little fruit or flowers. The plains and marshes are desolate, and the cities and towns are empty. The customs lack propriety and righteousness, and the people have little learning or skill. Their nature is fierce and violent, and they are also physically brave and valiant. Their appearance is ugly and wretched, and they wear garments of felt and coarse wool. Their writing and language are largely the same as those of the country of Khāsa (佉沙國). However, they are sincere in their faith and revere the Buddha-Dharma. There are more than ten monasteries and over five hundred monks, who study the Hīnayāna teachings of the Sarvāstivāda school. The present king is simple and honest, respects the Three Jewels, is elegant and refined in his demeanor, and is devoted to learning. Since the founding of the country, many years have passed. The people claim to be the descendants of the *Cīnadeva-gotra* (至那提婆瞿呾羅). This country was originally a desolate valley in the Onion Range (葱嶺). Long ago, a king of Persia (波利剌斯) married a princess from the land of Han and was escorting her back when they reached this place. At that time, a military rebellion broke out, and the roads to the east and west were blocked. He therefore placed the princess upon an isolated peak, which was extremely steep and high, accessible only by ladders, and stationed guards around it to keep watch day and night. Three months passed, and when the bandits had finally quieted down and they wished to continue their journey, the princess was already pregnant.
